Paul Adams: British-Israeli relations at lowest ebb in decades

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 21:46:31 GMT

Israel's furious response to the British government's decision to ban trade with Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank testifies to just how important this moment is.

Britain took the brunt of Israel's anger, but the fact that 12 countries chose to move together clearly sharpened the sense of outrage.

Officials in London always knew that such a dramatic shift in policy towards Israel-Palestine was going to elicit a hostile response, but seemed taken aback by the speed and ferocity of Israel's reaction.

The closure of the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem, which serves the West Bank and deals directly with the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah, and the removal of British representatives from the International Gaza Support Centre, the body set up last year to co-ordinate stabilisation and relief efforts in the Gaza Strip, are very hostile moves.

They tell you that Israel is deeply troubled by Tuesday's action by the UK and 11 other countries, which include France, Spain and Canada.

Products manufactured in settlements may not represent a significant proportion of Israel's exports, but the political symbolism of singling these out for special treatment is powerful.

For decades, the British and other governments have regarded settlements in occupied Palestinian territory as illegal but stopped short of banning products grown or manufactured there.

Now, having announced that Britain agrees with the 2024 International Court of Justice ruling that the occupation as a whole - including Israel's military presence - is unlawful, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband says the government's economic relationships must reflect that.

Hence the ban, not just on products but also on companies that provide construction, infrastructure or finance to settlements. The measures, which also include restrictions on arms sales that "materially contribute to the occupation", go further than many expected.

And it's not just the actions - it's the language of the foreign secretary's heartfelt, sometimes deeply personal statement that is so striking.

As a "proud British Jew... unwavering in my support for the state of Israel," Miliband spoke more directly and starkly than practically any of his predecessors.

That a British foreign secretary should say that "settler terrorism is rampant" and was responsible for the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians in parts of the West Bank, while the Israeli government "turned a blind eye to this" is truly remarkable.

Miliband calls this a "reset" in British policy. At times today, it felt like a radical rethink, and it leaves British-Israeli relations at their lowest ebb for decades.

Yes, the heated, febrile atmosphere that invariably accompanies an impending Israeli election may have contributed to Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar's brutal response, but most Israelis will have shared his sense of outrage.

Many Israelis find the violent, messianic ideology of some settlers deeply problematic. Some see them as a national embarrassment.

But that's not the same as saying they agree that settlements, built on land captured during the 1967 Six Day War, are illegal.

Most would disagree violently with the former prime minister, Ehud Olmert, who last year accused his successor Benjamin Netanyahu of turning Israel into an international pariah.

But they can feel the walls of international opprobrium closing in - from protests at Eurovision or sporting events, to international arrest warrants being issued against their leaders and now to bans on settlement products - and that makes them anxious and defensive.

For the Palestinians, on the other hand, this feels like progress.

The Palestinian foreign ministry commended the countries adopting sanctions but called for "urgent, concrete measures" to stop Israel's "illegal settlement enterprise".

In London, the Palestinian ambassador Dr Husam Zomlot called the government's decision "a turning point in the UK-Palestine relationship".

Britain's "courageous steps", he said, would help pave the way for the independence of the State of Palestine on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital.

But Zomlot knows that the reality of Israel's 59-year occupation has not ended, or even substantially changed.

The prospects for a viable Palestinian state remain vanishingly small, and there's little immediate sign that concerted action by 12 countries will reverse Israel's seemingly inexorable takeover of the West Bank.

Only the United States has that kind of influence, should it choose to wield it.

In 1991, President George HW Bush and his steely Secretary of State James Baker threatened to withhold $10bn (£7.4bn) in loan guarantees from the government of Prime Minister Yitzhak Shamir, when the famously tough Shamir refused to promise that it wouldn't be used to finance settlement activity in the occupied territories.

But Donald Trump has so far shown no desire to curb Benjamin Netanyahu's settlement plans.

Some parts of Trump's MAGA movement have turned against Israel in recent years, but the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, is a fervent Christian Zionist who shares Israel's view that the West Bank was promised to the Jews by God.

So Tuesday's action by the UK and its partners pits them not just against Israel but also against Israel's backer-in-chief in Washington.

More flight delays expected after hundreds cancelled by air traffic control glitch

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 21:46:21 GMT

Flight delays are expected to continue on Wednesday after an air traffic control problem cancelled hundreds of flights across the UK.

Tens of thousands of passengers were affected by the disruption and tracking website FlightRadar24 said up to 1,000 flights were cancelled after a glitch affecting air traffic control provider Nats.

Its boss Martin Rolfe apologised, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after Nats said resolving the issue had taken "longer than hoped".

With few aircraft able to take off, it is understood landings were restricted, leading to some flights being unable to depart overseas airports.

The fault was widespread across the UK, and beyond, with airports in Scotland and Ireland also reporting disruption. EasyJet made 200 cancellations and British Airways more than 100.

It is not the first time disruption has blighted Nats' control system. Ryanair and Wizz Air called for an overhaul of the organisation, with Wizz Air saying Nats was "not fit for purpose" in its current form.

When asked whether he was considering his position, Rolfe said there would be "lots of time for that later" but his focus now was on making sure the problem was solved.

Europe's busiest airline, Ryanair, reported on Tuesday that more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed by up to eight hours.

At Heathrow, one of the busiest airports in Europe, departures were initially paused around lunchtime. Traffic then resumed, before facing further disruption in the afternoon.

It is understood the airport ran out of space for incoming flights during the afternoon because planes had not been departing.

Thirteen Heathrow-bound flights were diverted to other airports in the UK and Europe.

Passengers have been advised to contact their airlines to check the status of their flights.

British Airways said in a statement that it was anticipating knock-on effects.

"We were forced to cancel or divert more than 100 flights on Tuesday afternoon," a spokesperson said.

"We're doing everything we can to keep our customers updated and make arrangements for them to continue their journeys.

"We ask customers whose flights have been cancelled not to travel to the airport and to bear with us if they're trying to get in touch, as our call centres are incredibly busy at the moment."

Airports across the UK said they were experiencing cancellations and delays and advised people to check their flight details before travelling.

According to FlightRadar, the worst affected airports were Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester and Birmingham.

Ryanair said affected passengers would be notified.

Phil White from Bexhill told BBC Your Voice that his flight to Lanzarote boarded on time but he was left sitting on the tarmac at Gatwick for hours.

"We've been told the radar is down and we can't take off," Phil said.

"It's comfortable enough but the pilots been on every 20 minutes saying they are waiting for information from air traffic control and when he finds anything out he will let us know."

Even if Nats has resolved the issue with its flight processing system, the disruption is likely to persist due to backlogs.

Rolfe said the issue was in Nats' flight data processing system. He said it was not the same system that failed during an incident in 2023 over the August Bank Holiday weekend.

Although the technical issue affected departures, arrivals were also hit as space on the ground became increasingly restricted.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said that "it will take time to fully resume flights, so continue to check with airlines".

"I am seeking assurances that lessons will be learned and systems that support aviation are up to the job," she wrote on X.

According to Nats, the flight processing system processes flight plans and other operational information used by air traffic controllers to manage air traffic.

The system continually updates flight information as aircraft progress through UK airspace, helping controllers maintain a safe and orderly flow of traffic.

Chloe Davis,18, from Cambridgeshire was left sitting on a Virgin plane at Heathrow waiting to fly to Orlando.

She told BBC Your Voice that she had been due to depart at 13:40 BST.

"I'm not concerned, I would just like to know what's going on," she said.

"There [are] planes parked up on the taxi way because there's no gates for them to go to."

LIV files for bankruptcy protection with $45m owed to players

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 21:20:22 GMT

LIV Golf was founded in 2021, with its first season taking place the following year

LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave.

A Chapter 11 petition, which LIV says is to "preserve the company's business" as it attempts to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, was filed in the United States on Tuesday.

The breakaway league says it has found a new investor in BC Partners, following the decision in April by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to pull its funding.

Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m).

Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m).

The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m).

The court documents show LIV estimates its assets at $100m-$500m (£74m-£370m) and its liabilities at between $500m and $1bn (£370m-£739m).

LIV Golf intends to commence its new majority player-owned league early next year and it is understood the Chapter 11 process allows it to start talking to players about their participation in LIV's future.

BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.

Sources have said contracts under the previous iteration of LIV Golf will finish because of this court filing, with amounts owed to players and other creditors addressed through the court process.

However, it remains unclear when players would then be able to enter discussions with other tours.

'Time will tell' - Rahm on LIV Golf future

Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0

Saudi Arabia to stop funding LIV Golf next season

Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by PIF, with major winners including Rahm and DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money.

However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil told the BBC at the final event in Indianapolis last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a "critical mass" of players to make the new league a reality.

DeChambeau said at the conclusion of that event he felt there was "a lot of potential moving forward" and he believed there was "something fun coming".

Speaking on Tuesday before this week's Irish Open, Rahm was tight-lipped when pressed on his future.

Asked if he knew what the coming months held, he told BBC Sport: "Yes and no. It hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis.

"There's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell."

Rahm added: "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell."

This video can not be played

"We'll see what happens" - Rahm on LIV future

The bankruptcy filing was made in the federal district court of New Jersey, where LIV Golf set up a subsidiary earlier in the summer.

Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business.

PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process.

When announcing its decision to withdraw funding, PIF said the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term" was "no longer consistent" with its strategy.

Despite its decision to stop bankrolling LIV Golf, PIF added it "remains committed" to its "substantial current and future investments in various sports as a priority sector".

On Tuesday, LIV confirmed international investment firm BC Partners as its proposed new investor in a letter to fans outlining its "next phase".

"LIV Golf has entered a court-supervised restructuring process that provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the league's next phase a reality," said the letter.

"Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf."

O'Neil added in a statement: "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf - one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem."

In yet another indication the free-spending days of LIV 1.0 are over, the letter said the new league would be "built around a sustainable business model".

Players are set to be given equity and individual commercial rights are set to be returned to players, giving them greater earning potential. In terms of prize money, LIV Golf purses are set to be lower than events on the PGA Tour - which has risen in part because of the existence of LIV - but higher than events on the DP World Tour.

The letter also outlined proposed changes, with field sizes expanding to 75 players, the introduction of a cut, creating qualifiers and having more teams that "embrace national identities", with the ambitions for teams to "grow into enduring global sports businesses".

LIV cancels final event to focus on 'next chapter'

LIV files for bankruptcy protection with $45m owed to players

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 21:20:22 GMT

LIV Golf was founded in 2021, with its first season taking place the following year

LIV Golf has filed for bankruptcy protection with at least $45m (£33m) owed to players, who will now have the option to leave.

A Chapter 11 petition, which LIV says is to "preserve the company's business" as it attempts to restructure after Saudi Arabia withdrew its multibillion-dollar funding, was filed in the United States on Tuesday.

The breakaway league says it has found a new investor in BC Partners, following the decision in April by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) to pull its funding.

Documents in the petition outline money owed to LIV Golf's creditors with the 30 largest unsecured claims. Two-time major winner Jon Rahm tops that list with an unsecured claim of $7.5m (£5.5m).

Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m - £4.2m), Dustin Johnson ($5.5m - £4.1m), Cameron Smith ($4.8m - £3.5m) and Tyrrell Hatton ($3.4m - £2.5m) are also among the top 30 creditors, as well as Brooks Koepka, who left to rejoin the PGA Tour in January but has an unsecured claim of $1.7m (£1.25m).

The total amount owed to the 14 current and former LIV players in the top 30 creditors is just over $45m (£33m).

The court documents show LIV estimates its assets at $100m-$500m (£74m-£370m) and its liabilities at between $500m and $1bn (£370m-£739m).

LIV Golf intends to commence its new majority player-owned league early next year and it is understood the Chapter 11 process allows it to start talking to players about their participation in LIV's future.

BBC Sport understands there is no obligation on players to sign on to LIV 2.0, regardless of whether they had previously signed multi-year contracts with LIV Golf.

Sources have said contracts under the previous iteration of LIV Golf will finish because of this court filing, with amounts owed to players and other creditors addressed through the court process.

However, it remains unclear when players would then be able to enter discussions with other tours.

'Time will tell' - Rahm on LIV Golf future

Strained smiles and uncertainty - the strange end of LIV Golf 1.0

Saudi Arabia to stop funding LIV Golf next season

Since LIV's controversial launch in 2021, more than $5bn (£3.7bn) has been spent by PIF, with major winners including Rahm and DeChambeau lured by lucrative contracts and vast prize money.

However, the future of the concept - and its star players - has been shrouded in uncertainty, with the 2026 season having ended early.

LIV Golf chief executive Scott O'Neil told the BBC at the final event in Indianapolis last month he had "high levels of confidence" in achieving a "critical mass" of players to make the new league a reality.

DeChambeau said at the conclusion of that event he felt there was "a lot of potential moving forward" and he believed there was "something fun coming".

Speaking on Tuesday before this week's Irish Open, Rahm was tight-lipped when pressed on his future.

Asked if he knew what the coming months held, he told BBC Sport: "Yes and no. It hasn't really changed from my last interview in Indianapolis.

"There's just a lot of things in place, right? There's a lot of things that could happen and it's one of those things where time's gonna tell."

Rahm added: "I still have a contract with LIV 1.0 that I'm more than willing to fulfil, so like I said, time will tell."

This video can not be played

"We'll see what happens" - Rahm on LIV future

The bankruptcy filing was made in the federal district court of New Jersey, where LIV Golf set up a subsidiary earlier in the summer.

Chapter 11 protection postpones a US company's obligations to its creditors, giving it time to reorganise its debts or sell parts of the business.

PIF is providing a bankruptcy loan of $49.6m (£36.6m) - called 'debtor in possession' (DIP) financing - to help fund the process.

When announcing its decision to withdraw funding, PIF said the "substantial investment required by LIV Golf over a longer term" was "no longer consistent" with its strategy.

Despite its decision to stop bankrolling LIV Golf, PIF added it "remains committed" to its "substantial current and future investments in various sports as a priority sector".

On Tuesday, LIV confirmed international investment firm BC Partners as its proposed new investor in a letter to fans outlining its "next phase".

"LIV Golf has entered a court-supervised restructuring process that provides us with the time and framework to address previous financial obligations and complete a transaction that will make the league's next phase a reality," said the letter.

"Put simply, this process is designed to build a stronger and more sustainable future for LIV Golf."

O'Neil added in a statement: "This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf - one built around the fans, an innovative, player-first ownership model, and a part of the global golf ecosystem."

In yet another indication the free-spending days of LIV 1.0 are over, the letter said the new league would be "built around a sustainable business model".

Players are set to be given equity and individual commercial rights are set to be returned to players, giving them greater earning potential. In terms of prize money, LIV Golf purses are set to be lower than events on the PGA Tour - which has risen in part because of the existence of LIV - but higher than events on the DP World Tour.

The letter also outlined proposed changes, with field sizes expanding to 75 players, the introduction of a cut, creating qualifiers and having more teams that "embrace national identities", with the ambitions for teams to "grow into enduring global sports businesses".

From shot-shy to shoot on sight - Villa find a way to win

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 20:55:18 GMT

Emi Buendia scored his first goal since netting in the Europa League final in May

It is a new chapter for Aston Villa and, against Club Brugge, they turned the page.

A first win of the season, albeit more nervy than anticipated, lit the spark for Unai Emery's side.

It may not have completely ignited the season yet but John McGinn, Emi Buendia and Nicolas Jackson gave them a winning Champions League return.

Villa won but could have drawn - or equally triumphed more handsomely - during a game which went from comfortable to edgy to relief.

It was only a second victory since that historic night in Istanbul when McGinn lifted the Europa League in May.

Since then it has been all change and, after another bleak Premier League opening, victory in Belgium was desperately needed.

With Fenerbahce and Viking to come at home in October, the path to Champions League progress is already opening up as Villa's new era slowly emerges.

The visitors were in a commanding and deserved position at half-time, McGinn's opener making him the club's all-time record European goalscorer with 12.

Buendia's strike and Jackson's first Villa goal - benefiting from Yann Sommer's rush of blood - had them cruising.

Brugge were poor and George Hemmings, Villa's first Champions League/European Cup teenage starter in 43 years, could have had at least one.

Yet the hosts made it uncomfortable for Emery's men with Nicolo Tresoldi's penalty after Aaron Wan-Bissaka's blatant handball setting up an anxious last half an hour, during which Tresoldi hit the post.

It can be viewed as a blessing in disguise that Villa had to battle their way through and ride out the hosts' pressure to earn their first win of the season. Adding the grit and determination to the quality of the opening half to prove they can get the job done.

Not that they needed the evidence themselves, Emery and his squad always have that faith and the internal desire to progress no matter the obstacle.

It was the same last season. A below-par 1-0 win over limited Bologna - thanks to another McGinn goal - got Villa going and they hardly looked back.

The victory kicked off the staggering run of 17 wins in 20 games which formed the backbone of returning to the Champions League and giving Villa momentum to win the Europa League.

Since then, of course, Villa's spine has been torn out and Emery has to integrate 10 new players into his methodical methods.

Three points in Brugge may not spark another relentless run but it gives Emery and Villa the foundations of this new era.

"It's a new Villa and it was a big test for the new players to dig in," McGinn told Uefa.

"It was Joao Gomes and George Hemmings' first Champions League game. It's not easy to go away at a place like this in difficult weather conditions. Club Brugge were pushing and pushing and pushing and we had to stand strong. We managed to do that.

"It was so important to show a real gritty performance and get a victory at a very, very tough place to play."

Nicolas Jackson helped Bayern Munich win the Bundesliga on loan from Chelsea last season

After just one shot on target in their opening three Premier League games the nine Villa had in Belgium would have been a comfort to Emery.

He said following Saturday's 0-0 draw at Hull it was vital to take the rebuild step-by-step and Tuesday's win was another positive move.

"The players have a responsibility too, the older players need to guide to keep our standard high, to show everybody that this is the only way to achieve our targets," Emery told the post-match news conference. "We are improving after Brighton and after Hull City.

"We must work hard - it is the only way. This is the process that we must try to set. We did one very important step forward, being resilient when we were struggling."

His players wasted no time in making that next leap by having 14 attempts in the first half, with Hemmings going closest to adding more goals.

Jackson, on his third start, got his first Villa goal following his record £65m move from Chelsea as he starts proving he is a fitting replacement for the departed Ollie Watkins.

The striker, who worked with Emery at Villarreal, will be one of the flag-bearers of Villa's new beginning as both the record signing and the player expected to score the goals to ensure they can compete at the elite level again.

"We don't care about the past, we just focus on the next one. Like every team, we have our ambitions. We just know it's a long journey, so we take it step by step try to win every game we play," said the Senegal international.

"I'm very happy to be here and happy to be with the team, manager and staff. Hopefully, there are many more to come."

Villa now host Nottingham Forest in the Premier League on Saturday before going to Coventry in the Carabao Cup and then travelling to Tottenham.

After returning from Belgium with three points following their stuttering start, they could go into the extended international break with a fresh perspective.

RNLI volunteers facing 'unacceptable' abuse, chief says

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 20:25:12 GMT

RNLI staff have faced "unacceptable" online and physical abuse since anti-migrant protests at the weekend, the charity's chief executive has said.

On Sunday, police faced off with demonstrators who blocked roads in Portsmouth in an effort to stop 140 people who arrived at the Eastney Landing ferry port area with the RNLI's assistance.

Chief executive Peter Sparkes said the abuse of volunteers was "wholly unacceptable in a civilised society".

He said there had been "deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding" about the charity, and condemned threats by "those who would hide behind a balaclava or a keyboard".

The protest in Portsmouth followed a separate demonstration the previous day, in which hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters brought the Port of Dover to a standstill.

Footage was subsequently posted on social media showing volunteers of the Poole-based charity labelled as "traitors".

In a statement issued on Tuesday, Sparkes said: "Recent events have generated deliberate misinformation and a misunderstanding about the RNLI – our purpose, our tasking, and particularly our lifesaving work in the Channel.

"Sadly, as a result, some of our volunteers and staff have been the subject of online and, in the worst cases, physical abuse.

"The RNLI's people represent the very best in our society, they selflessly give up their time to keep others safe."

He continued: "We will take whatever steps we can, to care for and protect our people and their families."

Digital Secretary Lisa Nandy said she had spoken with tech firms about how the names, addresses and photographs of RNLI staff and volunteers were reportedly shared online.

She was responding to Vikki Slade, the Liberal Democrat MP for Mid Dorset and North Poole, about "some very disturbing posts" on social media identifying "brave RNLI rescuers".

Nandy was asked what more the government could do to remove posts "that put children and adults' safety at risk through doxxing".

She told the Commons: "It is something that the government is concerned about [and] I'm personally concerned about."

Requests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying the migrants were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port, the BBC understands.

Sparkes described illegal migration as a "polarising subject" and urged people to "be mindful of misinformation" and the "impact it has upon others".

He said: "Be reassured that the RNLI and our crews strive only to prevent people like you and me from drowning at sea.

"Stand by them, not against them and their families.

"I am extremely proud of and grateful for their vital lifesaving work that meant 389 families welcomed their loved one homes safely last year."

Of the 9,058 RNLI lifeboat launches in 2025, 109 were to those "in distress in the Channel", Sparkes said, which makes up 1.2% of the charity's total rescue work.

He said nearly 95% of small boats were intercepted by the UK Border Force.

"Our mission, and our tasking is to rescue those women, children and men in danger of drowning," he added.

Ports denied request to land 120 migrants in RNLI boats

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 20:13:19 GMT

Requests to accept the landing of RNLI boats carrying 120 migrants intercepted off the Isle of Wight were refused by both Portsmouth harbour and Southampton Port.

When the migrants were landed on Sunday at Eastney, in Langstone Harbour, anti-migrant protesters blocked the road.

Associated British Ports (ABP), which operates Southampton, said it was not the closest port and it "did not have suitable reception facilities available".

The BBC understands the King's Harbour Master (KHM) Portsmouth also declined a coastguard request, but it would not comment directly on operational matters.

The protest followed a separate demonstration at the Port of Dover on the previous day.

The Langstone Harbour Master said the migrants were "recovered" onto two RNLI vessels in the vicinity of the Nab Tower.

They said they would have travelled at "quite a slow speed" to Langstone because the vessels were so overloaded.

An RNLI spokesperson said: "We are working with the relevant parties to understand the decision to deny access, and we are disappointed with the nature of the communication with our crews, who voluntarily give their time to save the lives of others at sea."

The narrow peninsula at Eastney has only one road leading in and out, which demonstrators used to block coaches carrying the migrants from leaving the area.

It led to a stand-off that lasted into the early hours of Monday.

Portsmouth City Council said it was a "completely unsuitable location to bring the boats ashore" and brought "needless disruption" to the area.

Langstone Harbour Master Billy Johnson said the coastguard was coordinating "a search and rescue operation" and there was "no reason not to accept" the landing of the vessels at Eastney.

"The problem was managing the public order aspect that was also taking place and the geography of the area made that very challenging for the police," he said.

"This is a new thing in the Solent and the degree to which it attracted public interest and the speed at which the public reaction was mobilised was unusual and surprising.

"The way the emergency services mobilised was really effective, with the police, Border Force, coastguard, the RNLI, ambulance and fire service working completely together - all of whom were hindered by the activities of protesters."

ABP said it received an enquiry about landing recovered migrants.

It said in a statement: "We had to decline the enquiry as the Port did not have suitable reception facilities available.

"If there had been a safety of life at sea issue where Southampton was the closest port or if we had received a formal direction from the relevant authority then we would have played a role.

"Neither was the case in this situation."

The leader of Portsmouth City Council, Steve Pitt, said: "The Home Office has some serious questions to answer about their lack of planning, inconsistent decision-making and ultimately, poor judgement."

In the House of Commons yesterday, Dame Caroline Dinenage, Conservative MP for Gosport, referred to the boat containing 120 migrants in the Solent as an "extraordinary mega dinghy".

She said: "MPs across the Solent region were scrambling for reliable information with complete radio silence from the Home Office. As a result we weren't in a position to calm fear and tension."

Responding for the government, Home Office minister Sarah Jones said the department would "learn any lessons that we need to" following the weekend's protests.

Asked why Eastney had been chosen as the landing site, she said: "We are of course making sure we understand what exactly happened in that circumstance."

UK announces sanctions on West Bank settlements prompting furious Israeli response

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 19:11:39 GMT

The UK has announced sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, accusing Israel's government of turning a blind eye to the "ethnic cleansing" of Palestinians by settlers.

Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the move marked the "beginning of a new approach" to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, which "not only calls out injustice and suffering but acts".

Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar responded by accusing him of spreading an "outrageous lie" and announced counter-measures including shutting the UK's consulate in East Jerusalem.

The UK sanctions will ban settlement goods but also act against companies and individuals providing services for settlement expansion.

The sanctions were launched alongside France and Canada, which in a joint statement with the UK said the action "marks a further turning point in our approach to protecting the two-state solution".

Settlements are illegal under international law, and there has been a rise in violence towards Palestinians in the West Bank by settlers in recent months.

In a statement to MPs, Miliband said: "The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.

"And all too often the Israeli government has turned a blind eye to this and worse, members of it have made statements and taken actions to support the forced displacement of Palestinians."

He said ethnic cleansing was defined by the UN as a "purposeful policy designed by one ethnic or religious group to remove by violent means another ethnic or religious group from certain areas".

Miliband said the official view of the government was that the Israeli occupation of the West Bank was unlawful because of the "entrenchment of its control, its intention to extend permanent sovereignty, and its expansionist agenda via illegal settlements".

He said this position, which is in line with a 2024 advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice, should be reflected in the UK's "economic relationship" with the occupied West Bank.

As a result, over the next six to nine months, the UK will introduce "a new comprehensive sanctions regime", he said.

The foreign secretary also announced a ban on advertising illegal West Bank settlements in the UK.

"The sanctions regime will target illegal settlements and settlement expansion, not Israel," Miliband added.

Later on Tuesday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the targeted measures were "aimed not at the Israeli people, but in support of the two-state solution".

Announcing the closure of the consulate - which represents the UK government in Jerusalem, the West Bank and Gaza - Israel's Foreign Minister Saar said at a press conference: "We know that we have many friends in Britain.

"Unfortunately, we have a hostile Labour government that is consistently operating against the State of Israel, and it has left us no choice but to respond to its hostile actions."

He added that 11 UK MPs, including Jeremy Corbyn, Diane Abbott and all five sitting Green Party MPs, would be banned from entering Israel, accusing them of "antisemitic and anti-Israel activity".

The UK also issued a joint statement with 11 other countries; France, Canada, Denmark, Spain, Finland, Ireland, Iceland, Norway, Poland, Portugal and Sweden.

It said the group was unequivocally committed to the two-state solution and would introduce national measures or support European restrictions on trading goods with West Bank settlements.

The UK announcement comes after Israel opened up tenders for the construction of some 1,200 settlement homes in the so-called E1 area - a strategically important area east of Jerusalem. The plans have drawn widespread international condemnation. Israel has held off on plans to build in the area for decades under global pressure.

Miliband told the Commons the UK's "new approach" was necessary because plans for the E1 development in the West Bank would render a two-state solution "unviable" by "cutting through the heart of Palestine".

Elsewhere, he said the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, which triggered the Gaza war, carried "terrible echoes of the centuries of persecution of the Jewish people" and stressed Israel had "the right to protect its people and defend its territory".

However, he added, "that cannot justify what has happened in Gaza".

He said: "International humanitarian law imposes clear rules for states fighting wars, including to ensure access to food and medical supplies, to avoid mass displacement of civilians, and to avoid the targeting of civilians. Serious and international violations of this law, if proven, amount to war crimes.

"What has occurred, including the actions of the IDF (Israel Defense Forces), have been examined in depth by a number of organisations, including the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry.

"The conclusions of these reports represent increasing evidence that war crimes appear to have been committed, and we support legal processes to determine this."

He added it was up to international courts to determine if Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

Israel's leaders have consistently rejected allegations of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. They have insisted that Israeli forces have operated in accordance with international law.

Miliband began his statement to the Commons by referring to his Jewish roots and childhood experiences of visiting Israel, as well as recent antisemitic attacks in the UK.

He described himself as "a proud British Jew" and outlined his steadfast support for the state of Israel.

He said: "My personal story and that of thousands of British Jews is one of the many reasons why I say to anyone here or around the world who questions Israel's right to exist as a homeland for the Jewish people - you are wrong, and we will call you out whenever you engage in this attempt at the erasure of Israel."

But the UK's Chief Rabbi Sir Ephraim Mirvis said it was a "truly a dark day for British Jews", saying the sanctions were "little more than political flag bearing for mendacious anti-Israel rhetoric" that would embolden people who "use hatred as a weapon against Jews".

The Board of Deputies of British Jews expressed "deep regret" over Tuesday's announcement, and urged both the UK and Israeli governments to "avoid pursuing what appear to be party interests over national interests".

Responding in the Commons, Conservative shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat claimed ministers were "enacting policies that the Foreign Office knows won't work".

He agreed that illegal settlements were wrong and "some Israeli ministers have indulged in hateful propaganda and incitement" but added "this isn't about Israel alone and it certainly isn't about reducing the complexity of the region to a single sentence. Sadly, the government is in the process of doing just that".

Israel's foreign minister Saar said on Tuesday evening he had spoken with Tugendhat and Tory leader Kemi Badenoch, thanking them "for their firm opposition to the hostile Labour government's announcement today and its series of anti-Israel policies since taking office".

He also said British representatives from the International Gaza Support Center in Kiryat Gat in southern Israel would be removed, and UK activities to train Palestinian Authority forces in Judea and Samaria - how the Israeli government refers to the West Bank - would be terminated.

Speaking earlier on Tuesday, the country's President Isaac Herzog said the decision would "fall on the wrong side of history", adding: "In the current context, it would be a gross interference in the democratic elections of a sovereign nation."

Herzog said the move would directly harm Palestinians and urged foreign governments to turn towards "constructive dialogue" and cooperation, adding "sanctions are not a solution".

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters the White House had no comment on the joint action, adding that "obviously we're not going to do what the UK did".

Earlier, Donald Trump's ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee earlier told the BBC that the US - Israel's most powerful ally - would "without a doubt" respond to the expected sanctions, warning of a "huge economic impact on British businesses".

He suggested action could be taken by individual US states as well as at a central, federal level.

The Palestinian presidency welcomed the UK's decision, saying it was "an important step towards confronting Israel's colonial system and its violations against the Palestinian people".

As part of the UK announcement, Miliband also announced sanctions on the financing wing of Lebanon's Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed group.

New sanctions in line with the US and European Union were also announced on Iran.

The intervention comes almost a year after Sir Keir Starmer's government recognised a state of Palestine, and said the UK had a moral responsibility to support a peaceful future for Israelis and Palestinians.

Israel rejects a two-state solution. It says any final settlement must be the result of negotiations with the Palestinians, and statehood should not be a precondition.

The Palestinian Authority backs a two-state solution but Palestinian armed group Hamas does not because it is opposed to the existence of Israel.

Hamas says that it could accept an interim Palestinian state based on 1967 de facto borders, without officially recognising Israel, if refugees were given the right to return.

Israel has built about 160 settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them.

There has been a surge in attacks by settlers on Palestinians and their property in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war, which was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.

Sabalenka fights back to keep US Open defence alive

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 19:07:02 GMT

Aryna Sabalenka is a four-time Grand Slam singles champion, with two titles apiece at the Australian Open and US Open

Aryna Sabalenka thought she had lost her US Open crown before leaving herself "speechless" as she battled back to beat Linda Noskova in three sets and advance to the semi-finals.

Taken to a deciding set for the first time in this year's tournament, the two-time defending champion trailed 4-2 in the third set and later 2-0 in the tie-break before recovering to close out a 7-6 (7-1) 3-6 7-6 (10-7) win in a little under two and a half hours.

It was the 28-year-old's 19th consecutive win at the tournament, having not tasted defeat since the 2023 final, while she becomes the first woman since Serena Williams in 2016 to reach six successive semi-finals at Flushing Meadows.

Victory also sees her temporarily keep hold of her world number one ranking, though she will be overtaken at the top regardless of how she fares in the remainder the tournament if world number two Elena Rybakina beats Zheng Qinwen on Wednesday.

Asked if she would be happy if she retained her US Open title but Rybakina replaced her at the head of the standings, Sabalenka said: "I'll be more than happy. Three-peat - sounds great.

"I'm just super happy that I put myself in the position where I have chance to go for the three-peat, even though I'm still far away from that."

Sabalenka will next face either American third seed Jessica Pegula or her compatriot Emma Navarro, seeded 26th, as she bids to reach a fourth consecutive US Open final.

The Belarusian has a history of letting her emotions get the better of her, most recently in her quarter-final defeat from a set up at the French Open.

But as in her previous match against Taylor Townsend, when she had her serve broken four times and trailed 3-1 in the second set, Sabalenka showed impressive composure to emerge victorious against Wimbledon champion Noskova, suggesting she may have turned a corner.

"I'm speechless right now. I was pushing to the limit in this match, especially in the third set," said Sabalenka.

"I honestly thought that that's it, the match is over, but probably that's what helped me to feel loose and go after my shots. [I'm] super happy to get the win."

Fighting to stay No 1 - Sabalenka's US Open mission

Listen: Sabalenka beats Noskova in epic, and do we need five sets?

Sabalenka began the match in cruise control, breaking in sixth seed Noskova's opening service game and racing into a 5-2 lead, before being broken as she served for the set.

Although she dominated the subsequent tie-break, the double fault she hit in her last service game – one of four in the match – would prove a feature of her performance, as would her failure to convert break points.

She wasted three early in the second set before conceding a break in the sixth game with a double fault at 30-40 as Noskova forced a decider.

After hitting two more double faults to be broken for a third time, she looked down and out after Noskova held to love for a 4-2 lead, but won the next three games to turn the match around.

She then won the tie-break - for a 10th successive time at the US Open, in a run dating back to 2021 - to complete her comeback, sealing the victory with a nerveless second-serve ace.

This was only Sabalenka's second quarter-final victory since March, with the top seed unable to replicate her early season hard-court success – which included titles in Brisbane, Indian Wells and Miami – on the clay or grass.

She suffered last-16 exits in Toronto and Cincinnati in the build-up to the US Open, but has rediscovered something approaching her best form at the tournament where she is yet to lose a quarter-final in six attempts.

"I have to say that knowing that physically my body can handle these matches again, I'm super happy with that," Sabalenka said.

"And of course, these kind of tight matches give you so much confidence that you're back and you're ready to do anything it takes to get the win. So this match definitely gives me a boost of energy and motivation."

For Noskova, this defeat, during which she hit more winners, fewer unforced errors, and saved seven of her nine break points, ends a run of 11 consecutive singles wins at Grand Slams.

Commentator Tim Montgomerie quits Reform following suspension

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 18:54:41 GMT

Conservative Party defector and political commentator Tim Montgomerie has told the BBC he has resigned from Reform UK, urging Nigel Farage to "get a grip" of the party.

Montgomerie defected from the Tories 18 months ago but was suspended from Reform UK last month after he criticised senior figures.

His decision to resign came after a conversation with Reform's party chair Lee Anderson on Tuesday. "I think they wanted me back in the party but meekly," he told the BBC. "And I wasn't prepared to do that."

Montgomerie said he still plans to support Reform and has no intention of re-joining the Conservatives.

"I want to still be a supporter, but that requires them being more like Reform and less like the AfD [Germany's right-wing Alternative for Deutschland]", he said.

The far-right AfD won a decisive victory in Germany's eastern state of Saxony-Anhal this weekend, in what commentators said was a watershed moment as no far-right party has controlled a German state since World War Two.

Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants.

In the wake of controversial demonstrations against migrants in Dover and Portsmouth linked to Tommy Robinson this week, Montgomerie suggested Nigel Farage needs to go further in asserting his authority and professionalising the party.

"Nigel needs to get a grip, he needs to lead the party", he said.

"The one thing he's been brilliant at is policing the right and stopping [far-right activist] Tommy Robinson joining.

"But for the sake of his legacy and the sake of decency he needs to sort it out, and bring people like Zia [Yusuf] under control."

Last month, Montgomerie told the BBC he was frustrated at Farage's "aggrieved" tone after the Clacton by-election - and told the Spectator podcast that Reform's home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf was not a "team player".

At the time, Reform said he had been suspended "in line with party rules" after public criticism of the party.

Montgomerie joined Reform after a long career as a Tory adviser and commentator, and he had run the ConservativeHome website.

In a video statement on X after news of his suspension emerged on the Guido Fawkes website, Montgomerie said he still believed in Reform's policies and its membership, and he was only trying to make the party "better and stronger" with his public criticisms.

Following his decision to quit, Montgomerie said: "I'm feeling very sad about it, I feel battered by it... When you get older there's less fight in you.

"Reform is at a junction: They haven't replaced the Conservatives which was plan A. I fear a battle of attrition between the two parties which will helps no one. The real danger now on the fight for political turf is that they go after sectional interests.

"Does Reform want to be a party of government or does it want to stand at the edge and just change the debate?"

A Reform UK spokesman said: "We wish Tim the best for the future and thank him for his support."

Glastonbury confirms ticket sale dates - and highest ever price

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 18:10:14 GMT

After taking a fallow year in 2026, the Glastonbury Festival has confirmed that tickets for next year's event will go on sale in October.

Tickets for the weekend will cost £408 including a £5 booking fee per ticket - an increase of £29.50 from 2025.

Headliners for the festival, which takes place from 23 to 27 June, have yet to be announced, but rumours are already swirling, with everyone from Harry Styles and Fontaines DC to Taylor Swift and Stevie Wonder said to be in the mix.

Tickets for the festival typically sell out in less than an hour, with thousands of fans joining online queues to fight for their place.

In a post on the official Glastonbury Instagram page, organisers said tickets with coach travel would go on sale at 18:00 BST on Thursday, 1 October.

General admission tickets go on sale a couple of days later, at 09:00 BST on Sunday 4 October.

As part of an ongoing campaign to stop touts, anyone wanting to attend Glastonbury had to be registered in advance. You can check your registration on its website.

In recent years, the festival has also introduced an automatic queuing system on the day of sale, with fans needing to be online before the start of the sale with a valid registration number.

Glastonbury, which features more than 100 stages, was already the UK's most expensive music festival, but next year's ticket prices are the highest ever - breaking the £400 barrier for the first time.

The increase is part of a pattern across the industry.

Analysis by BBC News found the cost of attending the UK's major festivals has surged over the past decade - rising above the rate of inflation.

Parklife tickets have increased by around £69 (71%) in real terms since 2013 - while Reading and Leeds had a much smaller increase, rising by about £40 (14%) over the same period.

In the same period, Glastonbury's ticket prices went up by about £85 - a 30% price hike.

The price hikes have multiple causes - from increased energy and infrastructure costs to post-Brexit labour shortages.

However, last weekend's Reading and Leeds festival held prices at their 2025 level, with passes costing £325, rising to £361 with early-bird entry.

Glastonbury said they would not be commenting on today's announcement but, in 2023, Emily Eavis acknowledged it was a "challenging time" for festival organisers.

"We have tried very hard to minimise the increase in price on the ticket but we're facing enormous rises in the costs of running this vast show, whilst still recovering from the huge financial impact of two years without a festival because of Covid."

The festival last took place in 2025, with Olivia Rodrigo, The 1975 and Neil Young topping the bill.

Glastonbury organiser Emily Eavis recently scotched rumours that Madonna would be among the headliners for next year's event.

"No, it's definitely not Madonna, I'll tell you that," she told BBC Radio 4's PM programme.

"But we have got three [other] headliners and we're very excited about it - it's all coming together really well," she added.

Asked about the possibility of a performance from Taylor Swift, Eavis laughed and said she didn't want to discuss the line-up any more.

British widow faces deportation from Sweden after 22 years

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 18:02:42 GMT

A 78-year-old British widow has told the BBC she is struggling to eat or sleep as the Swedish government threatens to deport her over a late post-Brexit residence application.

Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, moved to Sweden 22 years ago with her husband, who passed away from cancer three years ago.

The threat of deportation came after Swedish authorities said they should have made a formal application to stay in the country after Brexit.

Thomas has since had numerous applications and appeals rejected, and Tuesday marks the latest deadline for her to leave voluntarily.

"This is absolute hell," she said from her home in Sweden.

"I can't sleep, I can't eat. You get up in the morning, you don't know what's going to happen."

The Swedish migration minister told the BBC that the government would "examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected" by some consequences of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement.

When the UK left the EU on 31 January 2020, British citizens stopped being EU citizens, which meant they could no longer stay in Sweden with right of residence status.

During a transitional period, British citizens could apply for residence status under the withdrawal agreement between the UK and the EU - which ended on 31 December 2021.

Thomas said she and her husband were unaware that they needed to submit an application and she was only informed of the rule once she attempted to re-enter the country in 2023.

After years of appeals, the Migrationsverket, the Swedish government agency responsible for migration, told her last month that her voluntary departure deadline was 8 September.

Her lawyers are arguing against the deportation, but she is still waiting to hear from the government.

Thomas said the possibility of having to leave her son, grandchildren, friends and husband's grave has become too much to bear.

"I'm tired, I really am tired and I'm not young anymore," she said.

"Where is the empathy? I've lived here for more than 20 years - I've got friends, I've got family."

According to Eurostat data, between 2021 and 2025, 2,490 UK nationals were ordered to leave Sweden. This is almost a third of more than 7,500 UK nationals ordered to leave the 27 EU Member States over this time period.

The Migrationsverket said it could not comment on Thomas's case without her consent and did not respond to a question about how many British nationals are at risk of deportation.

However, it told the Guardian last week that 458 British citizens had been deported or forcibly removed since Brexit.

Last month, a family told the BBC how their father, who has dementia and vascular parkinsonism and is living in full-time care in Sweden, was also threatened with removal after more than two decades in the country.

Swedish Minister for Migration, Johan Forssell, told the BBC that the current framework was implemented by a previous government and that it "will therefore look closely at the situation and examine whether there are measures we can take to make the process easier for those affected".

He did not address Thomas's case directly but said "the government believes the rules should be applied generously".

"The UK is a very important partner for Sweden, and we want British citizens who live and work in Sweden to be able to remain here," he said.

"We are currently in dialogue with the relevant Swedish authorities to get a clearer picture of what measures may be possible," he added.

Håkan Svenneling, Thomas's MP from the opposition Vänsterpartiet (The Left Party), has criticised the government's "inhumane migration policy".

"That is why I hope that Sunday's election in Sweden will be a turning point where the opposition can form a government and change migration policy so that Joyce and other Britons with strong ties to Sweden can stay here," he told the BBC.

A spokesperson from the the UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office said: "We welcome the statement from the Swedish authorities that they will look at this issue. We are ready to support them in doing so."

New law to force tech firms to stop children taking or sharing nude images

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 16:48:29 GMT

The government has said it will introduce a new law to force tech firms to prevent children from taking or sharing nude images on mobile devices.

Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, were given three months in June to block access to nude images on smartphones and other devices used by under-18s.

But culture secretary Lisa Nandy MP told MPs on Tuesday that despite "significant commitments" from both companies, current proposals "do not meet the scale of this crisis".

She said ministers would look to legislate "as soon as they can" - with the caveat it may reassess these if firms develop and implement solutions sooner.

Alongside making tech firms block nudity on devices used by children at device-level, the government said its draft legislation would also make providers of apps used by children introduce similar blocks on nude imagery.

"This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world," Nandy said.

She told MPs that Apple and Google had already made "meaningful changes" to block nudity on smartphones used by children at the core of their systems, but more action was needed.

An Apple spokesperson said it launched its Communication Safety feature in 2021 to help stop children from seeing or sharing imagery containing nudity - and had since "continued to expand its capabilities".

"We share the UK's commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe," they said.

A Google spokesperson told the BBC it was an "industry leader in combating non-consensual intimate imagery and advancing child safety across our products".

They added Google was pleased to have "made progress" and remained committed to working on efforts to keep children safe online.

The government proposals have been welcomed by organisations and charities calling for tougher measures and technical solutions to stop children from not just seeing, but also capturing and sharing nudity on smartphones.

Ofcom data suggests that a growing proportion of younger children in the UK own a smartphone - and that the number of those do increases with age.

According to children's charity the NSPCC, content filmed on a child's device can be the starting point for grooming, sexual extortion and other forms of online child sexual abuse.

UK police chiefs have previously said restricting the ability of children's devices to take or share nude images would be a key step in preventing sextortion - crimes where a child is groomed into sharing explicit images and blackmailed.

Chris Sherwood, NSPCC chief executive, said legislative plans were a "necessary move" after tech firms failed to meet the three-month deadline.

But he said "children cannot face more delays, so Government must act swiftly and ensure these measures are enshrined in law at the earliest opportunity".

Andy Burrows of the Molly Rose Foundation said while the new proposals were "fundamental to their objective", it had been "a needlessly long and torturous road" to secure them.

"Ministers will need to demonstrate they are committed to delivering robust legislation without further delay," Burrows added.

Government proposals to prevent nude images being shared taken and shared by children were originally proposed as part of the government's violence against women and girls strategy.

But it faced criticism within its own ranks for being slow to enact it.

Its plans for a new law to enforce the measure would not prevent adults from accessing naked imagery on their device.

However, implementing solutions to block it for children may require checking whether the user of a phone, or app, is an adult or a child.

Online rights campaigners at the Open Rights Group have previously warned that implementing the change would mean "every adult would be forced through a digital ID checkpoint, and private images could be scanned by default".

The government has denied that the move would amount to surveillance.

Trump shares misleading video of King and fainting worker

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 16:31:16 GMT

US President Donald Trump has shared a misleading video on social media which appears to show King Charles shrugging and walking away from a man who fainted during a royal visit.

The footage, which has been edited, features in a video shared by Trump on his Truth Social platform which appears to show other world leaders being disrespectful. The video goes on to show a montage of clips where Trump is seen honouring fallen US troops, hugging veterans and shaking hands with law enforcement officers.

The clip of the King was taken from a longer video when, as Prince of Wales, he was visiting an Asda supermarket distribution centre in Bristol during the Covid pandemic in July 2020.

The full footage, which Trump did not use, showed Charles reaching out to the man as he fell before remaining close by as he received medical attention. The video posted by Trump edits out the King staying close to the worker.

Buckingham Palace said it was not something it would comment on. The White House has not responded to a request for comment.

The three-minute video was posted by the president on the US Labor Day holiday and opens with footage of French President Emmanuel Macron at the Elysee Palace as a guardsman appears to collapse behind him.

The Truth Social video also shows former President Joe Biden apparently checking his watch during a military repatriation ceremony and former President Barack Obama stepping off the Marine One helicopter and saluting US marines while holding a paper cup in his hand.

These are followed by a series of clips where Trump is seen picking up the cap of a US marine, saluting at a repatriation ceremony and comforting the families of fallen soldiers.

Captions saying "the side of Trump the media doesn't show you" and "the people's president" appear during some of the clips and the song A Thousand Years by Christina Perri plays throughout the video.

Trump has frequently spoken of his good relationship with Charles and described him as "the greatest king in my book" at the end of the King and Queen's state visit to the US in April.

Iceland summons US ambassador over Trump's stars and stripes map

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 15:55:19 GMT

Iceland has summoned the US ambassador after President Donald Trump posted a map on social media that appeared to show Iceland and several other countries covered by the American flag.

Trump posted the image on Truth Social on Monday, showing the US, Canada, Greenland, Iceland, Mexico, Central America and the Caribbean covered in stars and stripes. The entire landmass was labelled "United States of America".

Iceland's foreign minister said the post was "completely inappropriate".

Trump's territorial ambitions have repeatedly strained relations with neighbouring countries, including his push to acquire Greenland and calls to make Canada the America's 51st state.

His post of the map did not include a caption and preceded a flurry of posts of maps renaming the US state of New Mexico as "New America".

Responding to Trump's post, Iceland's Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir called in US ambassador to Iceland Billy Long, who formally took up the post last month, local media reported.

When an ambassador is summoned, it typically means they are being called for a formal meeting, where the host country will express displeasure over their government's actions.

The post also drew criticism from Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, who said on Monday that the position of Greenland's government and people had been made clear.

"The Greenlandic government and the Greenlandic people have said again and again that they do not want to be American," she told Danish news agency Ritzau in Nuuk.

"I hope no one is in any doubt about that, either in the United States or the rest of the world."

Trump's interest in Greenland has been a recurring theme on his social media accounts and in speeches since he took office again last year, claiming the island is necessary to the US to shore up its national security.

His post came shortly after the European Commission announced a €200m (£172m) investment in the Danish territory during a visit by Commission president Ursula von der Leyen and Frederiksen.

The European Commission said its investment would focus on education, internet connectivity, the use of raw materials in the country and hydropower energy.

Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico "is neither nor will be a colony or protectorate of any foreign country," after Trump's post.

"Proudly we are a free, independent, and sovereign nation," she wrote on social media.

Favourite Kane makes Ballon d'Or shortlist

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 15:27:09 GMT

Harry Kane scored 73 goals last season for club and country

Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane is one of three England players nominated for the 2026 Ballon d'Or.

Real Madrid's Jude Bellingham and Arsenal's Declan Rice join Kane, the favourite for the award, on the 30-player shortlist.

Inter Miami forward Lionel Messi, who is looking to win his ninth Ballon d'Or, has been nominated.

The 39-year-old scored eight goals as Argentina lost the World Cup final to Spain in July, with Messi since retiring from international football.

Lamine Yamal is one of six Spain players that won the World Cup to be included.

Having scored the winning goal in the final, Paris St-Germain forward Ferran Torres, who joined the French club from Barcelona in the summer, makes the cut.

Back-to-back Champions League winners Paris St-Germain have nine players - excluding new signing Torres - nominated, including last year's winner Ousmane Dembele.

Real Madrid forwards Kylian Mbappe and Vinicius Jr also make the shortlist, as do Arsenal defenders Gabriel and William Saliba.

The award is celebrating its 70th anniversary, having been created by France Football in 1956, and the winner will be announced at an ceremony in London on 26 October.

The "symbolic choice of venue" is in tribute to former England player Sir Stanley Matthews, who won the first Ballon d'Or.

Attacks victim's death 'potentially preventable'

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 15:18:10 GMT

The death of a student killed in the Nottingham attacks was "potentially preventable", a public inquiry has heard.

Barnaby Webber - along with Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates - were killed by Valdo Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020, on 13 June 2023.

On Tuesday, ahead of closing statements to the Nottingham Inquiry - which is examining the killings - the inquiry was told a "more rapid administration of blood products" could have meant Barnaby's death was "potentially preventable".

The inquiry also heard documents found in a bin at Calocane's address contained a list of explosives, which was not disclosed by Nottinghamshire Police until June this year.

A panel of medical professionals assessed the emergency medical response on the day of the attacks to assess "survivability", the inquiry was told.

In their assessment, the panel noted the hard work of the emergency responders in their care to the victims.

The panel found if blood products had been administered to Barnaby earlier and more rapidly, it could have increased his chances of getting to hospital with enough of a heartbeat to undergo surgery.

However, multiple other rapid and particular steps would have had to have taken place for him to have survived.

The inquiry heard Barnaby had a less than 50% chance of surviving his injuries, characterised as "potentially preventable", while Grace and Ian's deaths were "not preventable".

The families of the victims sobbed as the assessments were read out by counsel to the inquiry Rachel Langdale KC. Grace's father, Dr Sanjoy Kumar, left the hearing room.

Langdale said Nottinghamshire Police found the documents in a bin at Calocane's former property in Burford Road in Nottingham.

He wrote bullet points on one page about explosives under the heading "thoughts", including TNT and nitrate fertiliser.

Langdale said: "This piece of paper listing thoughts about a number of explosives was not identified or taken into account at the time."

She added it had not been made available by police to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) or to psychiatric experts.

Calocane was evicted from the Burford Road address on 11 June 2023 and travelled to London, before returning via to Nottingham shortly before midnight on 12 June, a day before his killings, the inquiry heard.

The Nottingham Inquiry started hearing evidence in February, with more than 100 witnesses questioned over three months.

Witnesses included police staff and officers, mental healthcare practitioners, Calocane's former flatmates and family members, the bereaved families and the survivors of the attacks.

A number of revelations emerged in evidence about errors in Calocane's care, his previous interactions with police and failings both during and in the aftermath of the attacks.

Calocane - who also seriously injured three others - is currently serving an indefinite hospital order in a high-security facility after pleading guilty to three counts of manslaughter, on the grounds of diminished responsibility, and to three counts of attempted murder.

The inquiry is currently hearing updates in evidence since the end of oral evidence earlier this year.

In her closing remarks, Langdale reiterated the evidence of former parliamentary ombudsman Sir Rob Behrens.

She said: "Too often these cases are dependent upon bereaved families campaigning at a time when they are least prepared to do so, and it is an outstanding public service that they perform."

Langdale added: "Although Sir Rob was talking generally about bereaved families, his words could have been written as a description of the bereaved families and their legal team in this inquiry. Indeed, without their efforts there would not have been a public inquiry at all.

"The evidence we have obtained has revealed one failure after another.

"There is a suggestion in some submissions that further oral evidence should be called. We submit that there's no need for further oral evidence from any source.

"Barney, Grace and Ian should be alive. And the survivors - uninjured."

Final submissions to the chair, senior judge Deborah Taylor KC, will continue on Wednesday.

Taylor said it was "disappointing" that over the break, evidence had emerged which "ought to have been identified" and disclosed earlier.

She directed core participants to provide any corrections to errors or omissions by no later than 31 December.

Contains some violence.

Langdale said Nottinghamshire Police also recovered a holdall bag belonging to Calocane - who is being referred to in the inquiry as VC - from his address in the days after the attacks.

There were three notebooks in the bag, which included a note written by Calocane saying he was a god and "was a tree that guards the key between heaven and hell".

In his closing speech, Tim Moloney KC, who represents the bereaved families, said a note made by Calocane on one of the sheets of paper appeared to say "Manchester Arena".

Calocane searched online for large venues in Nottingham and bookmarks on his web browser for the Albert Hall Conference Centre in the city and the Theatre Royal and Royal Concert Hall, the inquiry heard.

Moloney said the notebooks also revealed "relevant information including what we say was a deep-seated misogyny".

The items were not prioritised because efforts were focused on finding a bag which the killer had with him on the evening of the attacks, the inquiry heard.

"There was a failure to investigate VC's historical behaviour and actions," Moloney said.

He added "no-one asked VC why he was searching for explosives and large venues because they couldn't", referencing the police's failure to share the information.

Langdale described the failure to disclose the notebooks an "oversight by Nottinghamshire Police".

The inquiry heard further violent assaults by Calocane on colleagues at warehouses in Nottinghamshire were also not disclosed to the inquiry team until after the public hearings took place.

This included an assault on a colleague in a warehouse in Eastwood in 2021 and another in Normanton in February 2023.

Footage of the February 2023 attack, described by Moloney as "sustained attack with punches thrown", was shown to the inquiry for the first time on Tuesday.

In his closing statement, Moloney focused on the timeline of contact between Calocane and public services.

"We say the timeline contains a litany of unnoticed red flags, missed opportunities and individual and systemic failures," he said.

"The bereaved families firmly believe that if opportunities had been taken to effectively deal with the behaviour of VC, if there had not been so many failures by so many people in institutions between 24 May 2020 and 13 June 2023, then their loved ones would still be here today.

"They have good reason to believe that, because VC's history of contact with public agencies is one of repeated individual and systemic failures in the face of the clear and growing risk that he presented."

Moloney said there were failures by authorities to follow policies and procedures and adequately consider harm with "every incident" involving Calocane between 2022 and 2023.

"Police were too quick to let things go in the teeth of really quite serious incidents, and clinicians were too quick to adopt a least restrictive practice which ignored the rights of his victims as we say ultimately and the rights of the public," he said.

"Together, these practices diverted VC away from the criminal justice system or forensic psychiatry and he should have been going down that pathway.

"Together, these practices failed VC and the people he affected who sit in this room."

Adam Straw KC, representing Calocane's family, highlighted a list of failings by Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust throughout the duration of its care for the triple killer.

He said: "Many of the problems brought to light by this case are founded on inadequate resources.

"It was clear from many of the witnesses at every level that resources for mental health services are far too low."

Among his suggestions, he said there should be a ring-fenced "increase for mental health service generally", national guidelines on minimum staffing levels for various relevant roles and more support for patients' families.

"Had VC received full and proper treatment and management of his admission in May 2020, there is reason to think that this tragedy would have been prevented.

"The same is true of many other schizophrenic-homicides up and down the country," Straw added.

Renoir paintings worth millions stolen in French museum heist

BBC News Tue, 08 Sep 2026 13:35:28 GMT

Two paintings by the impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir have been stolen from a museum in the south of France.

Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer early on Tuesday, seizing four paintings but dropping two of the works in the museum gardens as they escaped, local Mayor Bryan Masson said.

The paintings, each worth €9m (£7.7m; $10.4m), are the latest high-profile pieces to have been stolen in a string of recent heists in Europe which have thrust the security of art in galleries and museums into the spotlight.

One of the most high-profile was in October last year, when a brazen heist at the Louvre Museum in Paris saw France's priceless crown jewels being stolen.

CCTV footage captured the thieves entering the Renoir museum gardens by cutting through a fence before they cut through structures holding the paintings' frames in place, the local mayor said.

The alarm went off at 05:48 (03:48 GMT), and police were at the scene within five minutes, Masson explained, saying the thieves fled the scene upon hearing the security alarms.

He later told reporters that the thieves seemed to be "well-equipped" and "well-informed".

They were "wearing helmets, gloves, and combat gear" and carrying "an electric knife and hacksaw," he added.

Investigators have found two zip-up bags at the scene, which may have belonged to the suspects.

The mayor said that two paintings were "abandoned" in the gardens and have now been recovered.
