We’re on the verge of seeing the quantum vacuum for the first time

New Scientist September 07, 2026

On the outskirts of Hamburg, Germany, pulses from one of the world’s biggest X-ray lasers race underground towards a stainless-steel chamber. Directly above, another huge laser waits. Soon, its beam will be sent down to meet the X-rays head on, bringing the two extraordinarily powerful beams of light together in an almighty burst of energy.

All very exciting, to be sure. But there is a serious side to these laser theatrics: the scientists behind them are hoping to see the vacuum. Not stray material in the chamber, or leftover gas, or particles of any kind, but the vacuum itself – what most people regard as pure emptiness, but modern physics says is brimming with quantum fields. Usually, these fields are perfectly undetectable, and the vacuum looks like nothing. But with enough light, even nothing can start to look like something.

“The hope is that, if it exists according to theory, we’ll be able to see it,” says Tom Cowan, an experimentalist at the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf laboratory in Germany. “If it’s not there, there’s a problem.”

Advertisement

Seeing the vacuum doesn’t merely require massive lasers, but also some of the most sensitive detection equipment ever devised. But the payoff could be great. The results will put our best theories of the vacuum to the test, and potentially give us a better handle on the dark matter that seems to occupy most of the universe. There is also an outside chance they could reveal that empty space is even stranger than quantum theory predicts.

No space, no time, no particles: A radical vision of quantum reality

The modern concept of the vacuum can be traced to the work of theorist Paul Dirac in the late 1920s. At that time, physicists already believed that the electromagnetic field filled all of space, but they still thought of matter as discrete particles, such as electrons and protons. Dirac saw that electrons could also be understood as energetic blips in an underlying field. Over a decade or so, his idea blossomed into quantum electrodynamics, or QED for short – the first successful quantum field theory.

By the 1970s, a more elaborate quantum field theory, the “standard model” of particle physics, had grown to encompass QED and account for all known matter and fundamental forces, besides gravity. When space is empty, these fields remain, but they aren’t totally placid. The uncertainty built into quantum theory predicts that a field can never be guaranteed to have any particular strength, even zero: there must always be the possibility of something a little more, the chance of a fluctuation.

This isn’t just abstract physics. As theorist Hendrik Casimir predicted in the late 1940s, quantum fluctuations can exert a measurable force. Put two metal plates extremely close together in a vacuum and the gap restricts the wavelengths of the fluctuating electromagnetic field that can fit between them. Outside the plates, the quantum fluctuations pile up, and the resulting imbalance draws the plates together. Today, engineers battle with this effect whenever they build nano-devices for smartphones, game controllers and other modern technology.

Still, no one has actually seen the quantum vacuum itself. Normally, seeing something – even something transparent – involves it changing the light in some way. Take water in a cup, for instance: light passes through it, reflecting and refracting off the electrons surrounding the water’s atoms. The distinctive optical pattern reaching our eyes is what tells us that the cup contains water, rather than nothing.

But when light passes through a vacuum, we don’t see a response from its fields at all, even if they are rife with fluctuations. The fields are perfectly invisible – they might as well not be there.

Except, maybe we haven’t been looking hard enough. In the mid-1930s, when QED was still in its infancy, the theorists Werner Heisenberg and Hans Euler showed that if light is strong enough, it should begin to strain the vacuum fields, such that they affect the passage of any more light passing through – an effect known as vacuum birefringence.

“One must attribute certain properties to empty space itself,” remarked theorist Victor Weisskopf, who furthered the analysis a year later. If they were right, the vacuum fields ought to be visible, after all – almost like some incredibly rarefied crystal.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Trouble is, no one had light bright enough to explore this uncharted realm of QED. In those days, the brightest light sources were arc lamps, commonly found in black-and-white cinema projectors, operating at a few kilowatts. But technology moved on. Once lasers arrived in the 1960s, maximum intensities ramped up to megawatts, then gigawatts and beyond.

More recently, “chirped pulse amplification” – recognised by the 2018 Nobel prize in physics – has opened the gateway to petawatt lasers, powerful enough to vaporise anything placed in their focus. Meanwhile, advances in particle accelerators have led to the creation of gargantuan lasers that emit X-rays, rather than visible or infrared light.

None of these instruments was invented to probe the quantum vacuum. High-power optical lasers were developed mainly to study how light interacts with matter, and to develop new methods of nuclear fusion. The scientists behind X-ray lasers mostly wanted to obtain the molecular structures of important proteins, and to watch chemical reactions in real time. Still, “you get a new hammer, and you look for a new nail to hit with it”, says Tom Heinzl, a theorist at the University of Plymouth, UK.

Two years ago, Heinzl was one of more than 50 authors who published a proposal to use one of the world’s most powerful X-ray lasers, the European X-Ray Free-Electron Laser (XFEL) in Germany, to test Heisenberg and Euler’s predictions of vacuum birefringence.

The idea, which had been brewing for nearly two decades, involved crossing the XFEL’s pulsed X-ray beam with that from a separate, 300-terawatt optical laser. The optical laser would strain the electron field, such that when the X-rays passed through, their orientation, or polarisation, would be very slightly rotated: the signature of the vacuum itself. “This is QED in an uncharted regime,” says Heinzl. “No one has tested it before.”

On the face of it, this could sound like juvenile antics – firing two obscenely powerful lasers at each other to see what happens. But the predicted effect is anything but dramatic. A single pulse of the XFEL, which lasts around a hundred-trillionth of a second, contains 100 billion X-ray photons. Felix Karbstein at the Helmholtz Institute Jena in Germany suggested that, out of all those photons, just one would have its polarisation flipped by the vacuum. No detector on Earth could hope to pan for that kind of signal. A trick was needed.

The potential answer came from several members of the experiment’s research team, including Cowan. Known as a dark-field technique, it involves placing a small, circular object in the middle of the X-ray beam, just after it passes the light-strained region. Most of the X-rays are blanked out, but not those that have been affected by the vacuum: in the process of having their polarisations flipped, they are simultaneously diverted into a dark halo surrounding the beam, where a detector can spot them more easily.

“It’s like looking at the sun during an eclipse,” says Cowan. “Thanks to the moon’s shadow, you can see the sun’s corona because it’s no longer overwhelmed.”

Last year, the team conducted a proof-of-principle experiment at the XFEL’s Helmholtz International Beamline for Extreme Fields (HIBEF) research facility to test the dark-field concept, and found that it did indeed block out the background signal. “Our goal wasn’t to do the measurement in that run,” says Ulf Zastrau, who leads research on matter under extreme conditions at XFEL. “Really we just learned what we have to do.” The researchers hope to attempt their first proper observation next year.

If they are successful, they won’t actually be the first to claim to have detected vacuum birefringence. Ten years ago, astrophysicists using the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope (VLT) in Chile detected polarisation in the faint light coming from a neutron star 400 light years away. Neutron stars are the dense remnants of massive stars with extreme magnetic fields.

For decades, scientists have tried and failed to explain how the force that binds the heart of atoms together really works. But new mathematical tools are finally prising the problem open

The researchers argued that if their star’s light had started off polarised, the magnetic fields ought to have scrambled it – so the fact that there was polarisation meant it could only have been generated by the surrounding vacuum. “The [results] that we measured with the VLT can’t be easily explained by our models unless the vacuum birefringence effects predicted by QED are included,” said Roberto Mignani at the National Institute for Astrophysics in Milan, Italy, at the time.

But almost immediately after the team’s claim was published, independent theorists began to dispute it, saying that the models depended too heavily on assumptions about the neutron star and its magnetic field. Earlier this year, results from NASA’s Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer strengthened the case for vacuum birefringence, but the analysis still depends on various model assumptions about neutron star behaviour.

By contrast, the polarisations of the X-ray photons at the HIBEF experiment will be clearly known, before and after. If any are detected in a different polarisation, there will be little debate that it was the vacuum that flipped them.

Of course, this depends on the QED predictions being correct – which, to be fair, they always have been. No other theory has ever proved so successful as QED in the history of science. Famously, one particle property, the magnetic strength of the electron, can be correctly predicted by QED to a relative accuracy of around 1 part in 1 trillion. “If you talk to a particle physicist and say you want to test QED, they’ll start yawning,” says Heinzl. “They’ll say that’s already been done decades ago.” In this view, a successful observation of vacuum birefringence would just be the icing on the cake.

But, as Heinzl points out, past predictions of QED have all involved relatively weak light fields, and the addition of numerous corrections or “perturbations” to get the right answer, while avoiding any infinities cropping up in the calculations.

For strong light fields, this type of maths almost always doesn’t work – the calculations sum to infinity, whatever you do. The Heisenberg-Euler prediction of vacuum birefringence is a rare, lucky case in which a strong-field QED effect can be calculated without resorting to perturbations, and without any infinities. It is quite possible that this strong-field regime of QED fails to live up to the success of what has been tested before, and that some other, yet-unknown theory governs strong-field behaviour. “That’s why we get excited,” says Heinzl.

In such unexplored terrain, one new thing that could show up is the signature of a new particle related to dark matter. In the universe as a whole, dark matter is believed to account for 85 per cent of all matter, yet no one knows what it is. One of the leading candidates is a hypothetical, electrically neutral particle known as an axion, which barely interacts with ordinary matter. Current experiments involve looking for photons that might have been generated by axions in the presence of strong magnetic fields. But so far, no luck.

As these searches continue, theorists have begun to consider broader possibilities of axion-like particles – even a rich “dark sector” of various new particles and fields interacting with one another. In this case, an axion-like particle could be too short-lived to be detected by existing experiments, but could make its fleeting appearance known in a stronger-than-expected birefringence effect at HIBEF.

It’s a long shot, says theorist Andreas Ringwald at the DESY particle accelerator lab in Germany, but a unique window nevertheless. “I think the experiment should be done,” he says. “It’s very well motivated. QED in this regime has never been tested in the laboratory before.”

There is even the question of whether QED itself is the whole story of how strong light affects the vacuum. Since the 1930s, physicists have explored other theories of electromagnetism, in which empty space responds differently. Some predict vacuum birefringence much like QED does, but not all, at least not to the same extent. HIBEF itself won’t be able to distinguish between these theories, but it will crack open the window to a new experimental testing ground that could potentially be explored more in future experiments.

As laser powers increase, physicists are looking not only to see the vacuum, but to force its quantum fields to erupt into real particles and antiparticles – the Schwinger effect, named after QED theorist Julian Schwinger, who described it (see “The vacuum volcano”, below). “The wonderful thing about physics is that, as you probe new experimental regimes, there’s always the possibility of surprises,” says David Tong at the University of Cambridge.

In truth, though, any deviation from strict QED predictions wouldn’t immediately be cause to throw away the theory. For over 30 years, the PVLAS (“polarisation of the vacuum with a laser”) experiment at the National Institute of Nuclear Physics in Ferrara, Italy, has been trying – and failing – to pick out vacuum birefringence from background noise by reflecting a dim laser beam back and forth though a magnetic field hundreds of thousands of times. In 2006, its team reported a deviation from QED predictions, which some theorists took as evidence for axions.

However, two years later, the team rebuilt the experiment, including replacing the laser, and found nothing. Likewise, any signal measured by HIBEF will need to be scrutinised for experimental artefacts.

The daring idea that time is an illusion and how we could prove it

And even with the dark-field technique and massive lasers, seeing the vacuum will be difficult. According to calculations by Karbstein, they can expect the vacuum to flip just two photons per hour. They can’t simply let the experiment run forever, as XFEL beamtime is sparingly distributed – most experiments are given just half an hour or so. In a limited time window, success isn’t guaranteed.

“It’s all about controlling background noise,” says Heinzl. “We might get lucky, we might not.” Yet, if just a handful of photons emerge from the blinding laser collision with their polarisation altered, then, for the first time, physicists will have seen empty space itself.

With sufficiently powerful lasers, the vacuum should become visible, twisting the paths of passing photons (see main story). But push the vacuum even harder and it should produce particles of its own – an eruption of electrons and their antimatter partners, positrons. The phenomenon was first predicted by theorist Julian Schwinger in 1951, and requires immensely powerful laser fields – above 1 quintillion (10¹⁸) volts per metre.

Researchers at facilities such as the Extreme Light Infrastructure in the Czech Republic, Hungary and Romania are hoping they might still break the Schwinger limit by crossing several beams at one spot, or reflecting a laser from a plasma “mirror” travelling at near the speed of light. So far, though, these all remain blueprints.

The best new popular science books of September 2026

New Scientist September 07, 2026

This month seems to be full of celebrity, whether as subjects of our latest science books or as their authors. There are new books from physicist Carlo Rovelli, doctor and presenter Xand van Tulleken, broadcaster Jim Al-Khalili and leading scholar of our relationship with tech, Sherry Turkle, as well as a biography of Stephen Hawking. As ever, we range far and wide, from great biographies to the world’s darker, problematic corners.

Carlo Rovelli’s latest offering, On the Equality of All Things, certainly looks like a broad-ranging virtuoso. New Scientist reporter Karmela Padavic-Callaghan has already gone the distance with the book, and their review will be published soon. They write that physics, as the science that describes all the ingredients of our physical reality and how they interact with each other, has a strong claim on how we understand our surroundings – but what about its grasp on meaning-making more broadly? Rovelli apparently tackles this question to great effect, arguing that with the advent of quantum physics, science underwent a revolution, but philosophers haven’t fully caught up, and he aims to offer them – and the rest of us – a crash course. Padavic-Callaghan finds his final lesson inspiring: “We face the world not as an ‘I’ faced with a ‘this’ but as a ‘me’ faced with a ‘you’. We are in the world. We are here. And we are home.” Rovelli is saying that seeing ourselves as abstract consciousnesses disconnected from the world and looking for truths beyond how the world touches us is a fool’s errand. “Interesting” barely touches the sides with Rovelli.

“If anyone can drag the wellness industry into the light and make you laugh while doing it, it’s Xand van Tulleken. Beautifully researched, clear-eyed and very funny,” said mathematician Hannah Fry of Make Me Well: A quest to understand the confusing world of wellness. Xand van Tulleken (one of identical twin brothers, both doctors, and both writers) sets out to take a hard look at a sector already worth billions – and largely unregulated. He digs into everything from the supposed benefits of vitamin D supplements and turmeric tablets to wearable health technology, blood tests and so-called anti-ageing pills. And he finds that the claims made for the above by influencers, tech companies, podcasters and their ilk mostly don’t stand up to hard science. This may be unsurprising to regular readers, but it can’t be documented too many times as we face an extraordinary surge in innovation, transforming drug design, genomics and diagnostics that yields ever more complexity and confusion. So how do we stay healthy, facing such an onslaught – and naked corporate greed? Quite likely, we could do worse than start here…

Advertisement

What a challenge: write the first major biography of theoretical physicist Stephen Hawking, a man who faced enormous physical challenges just to stay alive beyond his twenties, who lived on to defy the odds and contribute pioneering science – some of which has only quite recently been worked through. Factor in both the Hawking estate (which supported the work) and the whole scientific world (especially many of the stars also interviewed by the biographer) all watching closely to see the result. But it would be surprising if veteran science writer Graham Farmelo dropped the ball in Hawking: His life and work. Hawking is the man, after all, who travelled the farthest reaches of the universe from his wheelchair, and ended up shedding important light on the mysteries of black holes and our understanding of the beginnings of the universe, not to mention selling more than 25 million copies globally of his A Brief History of Time. Kudos all round.

Anyone who’s tangled with Carlo Rovelli’s elegiac approach to physics will come away enriched and full of wonder. His book The Order of Time, published in English in 2018, was a case in point – as much a meditation as an exposition. Jim Al-Khalili on the other hand is our go-to for a seriously comprehensive overview – plus his own share of lofty questions. New Scientist’s Joshua Howgego found his latest both excellent and meaty, as it tackled the various tricky problems in grappling with time. Al-Khalili, he wrote, is known as a “brilliant explainer of science and his focus here is explanation… He is at pains to be clear, fair and methodical.” Howgego found the earlier parts of On Time “supremely helpful” in teasing apart the deeply interconnected strands, separating them into two categories. First are the problems of “manifest time” (that’s how we experience it, flow, the sense of past and present), then, second, there is physical time (to do with how various fields of physics interpret time differently and how to resolve the tensions that result). Just one word of warning – it’s not a fat book, but it is dense. Enjoy.

It is billed as “an entertaining tour of the seemingly simple formula guiding the search for extraterrestrial intelligence”, and the first part of the title certainly raises a laugh – Cloudy with a Chance of Starships: How the Drake equation reveals the odds of life in the cosmos. The author Seven Rasmussen is an astrobiologist, so should know how to take the readers off on what is probably a rather irreverent trip round an equation that has become important to many within and around the scientific community: after all, who doesn’t want to know how likely ET really is? The Drake equation calculates the number of civilizations in our galaxy that humans could potentially contact and was first proposed in 1961 by another astrobiologist, Frank Drake. It begins, say the publishers, with well-known numbers for the rate of star formation in the Milky Way and the fraction of stars with planetary systems but gets more complex with a dive into areas such as the number of planets suitable for life, the fraction of suitable planets on which life appears and the likelihood of intelligent life emerging on a planet and becoming technological. The publishers say Cloudy with a Chance of Starships guides readers from the basics of astronomy to the frontiers of planetary science, calling it an “extraordinary book” which “shares a tantalizing vision of the dawning era of space exploration and invites enthusiasts of all ages to join in the discovery”. Buckle up then.

You might need a strong stomach for this one. Guilty Pleasure: The pornification of the internet, the economy, and everything else is billed as “the story of one of the most influential – and least examined – industries on earth” – that is pornography in the online age. Worth billions and generating, says the book, an almost unbelievable tenth of global internet traffic at peak times, it is changing our world at every level, from tech to work and culture to love and relationships – even our sense of self. Investigative journalist and FT reporter Patricia Nilsson draws on five years of reporting to show how the internet turned pornography into “a vast, secretive industry dominated by obscure owners, platform logic and profit at almost any cost”, as her publisher puts it. Nilsson takes on what can only be a difficult, unpleasant task that few would countenance. Sounds like we may at least owe her our attention.

There are few places on earth quite like bogs and boglands. Their ecology is truly unique, and they are home to abundant amphibian-eating plants and acid-flinging mosses. This is the world conjured by ecologist Merritt Turetsky in her book, Boglands: The hidden world of Earth’s most extraordinary ecosystems. She should know; Turetsky is a climate scientist, with hundreds of scientific articles on the importance of bogs to global climate. She advises governments, communities, and professional networks worldwide so they can understand the importance of bogs to the global climate. Above all, say the publishers of Boglands, “bogs are places of paradox, where past meets present in the remarkably preserved artefacts and bodies entombed in their depths, land meets water in an otherworldly landscape, and safety meets danger for those who dare to venture into the heart of the bog”. There’s a beguiling, if somewhat unnerving, invitation, and one bound to challenge how you see the natural world.

Insider books are often full of interesting knowledge you just can’t get at any other way – and James Webb’s Ancient Cosmos: A journey to the beginning of time certainly sounds like it will be one of them. Maggie Aderin has huge hands-on expertise and insights to share because she worked on the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), which, with its six-and-a-half-metre primary mirror, achieves a very high resolution. Working with science journalist Sarah Wild, the book promises to be an “essential guide to the latest James Webb images, revealing what these discoveries mean for our understanding of the universe and human history”. It’s quite a journey, beginning in our own galaxy and using the James Webb images as “route markers towards this cosmic dawn.. explaining some of cosmology’s greatest mysteries, from the shape of the universe to the nature of dark matter”. It will be interesting to see what it adds to her 2024 book, Webb’s Universe, reviewed in New Scientist, which featured JWST pictures including of the Carina and the Ring nebulae, The Pillars of Creation and the Cartwheel galaxy.

With wildfire, flooding and El Niño dominating the news agenda, global food scarcity can hardly be far behind. Enter earth scientist David R. Montgomery and his new book, Regen: A new future for farming, food, and health. His message is that a century of conventional farming has left our planet with sick soil, accelerating the interlinked crises of food security, biodiversity loss, water pollution and climate change. But thankfully he has a plan in the shape of regenerative farming, honed from a decade of research, interviewing farmers and seeing how they restored degraded farms all around the world. ReGen, say the publishers, “breaks down common myths around conventional and organic farming, animal agriculture and plant-based diets to frame ten policy recommendations for sustainably nourishing the world”. It also looks to build on Growing a Revolution, a previous book by Montgomery. Reviewing it, New Scientist called Montgomery “one of our most eloquent and precise earth science communicators… [He] has a knack for opening our minds to large, critically important questions.”

As of 2025, nearly a third of US adults rely on AI for companionship and emotional support. This is the scary background to Sherry Turkle’s latest book, Artificial Intimacy: Who we become when we talk to machines. She’s had years at MIT researching digital culture, writing 10 previous books exploring many facets of how technology has reshaped our outer and inner worlds, sometimes isolating us and leading us to “expect more from technology and less from each other”. Now, Turkle has an “urgent warning about how ever-increasing reliance on AI chatbots is eroding our capacity for empathy”, as we redefine human capacities for care, solitude and intimacy in terms of machines. She “evokes the seductive and beguiling nature of chatbots” as they work hard to be our “‘perfect’ companion.. and ask for nothing in return”. Intimate machines, says Turkle, are producing a generation more alienated, depressed and lonely than ever – and less equipped to reverse course, as machine relationships offer no practice for getting along with people.

You really need the subtitle here to get the whole, er, picture. The Universe: A graphic guide is unusual among general science books for adults, but it offers a perfectly serious, well-illustrated entry point to a topic that’s literally as big as it gets. Jillian Scudder, an astrophysicist and associate professor of physics and astronomy, is an ideal intergalactic tour guide, making sure that you work your way through the building blocks of life, the mysteries of dark matter, how stars are classified, the moon’s origins or why stars collapse. You need never worry about just what Cosmic Noon is either – the answer’s here, easily explained. And Lily Fossett’s illustrations are also gloriously unintimidating. Like a soothing cup of tea, The Universe is one of life’s instant small pleasures.

Given the current disquiet over the nature of autism, it may be a timely thing that Darian Leader, a psychoanalyst and writer, has titled his book Austisms. With Uta Frith, one of the original leaders in autism research, calling in May for a return to the drawing board in the face of rising levels of diagnosis, there are many issues muddying the waters. The radical split between the ways autism is perceived means that for some, it is a condition or a pathology, while for others it is an identity or a natural variation in human cognitive and behavioural diversity. Drawing on years of clinical experience and research, and the testimonies of autistic people, Leader’s book promises to be “an up-to-the minute account of the many indicative features of autism and how they have been assessed and treated over almost a century”, the publishers promise. Clarity amid the complexity and contradiction from an “illuminating guide” ought to be welcome.

If you love brilliant curation and stunning images of the natural world we need to save, then this compilation definitely sounds worth a shot – especially if you like your call-to-arms a bit glossy. The images range from tiny microscopic wonders and networks of fungi to medicinal plants and the animal species that share our world – drawn from every culture and era. The point, say the publishers, is that Ark “reveals the unique importance and beauty of the living things depicted and, in doing so, prompts readers to reevaluate humanity’s place in the natural world”. It’s been curated by Stephen Ellcock, who has made a name for himself as a curator, writer, researcher and an online collector of a huge number of images. He’s backed up by an impressive group of nature writers and academics: the foreword comes from Robert Macfarlane (Landmarks and Is a River Alive?), with essays helping to tie it all together by the likes of Harriet Rix (The Genius of Trees), marine biologist Helen Scales (What the Wild Sea Can Be and The Brilliant Abyss) and birder Stephen Moss (Ten Birds That Changed the World).

Youyou Tu, Flossie Wong-Staal and Chien-Shiung Wu are just three of the people celebrated in Marieke Bigg’s attempt to set the record straight – or at least straighter – about women and science. They appear alongside historical figures like ancient Greek mathematician Hypatia, 17th-century duchess Margaret Cavendish, Florence Nightingale, Marie Curie and more recent figures like Katherine Johnson, the US mathematician whose calculations of orbital mechanics while she worked at NASA were crucial to the success of the first (and other) crewed space flights. Tu is a chemist who won a Nobel prize in 2015 for the discovery of artemisinin, used to treat malaria – a breakthrough that saved millions of lives in southern China. Virologist and molecular biologist Wong-Staal was the first scientist to clone HIV and determine the function of its genes, a major step in proving that HIV is the cause of AIDS. And Wu was a particle and experimental physicist who worked on the Manhattan project, and later designed an experiment that was key to overturning ideas about the weak force. The experiment was named after her, but her two male colleagues were awarded a Nobel in 1957 for proposing the idea (they mentioned her in their acceptance speech). She had to wait until 1978 to be awarded the first Wolf prize in physics.

New Zealand Herald September 08, 2026

Police at the scene of a triple homicide investigation in Rotorua. Photo / Ben Fraser

A scene guard remains this morning at the Rotorua property where two children and a woman were killed on Monday.

Police were called to the Glenholme address at 10.30pm.

“On arrival, staff located two young children who were deceased and a critically injured woman, and sadly, she passed away at the scene,” Bay of Plenty Police Acting District Commander Inspector Logan Marsh said yesterday.

Marsh said the critically injured woman died despite extensive efforts by police and ambulance crews.

“We are treating the incident as a homicide, and an investigation is also underway,” Marsh said in a video on the Bay of Plenty Police Facebook page.

He said a man was found at the scene and was assisting police with the investigation.

A man later appeared in the Rotorua District Court on Tuesday afternoon charged with assaulting a person in a family relationship.

He appeared remotely via an audio-visual link, wearing white coveralls.

Judge Greg Hollister-Jones granted interim name suppression to the man and “three named” people.

He remanded the man in custody to reappear in court on October 2.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell told the Rotorua Daily Post the community was heartbroken.

“As the investigation continues, our thoughts are with the victims, their loved ones and all those impacted.”

She described the incident as a “horrific tragedy” and acknowledged the emergency services personnel who attended the scene.

Police said yesterday they were conscious of the distress the deaths have caused would do additional reassurance patrols in Glenholme and across Rotorua.

Marsh said the tragedy would be felt well beyond those directly affected.

“We know this event will be felt widely in the community and people will want answers.”

Marsh said support was being provided for the victims’ family and the police and ambulance staff who responded to the “extremely confronting scene”.

“Our focus now is on supporting the family, our first responders and getting answers to what occurred.”

Residents living near the property described a significant police presence in the area on Monday night, with officers conducting searches and making inquiries throughout the neighbourhood.

One resident said she saw police vehicles converge on the street, while another told media she was awakened by officers knocking on doors as they worked to locate the source of the emergency call.

A hearse was at the scene last night.

This morning, the quiet residential street remained under police guard, with investigators continuing their work behind cordons.

Police urged the public to avoid speculation as the investigation progressed, out of respect for the victims and their family.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown says he does not accept the finding that he put the council in disrepute after he described an RNZ worker as a “Muslim terrorist”.

An independent Conduct Commission investigation into comments made by Brown to an RNZ worker found he breached the council’s code of conduct.

The mayor’s comment was material “because it brought the council into disrepute and, although it was an isolated incident, it represented a major departure from expected standards”.

Appearing on Ryan Bridge TODAY, host Katie Bradford asked Brown if he accepted that finding, which the mayor said he did not.

“But it’s been and gone so I just have to live with that.

“I have a sense of humour which not everybody has unfortunately and I didn’t realise that that was a problem.

“You know we’re a dull society as it is and there are people determined to make it duller than it already is.”

In a statement to the Herald last week, Brown said: “I accept the report findings. I acknowledged at the time that I got this one wrong and apologised. We can now move forward.”

During his appearance on the show, while wagging his finger at Bradford, Brown insisted he did not call the man a terrorist, but said he looked like one.

“I said someone was a very scruffy person and looked like one ... That’s completely different.”

The mayor said he did not apologise at the time because the man “was laughing about it”.

Brown then attacked RNZ, questioning why taxes had to fund the broadcaster before threatening not to return to the show if “stuff like that” was raised again.

RNZ reported that Brown made an inappropriate remark to a staff member as he was being escorted into the public broadcaster’s Auckland office.

Responding to the staff member’s comment about security being tight, Brown said words to the effect “security can’t be very tight if we’re being escorted by a Muslim terrorist”.

The mayor also commented on the staff member’s beard. The man was of Indian descent.

The investigation, carried out under Auckland Council’s Elected Member Code of Conduct, was triggered by a complaint from a member of the public concerned Brown’s actions could normalise the “systematic issue of racism, hate and discrimination”.

The mayor’s chief of staff told the investigator “the mayor commented first on the RNZ employee’s lack of identification as a security guard and that he looked untidy”, and that the mayor then said; “you look like you could be a Muslim terrorist”.

Conduct Commissioner Paul Collins found the mayor’s “insulting remark” amounted to a material breach of the code.

“It breached the principle of respect and, although it was a single incident, it constituted harassment.”

The comments sparked fallout, with a Muslim advocacy group labelling the statement “downright racism”.

Brown apologised, saying it was a poor attempt at humour.

No sanctions were imposed, and Collins found Brown’s two previous apologies were sufficient.

Rotorua mayor backs National’s bed tax replacement: ‘Such a relief’

New Zealand Herald September 08, 2026

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell says receiving funds from the International Visitor Levy will be a huge relief for council and lift a burden from ratepayers. Photo / Laura Smith

Rotorua’s mayor says it’s a “welcome surprise” councils will take charge of how they spend new International Visitor Levy funding if National is re-elected.

National’s alternative to a bed tax announced by Prime Minister Christopher Luxon, Tourism Minister Louise Upston, and Finance Minister Nicola Willis would redistribute the International Visitor Levy tourists pay at the border.

Instead of the $100 levy going into Government baselines, they announced $100 million a year would go to the Department of Conservation, $50m to tourism projects, and the rest to councils.

Each council’s share would depend on the number of overseas tourists who stayed in its area.

This would also be topped up with more than $105m taken from future operating allowances.

The new policy is a replacement for a bed tax which National had originally agreed to consider but has now ruled out.

Auckland Mayor Wayne Brown said it was a step in the right direction but would still leave his council millions of dollars short compared with the take from a bed tax.

Rotorua Mayor Tania Tapsell, a former National candidate, said it was “such a relief” to hear of the new policy.

“We do need significant investment in our regions and actually this has come as a welcome surprise because we’ve actually got what we wanted as councils.

“We said we want to make the decisions for our communities and that’s exactly what’s going to happen – a significant amount of money guaranteed over the next few years.”

It was crucial councils decided how the money would be spent. The South Island would focus on infrastructure, Auckland on attracting events and Rotorua would look at destination marketing, Tapsell said.

She believed Queenstown, which would get more than $80m over the next four years, would focus on its infrastructure spending.

Rotorua, which hosts around 1 million foreign tourists a year, would get around $20m over four years.

Tapsell said the region would have got more with a bed tax; however, it was still a significant amount of money.

Using the visitor levy was preferable to avoid New Zealanders having to pay any levy, she said.

“This is quality over quantity.”

The new money would also lift a burden from ratepayers. Rotorua, with a population of 78,000, hosted 2 million visitors annually.

“This is going to help us without hurting the pockets of those domestic visitors.”

Sudima NZ operating officer Les Morgan also praised the levy announcement as a good first step.

He said a lot of work had been done on the bed tax and it was disappointing to have it “tossed aside”.

However, the levy was the second most-favoured option.

The raising of the levy from $35 to $100 had so far had little impact and showed visitors were prepared to pay it, Morgan said.

He was among those concerned that while it was positive that councils would receive the levy funding, it was not “fresh investment”.

It was redistributing existing money.

With the Government aiming for 4.7 million visitors by 2034, there remained “a huge funding gap” to pay for the infrastructure upgrades that would be needed.

“The money is definitely welcome but we most definitely need extra funding.”

Government acknowledges some pork labels may be misleading, refuses law changes

New Zealand Herald September 08, 2026

The pork industry is calling for "country of origin" information to be clearer. Photo / 123rf

By Sally Wenley of RNZ

The Government is refusing to make any law changes surrounding pork branding but acknowledges some labels may be misleading.

This follows the pork industry calling for “country of origin” information to be clearer, as some shoppers think they are buying New Zealand bacon or ham – but it’s not.

NZPork’s chief executive said some supermarkets’ pork products had extremely small labelling hidden on the back saying where the pig was bred overseas – but it’s marketed as being local.

Brent Kleiss said it’s infuriating and he’s not happy that no changes were being made.

He says a Parliament committee recommended the Government look at clearer labelling of pork products three years ago and has had no response since then.

However, in a statement, the Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs said the regulations ensured that information about the origin of regulated products – such as pork – was available to consumers in a way that was clear and informative.

Cameron Brewer said the complaint upheld by the Parliament committee related to how certain pork products were branded, rather than the origin information they were required to disclose.

“Although it might be possible for an imported meat product that complies with the regulations to be branded in a way that misleads consumers about the product’s origin, I am not aware of evidence that this is occurring on a scale that would justify further regulatory change.”

Brewer added that his Fair Trading Amendment Bill proposed to increase penalties for any misleading conduct that could affect consumers.

“I acknowledge your concern that some branding practices may give consumers a misleading impression about whether pork was raised in New Zealand.”

He suggested PorkNZ complain to the Commerce Commission if it had issues with the way pork products were labelled.

But Kleiss said farmers were not impressed – and they would be making a big noise about it.

“Our fear is that the minister may have been misled or made a decision to get it off his plate rather than actually tackle the issue head on.”

He said an issue was animal welfare – some countries were breeding and killing pigs unethically and local consumers didn’t realise how badly the pig had been treated before being made into bacon.

He was also frustrated with some supermarkets, saying he visited a Pak’nSave in Christchurch last week that didn’t have any New Zealand-bred and processed pork products.

Foodstuffs said it supported customers having clear and accurate information about the products they bought, including country-of-origin information, in line with the labelling requirements.

In a statement, it said availability of New Zealand pork could vary between stores depending on customer demand, supplier availability and the range of products stocked.

“When sourcing pork and other meat products, we consider a range of factors including food safety, quality, animal welfare, supply reliability and value for customers.”

The Minister for Social Development and Employment is refusing to apologise after tens of thousands of beneficiaries were declined food grants categorised as a non-essential item.

More than 8000 Special Needs Grant applications to help towards buying food have been declined by the Ministry of Social Development (MSD) over the past six years on the basis that food is “non-essential”.

Louise Upston told Ryan Bridge TODAY’s Katie Bradford that while she recognised food “clearly is an essential item”, the reason for declining applications had simply been recorded in the system incorrectly.

When asked if she would apologise, she remained firm that it was an administrative error.

“No, look, I think there’s two things here ... first food clearly is an essential item.

“... hardship grants will be declined for a range of reasons. What’s happened here is the reason has been incorrectly recorded in this system.

“It doesn’t change the decision that a hardship grant was declined.”

Meanwhile, MSD Canterbury regional commissioner Blair McKenzie acknowledged that clients would feel “confused and upset” and described the mishap as a record-keeping issue.

“We’re really, really clear that food grants should not be coded as non-essential.

“I do want to sit here today and apologise to anyone who finds themselves in that situation, it’s not a nice situation to be in.”

He said the 8000 applications made up around 0.1% of the total grants made over the past six years.

Food requests made up 96% of all applications under the Special Needs Grants.

“MSD has a range of about 50 codes they use to assess entitlements.

“Sometimes our staff get it wrong in terms of the code or the reason they might choose.

“But that aside, it’s affected 8000 New Zealanders and we do apologise for that.”

Upston said MSD made 1.3 million payments to Kiwis every week.

“In this instance they got it wrong, Blair’s apologised for that and we have made it absolutely clear that food is an essential item.”

Further training and guidance would be given to staff to ensure reasons behind decisions were recorded correctly.

“MSD staff do an amazing job, they work incredibly hard supporting New Zealanders who are often facing really challenging times and I don’t want this issue to reflect on the thousands of staff who work at MSD each and every day and they are amazing public servants.”

First XV rugby should matter, but not too much – Christchurch Boys’ High School headmaster Nic Hill

New Zealand Herald September 08, 2026

Christchurch Boys' High School headmaster Nic Hill has been raising concerns about First XV rugby for some time. Photo / CBHS Media Team

THE FACTS

In August, three boys aged 13 and 14 from Scots College in Sydney were charged with the aggravated sexual assault of a 14-year-old girl.

In response, Chanel Contos, the founder of Teach Us Consent, wrote about what she sees as a wider problem in elite boys’ schools. Her article explicitly examined schoolboy rugby and argued that cultures of physical status, group loyalty, sporting dominance and entitlement can overwhelm empathy and judgment.

Her writing is confronting. At times, she moves so quickly to judgment that she risks losing some of the people she most needs to persuade.

But the questions she raises are important. What do schools reward? What forms of masculinity do boys see celebrated? And what happens when adults build sporting cultures around status, dominance and winning, regardless of whether the school is single-sex or co-educational?

These questions matter in New Zealand too. I have been raising concerns about First XV rugby for some time, particularly about recruitment, escalating expenditure and the culture that develops when winning becomes too important. Too often, those concerns have been treated as peripheral to the real business of rugby. I believe they are the real business.

First XV rugby should matter. Boys should want to play for their school. They should train hard, compete fiercely, feel pride when they win and disappointment when they lose. They should experience belonging, responsibility and the pressure and privilege of representing something larger than themselves. Those things are worth protecting.

The problem comes when adults allow school rugby to matter too much. When schools recruit players, escalate spending on coaching, use inducements to attract sporting talent or build increasingly aggressive promotion around sporting success, the purpose starts to shift. What should be about young people can become an arms race driven by headmasters, coaches, parents and alumni, where money, recruitment and personal ego begin to shape decisions. In parts of school rugby, that has already happened.

The answer is not more complicated rules. It is a clearer moral standard.

Schools should be willing to say that recruiting students because of sporting ability is wrong and that win-at-all-costs behaviour is inconsistent with the purpose of school sport.

At Christchurch Boys’ High School, we have tried to make this explicit in policy by prohibiting recruitment based on sporting ability and behaviour that reflects a “win at all costs” attitude. I have encouraged other principals to adopt a similar standard. The responses have been revealing: “How would we compete?” “Our community expects this” or simply: “The horse has already bolted.”

Those answers worry me. They suggest that competitive pressure, community expectation and precedent are being allowed to set the moral standard. They should not.

Contact our South Island newsroom

I am not anti-competition. Competition matters because players invest something of themselves in it. The result should matter. Winning should feel good and losing should hurt. Competition also needs restraint.

Contos writes about environments where physical ability, status and group loyalty can become forms of social currency and where entitlement can overwhelm empathy. Boys are also growing up in a digital environment that often presents status, wealth, dominance and winning as evidence of male worth. Schools should challenge that message. They should not reinforce it.

Rugby can help.

For boys, it can teach them to harness aggression without cruelty, strength without domination, loyalty without tribalism and pride without arrogance. But that depends heavily on the adults who coach them. Decent coaches matter because boys learn as much from how adults behave as from what they are told.

School culture is shaped by what adults reward. If we signal that winning is important enough to recruit players from other schools, spend ever greater sums on coaches or treat teenage athletes as institutional assets, students notice.

The question for school leaders should therefore be broader than whether a practice complies with a rule. We should ask whether it is right. Is it good for the player involved? Is it fair to other schools? What kind of people is this helping form? Would we be comfortable plainly telling our whole community that this is how we choose to win?

The scale of recruitment, inducement and spending matters. There is no perfect numerical threshold, which is why judgment matters. Principals should ask what their school’s actions are doing to the people involved. Are we helping young people develop humility, judgment and care, or rewarding entitlement, status and the pursuit of advantage?

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) needs to stop treating uncertainty about formal jurisdiction as a reason to stand back. It has influence, resources and levers. It also has a national responsibility to lead. If NZR is prepared to take positions on competition structures, it should also be prepared to take positions on the behaviours and incentives shaping the game.

NZR could lead the development of a simple national standard for school rugby. Schools could commit not to recruit students because of sporting ability, not to use inducements to attract sporting talent and not to tolerate win-at-all-costs behaviour. They could also commit to communication and branding that is humble, dignified and respectful of opponents.

Some regions have already acted more firmly. Auckland schools introduced stricter rules around player movement and recruitment several years ago. The fact that standards vary so much across the country is itself a reason for NZR to lead.

That would not make First XV rugby less important. It would make it more worthy of its importance.

We should want boys to care deeply about representing their schools. We should want fierce contests, packed sidelines, pride in victory and genuine disappointment in defeat.

The adults around the game must ensure that pride does not become entitlement, belonging does not become tribalism, excellence does not become elitism and ambition does not overwhelm judgment.

School sport should help young people become good adults. In boys’ schools, that includes helping boys become good men. Winning should never become more important than that.

The owner-operators of an award-winning dairy company say they’re facing ongoing criticism despite apologising for promoting their brand with an image showing their Bentley parked in a mobility spot.

Hamilton-based Vibhah and Vineet Shiriwastow, who run wellness company Four Leaves Co, are still dealing with a backlash from some in the disabled community after promoting their latest product while their Bentley Continental was parked in a designated mobility space.

The image was shared on their Lullaa milk brand’s social media channels, where viewers soon spotted the faux pas and questioned why they had parked there.

The brand removed the image, but not before it was reshared in a public Facebook group that “names and shames” those caught breaching mobility parking rules.

Several members took offence at the brand’s light-hearted responses to commenters’ concerns, including one that said, “no mobility parks were harmed in the making of this TikTok”, and encouraged others in the group to lodge complaints.

Some had even sent the brand threatening and intimidating messages, while their Bentley had been recorded as a stolen vehicle on CarJam.

Speaking to the Herald, the Shiriwastows said they typically take a picture each time they deliver an order to stockists and the image in question was taken after they delivered products to FreshChoice as an internal record.

The pair said they had turned the car around, briefly stopped in the mobility space while the car was running, took the photo and left within about a minute.

“We owned our mistake, we rectified it, we acknowledged it, and we took that photo down,” Vineet Shiriwastow said.

“We knew we were in the wrong ... and we learned from that. That was it, and we apologised to everyone who personally emailed us.”

The Shiriwastows said they accepted the incident “shouldn’t have happened at all”, but despite conveying their regret to complainants, a minority continued to escalate the situation.

Vibhah Shiriwastow said they removed the image after learning it had been reshared and stopped responding to some queries because they believed their replies were fuelling the backlash.

The FreshChoice store had also fielded criticism after allegedly giving the pair permission to park temporarily, but Vineet Shiriwastow said it was a third party that shouldn’t be involved.

FreshChoice did not respond to questions.

Contact the NZ Herald newsroom

Nevertheless, the years spent getting the Lullaa product ready for market had been clouded by the backlash at home, and Vibhah Shiriwastow was “disappointed that we’ve actually had to come to this bridge to cross it”.

“In my time, I have not ever parked in a disabled car park to jump out to get as much as a pie,” he said.

“We’re human ... It takes a real person to actually acknowledge their mistake and own it.

“We’ve acknowledged and owned it, but people have turned it around on us to try and destroy our company, and this company is actually meant to be better for New Zealand.”

OpenAI claims to have solved maths problem that stumped humans for decades

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 21:29:10 GMT

Company behind ChatGPT says 10,000 of its AI systems cracked the Navier-Stokes problem in 88 hours

OpenAI claims to have solved a major mathematics problem that has stumped humans for nearly a century after spending millions of dollars on the artificial intelligence-led endeavour.

The company behind ChatGPT said it had cracked the Navier-Stokes problem, one of seven Millennium Prize Problems published by the Clay Mathematics Institute to highlight some of the biggest unsolved puzzles in the field.

However, the announcement swiftly became mired in controversy after mathematician Tristan Buckmaster, a professor at New York University, said OpenAI accelerated its work on the problem after hearing that he and another researcher at Anthropic, an OpenAI rival, were poised to announce their own breakthrough.

Buckmaster had further concerns because the pair’s work in progress was stored in OpenAI’s Codex model, which is used for writing computer programs, potentially making the work visible to the OpenAI team.

In a document posted on his website, he added: “I do not know what their model did, or how. I do not know whether our data was used. I am not accusing anyone of anything.”

At a press briefing on Tuesday, OpenAI researcher Sebastien Bubeck denied that the company had used the pair’s work or accessed material shared with OpenAI’s servers.

OpenAI’s announcement on the breakthrough gave more details, saying that the company was inspired to launch the effort after hearing rumours that two Millennium Prize Problems had been solved. It also said it could not rule out that data from the pair’s use of their products “helped improve our models.”

OpenAI said it tackled the Navier-Stokes problem with an internal OpenAI system that was more powerful than its latest GPT-6 Astra model. About 10,000 AI agents – AI systems that carry out tasks autonomously – worked on the problem at once and reached the solution in 88 hours.

“A major goal of our work is to empower scientists to advance research and technology that benefits all of humanity,” OpenAI researchers wrote in a blog. “We believe it is important to inform the world about the pace of AI progress and what to expect from upcoming models”.

The breakthrough is the latest to demonstrate how advanced artificial intelligence models consuming enormous amounts of computing power are encroaching on and reshaping the field of mathematics. In May, OpenAI claimed progress in another mathematical problem first proposed 80 years ago, while Google DeepMind has also claimed maths achievements with its models.

Bubeck said the solution to the Navier-Stokes problem was “a spectacular culmination of the arc we have seen over the past 12 months”.

The Navier-Stokes problem asks whether equations that are used to describe the movement of fluids like air and water fail under particular conditions. OpenAI’s proof suggests that they do, with the equations occasionally “blowing up” with the speed of fluids becoming impossibly infinite. It took OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra about 17 hours to verify the solution.

Mathematicians who solve any of the Millennium Prize Problems are in line for a $1m (£740,000) reward from the Clay Mathematics Institute. OpenAI, which is preparing for a flotation that could value the business at around $1tn, said it did not intend to claim the prize.

The clash with Buckmaster aside, the maths announcement also allows OpenAI to cast its technology in a positive light after a period of alarm over how safely it is being developed. OpenAI revealed in July that a swarm of agents had hacked into Hugging Face, a third'-party software store, during a cybersecurity test.

The incident, plus a similar episode at Anthropic, has led to renewed calls for curbs on AI development, with US senators calling last week for a permanent ban of AI “superintelligence” – the term for systems that outperform humans in all cognitive tasks.

Just don’t ask exactly how. There was something exhilarating about Vinícius’s acceleration and for all the fortune this did start to feel a little like a plan now: force the mistake, punish it. Madrid would force many more too, which they didn’t punish. They had also completed 125 passes in the final third; Madrid had completed 13.

The second half began with Martínez coming out to stop Mbappé, dashing through again, but Inter came back at them. Madrid’s midfield just didn’t exist. Which didn’t always matter as they ran through it. Courtois, though, does: he saved from Jones. There was a Nicolò Barella shot wide and Thuram scooped over. Then the stadium then stood to applaud when Courtois made an outrageous double stop on 55 minutes which, although the flag was up anyway, spoke of a kind of disbelief.

The issue was Porto being content to allow City to pitter-patter passes about their backline and middle third and there being no quickness of play or penetration. Discard the ponderous pace might have been Maresca’s message because when Foden switched flanks from the right and accelerated, Porto were splayed, and Haaland’s header from the cross required Diogo Costa’s gloves to keep the contest goalless.

A near-carbon copy came when Semenyo popped the ball over from the left but this time Haaland’s header sailed over. City were warming up: Foden, Cherki and Haaland all being denied, as Porto were caught in a chokehold in and around their area.

At Leicester and then Chelsea Maresca could draw criticism for a quasi-sideways style at times. Yet after the slowish passage, tonight’s XI had become direct and a threat, as when Bouaddi chipped the ball left from near halfway, it went forward at speed, and a panicked Porto cleared.

When Veiga went down after a challenge with Guéhi the match was halted, tempers frayed. The No 10 recovered – it appeared to be a head problem – and the action, finally, restarted before Szymon Marciniak blew his whistle for the break.

After the now seemingly de rigueur fireworks before every Champions League game, Porto had begun with confidence sky-high after winning all five Primeira Liga outings so far and, when wandering off for half-time, they remained content.

The mood changed almost instantaneously. City, at last, showed the ruthlessness needed at this level. Cherki, breaking into the area, swerved left, leaving Costa stranded. He fed Fernández and Haaland headed his cross into the turf and home – the visitors had a priceless lead.

What would be Porto’s response? To rove upfield and go close to the equaliser, was the answer. Maresca’s team can be open, as they were when André Silva had an age to dip right and let fly, the former Portugal forward’s attempt hitting the side-netting.

The lead was slender, as it was in Saturday’s 1-0 win over Coventry. Maresca acted as the hour passed, removing Cherki and Semenyo for Elliot Anderson and Iliman Ndiaye: two attackers for one forward and a holding player in Anderson whose role was to try and exert control for City, and aid Bouaddi in snuffing out any Porto threat.

A second goal would also stymie the hosts, so Ndiaye skipped across the grass, and unloaded, though the effort went straight into Costa’s clutches. Foden, too, tried to break in behind but the ball was shepherded back to the Porto keeper.

Whenever Farioli’s team moved forward City remained vulnerable despite Anderson’s presence. By the close, though, Haaland’s late right-foot stab ensured the result, and meant that even an interval dispute in the tunnel due to the Veiga-Guéhi clash was of scant import to City, despite tempers again meaning a further row.

Newcastle progress as Joe Willock strikes late to see off Millwall

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 21:07:57 GMT

Newcastle United did just enough in south-east London to progress to the next round of the Carabao Cup. Joe Willock scored the only goal of this boisterous, fun, slightly vague cup tie against a spirited Millwall team that wasn’t so much down to the bare bones, as the bones beneath the bones.

By the end there was a sense both sets of fans were more or less happy. Millwall for the vigour of the performance. Newcastle for the result, the clean sheet and any signs of early progress in the dawning of the age of Jaissle-ball.

“We were worth it, we faced it, we did it,” was Matthias Jaissle’s verdict, having sent out a strong team, Jacob Ramsey coming in on the right for the early-season hot-hands Anthony Elanga. And this was a significant win for Newcastle, who have been excitingly direct at times under their twinkly new manager, with his much-trailed blueprint for rapid transition, hyper-vertical attack and getting it forward quick-smart to the lads up front, but who still need to groove that system.

Millwall also aren’t sure what they are yet this season, although this is more to do with injuries. They currently have 13 players out, which is at least an improvement on the previous 15. Absurdly, Alex Neil has already come under some pressure after a couple of losses. Football needs its irrational edge. But there is also a limit.

Ryan Christie hit a hat-trick as Marco Rose celebrated his first win as Bournemouth manager with a 4-0 demolition of Lincoln in the Carabao Cup third round.

Substitute Rayan completed the scoring against the Sky Bet Championship Imps at the Vitality Stadium.

Jørgen Strand Larsen struck twice to propel Crystal Palace to a 3-0 success over Middlesbrough at Selhurst Park. Strand Larsen nodded home in each half before substitute Daichi Kamada lobbed Boro goalkeeper Sol Brynn to seal victory.

Chemsdine Talbi scored the only goal to earn Sunderland a 1-0 win against Premier League rivals Hull at the Stadium of Light.

Bradford came from behind to win 3-1 at fellow League One club Leyton Orient. Goals from Will Swan, Stephen Humphrys and Nick Powell overturned a Macaulay Gillesphey own goal.

At kick-off the sky was still a deep blackish blue above the lip of the Dockers Stand, the lights of the south London trains trundling past the unfilled corners of the ground, and the Den its usual self, a place that always manages somehow to generate that unique crackle of nonchalant hostility, no matter how midweek the crowd (and this one was a near-full house).

Newcastle had most of the ball early on, but looked like what they are, a team still finding its shapes and rhythms. “They are PONY, Wall!” was one measured home fan assessment of the Matthias Jaissle project at this early stage. It is a fair point perhaps. Newcastle’s manager does have a very precise idea of the patterns and tempo-shifts he wants from his team. This sort of systems-football can lead to periods of drift while players learn the brief.

Newcastle settled and began to dominate possession. Willock had the first real chance, snatching the ball from Romain Esse deep in the right back zone and shooting powerfully but too close to Filip Marschall.

In return Millwall offered graft, full-stretch defence and two deep banks of four in the classic old school style. With 36 minutes gone Caleb Taylor headed just wide charging on to a nicely flighted free-kick, their first effort at goal. And by half-time this had become something more like a cup tie as Millwall pressed down the left, ratted and pressed nicely in midfield, and delivered some potent set pieces.

Tino Livramento came on for Amar Dedic at the break. But it was Millwall who began at a clip, a zinging low cross from the right creating a scramble under the Newcastle bar, the ball eventually falling to Jenson Metcalfe, who shot with power just over the bar.

After which it was more diffuse pressure from Newcastle. Most teams would feel the absence of a midfielder of Bruno Guimarães’ passing quality. This one definitely does.

For a while the game looked like it was, an early season cup distraction for two chop and change teams, no lack of energy, but all feints and ducks and grapples, like a boxer warming up in the mirror. By the hour mark Newcastle had 70% possession plus 17 shots at goal, but somehow Millwall’s collection of hurled-together parts still looked more likely to create a telling chance.

Elanga came on, a measure of Newcastle’s desire to get this done. Millwall had the best chance of the game so far on 79 minutes, Tairyk Arconte, a real menace on the right, hitting the post with a shot that pinged back on to Lukas Hornicek’s body but somehow stayed out.

And moments later Newcastle scored with their first real moment of quality near goal. It was a lovely move to make it. Matias Fernandez-Pardo produced the key pass, a cute little shimmy and nudge outside to Lewis Hall. His cross found Willock in the centre, who finished it with a smart side-foot shot across the face of goal.

Millwall continued to press, without finding much penetration. And by the final whistle there was a concerted wave of noise coming from the full half-end of Newcastle fans, for whom the journey home into Wednesday morning would at least be a happy one.

Company review – Casey Affleck entertains us with creepy campfire tales

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 19:45:48 GMT

Venice film festival: Affleck’s third film as a director is a diverting gothic anthology about mysterious strangers, murder and – pointedly – wronged men

Gather ye ’round the glowing screen for a Casey Affleck campfire tale. It contains superstitions and murder and human oddities of all stripes. An old hermit in his shack. Something nasty in the woodshed. If you like the first tale, fill your boots, settle back, because here comes another and another; each sparked by the embers of its neighbour and playing out with the same deliberately theatrical panache. Affleck’s picture roams and rambles like a creepy cracker-barrel Jackanory.

Actually there is much to relish in Company, Affleck’s third film as a director, even if many of its elements feel like off-the-peg eccentricities; a little too laundered and self-consciously strange. It begins in tried and tested fashion with the arrival of a mysterious stranger on a dark winter’s night. The stranger takes a seat and spins a tale, at which point December 1975 melts into 1953, then 1903, before finally the film crosses the ocean to Europe at the tail end of the plague. Nick Nolte is a hermit pining for his lost daughter, while Ben Mendelsohn plays a mean, mordant farmer who reaches for his handgun too readily. Both men, one suspects, are destined for a bloody end.

Where is it leading, this tale of a woman who tells a tale of a woman? Into the woods and through the darkness, of course, although the film’s centrepiece story, set in the Rockies at the turn of the 20th century, provides a torch to dimly light our way. Here Adelaide Clemens and Scoot McNairy play Rebecca and Emmett, a hard-bitten farming couple who discover a teenage boy, Caleb, lying prostrate in the snow. Caleb is played by Atticus Affleck, the director’s youngest son, with a vulpine gaucheness which grows more assured and compelling the longer he’s on screen. Caleb tells Rebecca that he is much older than he looks; that he’s been “hither and yon” and visited Argentina and London. When she starts to suspect the boy may be behind a spate of grisly local killings, Caleb’s bleak pronouncements seem hardly designed to dissuade her. “This whole world is tall grass,” he explains. “You have no idea of the dangers underfoot.”

Affleck co-scripted Company alongside Ron Hansen, the author of The Assassination of Jesse James by the Coward Robert Ford, which was made into a fabulous 2007 film by Andrew Dominik. Affleck co-starred as Ford, a snivelling beta male with dark dreams of glory, unsure whether he wants to befriend or kill his idol, and there is a similar scary ambivalence to the character of Caleb, who settles in at the farm and appears in no hurry to leave. Caleb might be a fantasist, bumming for work in the mountains. He might be a demon, blown in from the backwoods or beyond.

As for Affleck, his career has peaked and troughed since those heady days of Jesse James. He won the best actor Oscar for Manchester by the Sea and cropped up as an army intelligence man in Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer. Off-screen, though, he has been dogged by accusations of sexual harassment (subsequently settled out of court) and it is perhaps no coincidence that his passion project is occasionally afflicted by pangs of self-pity and features men who have been wronged and weren’t believed by their peers. The hermit’s wife was killed by an errant, unrepentant physician. Emmett witnessed his father shot dead by a well-connected landowner. The law is a joke; the innocent are kicked to the curb. But these jarring asides stray too close to special pleading. They add little to the narrative; he could have easily cut them out.

Company is better – more satisfying – when it circles back to the fire and picks up the main thread; when it is sticking most closely to reliable American Gothic tropes. Affleck clearly loves this dark sub-genre and elects to play it straight, and his enthusiasm is infectious and embeds us in the yarn. His film is a diversion. Maybe it doesn’t wholly add up. But it contains a ripe gamey flavour with a crunch of buckshot in every bite. Don’t step into the woods after dark, it advises. And if a mysterious stranger taps at your door before dinner, think very carefully before introducing them to your guests.

Company screened in competition at the Venice film festival

Three people died at Burning Man this year, tripling the average number of deaths in connection with the annual festival that brings tens of thousands of people to build a temporary utopian community in the brutal conditions of the Nevada desert.

The increase in fatalities comes as news reports have highlighted that the average age of Burning Man attendees is increasing, with fewer participants in their 20s, and more in their 40s and 50s.

“Although we average one death a year at the festival, we have had two so far this year within the confines of the festival and I have received information regarding a third who died in transit to a hospital in Reno,” the Pershing county sheriff, Jerry Allen, told the Reno Gazette-Journal.

The festival, which has attracted upwards of 70,000 people in recent years, ended on 7 September. Founded in San Francisco in 1986 as a genuinely countercultural event, in which local artists built effigies and then set them on fire, Burning Man has increasingly become a jet-setting destination for the global tech elite.

Data from the annual Black Rock City census found that the estimated number of Burning Man participants in their 20s dropped from about 30% of total attendees in 2014, to only 10% in 2025, while the percentage of attendees in their 40s and 50s rose.

The first person who died this year was a man in his “mid-50s”, and the second was a 60 year-old man, the San Francisco Chronicle reported. Allen’s office confirmed that there were no signs of foul play with the first two deaths, both of which occurred at the festival held in the Black Rock playa, an arid stretch of federally managed land about 120 miles from Reno.

Last year, a 37-year old man was found dead in a pool of blood on the final day of the festival, in what authorities said they were investigating as a homicide. The case, which was the festival’s first known homicide in nearly four decades, remains unsolved, the Reno Gazette-Journal reported.

The Burning Man Organization did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the three deaths this year.

The Pershing county sheriff’s office said this year’s first death was reported in the early evening of 3 September, at Rampart, the temporary hospital in the festival’s Black Rock City. A man had been found on the street within the festival and had been given CPR for several minutes before a doctor pronounced him deceased, the sheriff’s office said. The second death was reported in the afternoon of the 5 September, when a man was reported to have been found deceased in his trailer he was sharing with his significant other.

More information on the deaths will be available in approximately six to eight weeks, after autopsies and toxicology reports are completed, the Pershing county sheriff’s office said in a statement. That office referred all questions about the third Burning Man-related death this year to Washoe county, where the county medical examiner’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
