Settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, Ed Miliband has said, in the UK’s starkest condemnation since the foundation of the Israeli state.

Andy Burnham, the prime minister, said he would “not stand by” as horrific suffering continued, writing in the Guardian that for too long the UK had been hesitant to act, “fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel”.

In the Commons, the foreign secretary said the government would now take the official position that Israel’s occupation of the West Bank was unlawful in its entirety, as he announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements.

The dramatic shift in the UK’s position comes after a summer of intense diplomacy against a backdrop of increasing settler violence in the West Bank, which has resulted in 12 nations – including France and Canada – announcing they would impose sanctions.

In a joint statement Burnham, Emmanuel Macron and Mark Carney said: “The time has come to take further action to uphold our commitment to protect the two-state solution, our interests and to stand up for our values, before it is too late.”

In response, the Israeli foreign minister, Gideon Saar, announced the closure of the UK consulate in Jerusalem and that 12 British MPs and activists – including Jeremy Corbyn and Labour MP Diane Abbott – would be banned from entering Israel.

Saar accused Miliband of “outrageous lies” and said the UK government was “systematically working against the state of Israel”. Washington’s ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, warned that the US could take retaliatory action over trade.

However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said Washington would “obviously” not follow the UK’s course of action, and did not want to see the West Bank destabilised, but declined to comment further. Burnham had briefed Donald Trump on the plan in advance.

In his statement to parliament, Miliband said the UK government would enact:

An import ban on goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories and a new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.

A comprehensive sanctions regime against providing services such as construction or financing for Israeli settlements and a ban on advertising them in the UK.

Personal sanctions against key individuals accused of promoting settler violence.

A new ban for arms licences and other exports that “materially contribute to the occupation”.

The foreign secretary said the UK’s actions would show that “Britain is not silent in the face of deep injustice, and nor is it powerless”. In an emotional statement, he described the agony he had heard from Palestinians in the West Bank whose homes had been destroyed and from doctors in Gaza who had seen children dying waiting for medical treatment.

The UK’s actions have been made increasingly urgent by Israel’s plans to expand the E1 settlement project east of Jerusalem, which could in effect cut off the north from the south of the West Bank, threatening the viability of any future Palestinian state.

Ministers expect the legislation to enforce the trade ban and sanctions to be in place within nine months, although they could be subject to legal challenge, which would result in a delay.

Miliband stopped short of describing Israel’s actions in Gaza as a genocide, as some on the left have demanded, saying the UK would wait for the determination of the international courts, but that there was evidence of “war crimes”.

Speaking in the Commons, he said: “The British government agrees that there is ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists.

“I recognise the gravity of saying this, but the truth is the least the people who face such suffering deserve. And it should be the prelude to justice.”

Miliband suggested that Keir Starmer had been reluctant to take action against West Bank settlers during his time as prime minister. “I’ll say very bluntly we should have acted earlier. And it has taken the new prime minister to come in and recognise the gravity of the situation,” he told MPs.

Burnham, who apologised for Labour’s stance on Gaza when he became prime minister, attempting to shore up votes on the party’s progressive flank, also said the previous government had been too slow to act.

Writing in the Guardian , he said: “We have called for years for a two-state solution in the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action. For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel.”

Miliband said he was taking the action as foreign secretary but also as a “proud British Jew” with relatives who had found safety in Israel after the Holocaust. “I am proud of my Jewishness and unwavering in my support for the state of Israel,” he said.

“And there is absolutely no contradiction between this and my support for the state of Palestine. Indeed, quite the opposite. The two-state solution is based on an explicit belief that the only route to security for both peoples is to live side by side in peaceful coexistence with freedom, security and self-determination.”

The foreign secretary said that to respond to threats against Jews around the world, the UK would also impose sanctions on Lebanese Hezbollah’s financing arm, Al-Qard al-Hassan, and reimpose major economic sanctions on Iran in line with the EU and US.

The action marked the beginning of a new approach towards Israel and Palestine, he said, one that not only condemned but took action. “Our argument is not with the people of Israel, with whom the UK has unshakeable bonds. Our argument is with the conduct of its government.”

Burnham wrote that the British Jewish community must not be blamed for the actions of the Israeli government. “[It] is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple,” he said.

“I met with the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.”

The shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said “illegal settlements are wrong” but suggested that Miliband was introducing policies the Foreign Office did not believe would work. Whitehall insiders denied this was the case.

But the veteran Tory MP Edward Leigh gave full backing to the sanctions. “I am proud to say as the longest serving member of the Conservative Friends of Israel that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and justice for all people in this world,” he said.

The move forms part of a broader attempt by Burnham’s government to reset British policy towards Israel, in part to regain the trust among Muslim and progressive voters in the UK they lost in the early days of the conflict.

It was overwhelmingly welcomed by Labour MPs, many of whom have been struggling with the issue in their constituencies, although some sounded a note of caution about the potential impact on local Jewish communities.

Emily Thornberry, the Labour chair of the foreign affairs select committee, said: “At last! I am so very happy to see a British government – a Labour British government – finally doing the right thing and taking a strong stance … no longer a bystander wringing their hands.”

England seek calm end to chaotic Test summer against penitent Pakistan

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 19:00:47 GMT

There are some chilly white-ball games still to come this month and with it the sight of Kevin Pietersen back in England training kit for the first time in 12 years. KP is down with the kids these days, 6/7 memes and the like, and starts a new life as the “specialist mentor” to Harry Brook’s young thrusters.

But the final Test of the summer that starts at Edgbaston on Wednesday does feel like an end of sorts, or at least one last push before a breather for the side that has undergone the more significant recalibration. And that is before we get on to Pakistan and a tour that has descended into a bonfire of players and a phone-snatching investigation into “discipline and conduct”.

None of what has transpired on the English side of the ledger was the plan back in March, save for sitting 2-0 up with one to play in this second home series. Ben Stokes has left the building, while Brendon McCullum has been boxed off into white-ball specialism. And as the Test team await Stephen Fleming’s arrival as head coach, those operating under the rebooted captaincy of Joe Root have been slowly deprogrammed from some of the extremes of the Bazball era.

All of this has taken place in a season where late-night drinking incidents have generated copious headlines and, more relevant to the Test cricket witnessed, the Dukes ball has dominated the bat. Wobble seam has been calling shots and a wicket has fallen every 40 deliveries on average. Not since the 1880s has this figure been lower for a summer in England which, given this has also been the hottest since the days of WG Grace, has been quite something.

It has been a far cry from 12 months ago, certainly, when all five Tests against India went five days, batters loosened their belts, and fast bowlers walked off at stumps with blood in their boots. Instead, Ollie Robinson has breezily nipped out 23 victims at eight runs apiece, while Ben Duckett’s 113 at Trent Bridge remains the only century to have been scored by an England player.

Root was keen to stress this context a day before the toss and not simply because his own average this season sits just under 30 amid a growing pattern of lbw dismissals. The last Test of summer is traditionally when players state their case to make the winter tours and Root was keen to assure his fellow batters that the dominance of the bowlers will be factored in when plans are drawn up for their next assignment in South Africa this December.

While Jacob Bethell will create a logjam in the top seven when he returns to fitness after knee surgery, players such as Emilio Gay, Jordan Cox and Dan Lawrence have instead been encouraged to focus on this week alone, the completion of a 3-0 clean sweep, and to consider the team’s needs at any given moment. “It’s understanding that the game is bigger than you and your individual achievements,” Root said when asked about Gay. “It is what you do collectively that matters.”

Whether a late outbreak of runs occurs on an Edgbaston surface that is brown and light on grass remains to be seen. And there may be more factors at play. This is the first time the ground has hosted a Test in September, while this is the 47th pitch out of 48 that has been prepared this year. The ball has swung during the recent County Championship fixtures also, with the increasingly autumnal overheads potentially more relevant than a tired surface.

As well as a desire for greater adaptability and nuance with the bat, rather than the prescriptive attacking mantra of before, another change from the previous England regime has been the return of the sports psychologist David Young this series. A key part of the setup that won the World Cup in 2019, and still contracted for 50 days a year overall, Young was not required by the Test team under McCullum because the head coach himself was the resident shrink.

England (likely): Emilio Gay, Ben Duckett, Jordan Cox, Joe Root (c), Harry Brook, Dan Lawrence, Jamie Smith (wk), Gus Atkinson, Jofra Archer, Ollie Robinson, Josh Tongue

Pakistan (possible): Azan Awais, Saim Ayub, Shan Masood, Abdullah Shafique, Babar Azam (c), Saud Shakeel, Ghazi Ghori (wk), Mohammad Ali, Razaullah, Ubaid Shah, Mohammad Abbas

Umpires: Chris Gaffaney and Paul Reiffel. Third Umpire: Allahudien Paleker. Fourth Umpire: Russell Warren. Match Referee: Ranjan Madugalle

Although, one wonders whether Pakistan are in greater need of Young’s services given how messy their tour has become this past week: seven players and two coaches have been shown the door, the same number have walked through it in the other direction. Even by Pakistan’s standards, it has been chaos; the kind that makes England’s Ashes calamity last winter look like a minor blip.

In Pakistan’s favour is the fact that the only way is up. And with Root admitting his backroom staff are slightly light on info about the newcomers, there is the element of surprise. For Babar Azam, who notably distanced himself from the mid-tour overhaul and the disciplinary issues that have since emerged, this Test is simply a “golden chance” for the next generation to make their mark.

Among them are Ubaid Shah and Razaullah, two young seamers who should bring a bit more zip in support of Mohammad Abbas, while the opener Saim Ayub offers a part-time spin option that could allow Pakistan to match England’s four‑pronged pace attack. Whether all this is enough to see the home side’s summer of unplanned recalibration finish on a bum note is another matter.

I believe in a two-state solution in the Middle East. That’s why we’re taking action to keep that hope alive

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 19:00:47 GMT

Our sanctions aren’t about the Israeli people, but about the unacceptable policies of the Israeli government, and the suffering they cause Palestinians

In a difficult and dangerous world, a decade on from Brexit, there is a risk that Britain loses the confidence to lead and stand up for its values. I’m not prepared to let that happen. It is more important than ever that Britain stands for something.

We have called for years for a two-state solution in the Middle East, but we must recognise that those words are meaningless unless we back them up with action.

For too long, we have been hesitant to act, fearful of being accused of being anti-Israel. Today we are announcing carefully judged, targeted steps that are not aimed at the Israeli people, but at the unacceptable policies of the current Israeli government.

The suffering of the Palestinian people is a scar on the conscience of the world. Innocent Palestinians, including children, continue to be killed in Gaza. And there is still a humanitarian crisis, with far too little aid getting in.

The scale of destruction is hard to comprehend. More than 70,000 people lie dead – at least 20,000 of them children. Families and communities have been torn apart. Millions displaced. And the population of Gaza is now penned into just one third of the territory.

I know that people across the UK feel very deeply about this issue – and so do I.

Before I became prime minister, I said our country’s response had been too slow and simply not good enough. That’s why I committed to changing the government’s approach.

I will not stand by as the horrific suffering continues to grow and the prospect of a two-state solution – the best hope for peace and stability in the region – comes under attack.

More settlements have been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years. The UN has reported more than 1,500 incidents of settler violence so far this year, aimed at driving out Palestinians. And the situation is growing worse, fast.

The Israeli government has now approved 104 new settlements since it took office in December 2022, and ahead of the October elections in Israel, it is allowing tenders for the construction of the E1 mega settlement to go ahead. This would cut a swathe through the heart of the West Bank – snuffing out the hope of realising a two-state solution. It cannot be allowed to happen.

That’s why we are announcing a new package of tough measures to put pressure on the Israeli government:

First, we will ban the trade in goods with illegal settlements in Palestine.

Second, we have formally changed the view of the British government to say for the first time that the Israeli occupation of Palestinian territory is unlawful – independent of, but in line with, the conclusion of the international court of justice.

And third, we will sanction individuals and companies that support, facilitate or profit from illegal settlements. That includes any businesses or investors that take part in the construction of the E1 settlement.

In addition, we are announcing a new package of desperately needed humanitarian aid to Gaza.

We are taking these steps because it is the right thing to do.

I have condemned the monstrous terrorist attack on Israel on 7 October 2023 in the strongest possible terms – and continue to condemn Hamas. However, it does not justify the Israeli government’s actions in Gaza or the West Bank.

The measures we are taking are about targeting illegal settlements and increasing the pressure on the Israeli government to change course. We are not imposing sanctions on Israel as a whole, which would punish the Israeli people, many of whom disagree with their government’s position.

The Israeli people are not responsible for the actions of their government. And nor is the Jewish community in the UK. Blaming British Jews for the actions of Benjamin Netanyahu’s government is wrong, plain and simple. And it is antisemitism, plain and simple.

I met the representatives of the Jewish community just last week. I know the fear they live with day by day. My government will stop at nothing to ensure they are safe and to stamp out antisemitism in every part of our society.

The measures we are announcing today are about protecting the only solution that could see the Israeli and Palestinian people living side by side in peace and security – something that people up and down the UK desperately want to see. The government I lead will keep working with our partners around the world to keep that hope alive.

Andy Burnham is prime minister of the United Kingdom

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 18:54:02 GMT

Aston Villa were 3-1 up after 43 minutes but were made to sweat for their first win of the season, emerging victorious from an entertaining Champions League opener with Club Brugge. John McGinn, who struck the only goal when Villa belatedly got their season up and running last September against Bologna, opened the scoring before Emi Buendía and a first goal for Nicolas Jackson in claret and blue appeared to put Villa out of sight at half-time.

The Belgian side have become familiar foes since Villa returned to the big time, the glitziest club competition of them all; a freakish Tyrone Mings handball gifted the hosts a penalty, and subsequently victory, in 2024-25 and on this occasion Aaron Wan-Bissaka conceded a second-half penalty to plunge a seesawing contest back into the balance.

“Today was a very important step forward, being resilient when we were struggling,” said Unai Emery. “It is very important to start with three points. Hopefully it gives us confidence for the next matches, in the Premier League this Saturday against Nottingham Forest.”

Emery had been at pains to radiate positivity despite another slow start – Villa picked up their first point of the Premier League season at the weekend and these goals represented their first of the campaign – but he was typically animated on the touchline in Brugge. He was particularly agitated midway through the second half when he felt, not for the first time this season, his substitutes were not ready for action. At Hull last weekend, it was Tammy Abraham and Wan-Bissaka, and a few days earlier Alejandro Garnacho against Arsenal.

This time the culprits were Alysson, Ross Barkley and Lamare Bogarde. “In the dressing room at half-time we were speaking about some players who were tired, [Boubacar] Kamara, Wan-Bissaka,” Villa’s manager said. “I tried to keep [them on for] 15 minutes, but when I asked the players to replace [them] they were talking through the set pieces, sorting individual issues, but I needed quickly their impact on the field, and they did afterwards.”

In the end, it was a blend of old and new faces that got Villa over the line. Zion Suzuki made a couple of fine saves, João Gomes put in a typically tigerish performance and Jackson got the goal an encouraging all-round display deserved. The 19-year-old George Hemmings did not look out of place on his Champions League debut. “The old players need to keep our standards high, to show everybody this is the only way we can achieve the process in our objectives and targets,” Emery said. “I am so happy.”

Pau Torres was the unlikely catalyst for two of Villa’s three first-half goals. McGinn’s opener was a product of the centre-back roaming unchallenged to the edge of the box. Presumably it crossed Torres’s mind to shoot, though just as he was getting giddy, he spread play to McGinn, who guided a superb first-time, left-foot strike into the far corner of Yann Sommer’s goal. In starting on Tuesday night, the Swiss became just the second goalkeeper to represent five clubs in the Champions League, but it was a night to forget for the 37-year-old.

Club Brugge replied when the lively Jan Virgili found a way past Wan-Bissaka – who was making his full Villa debut – and located Hugo Vetlesen in the box, the Norway midfielder sending a crisp finish beyond Suzuki. The hosts were level for less than three minutes, a slick Villa move culminating in Buendía wheeling away in celebration. Jackson’s deft backheel supplied Gomes, who twisted inside the box and then picked out Buendía who did the rest.

Ed Miliband has overturned decades of Foreign Office inertia on illegal Israeli settlements

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 18:34:03 GMT

Foreign secretary ends UK’s feigned helplessness with sanctions and condemnation of ‘ethnic cleansing’

Will UK sanctions have any impact on ‘settler terrorists’?

The indefatigable ability of UK Foreign Office ministers over decades to issue boilerplate statements of concern about the extension of illegal settlements in Israel has long been a matter of ridicule.

Even some of the Conservative ministers who issued them, notably Alan Duncan and Alistair Burt, have agreed. Duncan described the UK stance towards settlements as weak and naive, while Burt wondered at the ability of the Foreign Office to find new forms of diplomatic condemnation that never amounted to any specific action. Margaret Thatcher, often torn as prime minister between her natural sympathy for Israel and her fear of the Gulf states falling under the sway of the Soviet Union, similarly expressed her anger at the settlements.

But in the face of the Israeli disillusionment with a two-state solution – to which the UK had been committed at the UN since 1946, if not before – the UK produced little practical policy to prevent the spread of Israel’s illegal settlements.

The UK-Israel trade agreement prevented preferential tariffs applying to goods coming from territories brought under Israeli administration after June 1967. The business department also advised companies not to trade with the settlements – but many simply ignored the advice or, to secure the preferential tariff, relabelled their goods as from Israel. The then trade minister Chris Bryant told the business select committee in June it was very difficult to be certain of the origin of goods.

At the same time, the legal advice was that the UK regime could place sanctions on entities only if they were linked to settler violence, but could not put a contractor under sanctions simply for working on settlements.

It was this unhappy moral and legal mess that Ed Miliband inherited. As soon as he took office as foreign secretary, he said he refused to be a bystander to further suffering and the destruction of the two-state solution that settlement expansion represented. In this he had the support of the prime minister, Andy Burnham.

Above all, Miliband felt that the UK could not feign powerlessness, and to do so, or pay lip service to action, would prove disastrous to Israel’s own future. He was perhaps the only front-rank Labour politician who could push this argument through at such pace, overturning the inertia and caution built into Foreign Office legal advice.

His Jewish heritage – his mother, Marion Kozak, was a Holocaust survivor who fled to Israel – his life growing up with the Palestinian question and empathy for those subjected to antisemitism put him in a near unimpeachable position to adopt the role of Israel’s critical friend.

The US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, might this week say the Labour government is gripped by Jew-hatred, a charge he laid at Miliband’s door knowing he is Jewish, but Miliband’s riposte is simple. The best route to Israel’s security lay in Palestinian self-determination and the introduction of the two-state solution in its fullest form. To equate Israel only with the current Likud-led government as too many Conservatives have been prone to do, was a category error, he said: “Holding Jewish people responsible for the actions of the Israeli government is antisemitism, plain and simple.”

He is thus the first UK foreign secretary to describe what is happening in the West Bank as ethnic cleansing, and in so doing to in effect to accuse Israel of turning a blind eye to acts that amount to war crimes.

Miliband also ended the two years of delay in responding to the international court of justice advisory opinion in June 2024 that the occupation is unlawful. In what he admitted was an overdue statement of reality, he accepted the ICJ opinion that the occupation, and not just the settlements, were so designated. Accepting the ICJ opinion arguably places stronger obligations on the UK government to not assist the occupation. It may help to explain why the trade ban extends into services such as providing insurance for illegal settlements.

The biggest diplomatic rabbit Miliband pulled from the hat was the agreement of France and Canada to impose similar trade bans. France took the lead last year on recognition of Palestine; this year, it is the turn of the UK to lead on following through on the consequences of that recognition.

Paris appears to have been persuaded by the UK to stop waiting for the EU to reach an agreement on collective action, since it seemed unlikely the opposition in Germany and indifference in parts of the European Commission would end. A group of countries imposing the trade ban together of course makes Israeli reprisals harder, and serves to underline Israel’s isolation.

The perceived weaknesses are obvious.

Miliband still left it to the international courts to determine whether a genocide occurred in Gaza, something that might not be adjudicated for at least five years. There was mounting evidence of ethnic cleansing in Gaza, he said, but again it was for the courts to determine if that was so.

There is no pledge to protect the international court of justice or the international criminal court from the US drive to render them inoperable. As to a UK arms sales ban, an exemption continues for the sale of parts for F35 jet planes to the main US spares pool – all on the basis the F-35 jets “do not materially support the occupation” – the criteria the foreign secretary has set.

Miliband specifically condemned the Boycott, Disinvestment and Sanctions movement because it targets the whole Israeli economy and not just the occupied territories. The secondary legislation required to make sanctions as wide as envisaged may take as long as nine months, contrasting with the speed with which sanctions were enforced against Russia over the annexation of Crimea.

But to focus solely on what is absent is to miss the moment. Duncan, for instance, said: “At last, in the face of state-backed terrorism by illegal settlers, the British government has shown unprecedented moral courage.”

There is a risk of a cascading backlash from the White House – but Trump, trapped in a political labyrinth after he was persuaded to attack Iran, has little reason to come to Benjamin Netanyahu’s aid. Miliband has taken a risk, but after more than 70,000 deaths in Gaza, and the two-state solution on life support, it may be time to dare.

UK air traffic control problem strands hundreds of thousands of passengers

UK airport disruption: what are your rights?

Hundreds of thousands of air passengers had flights delayed or cancelled after another UK air traffic control technical glitch kept planes grounded for hours on Tuesday.

Airlines demanded action after a “technical issue” at the air traffic control services provider Nats caused the third large-scale stoppage in just over three years.

Flight monitoring website Flightradar24 said more than 1,000 flights had been cancelled at UK airports by about 8pm in an incident that started at about 1pm and affected departing flights at many of Britain’s biggest airports, including Heathrow and Gatwick.

Nats said on Tuesday evening that work was continuing to assist airlines and airports recover from the disruption, adding: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.”

By the time Nats said it had identified and implemented a fix to restart its flight processing system almost four hours later, most flights scheduled to depart from the London airports and others were yet to take off. The disruption had spread to include incoming flights to much of southern England.

Cancellations and delays were continuing well into Tuesday evening, and British Airways said disruption would affect operations through Wednesday at least, with passengers offered free rebooking until Friday.

Ryanair said more than 65,000 passengers had been delayed and 50 flights cancelled. The knock-on effects hit flights across Europe, according to easyJet. Eurocontrol said some inbound flights were being held at airports abroad, with disruption likely until the evening.

All London airports, as well as Manchester and Birmingham, were among the most directly affected. Flights to and from other airports around the UK, including Edinburgh and Belfast, were also disrupted.

According to the flight monitoring website FlightRadar24, easyJet had 137 flights cancelled, British Airways 111, KLM 26, Eurowings 22 and Ryanair 21 by 5pm.

Nats initially announced at 1.46pm that it was “investigating a technical issue which is causing some disruption to flight departures”. It later identified the problem in its flight processing system, and announced at 4.40pm that it had implemented a fix.

A spokesperson said the fault was not the same as the ones that caused previous outages and mass disruption in 2023 and 2025.

They said the system was only “starting to recover”.

“We are continuing to work closely with our airline and airport customers on recovery,” they said. “We apologise sincerely for the disruption to people’s journeys today and they should continue to check with their airline.”

The chief executive of Nats, Martin Rolfe, expressed his “huge sympathies to everyone who has been caught up in today’s disruption”.

“We absolutely take responsibility for this,” he told Sky News.

“We never want this sort of thing to happen. I completely understand how frustrating it is for passengers.”

He claims, however, “these things are relatively rare”.

“We resolved it to get back to our systems operating normally,” he added. “But of course, there’s a huge amount of disruption that’s now built up in the system.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, said: “I’m aware of a technical issue impacting flights at airports including Heathrow and Gatwick. Technicians have identified the issue and are fixing it as we speak. I know this will be frustrating for passengers and I’m sorry.

UK to force Apple and Google to block explicit images on children’s smartphones

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 18:25:01 GMT

Lisa Nandy says government will introduce legislation after talks end without breakthrough

Apple and Google will be forced to block explicit images on children’s smartphones by law in the UK after talks failed to produce a breakthrough, the government has said.

The legislation commitment puts ministers on a collision course with two of the biggest players in Silicon Valley, months after the government announced a social media ban for under-16s.

Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media and sport, said the government would start work on an act of parliament to stop under-18s taking, sharing or viewing nude images on their devices.

Talks with Google and Apple, whose operating systems dominate the smartphone market, had not reached agreement as a three-month deadline passed on Tuesday.

Nandy told the House of Commons the tech companies could still reach a deal but it was “almost certain” groundbreaking legislation would be required.

“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from some of the worst harms,” she said. “And to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace that we need it to, while harm is being done now.”

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, said the protections would be “built into the device and switched on by default”, and tech companies will be required to verify an adult user’s age before they are allowed to take, view or send nude images. The government also wants the restrictions to apply to apps used by children, which will require further legislation.

Nandy said: “This will ensure that the whole ecosystem changes, tackling the means by which children are most often abused or groomed in the online world.”

Sources familiar with progress in the talks have said there iwas a desire to reach a deal on both sides but significant hurdles remained including privacy concerns on the tech side.

Jess Phillips, the Labour MP and former safeguarding minister, said the legislation would stop the UK from producing self-generated child sexual abuse material, where children are duped or groomed into sharing explicit images of themselves.

However, she urged the government to ensure the UK was followed by other countries and to make sure that “while we lead the world, we’re not standing alone for too long”.

Hannah Swirsky, head of policy at the Internet Watch Foundation, which monitors the online spread of child sexual abuse material [CSAM], said: “It is deeply disappointing that tech firms have failed to act in full, but we are pleased that the government is now taking decisive legislative action to keep children safe.”

Last year the IWF said a quarter of the images or videos of CSAM it recorded were self-generated, representing more than 140,000 pieces of content over a 12-month period.

One of Keir Starmer’s final acts as prime minister was to give Apple and Google three months to stop under-18s from generating, sending or seeing nude images on their devices, by activating built-in features on the hardware or other technological solutions. Between them, Apple’s iOS and Google’s Android smartphone operating systems dominate the mobile phone market.

The nudity block implies the use of “client-side scanning”, where content is scanned by software on the device before it is encrypted or sent.

“Client-side scanning is the least evil approach,” said Lukasz Olejnik, a visiting senior research fellow in cybersecurity and privacy at Kings College London. “That said, it does put in place an infrastructure to scan content of messages.”

Privacy campaigners have also warned that adults would have to verify their age before switching off any nudity-blocking features. In June, the government said the proposals would “not affect the use of devices owned and used by adults who verify their age”.

Google said it was “pleased to have made progress” in talks with the government and was “fully committed” to working with legislators, experts, app developers and device manufacturers to “keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information”.

An Apple spokesperson said the company was preparing to strengthen its “communication safety” feature, which warns children when they are receiving or sending nude images and videos.

“We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online, and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen communication safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe.”

United Utilities fined nearly £1m after discharging raw sewage along Lancashire coast

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 18:04:11 GMT

United Utilities has been fined nearly £1m after illegally discharging raw sewage along the Lancashire coastline and polluting seaside holiday locations including Blackpool.

The water company pleaded guilty to five environmental permit offences relating to a pollution incident along the Fylde coast in June 2023, and was ordered by Preston magistrates court on Tuesday to pay £964,225 in fines and costs.

Sewage was released from pumping stations at Manchester Square, Anchorsholme and Chatsworth Avenue for more than 35 hours over several days in June 2023, affecting coastal communities in Blackpool, Lytham St Annes, Fleetwood and Cleveleys.

The Environment Agency issued “no bathing” advice for all eight designated bathing waters along the affected coastline. United Utilities’ modelling showed that a sewage plume had reached seven bathing waters and significantly affected water quality. Communities and businesses along the coast were affected significantly by the contamination, according to the Environment Agency. “In Blackpool alone, summer visitor numbers fell by hundreds of thousands compared with the previous year.”

Sewage was reported on beaches and at marine recreational facilities, including Fleetwood baths, while tests indicated the presence of E coli. Three shellfish beds were temporarily closed because of concerns about public health.

The incident began after the part collapse of a final effluent pipe at Fleetwood wastewater treatment works reduced the amount of sewage the site could receive, causing wastewater to back up through the network.

After rainfall, sewage was discharged from the three pumping stations. An Environment Agency investigation found that conditions required under United Utilities’ environmental permits had not been met. The company accepted the incident’s classification in category one, the agency’s most serious level.

Andy Brown, the Environment Agency’s water regulation manager, said: “This was an unacceptable pollution incident which had far-reaching consequences for residents and businesses along the Fylde coast.

“Our investigation found that United Utilities Water Ltd discharged sewage outside the conditions of its environmental permits. The company admitted those breaches, and today’s record fine reflects the seriousness of the offences and the harm caused.”

There were also secret sets from Pulp, Skepta, Haim and more, and acclaimed turns from Doechii, Alanis Morissette and others. But there was controversy around Kneecap’s appearance at the festival, as well as the act that preceded them: Bob Vylan, who led a chant of “death to the IDF”. Then-BBC director general, Tim Davie, said “I deeply regret that such offensive and deplorable behaviour appeared on the BBC,” and the furore led to an internal investigation. Since that previous edition, Eavis’s father, Michael, who founded the festival in 1970, has turned 90. Speaking to the BBC in October, he said: “It’s all been a long story of excitement. That’s probably what’s keeping me going.”He added: “I was always at war with the council and the village and the local magistrates and the police”, as he turned the festival from a gathering on his Somerset dairy farm into arguably the world’s greatest music festival. “And it came good. Which is extraordinary, really. The fight was really what made it work, there’s no doubt about that. It was certainly worth it.”

The 2027 festival takes place between June 23-27. Anyone wanting to buy a ticket must register with the festival by 5pm BST on Friday 25 September. Tickets can be paid for in full or with a £100 deposit, with the rest paid off in the first week of April. Under-13s attend for free.

Yes, cut red tape. But shareholder votes on boardroom pay are not ‘pointless admin’

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 17:57:42 GMT

Nothing good can come of ditching annual investor votes on remuneration reports or encouraging online-only shareholder meetings

The government, like every other one in living memory, is on a mission to reduce red tape for business. The former chancellor Rachel Reeves promised “a blitz on bureaucracy” and “pointless admin” and here comes the business department with a 12-week consultation on “modernising corporate reporting to support long-term economic growth”.

Never mind that cutting energy costs for business would, by an order of magnitude, do more to support growth than any bonfire of red tape ever will. The consultation is still worthwhile: clearing out accumulated clutter, exploring digital options and clarifying reporting “exemptions and exclusions” for small- and medium-sized companies could free up a bit of time for doing more business.

But two ideas in this burden-lifting exercise are terrible because they involve an unacceptable loss of transparency.

One is the idea of dropping annual shareholder votes on companies’ remuneration reports. The supposed justification is that, since a binding vote on a company’s overall remuneration policy would still be required on a three-yearly cycle, there is no point in having an annual advisory-only poll on how the policy has been implemented.

Such a weaselly idea could only have come from those FTSE 100 companies that resent scrutiny of their directors’ mega-bucks pay packages. Too bad: annual votes are a modest (and mostly ineffectual anyway) check on runaway boardroom rewards. Obliging the non-executives on the remuneration committee to justify their decisions to the outside world, in the knowledge the owners will vote, is a bare minimum requirement for retaining a bit of accountability in the system. If the chief executive has to squirm when, say, 30% of shareholders rebel, so be it. By rights, any reform ought to be in the other direction: it would be better to make the annual poll binding.

The government’s other bad proposal is to encourage the trend among quoted companies towards online-only annual shareholder meetings. It’s true that many such meetings struggle to attract attendances in double figures, so the desire to turn the thing into a glorified Teams call is vaguely understandable. But a well-established principle is at stake: even small investors in a listed company should have the right, once a year, to buttonhole the bosses and ask a question in the flesh.

The best solution in a digital age is hybrid meetings – let the shareholders decide if they wish to turn up or dial in. It is hardly an onerous requirement on the company to make a meeting room available. Again, one suspects the dead-hand of corporate affairs departments at work: with honourable exceptions, they don’t like the hassle of dealing with retail investors or campaign groups. Sorry, but that’s life.

One other piece of advice for the department: yes, it’s true that annual reports have grown monstrous in size – running to “98,000 words, longer than JRR Tolkien’s The Hobbit” on average, it complains. And, yes, burdensome reporting requirements explain part of the growth. But it’s also true that companies don’t help themselves by padding out their productions with acres of irrelevant corporate babble.

If, as the consultation says, annual reports are “a document primarily intended for investors and creditors”, make them easy to use. Part of the corporate instinct to write at Tolkien-like length stems, one suspects, is from fear of being accused of leaving anything out. The result, too often, is unreadable guff that doesn’t offer a concise account of the directors’ view of how the company is run and the risks and opportunities it faces.

By all means, reform some of the reporting burdens – there are probably plenty to go at. But don’t undermine the transparency offered by annual votes on pay and annual meetings. And don’t allow companies to use “regulatory requirements” as an excuse for boilerplate communication.

Commons breathes sigh of relief as UK finally takes a moral stance on Israeli settlements

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 17:40:51 GMT

Opposition to Miliband’s announcement of sanctions rings hollow – helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers turning up to debate

Nobody can say they weren’t warned. The Andy Burnham government might have looked like Continuity Keir with more positive vibes for the first six weeks or so, but on Tuesday a new line was drawn. When Burnham said he felt Labour had not done enough on Palestine and Gaza, he had meant it. His decision to impose trade sanctions on illegal settlements in the West Bank was to be his first break with the past.

Some opponents chose to get their retaliation in early, before Ed Miliband had even stood up to make the announcement in the Commons on Tuesday. Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador, declared on Sunday that Ed was guilty of “hating Jews”. Which rather implied he thought Ed hated himself.

Huckabee also wondered when we would get round to sanctioning Russia, China and North Korea. Er … We have, Mike. Try to keep up.

The Israeli president, Isaac Herzog, insisted that “the UK would be on the wrong side of history” if the sanctions were imposed. Presumably that means that doing nothing as Israeli settlers, with the explicit endorsement of the Israeli government, seize land, burn homes and kill children is the right side of history. It’s a strange world we live in.

Itamar Ben-Gvir, the far-right security minister, went completely rogue. His take was that this made “Las Malvinas” Argentinian territory. As though it was the sanctions that were the nail in the coffin for the Falklands. Still, there was some consistency there. The Israel government has never placed much weight on the rights of the Palestinian people to self-determination. So why should they bother to make an exception for the Falkland islanders?

Nor was all the oppo to be found abroad. Kemi Badenoch wrote a piece for the Jewish Chronicle in which she insisted that the government was desperate to win back Islamists and that Jews would no longer be safe in this country. Bizarrely, though, she made no effort to engage with what the Tories proposed to do about the Israeli settlements. Presumably nothing. Just give another nod and a wink to Benjamin Netanyahu as yet more Palestinians are forced off their land. I mean, it’s not as if the diplomatic efforts until now have had much effect.

By contrast, the Commons itself was an oasis of calm. Proof that just occasionally MPs are capable of behaving and arguing as adults. A proper debate with proper arguments, sincerely held. This could have been partly helped by fewer than 10 Tory backbenchers having bothered to turn up – we have to assume most of them don’t care much either way what goes on in the West Bank – but the Labour benches were all but full. For most of them, this was a statement that was long overdue. Though there was little triumphalism to be seen. More like relief. Burnham even showed up to lend support.

Miliband started by addressing his own Jewishness. He had reason to be grateful to Israel for providing a home to some of his relatives and he condemned all forms of antisemitism. But there was a separation to be made between the Israelis and the Israeli government. This was about righting a wrong, not giving in to hatred. And these sanctions would only apply to goods and services provided to or from the illegal settlements. This wasn’t a blanket ban on everything Israeli. It was about taking a moral stance. At no longer being a bystander while a foreign government broke the law. It was time to live our values and fight oppression and suffering. We were not powerless. It was the only way to maintain the dream of a two-state solution. Nor were we alone. France and Canada had also joined other countries in imposing sanctions.

The tone of the debate was immeasurably improved by having Tom Tugendhat reply for the Tories. Had Priti Patel still been the shadow foreign secretary, it would almost certainly have become a lot more bitter. Although Tugendhat was clearly operating with one hand tied behind his back. It wasn’t immediately clear what Tom really thought about the sanctions, but he was under instructions from Kemi to say they were definitely a bad thing and they needed to be opposed. So that’s rather what he had to do.

Tugendhat began with a long list of things with which he agreed in Miliband’s statement. That the settlements were illegal, that crimes had been committed, that Hamas were a terrorist organisation and that a two-state solution was the only workable outcome. You felt that in another world, Tom might have left it at that. But he had a job to do so he came out with a few comebacks. The sanctions wouldn’t work, British security would be compromised and 25% of the UK would die because we would no longer receive Israeli pharmaceuticals.

As with Kemi, Tom couldn’t quite square all this away with his default position of doing nothing. Tugendhat considers himself a man of action. Someone who would much rather be seen to be doing something. Now he was left to endorse the option of continuing to let Netanyahu get away with allegations of literal murder. As if all our allies automatically got a free pass. An annual allowance of dead children. Up to 100 and we promise to look the other way.

Much of the rest of the statement was taken with Labour MPs offering their appreciation to a government that had listened to their concerns. Nor was it just the home crowd. Edward Leigh declared he was the longest-standing member of the Conservative friends of Israel and he was 100% behind Miliband in this. Enough was enough. Kit Malthouse and Desmond Swayne felt much the same. When you have these three on your side, you’ve almost certainly more than made your case.

Oliver Dowden was a little more reticent. Couldn’t we have waited just a little bit longer? Until after the Israeli elections. Then Netanyahu might be out of office and a more moderate government installed in its place. It was hard to know what he was getting at. It’s not as if any Israelis are in much doubt about the nature of their current government. Britain imposing sanctions isn’t going to sway some marginal voters into thinking that maybe they needed more illegal settlements after all. Maybe it was just Oliver’s way of thinking out loud. He’s easily confused after all.

The Guardian view on Britain’s new Middle East policy: an unlawful occupation must carry a price

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 17:35:24 GMT

Ed Miliband has delivered Britain’s toughest indictment of Israeli conduct in Palestinian lands - and rightly says this has economic consequences

Rarely in recent years has the Commons felt like the cockpit of history. On Tuesday it did. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, placed Britain at the head of a 12-country coalition considering economic restrictions on Israel’s illegal settlements, with the UK, France and Canada committing to national trade bans.

The move comes after escalating numbers of attacks by Israeli settlers against Palestinian villages in the West Bank. International opinion seemed to shift decisively after Israel gave the go-ahead for 1,200 homes in the E1 settlement that would cleave the West Bank into two – using illegal settlements to bury Palestinian statehood for good. Mr Miliband added that evidence of war crimes in Gaza was mounting, making the overdue case for Britain to recast its economic and military relationship with Israel.

Mr Miliband, who is Jewish and lost more than 60 relatives at the hands of the Nazis, declared himself to be a friend of Israel. But clearly he thinks friends should talk straight to each other. Mr Miliband has delivered perhaps the toughest official British indictment of Israeli conduct in recent history, declaring that “ethnic cleansing” is taking place in the West Bank and accusing members of Israel’s government of supporting forced displacement.

Probably the most consequential move by Mr Miliband is to formally declare the occupation of the Palestinian territories unlawful, in line with the international court of justice’s 2024 opinion. The import ban logically follows. But private acts will have to change too. British companies could soon have to ask whether they are profiting from – or helping to sustain – an illegal occupation.

To emphasise this point, the foreign secretary also promised to take action against those providing construction, infrastructure and financing services, because a goods-only ban would leave untouched the commercial activity sustaining unlawful settlements. He also committed to target extremist settlers and to refuse to license arms sales that “contribute to the occupation”. By simultaneously sanctioning Iran and Hezbollah, the UK is signalling that it recognises the threats Israel faces while opposing its illegal actions.

No one can accuse Mr Miliband of ducking a fight. His statement will be pored over by the Trump administration, which has supported Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu. Being part of an international coalition will help to shield Britain from US ire. However, Mike Huckabee, the US ambassador to Israel, warned that some US states such as Florida could impose penalties against foreign governments deemed to be boycotting Israel.

Britain’s intervention comes in the midst of an Israeli election campaign. Opinion polls give neither Mr Netanyahu’s far-right coalition nor the opposition a sustained lead. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, a figure expected to be above the fray, absurdly claimed that Mr Miliband was interfering in the elections – as if the campaign itself could excuse ethnic cleansing. Israel closed the UK consulate in Jerusalem as a first response.

Tuesday’s announcement deserves a welcome. Mr Miliband has been characteristically brave. But the test is not what he said, but what he enforces in the weeks and months ahead. He promises a “sanctions regime” to take action against “companies and individuals” aiding settlements. Britain has accepted the principle that it must sever the business ties that uphold an unlawful occupation. The test is whether Mr Miliband can turn that into a comprehensive embargo, rather than a symbolic blacklist.

Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland did not match England’s success in reading and maths, although all four UK nations scored well in science.

Worries about children reading fewer books than in the past should be dispelled to some degree by England’s results, which show no decline in capability since 2022, when the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) last published results. The decision to place more emphasis on science, technology, engineering and maths (Stem), both at primary and secondary levels, has seemingly borne fruit.

Pisa scores do not record everything that schools are doing, and a positive set of results doesn’t mean that all is suddenly right with the system. The focus on Stem was partly at the expense of arts subjects, which were wrongly excluded from the Ebacc suite of favoured GCSE subjects promoted by the Conservatives. This is due to be scrapped by Labour, following the recommendation of Prof Becky Francis’s review. Prof Francis was also right to highlight the demoralising effect of compulsory maths and English GCSE retakes. The education secretary, Lucy Powell, has cited the development of modular replacements as a priority, along with improved technical qualifications, some of which she has suggested could take the form of new GCSEs.

Reform of special educational needs provision, and the laws surrounding it, is arguably the aspect of schools policy that will end up absorbing most ministerial attention. Earlier this week, the Guardian reported on a surge in applications for the education, health and care plans that compel councils to provide a specified level of support to individuals. The government must also find ways to address troublingly wide regional disparities. But concerns about attainment gaps and inequalities, and about the dismayingly high number of pupils who do not thrive at school, should not detract from schools’ striking successes. Many are meeting the demands of a challenging curriculum.

The stagnation and decline in other countries should not be viewed simply as a backdrop for England’s success. Andreas Schleicher, the OECD’s director for education, believes there are weaknesses in how schools adapt to technological change and has questioned whether heavy smartphone use is “compatible with sustained academic attention”. This echoes the concerns of academics who believe that overreliance on screens in schools is undermining learning. While other experts believe that the evidence points to more nuanced conclusions, it seems clear that caution is needed when assessing the role of technology in classrooms as well as in children’s lives in the round.

It would be overly simplistic to blame a poor set of international results on smartphones. After all, English teenagers use them too. But Prof Francis is right that England’s scores suggest there are “important things our education system is getting right”. Her review was aimed at avoiding too much disruption, given the impact on teacher workloads and morale. Further changes should not be rushed into – even by a new education secretary keen to make a mark. England’s schools deserve some praise.

Charley Hull has, unsurprisingly, been involved in a colourful start to Solheim Cup week. In an unusual scene, Hull, who is crucial to Europe’s quest to reclaim the Solheim Cup from the US this week, drove off alone at Bernardus Golf and caught up with her teammates after arriving on the 1st tee minutes behind them. In a clip that gained traction, Hull appeared to jokingly blame “drinks” from the night before. The English golfer did, however, seem to point towards her caddie at the time.

When asked about Hull’s delayed arrival, the European vice-captain Mel Reid, slightly strangely, focused firstly on the online speculation. “It is a completely false story,” said Reid. “Charley Hull was the first one to bed last night at eight o’clock and the first one on the bus this morning. She doesn’t even drink. So that is a completely false story that has been misquoted.

“She was late to the tee because I was responsible for her so I will take a little bit of responsibility for that. She just thought her tee time was a little bit later and trying to drag Charley Hull off the range is a feat in any tournament, especially a Solheim Cup.”

When it was pointed out to Reid that many observers were unaware of the “false story” anyway, she said: “I kind of want to shut this down before people start talking about it. She was late because one, I couldn’t drag her off the range and two, she thought her tee time was five minutes later.”

There is rarely a dull moment around Hull. Her participation in the recent Women’s Open was overshadowed by a prank she played on her caddie. Alongside Lottie Woad, she is one of two members of the world’s top 10 in the European side.

Hull’s individualism is one of her most endearing qualities. Anna Nordqvist, the European captain, denied that was in any way a problem but did concede Hull was given permission to arrive in the Netherlands later than her teammates.

“It has been really nice to see how much Charley has started to embrace the whole Solheim Cup atmosphere,” said Nordqvist. “It is nice to see how excited she is. Trump renames places and poses as superhero in bizarre social media blitz

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 17:12:48 GMT

Trump passed the long weekend posting a torrent of memes and musings on his Truth Social platform

The long weekend may have proved too long for Donald Trump, who passed the time by musing about annexing other countries, unilaterally renaming places he’s not allowed to rename and turning himself into a superhero.

Amid the torrent of memes and posts by the president on his Truth Social platform over the Labor Day holiday weekend was a bizarre AI-generated video depicting Trump as the Green Lantern DC superhero, wielding a glowing green power ring to erect his border wall, illuminate an “American manufacturing” scene, and command a fleet of warplanes and warships behind him.

Trump’s controversial forays into AI-generated images have seen him depict himself as a Christ-like figure, the pope, Atlas from Greek mythology, as Superman, and many others.

Over the weekend he also shared a map with a US flag emblazoned over most of North America and several countries in Central America, as well as Greenland, Iceland and many islands in the Caribbean. Iceland has summoned its US ambassador over the post. Trump also separately claimed the moon.

The president has spent much of his second term taunting Canada repeatedly with the suggestion of making it a 51st US state with “economic force”, and aggressively pushing for the annexation of Greenland, a self-governing Danish territory, which has sparked a major geopolitical row. He has also threatened military action in Mexico, Cuba and Colombia, threatened to seize the Panama Canal, and casually mused about taking over other countries including Micronesia and the Marshall Islands.

Also in the flurry of Labor Day posts was a map of the US state of New Mexico with the word “Mexico” crossed out and replaced with “America”. A few hours later, he posted what seems to be an AI video of him sticking an “America” label over the word “Mexico” on a “Welcome to New Mexico” road sign.

Trump’s suggestion that New Mexico should be renamed to “New America” comes as tense trade negotiations ⁠with Mexico ramp up. It also comes hot on the heels of Trump signing an order directing the federal government to change Lake Ontario’s name to “Lake America” amid his escalating trade war with Canada after negotiations last month failed to produce a deal.

He has also joked about renaming either the Atlantic or Pacific oceans, along with the strait of Hormuz, which has been central to his disastrous war against Iran, to “Trump strait”. He declined to elaborate on that latter idea when asked by a reporter in the Oval Office last week.

In the case of New Mexico, whose name predates the founding of the United States and is explicitly enshrined in its constitution, Trump has no legal authority to rename it – or indeed any US state. Any change to its name would have to come from the state itself and would require a formal constitutional amendment.

While his “Lake America” order directs federal agencies to adopt the name-change on US maps, documents and databases, Trump has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake, nor to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

That level of determination and the qualities he has should put himself in a good spot.”

The rise of hairy young women: ‘I know people who dye their armpit hair, so it stands out more’

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 16:58:06 GMT

When Phoebe Bridgers appeared at Venice international film festival with unshaven legs this weekend, it shouldn’t have made headlines – but did. What do young women make of the current expectations around depilation?

In 2026, female body hair feels as if it should be the least of anyone’s concerns. But although we may think we’ve come a long way since Julia Roberts’ unshaven underarm caused a furore at the 1999 London premiere of Notting Hill, depilation remains a staple of many women’s grooming routines – and when singer turned actor Phoebe Bridgers made her Venice film festival debut last weekend, her unshaven legs still made headlines.

Even so, her au naturel look may signal that attitudes are changing – particularly among younger generations. Vogue decreed that “rather than undermining the femininity of the look, unapologetic hair sharpened it”, and pictures of the 32-year-old’s hair-covered calves were generally praised by fans. But what do other gen Z and millennial women make of the decision to ditch the razor?

“Hell yeah!” is 27-year-old PhD student Anna Busuttil’s response. “I think it’s awesome; cool and rebellious,” she says – a view that chimes with that of most of the women I speak to outside University College London’s Bloomsbury campus. Busuttil says she sees a lot more women nowadays choosing not to remove their body hair. “I know people who dye their armpit hair a certain colour as well, so it stands out even more. I feel like leg hair is more taboo for women; it feels like such a ‘masculine’ thing, and legs are supposed to be a really sexy part of a woman.”

Francesca Hall, 25, agrees: she removes her leg hair, but doesn’t worry about her underarms. Yet she feels that, if anything, it’s becoming less common to go unshaven. “There’s been a general shift, culturally, towards more conservative ideas,” says the student union-worker. “It’s the same with veganism; it’s gone backwards a bit. My friendship group is quite queer, leftwing, and not everyone would remove their leg hair.” But, she says, not removing leg hair is more common “in those circles … I definitely think there’s a correlation there.”

“I’ve got really hairy legs!” says student Phoebe Green, 21, hitching up her long shorts so I can get a better look. “I don’t really pay attention to the trends that are going around; having leg hair doesn’t affect my life in any way,” she says. “I’ve definitely had a few comments, a few condescending dudes being like, ‘why aren’t they shaved?’ But I get a lot of compliments from girls, there’s a lot of solidarity.”

Children’s nurse Venus Whyte, 23, thinks that attitudes are changing among younger generations – albeit slowly. “I think society puts pressure on women to shave when they don’t really want to,” she says. “If I’m wearing something where my legs are showing, I would prefer to shave but that’s just what I feel comfortable doing.”

Not everyone thinks that leg hair remains the most taboo type of female body hair: for 24-year-old Wendi Fei, it’s armpit hair. She will shave hers for the first time ever this week, for her graduation ceremony. “It’s a formal event so I will be wearing a dress,” she explains. “I don’t think women really need to shave – men don’t need to do it – but some women think that it’s not beautiful.”

Bridgers was also at a formal event: she paired her unshaven calves with a Gucci skirt suit at the photocall for her first acting role, in A24’s psychological crime thriller Primetime. Online, Bridgers fans – or “Pharbs” – appeared to approve: “Sorry I actually might cry this is the first time I’ve seen a favourite artist of mine with her leg hair out while wearing feminine clothing like it’s the most normal thing in the world (which it should be!!)” wrote X user @starforthemagic; “wait this is literally so rare for public figures omg …. queen” agreed @yyelyahkwonn.

But for 22-year-old student Matilda Moore, social media can sometimes be part of why women feel required to conform to certain beauty standards. “Women shouldn’t have to worry about removing body hair – it’s down to individual preference,” she says, “but I still see, sadly, on social media, that women can get a lot of backlash for how they present themselves, which I think is unfair.”

Postgrad student Sarah Cender, 26, agrees that while many of her friends would be happy not to remove their body hair, they worry about how they might be seen by their peers. “I don’t think that it matters – but other people might judge you or see you differently,” she says. Laser hair removal has become more common than shaving or waxing among her friendship group: “so you can just get rid of the hair permanently”.

“I have lots of friends who religiously get laser everywhere,” agrees Hannah, a legal and corporate services manager at a trend forecasting company, “but I can’t even be bothered plucking my eyebrows, you know?” The 30-year-old feels that, today, people are more empowered to do what they want when it comes to grooming, especially compared with when she was younger. “I am just pretty lazy, I’ll be honest,” she laughs.

Her thoughts on Bridgers’ look? “Go her! I rate that.”

In Dover and Portsmouth at the weekend, mobs of masked vigilantes in balaclavas acted in an intimidating and racist manner (‘Army of Christian patriots’: how a black-clad vigilante group swarmed Portsmouth, 8 September). Critical infrastructure was blocked, with roads, boats and transport disrupted. Police officers were injured and vehicles damaged. Imagine if this had been a masked pro-Palestine protest or an unauthorised environmental action disturbing the flow of traffic, intimidating the public and injuring police officers. There would have been hundreds of arrests. To be consistent, it’s time to call for extremist racist organisations such as Patriot Platform to be designated as “terrorists”. Or, at the very least, for the government and police to use the many powers they have to take robust action against the participants of this kind of shocking whipping up of hatred that has already led to racist pogroms in many parts of the UK. I was punched in the face. I am due to give evidence in the resulting court case.

The contradiction is hard to miss. A movement that presents migrants and refugees as a threat to women can apparently tolerate intimidation and violence against women who stand in its way.

Blake’s townhouse could be open to all

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 16:49:17 GMT

We were pleased to see your editorial about writers’ houses (18 August), and the response from Richard Clemmow, a trustee of the Blake Cottage Trust (Letters, 25 August). However, we must disagree with Clemmow’s statement that William Blake’s cottage in Felpham, Sussex, is the only one of his residences that could ever open to the public. The other surviving house where Blake lived, 17 South Molton Street in London, is not “disappearing behind new development”, but is at present being carefully restored by its owner, the Grosvenor Estate. With inspired support, the leasehold could be acquired and it could be made into a culturally significant museum.

The William Blake Fellowship has been in negotiations with the Grosvenor Group/Grosvenor Property UK about this project for several years, and has the support of Sadiq Khan, Tate Britain, the V&A, English Heritage and thousands of Blake lovers, artists, poets and musicians who have signed our petitions and our letter to the Duke of Westminster, and sent messages of support. This project is gaining momentum and may even, with luck and vision, also be able to open to the public for the bicentenary of Blake’s death on 12 August next year. Helen Elwes and Stephen MicalefThe William Blake Congregation

Readers respond to George Monbiot’s article on Andy Burnham and political donations

George Monbiot condemns Andy Burnham for his alleged subservience to the interests of the wealthy (Andy Burnham has already made a mistake that will cost him his premiership: he lost his nerve over political donations, 2 September). If true, I agree. But the same could be said of any interest holding sway in our politics. Lobbying groups, activists, unions, thinktanks, people who obsess about this, that or the other. It is surely not OK for our democracy – at local or national level – to have its priorities dictated by those with the shrillest voices, as well as those with the deepest pockets.

Speaking from Scotland, I think that our public realm is a case in point. It seems special interest groups are, to all intents and purposes, the main driver of government policy now. And all too often, said influence is framed by an ideological mission that does not necessarily align with that boring, broad swathe of folks who don’t follow politics closely, and don’t see government as a means to progress personal hobbyhorses or single-issue causes.

The latter are, in their own insidious way, as injurious to democracy as the whispers of the wealthy in the ears of politicians. So too is turning a blind eye to such undue influence because its aims chime with your own beliefs. Leaders of any party must endeavour to serve not some, but all – without fear or favour – including those who didn’t vote for them. Not easy. No guarantee of success. But abandoning that principle makes our politics all the poorer. Colin MontgomeryEdinburgh

I was surprised to see George Monbiot paying feasance to that liberal shibboleth, “the general interest”. If a society is fractured by inequalities of class, race, gender, sexuality, etc, then there can be no “general interest” until these are overcome. Ensuring trade union influence over Labour policy through the continuation of union donations acts as leverage against policy being captured by the likes of Lord Alli and Lord Sainsbury.

When Monbiot goes on to say that “Labour governments know they can safely bash benefit recipients, who aren’t unionised, while they tread very carefully – far too carefully in my view – around the interests of oil workers”, he misses the obvious point that the way, then, to protect benefit claimants is to organise them. Unite, for instance, already has a community membership for students, claimants and pensioners, and has organised days of action against benefit cuts and sanctions. Monbiot’s proposal would not strengthen the power of benefit claimants, it would simply weaken the power of trade unions. Nick MossLondon

George Monbiot is right; Andy Burnham lacks the courage to take on vested interests, and nowhere is this more apparent than over climate breakdown. During an extensive Panorama interview with Laura Kuenssberg, the climate crisis was not mentioned once, despite record temperatures, drought affecting half the country and unprecedented wildfires raging throughout Europe. The cap on bus fares will be financed by abandoning international climate payments; and now Burnham wants to take a “pragmatic” approach to drilling in the North Sea.

Next year we will breach the 1.5C limit stipulated in the Paris agreement, and this will be followed by the disappearance of coral reefs and the eventual disintegration of the Western Antarctic ice sheet – irreversible events that will undermine the marine food chain and raise sea levels by six metres. Andy Burnham’s lukewarm approach won’t look so pragmatic to our descendants when coastal cities worldwide are under water. Dr Robin Russell-JonesFounder, Help Rescue the Planet

Mr T: I Pity the Fool review – a rare chance with an electrifying star … and they blew it

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 16:06:13 GMT

The former A-Team legend tells his extraordinary story with endless charisma, but this show is so rushed that they even misspell his name. No wonder he isn’t happy with it

Here’s a question: when was the last time you had as good a time as when you were watching The A-Team as a child? I know.

Many of the best moments of the wholly unexpected documentary Mr T: I Pity the Fool recall his legendary turn as the soldiers of fortunes’ genius engineer, pugilist and instant fan favourite (not that we used the phrase then) BA Baracus. According to Mr T, the show was built around him; when you see now how well it plays to his talents and charisma – a proper tough guy, but shot through with warmth and humour, giving a perfectly outsize performance and never overplaying his hand – it makes a lot of sense, however much it would annoy George “Hannibal” Peppard to hear it.

Mr T is now 74. I know. He looks a bit older, but the charisma is absolutely intact. He sits alone in a darkened room, occasionally being played old footage of his career’s highlights and lowlights, dressed in a stars-and-stripes boiler suit and bandana. You cannot take your eyes off him.

He has done very few public interviews since his heyday, but the clips they show from that period are electrifying, especially his thrillingly uncompromising one with David Letterman in which he unsmilingly explains his look to the increasingly cowed host. The Mohawk-style haircut and feathered earrings honour his African Mandinka warrior heritage. The gold chains are a transmutation of the shackles his ancestors were put in. He doesn’t get involved in “Black exploitation movies – no dope-dealing movies, no pimp roles … Give me the type of role you’d give Charlton Heston.” The audience laughs, not uneasily, missing and making his point.

At the same time, his rise to fame and riches has an inescapably “only in America” feel to it. He was born Laurence Tureaud (spelled Tero throughout the documentary), one of 12 children to his loving and beloved mother Willa Lee, and brought up in an impoverished housing project in Chicago. He and his brothers worked on their fitness together – by the time he was 15, he already looked like an athlete-cum-bodybuilder.

He renamed himself Mr T “so that the first word out of people’s mouths was always ‘Mister’”, after watching his father and brothers – including a Vietnam veteran – being habitually addressed as “Boy”. When his mother was robbed by local “thugs”, he went looking for them; although the story is left unfinished, it is implied that he carried out some serious physical damage. If so, it was a rare lapse in what seems to have been an otherwise hugely disciplined life.

He worked three manual jobs until bouncing gave way to bodyguarding and an entree into the world of television, which led to him being spotted by Sylvester Stallone and cast as the antagonist Clubber Lang in Rocky III. He turned up word-perfect to the audition – discipline again – met the ad-libbing requirements and worked on the accent the part originally required. The film was a hit – and so was Mr T.

Then came The A-Team, enormous popularity and wealth (Mr T commercials and merch was everywhere), an almost inevitable inflation of ego – and then, in the mid-90s, a cancer diagnosis that, along with his increasing demands, caused his star to wane. Since then, he has become a man of God and finds fulfilment in good works and preaching.

That, at least, is how the documentary tells it. In the accompanying publicity tour, Mr T has made clear that he finds the film dishonest and unfair. He says that he wasn’t forced but chose to step out of the limelight, having fulfilled his ambition to set his mother up in comfort for the rest of her days. As a child, he had promised her a house and pretty dresses. “If that’s the lord’s willing,” she replied.

Other objections include the time given to his former agent Peter Young (whom he says he had to sue and who is the main contributor of claims about Mr T’s diva behaviour and “bad decisions” professionally) compared with his longtime pastor, the Rev Henry Hardy, and the omission of counterweights to the hardman narrative.

It is certainly a small, slight documentary. In a 50-minute runtime, some omissions are to be expected, but even without knowing about its subject’s resulting displeasure, the emphasis on the violent incident reads oddly and the misspelling of his name raises questions about the quality of the research. There is a sense of eagerness with which the picture of Mr T as a monstrous egomaniac is painted. At best, it feels like a rushed job. At worst, it feels like the imposition of another negative narrative on a Black man by fools who are more to be censured than pitied.

Mr T: I Pity the Fool is available on Netflix
