A nostalgia-bait return to the witchy 90s comedy is as strange and messy as the first but there are warm seasonal pleasures to be had

Much has changed in the universe, cosmic and otherwise, since the Owens witches last graced the big screen with their practical magic of sleeping draughts, midnight margaritas and generational love curses. For one, movies like the 1998 cult-ish classic Practical Magic – a compellingly bizarre mashup of genres, aspirational 90s fashion and sisterly affection starring Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman in their movie-star primes as lovelorn sorceresses in Puritan-lite Massachusetts – largely stopped reaching theaters. For another, nostalgia cycles only intensified and tightened, our algorithms clogged with unsolicited sequels and dupes for Bullock’s impeccable vintage 90s Levi’s.

Which makes Practical Magic 2, reuniting both Kidman and Bullock, and Stockard Channing and Dianne Wiest as their lovingly eccentric aunts, somewhat of an anomaly, at once a seeming inevitability and, as a matrilineal romance comedy (though decidedly not a romcom) starring two 60-year-old women, an oddity. There’s no circumventing nostalgia bait, but Practical Magic remains so idiosyncratic in tone and, well, kookiness, that a sequel somewhat appeals.

The new film, directed by Susanne Bier from a script by original co-screenwriter Akiva Goldsman alongside Georgia Pritchett and Kelly Marcel (and again based on a book by Alice Hoffman), doubles down on the distillable ingredients of the original – hairpin tonal turns; strange CGI flourishes; needle drops by Stevie Nicks, that patron saint of witchy white women – though perhaps to a fault. Once again, Bullock’s Sally, the older and more neurotic/sensible of the central sisters, has given up practicing magic, much to the chagrin of Kidman’s looser, airier Gilly. Though she ended the first film believing that she broke the centuries-long curse that every man an Owens woman loved was doomed to die, life offered no such happy endings; her second husband, played in the original by Aidan Quinn, lasted only a few years, prompting her to supernaturally erase any memories of magic from her daughters’ minds, lest they too knowingly love a man to death.

This requires a little magical fudging of the timeline: though the original took place in March 1998– so says Quinn’s investigator Gary Hallet when interviewing Sally for the suspected murder of Gilly’s serial killer ex (it’s kooky!) – new headstones place the events in early 2000s. That’s all the better for Kidman and Bullock, both older now than Channing and Wiest were in the original but with fewer laugh lines, to hover somewhere in the uncanny valley of Hollywood middle age and keep Kylie (Joey King) and Antonia (Maisie Williams), who should be in their mid-30s, in the young 20s heyday of first real love. (Sorry to the recast Evan Rachel Wood and Alexandra Artrip.)

This will prove irksome if you, like me, are timeline-sensitive, but the original’s playful sense of tone, logic and rules in general was admittedly central to its appeal. I find it endearing that the magic in the Practical Magic franchise allows for generational curses, purgatorial spirits and the automatic stirring of coffee cups but not, say, levitating suitcases upstairs, forcing poor Kidman to lug oversized bags through three separate scenes.

So it goes – though Gilly obliquely warns Kylie that “love is our undoing” with “heartbreak feels good in a place like this” camp sincerity (complimentary), Kylie goes on loving anyway. And when her doting college boyfriend Gideon (Xolo Maridueña) ends up cursed in a coma, she, like her mother before her, tearfully rages against the powers that be and, guided by a recently unearthed Book of the Raven, flees to the Owens’ ancestral homeland of England. Sally and Gilly, whose old-pro sparring could sustain a lesser sequel, chase after her, leaving poor Williams and Channing – by far the film’s most luminous screen presence – stranded at the hospital in Boston. A shame, as I would love Aunt Fran’s take on the men they meet abroad, a fascinating dichotomy of masculinity in the hetero-pessimist age: one, an occult professor played by 6ft 5in internet boyfriend Lee Pace, openly pines for Sally, encouraging her to feel her feelings and embrace her power while covered in tattoos; the other, a brooding warlock with a mask of affability (Solly McLeod), craves Kylie’s power, seething with a resonant, almost too pointed sense of aggrieved entitlement.

The plot beats, guiding all the women through said men back to both magic and each other, are characteristically odd and mostly beside the point; if you’re watching the Practical Magic sequel, it is probably to see Kidman and Bullock channel their unique movie-star sorcery – beguiling eccentricity and earthy exasperation, both singularly endearing in their primes – and they conjure it with muscle memory that is fascinating in its own right.

Still, there is some comfort in the Owens’ narrative circularity; in the occult realm, as in the real one, we never truly escape our inheritances nor ourselves, even as times (and men, and hair) change. The overarching, if occasionally overwritten (“no magic is stronger than sisterhood”), theme of feminine solidarity through cyclical adversity is winning enough. The midnight margarita redux may feel obligatory, but there’s just enough magic here to still, despite everything, cast a peculiar spell.

Practical Magic 2 is out in US and Australian cinemas on 10 September and in the UK on 11 September

Matthew Brennan enhanced his status as the standout sprinter at the Vuelta a España by winning a fourth stage on his Grand Tour debut.

The 21-year-old British rider was delivered to the front of the bunch with 100 metres left by an ideal leadout from Wout van Aert, his star teammate at Visma-Lease a Bike who had already won two stages at this race.

Crossing the line, Brennan raised his right hand with four fingers out in a victory salute. Bryan Coquard was second and Vito Braet third. Van Aert was sixth at the end of a 181km ride in blazing heat from Cortegana to Palos de la Frontera.

“It’s unbelievable. Four stages and the plan was for one,” Brennan said. “As a team we’re on six, I’ve lost count.” Of Van Aert’s work setting up the win, Brennan said: “It’s incredible that he can bring you in such a perfect position in such a chaotic race.”

After 16 stages, the overall leader, Enric Mas, retained his advantage in the red jersey of 2min 6sec ahead of Felix Gall. Primoz Roglic is four seconds further back in third.

Wednesday’s stage is another flat ride into Seville before a 32.5km time-trial on Thursday that could be key for Roglic’s hopes. The Vuelta finishes on Sunday in Granada.

British family of man abducted by Saudi Arabia speak out over nine-year ordeal

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 15:45:18 GMT

Mira Lozi says quiet diplomacy has failed to free Rami Naimi who was first seized in Dubai in 2017

A British woman has spoken out for the first time about the alleged abduction, torture and coercion of her husband at the hands of Saudi authorities, after nine years of “failed” quiet diplomacy.

The businessman Rami Naimi was first abducted in Dubai in 2017 on his return from a trip to Australia with his father. After being tortured, he was released the following year.

The father of three, who is the son of Ali Al-Naimi, a former Saudi oil minister and head of the state oil company Aramco, was detained again in 2022 and held for two years. Last year he was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial.

He was initially detained alongside 400 of the kingdom’s most powerful people in an infamous round-up at the the Ritz-Carlton hotel in Riyadh, which became the biggest and most contentious purge in the modern kingdom’s history.

Speaking out for the first time after years of what they described as a failed diplomatic process, his family has alleged abduction, disappearance, torture and coercion at the hands of Saudi authorities.

Naimi now faces a second trial for allegedly following certain accounts on X critical of Saudi Arabia and for attempting to leave the country without permission – both of which he denies.

“The first thing I wanted to do was speak out, but I was told no,” said his wife, Mira Lozi, speaking alongside her son at a campaign launch to bring Naimi home in London on Tuesday.

Lozi, currently fighting cancer, fought back tears as she said she had been encouraged to keep silent since 2017 to help secure his release.

“For nine years my children and I have lived through a nightmare,” she said. “Saying the truth today is like a liberation, enough is enough and we’re just hoping that we can end this nightmare and all the governments will be able to help us.”

Naimi left Saudi Arabia aged 13 and travelled for years between the UK, US and Middle East as a businessman. His family claim he was abducted in Dubai in 2017 after returning home from a book tour trip from Australia with his father.

They say he was blindfolded and forcibly taken by car to Abu Dhabi and then by private jet to Saudi Arabia. He was surprised to find himself with the others who had been rounded up, his family said, as he is not a journalist, activist or politician.

His abduction in 2017 came as the kingdom’s elite were detained at a five-star hotel in Riyadh during a purge in which princes, tycoons and ministers were stripped of their fortunes. Accounts later surfaced detailing torture and coercion, and the event preceded the murder of journalist Jamal Khashoggi, whose assassination at the Saudi consulate in Istanbul in 2018 sparked revulsion around the world.

Naimi was held at the hotel and tortured, electrocuted, waterboarded and psychologically abused for three months, his family said. He was told, falsely, that his father was being tortured next door. He was released in January 2018 after signing a “settlement agreement”.

He was subsequently forced to sign a document pledging to surrender 5bn Saudi riyals, later “discounted” to 1bn riyals (£200m) – which the family says neither he nor they possess. Naimi was placed under electronic surveillance and banned from leaving the kingdom.

His family said he was disappeared again for nearly two years in 2022, and subjected to further torture, and emotional and psychological abuse. They said they had no idea if he was alive or dead, and learned only through the help of his legal team and diplomats that he was being held in Saudi’s notorious Al Ha’ir prison.

It was after his release in March 2025, with an electronic tag and subject to a travel ban, that he learned of charges against him claiming he had “exploited” his father’s official influence. Naimi faced allegations he acted as an agent for a US company in Saudi Arabia and helped Aramco to secure a contract to provide technology to prevent diesel smuggling.

After seven years without charges, Naimi, an EU citizen, was sentenced to six years’ imprisonment after a secret trial. Now he is unable to leave Saudi Arabia and his communications with his family remain monitored. He has no idea, the family said, of their decision to go public with his case.

“Until today we have no idea why Rami was targeted,” said Lozi, who is too frightened to return to Saudi Arabia or travel to the United Arab Emirates.

“It really is something out of a movie. It’s shocking and we just want to end this nightmare,” said his 21-year-old son, Ali, who was 12 when his father was abducted.

In recent years the UK’s relationship with Saudi Arabia has come under scrutiny over the flow of arms between the two countries, Riyadh’s use of public executions and targeting of exiled activists and dissidents.

“Any family making a decision like this needs to be supported by the government,” said human rights lawyer Caoilfhionn Gallagher KC, who is leading the case.

As the family hopes to meet the new prime minister and foreign secretary, Gallagher said the recent appointment of a special envoy for Britons detained overseas did not go as far as campaigners, experts and parliamentarians had called for.

Gallagher described it as: “Tea and sympathy for a very limited group of people.”

Last month the Guardian reported that X had become the latest US social media company to block the accounts of Saudi dissidents so they are no longer visible inside the kingdom, following orders from Saudi authorities.

The UK Foreign Office declined to comment. The Saudi embassy in London has been approached for comment.

Richard Alston’s dance illuminated the music, let you delight in the moment – and stole my heart

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 15:35:53 GMT

The radical British choreographer, who has died aged 77, was as warm and graceful as his astonishing body of work

The first contemporary dance I really loved was made by Richard Alston. In the 1990s, I was going to dance class a few times a week and watching the smattering of companies that would tour to Newcastle, where I grew up. There was dance that was pretty or provocative or intellectually stimulating, which I enjoyed or appreciated, but the dance that really had my heart was by Alston, who has died aged 77.

I was a pianist, too (and later a music student at Sussex University, with its on-campus theatre where Alston toured) and it was Alston’s deeply musical instincts that got me. They were honed in the gramophone library at Eton, where he’d pull out records by Bach and Billie Holiday or surprise the grazing cows with a blast of Wagner. We had different backgrounds, but musical alignments: a love of baroque, late Romanticism, 20th-century modernism.

I saw his work performed by London Contemporary Dance Theatre, Rambert and his own company, formed in 1994. In the late 90s, Alston made two pieces to the music of Brahms, Waltzes in Disorder and A Sudden Exit, the latter set to piano pieces Opus 118 and 119, including some intermezzos that I’d played myself, or at least was trying to master. Alston’s dancers illuminated the music for me in ways I hadn’t heard myself, even though I’d played the pieces hundreds of times. There’s a deliciousness in seeing music you know so well becoming embodied before your eyes: all the neurones in your brain firing like mad in anticipation of what’s coming and the satisfaction of the response, but with the discovery of new layers and ideas thrown in. It’s a physical, visceral experience, and at the same time one where you can dissolve into an exquisite merging of the senses.

Alston also brought out something beautiful in his dancers, especially the men, in particular Martin Lawrance, Jonathan Goddard and Liam Riddick. It wasn’t about flashy virtuosity from the outside, but the ability to adjust the volume and retune frequencies within each step, the effect like the nuanced touch of a pianist, the bow strokes of a violin. His dance, with its clarity of line, lilting curves, elegant poise and sleek flight, wasn’t matchy-matchy with the music, or a visual version of the score. For him, music was an equal partner in creation. He was deeply respectful of the score, once telling me about being intensely irritated after seeing some dancers “frolicking around” to Steve Reich, with no sense of the music’s own history or intention. “You really have to treat music better than that,” he said.

Watching Alston’s work I always felt relaxed, even if the music was fast and flying (in busy baroque counterpoint in 2000’s The Signal of a Shake, say, or his own dance to Reich, 1990’s Roughcut), because of the sense of rigour underpinning the choreography, and the certainty and clarity of Alston’s craft, which allows the viewer to be fully in the moment knowing that everything’s taken care of. Yet although Alston may have come to be seen as safe, tasteful, restrained, he was actually a radical, especially as one of the first intake of contemporary dance students in London in the late 60s, at the forefront of forging this new art form in the UK. And he was also radical in his work and his bold musical choices: composers such as Ligeti, Boulez and Birtwistle – sometimes tricky music which he could make sense of, and give shape and grace.

When I met Richard, he was just as warm and graceful as his dance; a lovely man of thoughtful intelligence, curiosity and enthusiasm. For this would-be dance writer all those decades ago he was an inspiration, and he will be greatly missed.

A constipated baby and a kid that looks like Boris Johnson: why would anyone bother stealing a Renoir?

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 15:33:41 GMT

The chocolate boxiest of all the impressionists has long had his haters – even Manet thought he was rubbish. Little surprise then that the thieves ditched two works on the way out

Stealing from the Louvre you can understand. I mean, who wouldn’t want a Géricault or Leonardo to hang in the downstairs loo? Same for the Musée d’Orsay too, even the Pompidou – they’re French museums absolutely rammed full of stunning art, all just begging to be audaciously heisted. But the Renoir Museum? It’s hard to see why anyone would bother.

As French art fans reel at the news that two Renoir paintings were stolen from the Cagnes-sur-Mer museum that bears his name this week, the rest of the art world has been saying really? Him? Renoir? He’s … awful. It’s like doing a heist of flares in the era of skinny jeans.

Did the thieves know something the rest of us don’t? Or was this just a crime of opportunity, taking advantage of a regional art museum with shonky security?

Pierre-Auguste Renoir was one of impressionism’s head honchos, a leading figure in one of 19th-century art’s most important movements. But time hasn’t been too kind to poor old Pierre. Where his contemporaries like Monet, Cézanne and Degas have been heralded as modernist revolutionaries, artists who shaped the future of western painting and helped set the path that all of their successors would soon follow, in recent years Renoir has been denigrated, mocked, protested and hashtagged.

In 2015, a group who called themselves Renoir Sucks at Painting picketed the Museum of Fine Arts in Boston, and then protested outside the Met in New York, with placards that read “God Hates Renoir” and “ReNOir”, demanding the museums remove his work from display. And they had their sympathisers: the hashtag #RenoirSucksatPainting trended soon after, they sold hundreds of anti-Renoir T-shirts, and their Instagram was full of photos of people giving the finger to Renoir paintings or pretending to vomit in front of them.

And his crime? Kitsch and chintziness. His work is soft focus and gentle, his figures are plump and joyful, it’s all happy haze and night-time revelry. He lacks the hard-edged absolute dedication to angular, prismatic experimentation that made the impressionists so famous. He is the safest of the group, the chocolate boxiest, the easiest, the horniest. And that has made him the most hated.

It’s not a new thing. Even his contemporaries disliked him. Édouard Manet said he had “no talent” and Mary Cassatt described his paintings of women as “the most awful of all”. Add to all of that a hefty dose of antisemitism (he refused to take part in exhibitions that featured Jewish impressionist Camille Pissarro), a big pinch of misogyny, and you’ve got a recipe of aesthetic distaste that can last centuries.

However in PR terms, the timing of this latest in a long string of French art robberies couldn’t be better. The National Gallery is opening their major Renoir and Love exhibition next month, a show they hope will have the same blockbuster success it had at the Musée d’Orsay in Paris this summer.

I want to defend Renoir, if only for the sake of debate, but I’ve hated his work for decades. I like him when he’s weird, when his nudes look like a super-psychedelic, ultra-horny version of Rubens with endless, surreal, undulating rolls of pink flesh. And I like a lot of his hazy, strange landscapes, though not as much as the work of any other impressionist. But for the most part, the haters are right.

I mean look at the works the thieves made off with after cutting through the fence with bolt cutters in the early hours of the morning. The first is Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano, her tiny head dwarfed by shoulders so vastly broad she could play rugby for Saracens, all watched over by a tiny painting-within-a-painting of a constipated looking baby. The other, Jeune Femme au Puits, is an unfinished smudge of a woman pulling a bucket out of a well. An art detective said the thieves would “have no idea what to do” with the paintings, well, they probably have some idea, and it involves the dustbin.

The best bit about this week’s heist on the Côte d’Azur is that the thieves actually took four paintings, but decided to leave two behind as they ran for it, including a portrait of a little boy who looks almost exactly like Boris Johnson. In all my years as an art critic, I’ve never managed a piece of criticism as incisive, cutting and direct as a bunch of criminals looking at a painting that they’d already nicked and thinking “leave it – it’s not worth it”.

Gladys the giant pumpkin: is this the biggest fruit in the world?

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 15:12:21 GMT

At one stage, on its way to becoming a smashing success, this plucky pumpkin was packing on 40lb a day

Name: Gladys.

Age: Gladys was germinated on 19 April and pollinated on 30 June.

Weight: About 544kg (1,200lb).

Quite a big girl then. Gladys is an Atlantic giant pumpkin.

Quite a big pumpkin then. Indeed. About the weight of six or seven average-sized adults.

Appearance: A 4.3-metre (14ft) circumference, spread over 600 sq ft, with hundreds of leaves and an intricate network of secondary vines and roots. It’s also a bit gross, to be honest. To me it looks a bit like … actually, I’m not going to say. Look at the picture, you decide.

Who grew it? Ben White.

The Arsenal right-back? No, the Essex heating engineer. White is also an amateur gardener and “Vegetable Tamer”, according to his Instagram.

How did he do it? He grew Gladys in an 18-metre polytunnel, tending to her lovingly with water and nutrients, and keeping her cool with a fan. “It isn’t just about growing a massive pumpkin. It’s about seeing how far you can push a plant towards its genetic potential,” he posted. He also said he “feels like a father” to her.

Aw, that’s nice. There must be magic involved. “No tricks,” says Ben, who has a decade of big-pumpkin-growing experience and showcased one at the 2021 Chelsea flower show. At Gladys’s peak “she was piling on 40+lbs a night”, he wrote.

Did he call her Gladys because she grows at night, and has pips? I don’t know. Nor do I know if she turns into a carriage at midnight. The point is that she is massive, smashing the original target of 1,000lb.

The biggest ever? You’d think, but actually not even close. Last October, after 50 years of growing bigger and bigger pumpkins, twin brothers Stuart and Ian Paton from Lymington in Hampshire finally broke the world record with one that weighed 1,278kg with a circumference of 6.4 metres.

Surely that’s the biggest vegetable ever? Pumpkins, though treated as veg in the kitchen, are actually fruit if we’re talking horticulturally.

Those pips! Usually referred to as seeds, but yes. If we’re talking strictly veg, I give you a 62.7kg cabbage grown by Scott Robb in Alaska; a 27kg cauliflower grown by Peter Glazebrook in Nottinghamshire; an onion grown by Gareth Griffin in Guernsey that weighed an eye-watering 9kg …

Enough! But they don’t really compare to Gladys, do they? Presumably she’s being fattened up for Halloween? Actually not. White is going to take her to a competition at the Canna UK National Giant Vegetables Championship at the end of this month.

By which time she won’t have beaten the Paton brothers’ world record, will she? No, but White plans to put Gladys on display to raise money for the Essex and Herts Air Ambulance. “It gives the challenge a purpose beyond simply trying to grow an enormous pumpkin,” says White over email. “Last time our giant pumpkins (Gloria & Greta) and the community raised £1,100.”

Do say: “Smashing!”

Don’t say: “But why?!”

America: the gulf, the lake and now the state – what’s next on Trump’s huge renaming spree?

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 13:41:13 GMT

Farewell, New Mexico. The war isn’t going well and nowhere on Earth is safe from the US president’s favourite displacement activity

Busy times for crayon-wielding US president Donald Trump, Earth’s most tireless freelance cartographer, who at the weekend celebrated the US labouring under the highest diesel prices in its history while his “two-week” Iran war edges into its seventh month with a social media spree in which he pushed renaming New Mexico as New America.

In some ways, it was a surprise to see Trump go for merely rebranding a state at this point, given that it was only so recently that he declared: “If you think about it, we have a gulf, and we have a lake. Now all we need is an ocean.” This is believed to be a reference to the Gulf of America, formerly – and indeed currently, in every meaningful sense – the Gulf of Mexico. It was also a nod to Lake America, as precisely no one calls Lake Ontario despite Trump supposedly retitling it by executive order last month, in another fit of pique over his trade war with Canada. Candidates for this heavily trailed American Ocean clearly include the Pacific and the Atlantic – though why the other oceans should be locationally ineligible increasingly feels unclear. At this rate, geography exams in the US are also about to get a whole lot easier.

In the end, you sense, most of the places in the US will go to the chop shop, and either have “America” bolted on the back, or have the Trump name fused on to them as a prefix. See the Donald J Trump and John F Kennedy Memorial Center for the Performing Arts, or the Donald J Trump Institute of Peace in Washington DC. Or, indeed, the President Donald J Trump International Airport in Palm Beach, Florida. A new class of warship may also be procured for naming privileges.

As for potential rebrand candidates/victims, how your area votes clearly affects the order in which its landmarks – or itself in its entirety – will be slapped with a fun new identity. When proposing the New Mexico renaming, Trump casually noted that it was “one of the great vote-cheating states of all time”. I wouldn’t be feeling all that confident if I were the Georgia state capitol, or the Trump America capitol as it may imminently be known.

Meanwhile, it must be said that all this frenetic activity does feel born of Trump’s conviction that it should surely be possible to shitpost his way out of anything, even a war. After all, the Iran war, which I seem to remember was won on day one, has now been going on for more than six months. This feels confusing. First it was going to be two weeks, then four to five weeks. Four days into Operation Epic Fury, Trump explained that the US was “already substantially ahead of our time projections”, while the secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, added: “It could move up, it could move back.” Having said that, evidence suggests it could only move up, although Trump wrapped up his first week of the conflict back in March by assuring the American people that his campaign continued “to totally demolish the enemy far ahead of schedule and at levels that people have never seen before”. Two days after that, the conflict was downgraded to “a short excursion”, with non-committal historical allies dismissed with a triumphant: “We don’t need people that join Wars after we’ve already won!” The war was “complete, pretty much”, he said two days later.

And yet, was it? A couple of weeks in, Trump was explaining he’d know when the war should be over because he’d “feel it in my bones”. Alas, he seems to have failed to get the arthritic signal to pull out as late as three weeks in, despite assuring everyone that – contrary to appearances such as still bombing the shit out of things – the war had in fact been over “in two or three days”. Flash forward to a month in, and they were still “way ahead of schedule”, although once the five-week mark was hit Trump was dropping casual asides like “a whole civilization will die tonight”. Six weeks in, things were going “swimmingly”. Although, not to nitpick, but were they?

That was April. In May, a deal with the Iranians could apparently “happen any day”. By the end of the month, it could have potentially happened “over the weekend”. Same thing a weekend later. A whole two months after that, unfortunately, Trump shifted from the war being over to declaring that his notional/imaginary agreements to end the war were in fact the thing that was “over”. He no longer wished to negotiate with Tehran. Jump ahead to the present day, in fact, and he has spent quite a lot of the past week bombing the shit out of things again. Which is very much the behaviour of any state that won a war back in the first days of March. Unhelpfully, the former US defence secretary Leon Panetta estimated at the weekend that the war would drag on for another six months.

All of which suggests there has really never been a better time to rename New Mexico. Those eternal searchers for a so-called Trump doctrine are surely beginning to see that it essentially boils down to wimping out of the big, painful calls that could literally move the dial – for example, boots on the ground – and existing in an eternally figurative zone where you can simply post the problem away. Here, there is no better way to signal that the war is over than to unilaterally rename the strait of Hormuz either the strait of Trump, or the strait of America. As some psychologists like to say: you have to name it to tame it.

Marina Hyde is a Guardian columnist

State handouts, 10,000 lasers – and Trump’s election: six things we learned from the Elon Musk film

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 13:34:15 GMT

Alex Gibney’s marathon documentary delivers numerous eye-raising insights into the broligarch’s business deals, early idealism and apocalyptic appetite for fathering children

Veteran documentarian Alex Gibney’s film about the richest broligarch on the planet has been one of the most eagerly anticipated films at the Venice film festival this year. The Oscar-winning 72-year-old, who has in previous films taken on the US military, the Catholic church, Vladimir Putin and Scientology, has been investigating the tech tycoon’s ascent and speaking to people in his orbit since late 2022, before his Maga turn and Trump 2.0.

The result clocks in at just under four hours and presents a comprehensive answer to how on earth one man managed to amass so much money and political influence. It is shocking less for any individual new pieces of information Gibney has unearthed than for its totality. Here are six things the film tells us:

Musk is a genius – at tricking the government into giving him assistance

At Maga rallies, Musk has been introduced as “America’s biggest capitalist”, but Gibney reminds us that he’s always been more than happy to go begging to the state for handouts – such as by cosying up to Obama to gain government contracts for SpaceX to launch satellites for Nasa and the military. The film zooms in on a Tesla press event in June 2013, where Musk unveiled a new “battery swap” system that promised to remove and replace the drained battery pack of a Model S with a fully charged one in just 90 seconds. As it turns out, the technology was never rolled out, and interviewees tell Gibney that a demonstration site at Harris Ranch was barely used for the process. Instead, the film-maker suggests that Musk’s over-promise allowed Tesla to get more ZEV credits from the Californian government, which are awarded to electric car makers based on range and which Musk could then sell to more polluting manufacturers.

In spite of everything, there was something admirable about Musk once

Gibney’s film serves as a reminder that Musk has never been in possession of charm or charisma – the petulant perma-poster retweeting praise is not far from the self-regarding twentysomething start-up bro. But what he did with the funds he earned from selling shares of his first software companies, Zip2, X. com and PayPal, was unusual, Gibney concedes. Where others turned to venture capital, Musk turned to engineering. It’s partially an act, we learn from his ex-wife Justine when she recalls how self-consciously he picked his wardrobe, telling her “I can’t look cool or hip, because I need to look like an engineer”. But in footage of Musk biting his nails with fellow engineers during SpaceX rocket launches his enthusiasm and emotional investment is genuine, and at times infectious.

Musk’s procreation drive is motivated by a fear of civilisational breakdown

Musk has 14 publicly known children, and sources tell Gibney that there are probably more. Some of them were conceived in romantic relationships but more recently the circumstances of their birth seem to have been entirely transactional, via sperm donations to employees of his companies. In a text message to one of his ex-partners, influencer Ashley St Clair, Musk said his desire to have “a legion of children” was driven by a fear of “civil war”. The documentary mostly places the roots of that fear in his South African childhood (in one scene, his father Errol Musk talks with no visible remorse of shooting three intruders in their home). “It’s no doubt he had a traumatic childhood,” Gibney said at a press conference in Venice. “He’s now playing out the trauma on the rest of us.” But, oddly for a man who was long a prominent atheist, the film also hints at a religious dimension to his vision of the apocalypse. The sordid business of negotiating disbursements and NDAs with the mothers of Musk’s children are handled by his right-hand man Jared Birchall, a devout Mormon whom St Clair calls his “henchman” and “demon”.

To Musk, empathy is good in principle but not in action

Recently, Musk has held forth at length about his view that “suicidal empathy” – people who have more empathy for criminals than the victims of criminals, in his view – is behind the decline of western civilisation. Empathy isn’t bad, he says in the doc, it’s just that it’s become too shallow. But interviews in the film raise the question of whether Musk is capable of empathy at all. This is a man who tells his wife that “if you were my employee, I would fire you”, and urges her to tell his estranged trans-daughter Jenna that “I’ll always love her” – and then cuts off her health insurance the next day.

Musk knew with a disconcerting degree of certainty that Trump would re-elected

In the film, St Clair describes the events of Trump’s election in November 2024. Musk, she tells Gibney, had a “degree of certainty” about the results before they came in that “I had never seen before”. He told her that he would “unleash the anomaly in the matrix” and that “we have 10,000 lasers in space”. Gibney leaves that comment hanging.

The godfather of AI is worried Musk might rig the next election

Geoffrey Hinton, the Nobel-winning British-Canadian computer scientist known as the “godfather of AI”, used to be friendly with Musk, but the pair fell out after Hinton declined his offer to join the xAI board. In the film, he makes clear that he does not trust Musk to weigh up the risks and benefits of AI responsibly, and there’s more. “It’s fairly clear to me that Trump is hell-bent on corrupting the midterm elections,” Hinton says onscreen. “If you wanted to corrupt those midterm elections and you wanted to use AI, all you needed to do was get detailed information on US citizens. And what Doge did looked like just what you would do.”

Trump’s approval rating is plummeting – as his fortune grows and grows

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 13:12:18 GMT

The US president says criticising his soaring investment portfolio is ‘very unfair’. Tell that to the millions of Americans struggling with the cost of living

If I had a dollar for every time Donald Trump said something inane, I would be a very rich woman. But even with an income that steady, I could never hope to be as flush as the president. A Forbes calculation from March puts his net worth at about $6.5bn – and it’s growing rapidly. Trump made $2.2bn in 2025 via business interests that ranged from selling cryptocurrency and Trump Bibles to offering early access to his (often market-moving) Truth Social posts.

To be fair, Trump isn’t making all this money just so he can buy golf clubs and gold toilets. No, he’s amassing these billions for the good of the little people; it’s altruism, not avarice! “I do this for our Country, not myself,” the president wrote on Truth Social on Sunday night alongside an AI-generated picture of him trading Intel stock. “I’ve made Hundreds of Billions of Dollars on Stocks, and many other type Holdings, for the U. S. A., not myself, and all I do is get criticized by the Radical Left Dumocrats. Very unfair, but what can you do!”

Oh, I have some ideas about what you can do, Mr President. Unfortunately, I can’t print most of them. I also can’t explain why Trump said he’s made hundreds of billions, apart from pointing to his propensity for exaggeration. It seems his post was referring to the fact that the US government took a 9.9% stake in Intel last year. That stake was worth $8.9bn at the time and as of Friday is worth nearly five times as much.

According to the Trump administration, this is a win for everyone. In May, the White House released a statement calling Intel’s surging stock price “a direct windfall for American taxpayers”. Weirdly, I seem to have missed my portion of that windfall. Intel’s stock price has had little impact on my life. What is having an impact is the soaring cost of necessities such as electricity and groceries.

But I shouldn’t be grumpy, should I? I should be grateful that our intrepid president is balancing the demands of the day job with stock trading for the good of the country. According to Trump’s latest government disclosure, he made more than 1,000 equity trades in June. And his picks are doing very well: a report published in August by Democrats on Congress’s joint economic committee argued that Trump’s holdings in oil and gas stocks had risen by nearly $16m because of the war with Iran. “Experts on government ethics have flagged how rare it is for presidents to hold and trade stocks in individual companies, especially since Trump’s war in Iran and his other favors to the oil industry have all pushed up the value of Big Oil stocks,” the report read.

Trump’s shamelessness may be rare, but he isn’t the only politician with serious conflicts of interest issues apropos stock market dealings. A 2022 New York Times investigation found that, from 2019 to 2021, 97 lawmakers or their family members traded financial assets in industries that could be affected by their legislative committee work. In 2020, for example, the wife of the now retired Democratic congressman Alan Lowenthal sold her Boeing shares a day before a House committee on which Lowenthal sat released a damning report about the company. Lowenthal told the Times that he was not involved in this trade at all, so I imagine it was just a funny coincidence.

Still, these sorts of funny coincidences don’t do much to build up trust in the US government, do they? A majority of Americans support commonsense legislation to stop lawmakers and their family members from trading individual stocks. After a lot of resistance, a bill to this effect is winding its way through Congress. The bill does not affect the president or the vice-president, however.

Money can’t buy you everything, of course: while the president’s stock portfolio is rising, his personal stock is plummeting. According to an FT poll this week, Trump’s approval rating has hit a record low, with only 33% of registered voters saying they approve of his performance.

But don’t take that as a sign that the US is coming to its senses or that Republicans are cognisant that dear leader’s war is bleeding the country dry: the same poll found that 72% of Republicans still approve of the president. That figure is down from 82% in May, but it’s still an awful lot of people. Either these Trump loyalists are bigoted fools or they are getting the Intel windfall checks that I’m missing.

Anti-AfD protests sweep Germany as far right closes in on two more states

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 12:54:24 GMT

Alarm that Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania may fall next after party’s Saxony-Anhalt election victory

‘It breaks my heart’: victory sparks dismay

Europe live – latest updates

Thousands of Germans have staged protests against the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) after the party’s watershed victory in a state election, warning it posed a danger in two more polls this month.

Demonstrators at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate held a peaceful pro-democracy rally denouncing the anti-immigrant, pro-Russian AfD, which has called for mass deportations of asylum seekers and a rollback of state support for renewable energy and public broadcasting.

The party captured its best-ever state result in the former communist eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt on Sunday, with clear momentum heading into regional elections in the capital and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, on the Baltic coast, on 20 September.

Police reported 5,000 protesters, while organisers said they drew more than 14,000 people in a campaign to mobilise voters against the AfD. Posters in the crowd read: “Fascism is no alternative”, “Stop the Nazi AfD: end racism and cuts to social services” and “History has its eyes on us”.

With less than two weeks to election day, demonstrators at the Berlin rally cautioned against resignation and cynicism after Sunday’s shock result.

The AfD’s nearly 44% vote in Saxony-Anhalt, the best for a nativist party since the Nazi period, is a “disgrace that makes you furious and stunned”, Jens-Christian Wagner, the director of the memorial at the former Nazi concentration camp Buchenwald, said from the stage.

Wagner sounded the alarm that the AfD, although it fell just short of an absolute majority, was on the brink of taking power in Saxony-Anhalt, a first for the far right since the second world war. That “should not be accepted in silence”, he said.

Max Schneller, 17, a member of the far-left Linke, from Saxony-Anhalt, said activists in the state would fight any attempts by an AfD government to target minorities. “We will not start categorising our neighbours according to their origin, religion or skin colour – we are too humane to hate,” he said to loud applause.

The AfD is three votes short of the support necessary to form a government under its candidate, the media-savvy firebrand Ulrich Siegmund, who hopes to peel off dissenters from the remaining parties willing to play kingmaker.

Germany’s domestic intelligence agency has since 2023 listed the state chapter of the party as rightwing extremist, saying it poses a threat to democratic norms.

Hundreds of anti-AfD protesters also gathered in Potsdam, near Berlin, with rallies also organised in Münster, Göttingen, Dresden, Aachen, Bamberg, Darmstadt, and Halberstadt, in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD captured nearly half the votes, local media reported.

In Halle, the region’s second largest city, leftist groups and civil society organisations have been staging a protest camp since election day.

The AfD is leading in voter intent polls in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, with about 35%. However, the centre-left Social Democratic party (SPD) of the state premier, Manuela Schwesig, mounted a remarkable comeback over the summer and is now scoring above 30%.

In Berlin, one of Germany’s 16 federal states, the picture is more mixed, with several parties jockeying for first place. It is governed by a coalition of conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) and the SPD.

The CDU, the party of chancellor Friedrich Merz, whose record unpopularity is reported to have weighed heavily with voters in Saxony-Anhalt, holds a wafer-thin lead in the capital, with about 20%.

Hot on its heels is the Linke, which has focused on soaring housing costs in its campaign, and the AfD, followed by the SPD and the ecologist Greens, both polling in the mid-teens.

Merz has vowed to stay in office and fight for a signature package of painful reforms, arguing the only way to defeat the AfD is to get Europe’s top economy moving again and repair its creaking social welfare system.

However, the SPD, his junior coalition partner, has indicated its willingness to backtrack on some of the most unpopular measures to shore up support for the embattled government.

Analysts say the dispute could further destabilise the shaky coalition.

Here in Liverpool, buses are back under public control – and that’s great for the only people who really matter

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 12:48:35 GMT

For decades we were told that privatisation would deliver better services. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story

Steve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city region

One of the best-known scenes from the TV series The Inbetweeners is the four angst-ridden teenage characters shouting abuse at people queueing at a bus stop. Only losers take the bus, is the point – except they use a much ruder word. There’s also a statement, misattributed to Margaret Thatcher, that any man over the age of 26 using a bus was a loser. This idea is deeply ingrained.

But when I was an MP it became obvious that there wasn’t the same stigma attached to jumping on the bus in London as there often was in other big cities. It often wound me up that the rest of the country was expected to accept a suboptimal public transport system – so much so that it could be joked that only losers would use it – while London retained its excellent bus service, which it ran under public control.

And I remember thinking: why can’t we have something like this at home in Liverpool? Well, last weekend Liverpool city region combined authority began to roll back the Thatcherite belief that private was all good, while public was all bad. For the first time in four decades, buses in the Liverpool city region have begun to be brought back under public control, starting in St Helens in Merseyside before spreading across the rest of the region.

What does this mean? Instead of private operators deciding where and when buses run, we will set the routes, fares and standards. Our franchised buses will still be operated by third parties. But we will set the rules, decide what kind of network our communities need and hold operators accountable for delivering it. It is the biggest change to public transport in our region for generations. Nobody standing at a bus stop at six in the morning cares about the finer points of franchising legislation. But they do care whether the bus turns up; whether they can get to work on time, get their kids to school or college, or make it to a hospital appointment.

Public control means we can start putting passengers first, with more frequent services, more evening and weekend buses, better connections to hospitals and railway stations and simpler fares. And we have kept single bus fares capped at £2, the price they have been for the past four years.

Change will be immediate. A new express service now connects St Helens directly with Liverpool John Lennon airport. For a family heading on holiday, that may mean avoiding airport parking charges. For somebody looking to work at the airport, it could open up a job. These changes will make a massive difference to people’s lives.

And, for me, that gets to the heart of the argument for public control. A bus route that helps somebody take a job, gets a student to college or allows an older person to remain independent has a value that won’t always show up on an operator’s balance sheet. Markets have their place. But public control allows us to ask not simply, “does this route make money?” but “do our people need it?”

That principle doesn’t stop with buses. We have bought a £500m fleet of new trains and are working towards bringing Merseyrail services into public ownership in 2028. In the coming weeks, the Royal Daffodil – our first new ferry ’cross the Mersey in 60 years, built by a loyal local workforce – will make its maiden voyage.

For decades we were told that privatisation and deregulation would inevitably deliver better services and that the government’s job was to get out of the way. The experience of millions of passengers tells a different story.

When he was mayor of Greater Manchester, Andy Burnham and I spent years working together to make that case and show what can be achieved when local leaders have the power to shape the services their communities rely on. Now we have a Labour government bringing our railways back into public ownership and giving local leaders more power over the essentials that ordinary people depend on.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

After decades in which the state steadily retreated from people’s lives, we have an opportunity to prove that active government can be a force for good again. That is what started in St Helens last weekend.

I want the Liverpool city region to have the best public transport system in the country. I want people to come here, get on one of our buses, trains or ferries, see what we have built and go home asking the same question I used to ask in London: why can’t we have this at home?

Steve Rotheram is mayor of the Liverpool city region

Monty Don is quitting Gardeners’ World – and you’re right to be devastated about it

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 12:37:53 GMT

Handsome, charming and vulnerable, the host made horticulture TV hotter than ever. What a huge hole he will leave

After 23 years at the helm, Monty Don has announced that he is leaving Gardeners’ World at the end of the series. All said, you are right to be distraught about it.

Gardeners’ World is a show with a long history – it was commissioned by David Attenborough as a way to showcase the potential of colour television – but Don arguably did the show better than anyone. Under his watch, the show and the host managed to mesh perfectly. He became it and it became him.

Don’s strength was that he approached the show as a self-taught gardener. This meant that it suddenly became more welcoming to newcomers and outsiders who had possibly been a little intimidated by the show.

This was a masterstroke. Previously, watching an episode could be like trying to download a horticulture encyclopedia all in one go, but Don – who always primarily viewed himself as a writer – was able to talk about gardening in more emotional and philosophical terms. Under him, the “why” of gardening became more important than the “how”.

Nevertheless, it took a while for him to bed in. After a minor stroke took him out of action after five years in the job, he returned having made the decision to present from his own home, Longmeadow in Herefordshire. This changed everything. It meant that, instead of seeing gardening happen in the abstract, we watched it happen to him. Over the years, audiences saw Longmeadow develop season after season. Sometimes the garden flourished. Sometimes it failed. But whatever happened, it strengthened the bond between viewer and host immeasurably.

A lot of this is down to Don’s presence as a host. Much has been made about how handsome and charming he is – when I met him last year, during the recording of an AI Michael Parkinson podcast that bewildered us both, there was no denying that he was either – but as he grew older, it was Don’s vulnerability that appealed the most. He became more used to silence, and was unafraid to express his uncertainties. Under his watch, Gardeners’ World became a programme about patience and resilience. Little wonder it surged in popularity during the pandemic.

Needless to say, talk will soon turn to Don’s successor. This is a role that needs to be chosen carefully, because this is a job for as much of your life as you are willing to give it. Although some presenters have enjoyed shorter stints – the original host Ken Burras lasted one year, while Arthur Billett managed three in the 1970s – Gardeners’ World is a programme that is at its best when it is given the space to unfurl according to the sensibilities of the person in charge.

Nobody typifies this more than Don, who took a show that had subtly increased in pitch and frequency under Alan Titchmarsh and went about making it earthier and ever so slightly more romantic. Before Titchmarsh, of course, the show had been in the hands of Geoff Hamilton, who lasted almost as long as Don did.

Fortunately, Gardeners’ World isn’t Top Gear. The BBC will be keenly aware that the last thing it should do is hand the programme over to someone big and starry, who’ll get bored and drift away after a few months.

The better bet is to recruit from within. Adam Frost has already presented episodes by himself, and is now in the middle of creating a garden from a blank canvas on the show. Then there’s Frances Tophill, who could approach from a more explicitly conservation-based approach. There is also Jamie Butterworth, who last year got called “the Jamie Oliver of gardening” and “Monty Don’s protege” in the space of a single headline. All would be worthy replacements.

But that is all to come. For now, it is time to herald Don, and the hole he leaves. The good news is that in no way did Don’s announcement signal a full-blown retirement. “There are more books to write, more programmes to make,” he said.

This is heartening news. Outside Gardeners’ World, Don has made some fine gardening travelogues – taking him to Italy, Spain, Japan and the US, among others – which fits, since he got his TV break in the 1990s on holiday programmes. More of these would be most welcome, as would anything else he chooses to do, quite frankly. He remains the best to ever do it.

Musk review – epic study of the world’s richest and most banal man

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 12:32:58 GMT

Venice film festival: Alex Gibney interviews former colleagues, wives, the trillionaire’s father and a CG avatar in this absorbing documentary

‘Elon is a nuke.” The speaker is Ashley St Clair, a former conservative Maga influencer and one of Elon Musk’s former girlfriends-slash-baby mommas.

She is a fascinating expert witness in Alex Gibney’s four-hour epic study of the world’s richest and dullest man: the overgrown brattish South-African-born trillionaire plutocrat, ersatz visionary and Trump courtier who owns Tesla cars, SpaceX rocket ships, Starlink satellites on which nation states’ military capabilities are increasingly reliant, X (formerly Twitter) which shapes the collective “incel” id of billions and GrokAI whose vast server farms daily guzzle oceans of precious water.

As head of Trump’s incompetent cost-cutting Doge (Department of Government Efficiency) unit, Musk actually increased the US deficit by sacking thousands of revenue officers whose job was to rake in tax – while reportedly accessing and improperly sharing Americans’ sensitive social security data.

He does indeed look like a nuke, efficiently designed, destructive, seemingly unguided and uncontrolled.

Gibney’s excellent film covers a lot of ground in its extraordinary story, although we don’t get to hear about the mysterious process that changed a balding youngster into a follicularly unchallenged mature man.

Musk is a uniquely disquieting baseball-capped figure, grinning and giggling and smirking on a thousand sycophantic podcasts like a modern, hyper-evolved version of Anthony Trollope’s wealthy charlatan Augustus Melmotte in The Way We Live Now. But given Musk’s boyish love of space travel and sci-fi, Gibney wittily compares him to the hero of the 1936 film version of HG Wells’s The Man Who Could Work Miracles about godlike space aliens who capriciously confer supernatural powers on a banal, ordinary earthling.

Gibney doesn’t get to talk to Musk (or Trump) though in the spirit of Musk’s AI interests, he creates a photorealistic CG avatar who mouths all the things the man himself is reported as saying (a rather contrived visual joke, actually, which the film didn’t need). He speaks to many professional colleagues, and to Musk’s formidably opinionated father Errol Musk who fills us in on Elon’s formative years in the tense world of South Africa in which young Musk was bullied and beaten up.

Gibney speaks to Musk’s first wife Justine Musk (née Wilson), a passionate and intelligent woman who tells us about the tragedy of one of their infant children dying of Sids and then the hurt she felt when Elon felt the need to grandstand about this on social media, claiming the child had died in his arms (it was her arms, she says). And given that heart-wrenching death, how crass it was for him to announce later on social media that his trans daughter had “died” of “woke mind virus”. Much later, Musk showed a creepy enthusiasm for procreating many children with various women; Musk reportedly built compounds for his extended families like something from The Handmaid’s Tale.

Back in the 90s as a pushy, bright young tech innovator, Musk had started out by inventing and selling an online Yellow Pages-type site, got involved in Peter Thiel’s PayPal and cleaned up again when this was sold to eBay. He got involved in the electric automobile industry, giving us Teslas, while misleading the public about their range.

His SpaceX adventure and his preposterous and ignorant effusions about colonising Mars were spectacular advertisements for his personal brand – so important for inflating stock market valuation – especially when he did indeed invent rockets that could be landed and re-used. But the question of how and when these rockets will carry us to inhabitable planets remains unanswered. Both his cars and his rocket ships got him on the receiving end of millions of dollars of federal money and lines of credit.

And at the beginning of the 21st century he was still the darling of the liberal world and the Obama administration for an apparently compelling eco-vision for non-fossil-fuel cars.

All this changed when Joe Biden seemed to be casting a cold eye on Musk’s businesses, and Musk went all in on promoting Trump 2.0 in 2024 and was rewarded with that grotesque Doge sinecure, damaging American public finances – from which he had benefited so lavishly.

What is so absorbing about Gibney’s documentary is that it has the structure and rhetoric of a film that could be about, say, Elizabeth Holmes, disgraced inventor of the phoney blood-test, or Sam Bankman-Fried, the cryptocurrency fraudster, or Billy McFarland, promoter of the Fyre festival. All of these were media darlings in their day, supposed visionaries and feted disrupters, talking the talk in front of saucer-eyed believers.

Unlike these illusionists Musk does have actual palpable success, with Tesla being a long-standing profitable company and Space X, among other things inventing successful re-usable rockets, allied with a skill they don’t have in moving on from commodity to commodity, while controlling the means of production in social media and cultivating the presidency. Just as well because, if Musk were ever to fall, it would truly send shock waves through Wall Street, Washington and Silicon Valley.

How meteorologists recreated weather that helped decide second world war

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 11:59:58 GMT

Experts helped guide weather scenes in Pressure – a film depicting dramatic buildup to 1944’s D-day landings

Dressed in a Royal Air Force uniform and sporting a trim moustache, Andrew Scott looks slightly queasy – as well he might. Behind him is a huge map of the Channel, and in front of him is Brendan Fraser, looming with a request: “I need a forecast,” he says.

Starring in the film Pressure, based on a true story, Scott plays the meteorologist Gp Capt James Stagg – the man who must tell Gen Eisenhower – played by Fraser – whether conditions will be suitable for the D-day landings scheduled to take place on 5 June 1944. But a large storm is approaching the Normandy coast.

The film, showing in cinemas in the UK and Ireland from 9 September, unites two topics that ceaselessly fascinate the British: the second world war – and weather.

It is also a rare treat for meteorologists, who are not hugely represented on the big screen and are delighted to be portrayed as the heroes of a film.

Dr Stephen Burt of the University of Reading, an adviser for the film, said the challenge Stagg and his colleagues faced was enormous. “To do a forecast beyond 24 hours was, in the 1940s, like trying to land a man on the moon,” he said.

Scientists had only recently started to use upper air data to predict the weather, he said, and largely relied on surface measurements of pressure, temperature, dew point, wind speed and direction, and experience-based intuition.

One difficulty is that most of our weather comes in from the Atlantic. “Nowadays we have satellites and so on and we can see what’s coming, we have observations coming from the US,” he said. “But then there were … just a couple of ships, a couple of submarines maybe and some aircraft observations. And that’s it.”

Crucially, the week before D-day was the hottest May week on record, Burt said – a high that was only broken this year. Then a huge storm blew up, with another close behind.

Prof Ed Hawkins of the University of Reading, an expert in historical weather data collection and examination, including D-day, explains that there were three teams working on the D-day forecasts – although only two are depicted in the film – all feeding into Stagg. But they took different approaches and produced different forecasts.

It was up to Stagg to reconcile the results and present a recommendation to Eisenhower that would, ultimately, affect 160,000 Allied troops. “Stagg was in a very difficult position. He left his very pregnant wife to come and do this very important task,” Hawkins said.

The teams were split about the forecast for 5 June – with Stagg concluding the conditions would be too perilous. The landings were postponed. But by the evening of 4 June a consensus emerged: there appeared to be a small but suitable window on 6 June. The invasion was back on.

“They managed to do the forecast, and the invasion, and get away with it,” said Burt.

Burt and his colleagues agree that even modern systems based on artificial intelligence have struggled to accurately predict conditions for 6 June 1944 using data available from the time.

“[I’d] still have been chewing my fingernails on morning of the sixth,” said Burt.

Catherine Ross, a Met Office archivist, said film-makers used exact replicas of records from June 1944. “We were able to provide images of every single weather chart that was being produced at the time. We had codes and examples of how the observations were sent in and all sorts of documentation,” she said.

She notes that even before modern technology, allied forecasters were on the front foot in terms of access to data. They already had data from the UK and across the Atlantic. “But because of Bletchley Park they had broken the Enigma code, so they had access to all of the German weather observations as well,” Ross said.

While the German forces may have been aware of the storms, they were not aware of a potential break in the weather. “Sometimes there’s no Atlantic on the [German] chart, which is where the weather was coming from in early June 1944,” she added.

It is no spoiler that D-day was a success for the British, but the film sheds new light on the drama that unfolded behind the scenes.

“It’s the most famous forecast ever made by the Met Office. It’s probably one of the most important weather forecasts in history,” said Ross.

This article was amended on 8 September 2026. The military rank given to James Stagg was that of group captain (Gp Capt), not captain as an earlier version said.

I went to Ikea with my son – and was confronted with my parenting failures

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 10:00:00 GMT

The pre-university shop is the moment you find out how much domestic wisdom you’ve managed to impart. In my case, none

I have yet again found my ultimate tribe in a high-street shop, this time Ikea. As far as the eye could see, there were middle-aged women trying to choose kitchen essentials for their late-teenaged sons, for whom the next chapter of life, in which they move to another city and never once use a kitchen, cannot commence fast enough. I don’t know where all the girls were – did they do it all online? Have they been collecting teapots for years, as part of a wistful university trousseau?

The negotiation started with a chopping board, which my son said he absolutely did not need or want. I said, “How are you going to chop vegetables?”, and he said he would cross that bridge when he came to it, and I said: “Oh my God, you’re going to get scurvy.” Behind me a woman and her son were arguing about whether or not he needed a cheese grater, which ended in her saying: “I think you might be about to starve.”

The household-item shop is a uniquely confronting experience, I realised halfway through, and one I had in no way prepared for. It’s the moment you find out how much domestic wisdom you’ve managed to impart. When you get a question like “Can you wash sheets?”, it turns out the answer is: “None.” I remember going round a far larger Ikea with my own mother, when I was in my 30s and my youngest was a baby, and my mum noticing, on the way in, that my daughter had nits. I say “nits” – it was one tiny nit. “Give her a chance,” I said. “She’s barely got any hair.” My mum, taking this as proof that I wasn’t serious enough about hygiene, tried to buy every bath-related item in the shop – at the top of her voice. By the third hour, there was nobody in there who didn’t know about the nit.

Ikea should have a sign at the door, saying: “Parents! If you’re having this conversation now, it’s already too late.” It would probably sound quite melodic in Swedish.

Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnist

I am sending the assisted dying bill back to the Lords – and this time, peers must do the right thing

The Guardian Tue, 08 Sep 2026 09:00:54 GMT

The will of the elected chamber – and a popular, compassionate piece of legislation – must not be frustrated again by a small minority of peers

Lauren Edwards is the Labour MP for Rochester and Strood

I was elected to Westminster two years ago, when the country was crying out for change and looking to parliament to tackle the big issues that had been forgotten for too long. When that change didn’t come fast enough, trust in politics once again started to ebb away. We have one last chance to prove we can deliver on people’s priorities.

Assisted dying didn’t feature in the manifesto I was elected on. Nor should it have done. Matters of conscience such as this are rightly left to individual MPs to decide upon. There will always be a range of views within all political parties. But this issue has been supported by a substantial majority in the country for a very long time. Reputable independent polling has shown support for assisted dying consistently at about 75%. The latest British social attitudes survey from the National Centre for Social Research found that “it is clear we are observing a continued high level of public support for legal change to allow assisted dying in some circumstances”.

Having examined the issue with great care, MPs decided in the last session to support the terminally ill adults (end of life) bill. On the Labour benches there was a clear majority in favour, as there was on the Lib Dems’. The Greens supported it unanimously. It is the most pressing, progressive reform of this parliament. But it was blocked in the Lords earlier this year by a small minority of peers, led in part by ex-Tory ministers such as Thérèse Coffey and Mark Harper.

On Friday, I will be asking MPs to send the bill back to the Lords. There they can amend the bill if they choose, just like any legislation, and if the Commons agrees, that’s fine. But they should not be allowed to frustrate the will of the elected chamber a second time.

I am not reopening divisions in the Labour party or in parliament, as some have claimed. Exactly the reverse is true. MPs have already made their decision. In a democracy, we settle our differences by voting on them. Last time, opponents in the Lords prevented a vote taking place on the bill’s provisions.

The voters put us here to tackle the big issues they care about, not to constantly kick them down the road. After a shaky start, this parliament has the chance to show that it can deliver; that we won’t shirk our responsibilities and will start to restore the public’s faith in our democratic system.

Other major social changes such as a woman’s right to choose and gay rights were bitterly contested at the time. But once passed, the reforms were quickly accepted and ceased to be controversial. It is time to do the same and give terminally ill people the choice to exercise some control over the manner of their deaths. We owe it to them, and to the vast majority of voters who support them, not to sit back and allow a minority of unelected peers to stand in their way.
