The 25 Photos That Changed Fashion Forever

The New York Times September 08, 2026

T 25

Two photographers, a fashion designer, a stylist, a creative director, an editor and a supermodel debate the images that have had an indelible impact on how we dress.

T 25

Two photographers, a fashion designer, a stylist, a creative director, an editor and a supermodel debate the images that have had an indelible impact on how we dress.

Credit...

Supported by

By Nick HaramisElly FishmanKate GuadagninoEviana HartmanJameson Montgomery and Kin Woo

In many art circles, fashion photography doesn’t always get the respect it deserves. Plastered across billboards and printed in magazines, these images — of moisturized and windswept models, cradling $5,000 handbags on the beach, by the pool or atop a tenement building — are plainly commercial. Although they exist to sell you something, they can be insidious (and inescapable) reminders that a certain level of wealth or perfection will always be out of reach. “Fashion,” the American photographer Richard Avedon once said, “is about who you want to be, not who you are.” But despite their limitations, print editorials and brand campaigns are, for many, a portal into a new world, proposing fresh ideas about identity and beauty. They can also provoke: In 1992, a United Colors of Benetton ad featured a photo, originally published in a 1990 issue of Life magazine, of the AIDS activist David Kirby on his deathbed; in 2010, after Italian Vogue printed an oil-spill-themed fashion story shot by Steven Meisel, The Guardian would ask if the spread was “slick or crude.”

Choosing the 25 most influential fashion photographs of the past century is an impossible task. Partly, that’s because influence is hard to trace. Without knowing firsthand, one can’t really say whether Marc Jacobs’s 1993 grunge collection (the one that got him fired from Perry Ellis) was inspired by the work of Joseph Szabo, whose photographs in the 1970s captured the angst and glory of suburban adolescence; or whether today’s street-style photographers admire or even know about the midcentury American photographer Saul Leiter. There’s also the fact that some fine-art photographers have had a great deal of influence on fashion, even though they aren’t considered fashion photographers and wouldn’t refer to themselves as such. In general, fashion photography was defined broadly enough here to include the work of fine artists, street-style photographers, backstage and nightlife photographers and paparazzi. And it didn’t matter if an image was meant as a fashion photograph, so long as the picture later inspired a designer, collection or trend, or it changed how we might think about style.

One morning this past July, a group of experts convened at the Times building in Midtown Manhattan to debate and make the list below. Huddled in a conference room for nearly three hours, six image makers — the New York-based stylist and T contributor Ian Bradley; the Canadian model Linda Evangelista, one of the original “supers” in the late 1980s and ’90s; the American fashion designer and Khaite founder, Cate Holstein; the Dutch American photography duo Inez van Lamsweerde and Vinoodh Matadin; and T’s creative director, Patrick Li — considered the merits of about 60 pictures they’d nominated, spanning roughly 100 years. (Ahead of time, each panelist was asked to submit 10 nominations, and they weren’t allowed to choose ones they’d worked on.)

As one might expect, there were many arguments. Evangelista petitioned not to include “Priscilla,” Szabo’s 1969 portrait of a girl smoking alone at New York’s Jones Beach, since the subject, she reasoned, looks too young to have consented. Matadin unwittingly eliminated a famous album cover with a casual observation — “It was clearly based on a work of ours” — and Li talked about how graphic design can make an image more indelible. Although diversity was a consideration, most of the photographs they included orbit global fashion capitals (New York, London, Milan, Paris and Tokyo), with an emphasis on New York, where several of the panelists live.

In the end, the following list, which isn’t ranked — it’s presented roughly in the order in which the entries were discussed — can be only so definitive. The selections are bound by the preferences and personal experiences of the judges, or even by their moods that day. But there’s one thing they could all agree on: Whether you think it’s art or frivolity, fashion photography is about so much more than clothes. — Nick Haramis

When the American actress Brooke Shields was 15, her appearance in a 1980 Calvin Klein Jeans campaign brought the controversy already swirling around her — about the sexualization of minors in the media, largely on account of her starring role, at age 12, as a child coerced into prostitution in Louis Malle’s 1978 film, “Pretty Baby” — to a fever pitch. Taken by the American fashion photographer Richard Avedon, one of the series’s most enduring images features Shields, her hip cocked and her lined eyes trained on the camera, wearing tight denim and a silky maroon top that she might be buttoning or unbuttoning. Even the fact that the picture is in color feels like a concession to sensuality for Avedon (who died in 2004), as he typically worked in black and white. The idea for the ads, he told an interviewer years later, was to make them “completely quotable,” which led to a script by the copywriter Doon Arbus (daughter of Diane, also included on this list) that was filled with double entendres. The most provocative line in the TV commercials — “You want to know what comes between me and my Calvins? Nothing.” — implied that Shields wasn’t wearing underwear. (She’s since said she didn’t understand the innuendo.) The marketing’s reception underscored the public’s capacity for moral outrage while also proving that sex sells: Even as networks pulled the ads, demand for the jeans skyrocketed. — Kate Guadagnino

Ian Bradley: This was a milestone celebrity endorsement for the brand.

Cate Holstein: Calvin paved the way for so many other campaigns, and this was his first big one.

Patrick Li: As I was putting together my list, I kept thinking about how the best images either reflect a moment or foretell the future. For me, that’s most evident in Avedon’s Andy Warhol mural [a 1969 black-and-white triptych of the artist and his creative circle], which celebrated the downtown New York art scene of that era and ushered in a new approach to group photography by collaging together several different shots.

Linda Evangelista: Prior to becoming a model, I worked at a 7-Eleven-type store in St. Catharines, Ontario. All I did was buy magazines and fantasize about getting out of my hometown to model. Avedon’s pictures made me dream. I could be wrong, but I believe he shot his fashion on a gray background and his nonfashion on a white background, so I don’t know if the Warhol mural is considered fashion. I know this because I did a [spring 1994] Versace campaign with him. I’d just had lung surgery and was drugged, but my agents convinced me to do it. I asked if he’d shoot it on a white background, and he was fed up with me, so he did, but he’d also promised to retouch my nipples and didn’t.

Holstein: When I think of Avedon, his 1957 portrait of Marilyn Monroe is the first that comes to mind. I don’t know that anybody’s ever seen a photo of someone looking so glamorous yet sad. And it would seem to inspire Steven Meisel’s Versace campaigns.

Li: That one also speaks to a moment before photo approvals, because Monroe’s PR person would never have approved it.

Inez van Lamsweerde: Vinoodh and I ended up choosing this Brooke Shields picture.

Li: Which, not for nothing, has a gray background.

In “Saturday Night Fever” (1977), John Travolta’s Tony Manero is the king of his local disco in Bay Ridge, Brooklyn, and a typical pop culture-steeped teen, with posters of Bruce Lee, Al Pacino and Farrah Fawcett hanging in his bedroom. Two years after the movie’s release, the French photographer Guy Bourdin came out with his own, more emphatic depiction of celebrity worship, casting Travolta, who was by then a global superstar, as the object of desire. In this image — an ad for the now-defunct French shoe label Charles Jourdan, with which the exacting Bourdin, who died in 1991, had a long relationship — a model does a backbend onto a sofa, with a framed photo of Travolta propped between her legs. She might be offering herself up to the actor, or perhaps we’re catching her midswoon. Bourdin’s much-imitated pictures were known for their voyeuristic and surreal qualities (he was a protégé of the American French Surrealist Man Ray, whom he met in the early 1950s), and for their attention to composition and color. Here, the saturated palette — the green and red of the woman’s satiny dress and sash combined with the hot pink and jet black of the carpet and couch — contributes to the sense that we’ve entered a bewitching other world. — K. G.

Van Lamsweerde: We own this picture; it’s in our home. The way he incorporated a black-and-white photo into the color image is unbelievable. There’s something about the disturbance of the color saturation with that image of John, and the fact that he’s looking at the camera and she’s not.

Vinoodh Matadin: It was from a time when they had three months to take one series. Now we do 30 pictures in half an hour.

Nick Haramis: Ian and Patrick, you each nominated a different image from Bourdin’s collaboration with Charles Jourdan.

Li: I’m not sure a lot of these images could be made today.

Bradley: So much of it would be social media outrage bait.

Li: But that doesn’t diminish its beauty or influence.

Around the time that Rei Kawakubo’s Comme des Garçons was upending the notion of what fashion could be with its deconstructed, unfinished and asymmetrical clothes, this image challenged what a fashion photograph could look like. Taken in 1983 for the Japanese brand’s catalog, it encapsulates many of Kawakubo’s fundamental ideas: the silhouette of the black dress obscures, rather than accentuates, the subject’s body; the scarf is wrapped around her face. And just as Comme des Garçons went from being disregarded — critics had derided its 1981 Paris debut as “Hiroshima chic” — to a foundational influence for generations of designers, the kinetic abstraction of this photograph became a touchstone for editorials. (It’s hard to imagine an issue of American Vogue without a model leaping through the air.) The project was a departure for the Swiss photographer Hans Feurer, who died in 2024; his work often depicted athletic women in exuberant colors or settings. And though the American model Susan Hess worked with many of the period’s top designers, she’d eventually leave the industry to pursue an acting and filmmaking career. Nevertheless, their collaboration remains an indelible souvenir of a moment when fashion made room for designers who weren’t following trends but defying them outright. — Eviana Hartman

Bradley: It helped ground the avant-garde by making it joyful.

Haramis: It’s interesting that we read joy into this picture given that you can’t see the model’s face.

Bradley: It’s in the body.

Matadin: For me, this is about total freedom and pushing against the establishment. In that way, it’s a perfect image for the brand.

Holstein: It also marks the beginning of what we know as the 1980s — the wackiness, the happiness.

Evangelista: What I loved about Hans is that unlike so many photographers, he wasn’t afraid of fashion. But he used a very long lens to blow out the background, so he couldn’t direct. Like, you couldn’t hear him because you were so far away.

Van Lamsweerde: He was such a master at capturing a mistake — this is a lucky shot, but you must get the right lucky shot.

The British photographer Nick Knight, 67, known for his work with brands like Jil Sander and Yohji Yamamoto, was early to adopt digital manipulation, embracing programs like Quantel’s Paintbox years before the widespread reliance on Photoshop. One of his most celebrated images, made in 1997 for the 20th edition of Visionaire magazine, features the American model Devon Aoki in a cowl-neck, pink satin brocade dress from Alexander McQueen’s spring 1997 collection. Her left eye is a milky shade of blue (it’s a contact lens), and her forehead has been x-ed out with an oversize safety pin and what appears to be a deep gash full of pink flowers, details added in postproduction. “I like the idea of the fragility and strength mixed together,” Knight said in 2020 about this picture, which not only presaged the rise of AI editing tools but also inspired the iconic cover for the Icelandic singer Björk’s 1997 album, “Homogenic,” shot by Knight and art-directed by McQueen. — Jameson Montgomery

Bradley: Nick Knight is technology. He predicted the future of Photoshop and altering images, and he’s had such memorable collaborations with designers.

Holstein: To me, fashion is more of a concept than anything. It’s about pushing things forward and taking us into a new era. This one brings us into the 2000s. And to be shooting with Devon at the time …

Bradley: She was the face.

Holstein: And she reflected a new way of looking at beauty.

The American photographer Robert Mapplethorpe sometimes used the curator Sam Wagstaff’s white-walled Greenwich Village penthouse as a photo studio, and it was there, in 1975, that he shot Patti Smith for the cover of her debut album, “Horses.” Lovers turned friends, Mapplethorpe and Smith were each other’s muses, and though they might have harbored different ideas about glamour ­— later in his career, Mapplethorpe, who died in 1989 at age 42, started taking pictures of celebrities and society types — it was a raw, insouciant vision that won out that day. One side of Smith’s face is bathed in natural light as she stares at the lens; the cuffs of her white shirt have been cut off, a ribbon hangs from her neck like an unknotted tie and she has a men’s suit jacket slung over her shoulder. As Smith said in a 2010 interview, “It has a little bit of Baudelaire, a little bit of Catholic boy, a little bit of Frank Sinatra and a lot of Robert.” Arista Records executives pleaded with Smith to allow an editor to airbrush the image, but she refused. And just as the poetic punk of “Horses” was a revelation, so was its cover, which introduced those beyond Lower Manhattan to a new photographic talent and to one of the greatest androgynous dressers: this self-possessed woman who redefined rocker chic. — K. G.

Holstein: Talk about changing the idea of beauty.

Li: This was taken at such an important moment in the women’s movement. It’s interesting to compare the kind of undone androgyny of this photo with Helmut Newton’s work at the time: two sides of that same idea. To me, this is a forever image that’s influenced not just fashion but the culture.

Haramis: We can’t discuss influence without acknowledging the relationship between fashion, photography and music. Many of the group’s nominations — Joseph Cultice’s work with Marilyn Manson, Jean-Paul Goude’s portraits of Grace Jones — were album covers.

Bradley: Maybe that’s why this picture feels so liberating — because of the music we associate with it.

Holstein: A lot of Mapplethorpe’s work felt that way. And you can see the influence he’d have on [the French fashion designer and photographer] Hedi Slimane.

Dubbed the “King of Kink” by the press, the German photographer Helmut Newton may be best known for his provocative images of women in various states of undress. But in one of his most emblematic shots, the subject is fully clothed. For French Vogue in 1975, Newton photographed the Danish model Vibeke Knudsen standing under a streetlight near his apartment in Paris’s Fourth Arrondissement. Capturing Knudsen in black and white, smoking a cigarette in a pinstriped Yves Saint Laurent tuxedo with slicked-back hair, Newton presented a deeply sexy version of androgyny. “I’m fascinated by ambiguity in a woman,” he told The Times in 1998. “There’s something of a boy in a certain kind of woman.” While Saint Laurent’s designs inspired photographers from Avedon to Irving Penn, his relationship with Newton — with whom he collaborated on many campaigns and look books — was particularly fruitful, born out of mutual admiration and a shared aesthetic. “Saint Laurent inspired me to take some of my best fashion photos,” said Newton, who died in a car accident in 2004. “There are so few people with whom I completely agree.” — Kin Woo

Li: This is undisputed. We don’t need to waste time talking about it. The fact that this was taken around the same time as Smith’s portrait is meaningful.

Matadin: It reminds you that history has different narratives.

Li: And it’s a bit ambiguous. You don’t know exactly what’s happening.

Bradley: It’s chic and queer.

A bruised, bedridden woman writhes in agony (or ecstasy?) as a nurse unpeels the bandage from her face. Another woman, her oversize sunglasses held in place by her cranial cocoon, seems oblivious to the ordeal behind her, fixated on either her reflection or her phone. A third patient, in a fluffy shrug, assesses her pharmaceuticals, served like afternoon tea on a silver platter. The American photographer Steven Meisel, now 72, seems to be saying that beauty is a battlefield. What was provocative in 2005, when “Makeover Madness” was published on the cover of Italian Vogue — and across 80 pages inside the magazine — is almost banal to our eyes today, making it one of the most prescient images from the aughts. (It’s hard to imagine Balenciaga’s spring 2020 facial prosthetics, for example, existing without these pictures.) This series, which features Evangelista plus a handful of other models and includes depictions of liposuction, breast implant surgery and facial injections, eerily anticipated our current era, in which influencers document their surgical journeys to Seoul and getting a face-lift is a status symbol rather than a secret. — E. H.

Li: I know we weren’t supposed to nominate the work of anyone here, but it’s too hard not to. I love this series so much. Linda, I’m curious about your experience.

Evangelista: Steven sometimes picks up on current events. There was so much buzz at the time about plastic surgery. It was the beginning of it becoming less hidden. And it was glamorous because you’d go to a hotel to heal. During those Franca days [Franca Sozzani was the magazine’s editor in chief from 1988 until her death in 2016], there weren’t a lot of preproduction meetings. We just guessed where to draw the surgical marks in Sharpie. It was a total spoof on plastic surgery, but he made it beautiful and glamorous. For me, that’s always been so important when shooting fashion: If you’re making a face, if you’re crying, if you’re screaming, if you’re in ugly clothes, if you’re being tortured — no matter what the situation — the subject still must be beautiful. And I think he managed that.

Li: I would argue, too, that this work is about bringing taboos to light. That’s how the culture moves forward.

Evangelista: This had foreshadowing in it. I remember people said, “Why would you do it?” And I was like, “Why wouldn’t I?”

Van Lamsweerde: What I find astounding about this period of Meisel’s work is that it’s all so perfect, even the tragedy.

In the summer of 1993, Stella Tennant, a 23-year-old student at England’s Winchester School of Art, was scouted by the fashion editor Isabella Blow to star amid a new crop of models in a portfolio photographed by Meisel for the December issue of British Vogue. It was Tennant’s first modeling job and, despite making a lackluster entrance — “Stella came off the train from Scotland smelling of goats,” Blow later told the writer Hamish Bowles — she enchanted Meisel, who’d go on to cast her in a Versace campaign the following week. Meisel’s portrait of Tennant, then a boyish young woman with short, shaggy hair, black-rimmed eyes and a pierced septum, helped kick-start a decades-long career that lasted until her death in 2020, at age 50. Though she’d never become a household name, Tennant’s patrician elegance and chameleonic quality made her a favorite of designers like Phoebe Philo and Helmut Lang, as well as influential photographers including Arthur Elgort, Paolo Roversi and Tim Walker. “I fell in love with Stella,” Meisel recalled of that initial encounter. “She gave everything and I adored her.” — K. W.

Evangelista: For a couple of the photos I chose, it was like the photographer was presenting someone to you. It’s the same with [the American photographer] Peter Beard and [the Somali American model] Iman. This was Steven saying, “I’m giving you a gift, and she’s going to rock your world.” I worked with Stella on her second shoot, for Versace, and I felt so uncool around her. She was shy and timid but so damn cool.

Holstein: Once again, this changed beauty standards. It defined an entire generation.

Bradley: It was a new proposal for what the modern It girl could be.

Matadin: A big part of Steven’s legacy is finding the girl and making her.

Haramis: That’s influence: “I’m seeing this person a certain way. You will now all see her that way too.” There’s no reason we can’t include two works by the same photographer.

The American photographer Irving Penn never stopped working. He spent more than six decades taking pictures, beginning in the 1940s, soon after he was hired at Vogue (initially as a graphic designer), and continuing right up until his death, at age 92, in 2009. His work, which includes 165 Vogue covers (more, by far, than any other photographer), is notable for its visual clarity and artful composition, with many of his images cropped in unexpected ways — a shift from the traditionally centered photos that’d long dominated fashion magazines. In one, from 1951, the American model Sunny Harnett rests an arm atop a table, the billowing sleeve of her blouse taking up most of the frame. Though Harnett’s face is visible, Penn opted to cut the image at her eye, shifting focus to the pin tucking and lace detailing of her top. A gelatin silver print of the photo is now in the permanent collection at New York’s Museum of Modern Art, which described it in a 2019 catalog as “so exquisitely balanced that we accept as inevitable the photographer’s daring cropping of the model’s head.” — J. M.

Li: I’ve never seen an image that celebrates a sleeve as much as this does. If we’re talking about fashion, it’s hard not to include something like this. The crop of the photo, just at the eye — there’s something so weird and transcendent about it.

Van Lamsweerde: Yeah. It’s incredible.

Evangelista: I nominated a Penn photograph of his wife [the Swedish model Lisa Fonssagrives]. I love a wife as a muse. They did so much work together, and he was so crazy in love with her.

Li: Penn’s work with Lisa is indelible. But as a single photo, this —

Van Lamsweerde: It sums Penn up.

Evangelista: But every Penn photo sums Penn up. A cigarette butt does. Flowers do.

The American photographer David LaChapelle, 63, redefined the celebrity portrait, shooting entertainers and world leaders ranging from Lil’ Kim to Hillary Clinton on surreal, cinematic sets that often blend religious iconography with Baroque or Renaissance motifs. In 1996, New York magazine called him “the Fellini of Photography.” LaChapelle came of age in 1980s Manhattan, starting out as a photographer for Interview magazine before shooting for Vanity Fair and Rolling Stone. One of his most unforgettable images is from a 1996 commission for Details magazine featuring the American rapper Tupac Shakur, then 24. “Solitary II,” as the image is titled, features the hip-hop star — who’d recently been released after serving a prison sentence for sexual abuse — adorned with heavy gold jewelry, a “Thug Life” tattoo across his abdomen, reclining in a bathtub. The image could be read as suggesting that the arts-school-educated Shakur (he majored in theater) was washing away his violent past in preparation for a creative rebirth. Instead, five months later, he was killed in a drive-by shooting in Las Vegas. — K. W.

Bradley: This Tupac series represents hip-hop moving into the world of luxury fashion. He walked in a Romeo Gigli men’s wear show shortly after this. It was right before his death; his security guards walked the runway too.

Haramis: At this point, mainstream rap was still largely homophobic. But with this image, LaChapelle almost seems to be encouraging Tupac to embrace a certain kind of queerness, or softness at least.

Bradley: Yeah, he’s playing that up. Tupac got a lot of flak for this.

Van Lamsweerde: It’s fabulous.

Tony sits on the edge of a bed decorated with a gold satin bedspread. Binky stands between his legs, her arms coiled around his. An oval mirror reflects a sliver of the scene from another angle, suggesting a world beyond the frame. The moment appears spontaneous, but like all of Deana Lawson’s work, it was carefully composed and meticulously directed. Lawson, 47, who was born and raised in Rochester, New York, made “Binky & Tony Forever” in 2009, when she was in her 20s and living in Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn. She’d met Binky, a makeup artist, on a shoot and invited her, along with her friend Anthony, to pose in the photographer’s own bedroom; she wanted the image, which was later used as the album cover for Blood Orange’s “Freetown Sound” (2016), to capture young Black love. The photograph is part of her broader project to build an expansive portrait of the Black diaspora, uncovering moments of beauty and grace within the everyday spaces of working-class life. As the novelist Zadie Smith wrote in The New Yorker in 2018, “Outside a Lawson portrait you might be working three jobs, just keeping your head above water, struggling. But inside her frame you are beautiful, imperious, unbroken, unfallen.” — Elly Fishman

Van Lamsweerde: Oh, this picture’s so good.

Bradley: Deana’s a fine artist, but I think fashion photography in the last five years has become a lot like this.

Li: It’s on every mood board.

Bradley: And these homey interiors — I love this set.

Li: I don’t think these are sets.

A 20-something woman with a blond pixie cut and bow-trimmed hat stands in the foreground, the skyscrapers looming behind her framing her worried face. Her white shirt and tweed jacket suggest she has — or is in search of — a job, and her eyes are fixed on something out of frame that we’re left to imagine. This is one of the better-known images in Cindy Sherman’s “Untitled Film Stills” series, for which the artist posed as different actresses promoting make-believe movies. As a child on Long Island’s North Shore, Sherman, now 72, liked playing dress-up, a habit she carried into adulthood. She started taking pictures of herself in costume in college and embarked on “Untitled Film Stills,” whose black-and-white images nod to the directors Alfred Hitchcock and Michelangelo Antonioni, in 1977, the year after she graduated. In “#21,” she embodies a career girl; elsewhere she appears as a vixen and a housewife. Taken as a whole, the pictures suggest that while the roles traditionally available to women are prescriptive, liberation can be found in toggling knowingly between them. First shown in 1980, the series launched Sherman’s career and helped make her a darling of designers ranging from Rei Kawakubo to Marc Jacobs, for whom she’d go on to shoot campaigns. — K. G.

Li: For me, this is the gold standard of modern image-making. It’s purposefully nostalgic but futuristic at the same time. It’s narrative, with the additional layer of projection and identity.

Evangelista: I wanted to include her because I really like the “Clowns” series [2003-4]. And then I thought, “Is the reader going to get the clowns?” But if they don’t know Cindy Sherman, they should.

Haramis: And what is fashion if not the opportunity to become a different version of yourself? Nobody encapsulates transformation quite like her.

Bradley: It’s also about the power of doing it to herself.

Van Lamsweerde: That makes a big difference. We’re in the business of constantly projecting something of ourselves onto the model, who then must embody it and reflect it back. For her to not have that layer, to not worry about whether she’s offending someone or being cruel, that’s also why I think this body of work is so unbelievable. There were no limits.

Evangelista: But is Cindy Sherman a fashion photographer?

Van Lamsweerde: I think she’s the biggest influence. Even when she did the pictures for [the French fashion house] Dorothée Bis in 1984, they were genius.

Shortly after getting an MFA from Brooklyn’s Pratt Institute, Joseph Szabo, hoping to pass along his passion for photography to the next generation, took a job teaching at Long Island’s Malverne High School. After his enthusiasm was initially met with indifference, he started taking pictures of his students instead. Inspired in part by the French Hungarian photographer Brassaï’s portraits of libertine Parisians in the interbellum 1930s, Szabo, born in 1944, captured the wild social lives and rebellious attitudes of suburban New York teenagers in the 1970s and ’80s — which he felt were a world apart from his own upbringing in conservative Toledo, Ohio. In one photograph from 1977, a couple in jeans stand on a curb while passionately kissing, a half-smoked cigarette dangling between the girl’s fingers. Though Szabo wasn’t a fashion photographer, the stylist Grace Coddington has cited the rawness of his work as inspiration for her own. — J. M.

Li: I nominated 1969’s “Priscilla” [a photo of a girl smoking at Jones Beach on Long Island]. It speaks to fashion’s obsession with youth.

Evangelista: How old is she in that photo?

Li: She looks about 13, I think. He didn’t know her, and he never found her again.

Bradley: I think of “Priscilla” in the same vein as Davide Sorrenti’s Jaime King photos from the ’90s.

Holstein: And Larry Clark’s [1995 film] “Kids,” which was so formative for me during my adolescence. I’m excited about the darkness, the subculture.

Li: Transgression is important.

Evangelista: I don’t like that one. It’s disturbing. She would have had to consent to this on her own.

Holstein: I mean, 13 isn’t 9. I was smoking at 13.

Haramis: And one doesn’t have to agree with it for it to be influential.

Van Lamsweerde: But with “The Kiss,” you can really see the people in the background, the hairstyles, the whole thing.

Bradley: It’s a bit more optimistic.

Haramis: It sells the fantasy of youth, too, the promise of being young and in love.

Van Lamsweerde: For us, the kiss is always a theme. The fact that these two faces are sort of melting into an abstract shape together is unbelievable.

With 20 photographs, the American artist Carrie Mae Weems transformed a mundane, domestic surface into the stage for one woman’s life. Beneath the glow of a hanging lamp, Weems’s central character — played by the artist herself — falls in and out of love, raises a daughter, entertains, reflects and, finally, sits alone playing solitaire. When “Kitchen Table Series” debuted in 1990, art often depicted Black women in scenes of oppression or struggle. Weems wanted to present a meditation on their interior lives, one that shows how identity is forged through everyday rituals — including getting dressed. In a wardrobe that shifts from silk nightgowns to a thick sweater layered over a summer dress, she documents inherited beauty rituals (applying lipstick, brushing hair) and demonstrates how a story can be conveyed through style. Weems, now 73, was the first Black woman to mount a retrospective at New York’s Guggenheim Museum. In a 2009 interview, she said, “I use my own constructed image as a vehicle for questioning ideas about … family, monogamy, polygamy, relationships between men and women, between women and their children and between women and other women.” The artist added, “My work endlessly explodes the limits of tradition.” — E. F.

Li: I appreciate the rigor of the series, the narrative of a life unfolding.

Van Lamsweerde: I think a lot of artists have been influenced by this picture.

Matadin: [The American artist] Rashid Johnson referenced it in the video “Black and Blue” (2021).

Bradley: Fashion has never really been able to match the weight of these photos. Bottega Veneta tried to do it [Weems took portraits of the rapper and actor ASAP Rocky and his two sons for the brand’s 2024 Father’s Day campaign], and it wasn’t as rich.

Holstein: It’s difficult for artists to cross over into fashion.

Evangelista: Everything changes when you bring in a big handbag.

Nan Goldin was 20 when she started taking the photos that would become “The Ballad of Sexual Dependency,” her confessional collection reflecting on love, addiction, violence, power and, eventually, the AIDS crisis. Shot between 1973 and 1986, the nearly 700 images established her as one of the most important photographers of her generation and came to define an era of downtown New York. Raised outside Boston, Goldin left home at age 14, three years after the suicide of her older sister, and eventually found a chosen family among East Village artists, musicians and drag queens. Her friends became her subjects, too, as she carried her camera through the apartments, bars and bedrooms that formed the backdrops of their shared lives. “These pictures come out of relationships, not observation,” Goldin, 72, said when Gagosian exhibited 126 images from “Ballad” earlier this year. “They are an invitation to my world, but now they have become a record of the generation that was lost.” In one of them, “The Hug, New York City,” her harsh flash catches two figures locked in an embrace, their faces obscured as shadows spill across the wall. The offhand intimacy of the picture collapses the boundary between documentary and autobiography, a radical proposition when “The Ballad” first appeared, as a slide show, in 1979. (It was published as a book in 1986.) Four decades later, Goldin’s gritty style has become ubiquitous on social media and has paved the way for the likes of Ryan McGinley and Tyrell Hampton. But despite her many acolytes, she remains a singular voice. — E. F.

Holstein: I find so much emotion in this photo, even though you can’t see anybody’s face. And it really is about fashion; the dress is the main character.

Van Lamsweerde: It’s fantastic.

Evangelista: I love the grip.

Haramis: As with a lot of Nan’s work, there’s a suggestion of violence in the romance.

The Dutch photographer Ed van der Elsken’s serene yet puzzling 1967 shot of a woman with a broken leg taking in an Alpine view, part of a travel-themed portfolio for the Amsterdam-based magazine Avenue, is both timeless and ahead of its time. Its subversive twist on sexuality foreshadows Newton’s controversial use of orthopedic gear in sexualized imagery, while its undone aesthetic seems an obvious progenitor of Y2K-era erotic iconography, from the opening frames of Sofia Coppola’s “Lost in Translation” (2003) to the American filmmaker and photographer Richard Kern’s hypersexualized portraits of nearly naked women. No information about the convalescent woman appears to exist in the public record. Was this one of van der Elsken’s brief encounters with a stranger on his travels, or was the tableau — and the injury itself — staged? The title enhances the ambiguity, with the image capturing both the glamour of a European ski vacation and the pain that can linger after the trip’s over. — E. H.

Matadin: The New York art scene was obsessed with his pictures of Vali [Myers, a model featured in van der Elsken’s 1954 book, “Love on the Left Bank,” which Patti Smith has cited as an inspiration for her move to New York]. Goldin was influenced by him.

Van Lamsweerde: And this is literally the opening scene of “Lost in Translation,” with Scarlett [Johansson] lying in front of the window. This is another picture we own; Sofia has it, too.

Evangelista: That poor girl. Life happens.

Haramis: And yet, it’s so glam.

Evangelista: So glam.

In the early 1990s, the studied glamour of Bourdin and Newton gave way to a naturalistic approach pioneered by young British photographers like Corinne Day, Craig McDean, Glen Luchford and David Sims. The image that kicked off this new era was Day’s portrait of a freckled 16-year-old Kate Moss, fresh-faced and laughing, wearing a feathered headdress and a string of beads. Appearing on the cover of The Face magazine in July 1990, the picture, which was taken one freezing spring day on a beach in the south of England, was accompanied by a headline that read, “The 3rd Summer of Love,” a reference to the country’s exploding outdoor rave scene. It was the start of a long creative partnership between Day and Moss that would include a controversial 1993 British Vogue shoot of an ultraskinny Moss wearing mismatched underwear in her London flat, making her the poster child for what became known as “heroin chic.” After the photographer’s death in 2010, Moss said, “She saw beauty in people’s awkwardness and vulnerability where others didn’t.” — K. W.

Evangelista: Do we have David Sims or Juergen Teller or Corinne Day?

Haramis: We have Corinne’s portrait of Kate, and that’s around when it all started.

Holstein: Kate should really be in here.

Bradley: I nominated Mario Sorrenti’s Calvin Klein Obsession campaign from 1992, but I’d say this Kate picture cancels that one out.

The French graphic designer, illustrator and photographer Jean-Paul Goude met the Jamaican singer Grace Jones in the mid-to-late 1970s, when she was performing at a New York gay bar. Soon, they were romantic partners and “she became an obsession,” he told Women’s Wear Daily in 2009. “We did everything together,” including collaborating on several album covers. For Jones’s fifth record, “Nightclubbing” (1981), Goude captured the performer with a flattop haircut wearing a square-shouldered Armani tuxedo, her skin dusted with an inky blue pigment. In making the image, Goude told the Guardian in 2018, he “wanted to focus on Grace’s masculinity — to use what other people thought an embarrassment and turn it around to her advantage.” In the almost half-century since, the resulting photo has lost none of its potency and continues to hold sway over designers like Anthony Vaccarello, who in 2016 paid tribute to Jones’s look in his debut collection for Saint Laurent. “I maintain it’s the best role Grace ever played,” Goude, now 85, once said. “And one of the best things I ever did.” — K. W.

Van Lamsweerde: The perfection of that shoulder.

Evangelista: The power of that cigarette.

Matadin: For a model to become a pop star in those days was revolutionary.

Evangelista: Do you know if the picture has been chopped and extended? I heard he [did his postproduction] with scissors and then airbrushed. This makes me dream.

As a teenager growing up on New York’s Lower East Side, Melvin Sokolsky came across a reproduction of the 15th- and 16th-century Dutch artist Hieronymus Bosch’s fantastical, richly detailed triptych “The Garden of Earthly Delights” (circa 1490) in a book and became fixated on a detail of a nude couple lounging in a transparent bubble. The image stayed with him for decades and ended up being the inspiration for what remains his best-known work: a 12-page editorial that ran in the March 1963 issue of Harper’s Bazaar and features his muse at the time, the French model Simone D’Aillencourt, floating over Paris in a human-size Plexiglas bubble. In the most iconic frame, D’Aillencourt wears a double-breasted suit and silk coat by the French designer Philippe Venet as the bubble, suspended from a crane by an aircraft cable, kisses the surface of the Seine. Sokolsky, who died in 2022, later recalled in an interview that at one point the bubble was lowered too far, submerging D’Aillencourt up to her ankles — and ruining an expensive pair of shoes. It was a small price to pay for an image that continues to inspire: The idea has been revisited several times, including for a 2001 Vogue shoot with the actor Ben Stiller by Annie Leibovitz and a 2014 Bazaar story featuring the actress Jennifer Aniston and shot by Sokolsky himself. — J. M.

Bradley: It’s very sci-fi.

Matadin: To think that it was made without a computer.

Li: Linda, it’s like your Peter Lindbergh Meatpacking photo [for a 1992 issue of Harper’s Bazaar], where you’re flying away.

Evangelista: Oh, the one where I was chafed and cut. I was so excited to go up on the crane and didn’t know that all my body weight would go into the harness. [The American stylist] Paul Cavaco tried to help me stuff things in there for support. We found a shoehorn and some sanitary napkins.

Holstein: Girl …

Evangelista: I couldn’t understand how Mary Martin did it on Broadway in “Peter Pan” (1954), because it wasn’t comfortable. Anyway, Sokolsky’s model has probably been told, “Don’t breathe, you don’t want to steam up the ball.” But look how airy her feet are.

After first laying eyes on Jackie Kennedy at a gallery on Manhattan’s Upper East Side in 1967, the American paparazzo Ron Galella followed her home and remained a pesky presence in her life for well over a decade. “Smash his camera,” she told a Secret Service agent not long before the two ended up in court for the first time, in 1972. Still, Galella had his fans, Warhol among them, and he’s been credited with pioneering not only a genre of photography in America but a new kind of stardom, paving the way for street-style photographers like Scott Schuman and Tommy Ton. In October 1971, he took the picture that he’d call, in a 2010 documentary, his “Mona Lisa.” Having spotted the former first lady, who was by then Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis, exiting her building near Central Park, he hopped into a cab to trail her. At one point, the driver honked and she looked over, the wind in her hair, oversize sunglasses in her hand and the hint of a smile on her lips. If Galella’s memorialization of this moment represents Onassis’s inability to move freely through the world, it also suggests the opposite, encapsulating a period when she was more likely to be wearing jeans and a ribbed henley than a skirt suit and pillbox hat. It’s this Jackie whom, 55 years later, we’re still trying to emulate. — K. G.

Evangelista: This is a rare paparazzi picture that’s good, and I love the fashion. It’s not the Jackie O. we knew. This had to have inspired all of Anna Wintour’s earliest issues.

Bradley: It created the American Vogue formula: Put her in a henley.

Haramis: Cate, you’d nominated a paparazzi photo of her son, John F. Kennedy Jr., and his wife, Carolyn Bessette Kennedy, from 1999.

Bradley: I started with J. F. K. Jr. and Carolyn too, but then I thought about that Jackie picture. I feel like their entire haunting by paparazzi was about trying to get to that Jackie moment.

Haramis: But as a photograph …

Van Lamsweerde: Well, Jackie’s is a real picture.

A Swiss-born Jewish immigrant who moved to the United States after World War II, Robert Frank spent 10 months in the mid-1950s crisscrossing the country on a Guggenheim fellowship, observing his adopted home with the curiosity — and skepticism — of an outsider. Traversing 30 states in a used Ford, he shot more than 760 rolls of film, eventually editing them down to the 83 photographs collected in his seminal 1959 book, “The Americans.” In one of the book’s photos, “Rodeo, New York City,” a cowboy — dressed in a broad-brimmed hat, embossed leather boots and slim jeans held up by an ornate belt — leans against a trash can on a Manhattan sidewalk, holding a cigarette. By placing the mythos of the American West in the middle of the metropolis, Frank, who died in 2019, collapses two competing visions of the nation into a single frame. He also uplifts the urban cowboy, a fashion trope that’s been reinterpreted by everyone from Ralph Lauren to Beyoncé. — E. F.

Evangelista: This is America.

Holstein: It makes me think of the Marlboro Man and American hypermasculinity.

Evangelista: I love how small his hips are.

Holstein: If you squint your eyes, he almost looks naked.

Li: It’s nice to have a men’s image in the mix.

Bradley: I agree.

The heavy-lidded subject, his hair set in plastic rollers, looks squarely at the viewer. Taken with a waist-level Rolleiflex camera, “A Young Man in Curlers” feels like you’re eavesdropping on a conversation between photographer and subject. Diane Arbus, who lived in New York, often turned her camera toward those who were overlooked and misunderstood by mainstream America. She took this photograph the year before her work was featured in the Museum of Modern Art’s landmark 1967 exhibition “New Documents.” The group show anointed a generation who rejected the polished formalism of earlier fine-art photography in favor of an observational, more personal approach. Writing about it, John Szarkowski, MoMA’s longtime director of photography, said that the artists shared “the belief that the commonplace is really worth looking at, and the courage to look at it with a minimum of theorizing.” — E. F.

Holstein: I’d originally nominated another Diane Arbus picture, but I swapped it out for this one because I couldn’t stop thinking about it — the gender ambiguity, the vulnerability. Compositionally, I love it.

Evangelista: When were Weegee’s taken? [Arthur Fellig, who went by the pseudonym Weegee, was a photojournalist known for his stark black-and-white pictures in the 1940s and ’50s.] I feel like it gives you Weegee. He had those photos of cross-dressers being busted in the back of the police wagons.

Bradley: Although there’s vulnerability, there’s also a sense of power here. Very “I’m at home relaxing with a cigarette.” She’s about to put her face on, put the dress on and have a night out.

For Warhol, Polaroids were both a source of artistic inspiration and a form of record-keeping. His instant photos serve as a visual diary dating from the late 1950s up until his death in 1987. Many of these images — the subjects of which include everyone from Saint Laurent and the boxer Muhammad Ali to Warhol’s pet dachshund, Archie — also served as the basis for his paintings and silk-screens. In a series of particularly historic shots, taken on Oct. 4, 1982, Warhol captured the then-ascendant 21-year-old American painter Jean-Michel Basquiat after their first lunch date, which had been arranged by the Swiss art dealer Bruno Bischofberger. In his journal that day, Warhol described the meeting as well as another Polaroid he took, the only one of the two artists together, which Basquiat transformed into his own artwork, “Dos Cabezas, 1982.” Wrote Warhol: “I took a Polaroid and he went home and within two hours a painting was back, still wet, of him and me together.” Think of it as instant gratification twice over. — J. M.

Bradley: Warhol’s Polaroids are significant, and this one is the source of endless men’s wear inspiration.

Holstein: Basquiat was walking in Comme shows — he was so incredible.

Evangelista: Didn’t Raf [Simons] style a show with a collar half out like that?

Bradley: It was Jonathan [Anderson] for Dior.

On an unseasonably warm day in late 1989, five models — Evangelista, Naomi Campbell, Cindy Crawford, Christy Turlington and Tatjana Patitz — assembled in New York’s Meatpacking District for British Vogue’s first cover of the new decade. The magazine’s then-editor, Liz Tilberis, had asked the German photographer Peter Lindbergh, a master at capturing casual elegance, to “photograph the new woman of the Nineties,” as Crawford wrote in an essay for the same magazine in 2016. “Peter’s reply was that he couldn’t do it with just one woman.” Though group shots have since become commonplace, Lindbergh, who died in 2019, made what was then the radical decision to feature five faces on equal footing. The easy clothes (Giorgio di Sant’Angelo bodysuits paired with faded Levi’s, all of which belonged to the models) and natural grooming were different, too. “We were quite undone. Coming out of the ’80s, which was all big hair and boobs pushed up, it felt refreshing and new,” Crawford wrote. In the years that followed — propelled by George Michael’s “Freedom! ’90” video featuring all five cover subjects — models became supermodels, supermodels became celebrities and fashion became inseparable from pop culture. — E. H.

Van Lamsweerde: I mean, come on.

Li: It’s iconic.

Bradley: Also, the styling!

Evangelista: Those are our jeans and probably our Giorgio di Sant’Angelo tops, because that’s how Giorgio would pay us to walk in his shows. Our hair could have been better.

Holstein: It’s very “Edward Scissorhands.”

Evangelista: That was the picture George Michael saw before the “Freedom” video, which took everyone to a new level. I’m grateful for that day.

Van Lamsweerde: The influence is huge.

“With young people, everything is much more on the surface,” the Dutch photographer Rineke Dijkstra, 67, once said. “When you get older, you know how to hide things.” Her observation is visible in all her work, but particularly in this shot, the best-known photo from her series of large-format beach portraits of teenagers taken in the early and mid-90s. Two years before she started the project, Dijkstra had had a serious bicycle accident and begun swimming as a form of rehabilitation. One day, she decided to take a self-portrait after emerging from the pool, using a stationary 4x5 view camera that rendered a rich degree of detail and emotional depth. The resulting photograph spawned the series, which began as a commission for a Dutch newspaper and made Dijkstra’s career. The subject of this shot stands before the camera in a lime green swimsuit, slender limbs draped, lip bitten shyly. The flash renders her almost beatific. Critics have questioned whether the girl’s Botticelli-esque pose reflects an unconscious awareness of art history (Dijkstra has said she gave little direction to her sitters), but what makes the shot transcendent is the awkwardness that belies its beauty. — E. H.

Van Lamsweerde: Rineke and I overlapped at the Gerrit Rietveld Academy in Amsterdam. We were constantly trying out different lighting setups; I’d pose for her and she’d pose for me.

Matadin: And I’d pose for both.

Van Lamsweerde: What’s so beautiful about Rineke’s work, and why it’s so resonant today in the fashion world, is that she captures reality while also lifting people up. Maybe they’re tragic, but they’re always overcoming it.

Matadin: Luxury brands now use these methods [for their campaigns] because their clothes are so outrageously expensive. It’s almost like they use her way of shooting people to be like, “Look, we’re still regular people.”

Van Lamsweerde: But it never has the same feeling. What’s so brilliant about this body of work is that you see the dreams of these people. You see how they wish to be glamorous, or more than what they think they are. We’re always saying that a fashion photograph shows you the road to happiness is through glamour.

Haramis: And these girls are glamorous, despite their insecurities.

Evangelista: These photos couldn’t be further from what we see today. There’s no vulnerability — nothing’s real anymore.

Part of the fun of making these lists is arguing over what goes on them. During the roughly three hours we spent putting this together, we debated criteria like originality, impact and intent. We wanted to include everything from fine art to paparazzi shots — any image that shifted our ideas about beauty and style. But in the end, we had to leave out plenty of our favorite photographers: Lillian Bassman! Herb Ritts! Deborah Turbeville! Philip-Lorca diCorcia! Mario Sorrenti! Which of yours did we miss?

Is This Miami or L. A.? Southern California Is Hot and Steamy Again.

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Extreme Heat

Advertisement

Supported by

Temperatures soared across the region on Tuesday. The muggy weather will get worse before it gets better.

By Amy Graff

Amy Graff is a reporter on The Times’s weather team. She is based in San Francisco.

Big waves pounded coastal Southern California on Tuesday as scattered rain showers swept through hot, humid air.

The weird weather was driven by a deteriorating tropical storm hundreds of miles offshore, and while calmer ocean waters and clear skies were expected in the days ahead, temperatures and humidity levels will soar.

Downtown Los Angeles was forecast to reach 98 degrees on Wednesday, but with the heat index the National Weather Service warned that it would feel like 116 degrees.

“It feels very much like Miami,” Rich Thompson, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service office in Oxnard, Calif., said on Tuesday. “Tomorrow is going to be the worst of it.”

The air spread between Los Angeles and San Diego has been unusually sticky most of the summer, and Mr. Thompson said this week could bring the worst yet.

Heat advisories and extreme heat warnings were in place across the region through Thursday. Triple-digit heat was expected in desert areas including Palm Springs, where temperatures could hit 109 on Wednesday and Thursday.

“Humid conditions will add to heat discomfort,” the Weather Service wrote in an advisory.

Heat advisories also extended into a portion of Northern California including the Sacramento Valley, where the state capital could hit 100 degrees on Wednesday and the Bay Area, where San Francisco was forecast to reach 86 degrees.

There is good news: Cooler weather was expected by Friday, particularly at the coast.

The remnants of Hurricane Marie were 800 miles southwest of San Diego on Tuesday. The storm developed last week, and over the Labor Day weekend it whipped up the ocean waters and sent a plume of moisture to Southern California.

A region that stays mostly dry in September received rain over the holiday weekend. Downtown Los Angeles recorded 0.73 inch of rain through Monday, well above the September average of 0.13 inch. Places in the mountains of Los Angeles and Ventura Counties received nearly two inches of rain. Light rain fell in much of Orange County.

Scattered showers moved around the region on Tuesday, but the chance for rain is expected to be over by the evening.

The rain was accompanied by active surf at beaches, and wave heights reached eight to 12 feet up and down the coast.

“We had some beach erosion and coastal flooding with the large swells,” Mr. Thompson said.

In Long Beach, officials ordered residents of over a dozen homes to evacuate as the waves crashed over a sea wall.

“The triggering point was there were reports last night of several large cracks in the concrete, and those cracks extended into the interior walls of the homes,” said Capt. Jack Crabtree with the Long Beach Fire Department.

A dozen homes and garages were also soaked and damaged by the swollen surf, he said.

The oversize waves were expected to subside by Wednesday.

“We have had very hazardous swimming conditions,” Casey Oswant, a meteorologist with the Weather Service office in San Diego, said.

The Life That Rose From the Ashes of Ground Zero

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Bret Stephens

By Bret Stephens

Opinion Columnist

Three days before 9/11, I hosted an out-of-town friend who wanted to take in the view of New York from above. I suggested a drink at Windows on the World, in the north tower of the World Trade Center. We arrived a minute too late to catch the last elevator to the 107th floor.

“Next time,” I remember telling her. Of course there wouldn’t be one.

Many years of living in a city creates a kind of archaeology of private memory. A street corner, a bar, an office building, a playground, a spot where a favorite restaurant or bookshop used to be — each recalls a buried layer of life, and each has its own circumstances, its web of relationships, its emotional color.

In 1998 I got a job with The Wall Street Journal, which at the time had its offices across the street from the Trade Center. My subway stop was at Cortlandt Street; my gym was on the top floor of the Marriott that stood between the towers. That summer I overnighted a hard copy of my master’s thesis to London from the courier service in the sunlit lobby of the south tower and said to myself, “School’s over forever.”

Now and then the thought of another terrorist attack, like Ramzi Yousef’s 1993 underground bombing, crossed my mind. But I never imagined jetliners slamming into buildings, incinerating perpetrators and victims alike.

On the day itself I was in Jerusalem on assignment for The Journal. I watched the towers come down on TV and wondered who among my colleagues had been killed. (None had, miraculously, despite some close calls, and they performed the additional miracle of putting out a paper the next day for which they won a Pulitzer Prize.) For one of the few times in my life I felt an overwhelming desire to pray. At the Western Wall I found this in the Book of Psalms:

Lift up thy steps because of the perpetual ruins, even all the evil that the enemy hath done in the sanctuary. Thine adversaries have roared in the midst of Thy meeting-place; They have set up their own signs for signs.

I moved to Israel for a new job soon afterward. When I came back to New York three years later I had a family, as well as an office with a direct view of the giant pit called ground zero. For a long time nothing seemed to happen inside it, or if it did, it was at a glacial pace. It struck me as emblematic of a post-9/11 national paralysis, “testifying,” as I wrote in a bitter column from 2009, “to a society in which everyone gets their say and nothing gets done.”

I was wrong.

Ground zero may have been stuck in legal gridlock — and coated in more toxic dust than was previously acknowledged. But the neighborhood around it was springing to life, thanks to a combination of civic spirit, government subsidy and capitalist creativity. Between 2000 and 2026 the number of downtown apartments nearly tripled, from 13,000 to 37,000, according to The Journal. Battery Park City, the neighborhood directly west of the old towers, became an oasis for families with young children, including our three. I never worried for the safety of my kids in the 16 years that we lived there.

Except once. On Halloween of 2017, two of our kids were out when I heard a crash and what might have been a gunshot, then one police siren after another. My 12-year-old son came home to tell us that he had seen a truck smashed at the corner of our street with blood on its windshield. An Uzbek man named Sayfullo Saipov had driven a rented Home Depot truck down the Hudson River bike path, killing eight people and injuring many more.

President Trump used the occasion to rail against immigration — and Chuck Schumer. But what I remember was the calm good judgment of our neighbors, many of them immigrants themselves, who sheltered the students at P. S. 89 just as they were being let out from school. It was America at its best. The kids trick-or-treated that night as usual.

And ground zero did come back. On Monday, another old friend came to town and we toured the site together. The early September weather was perfect, just as it had been 25 years ago. Thousands of people, locals and tourists alike, shopped and chatted and gawked at the sights around us.

We visited the shrine of St. Nicholas, a stunning replacement for the unassuming Greek Orthodox chapel that once stood a stone’s throw away on Cedar Street. We walked through the oak-shaded plaza encompassing the memorial pools ringed by the names of the fallen. We went down to the vast underground mall that looks (in the best possible way) like the rib cage of a gigantic dinosaur and which, from a certain spot, gives a neck-craning view of the spire atop the tallest of the towers surrounding the site. We both remembered the plaza of the old World Trade Center, so intimidating and sterile. What we have now is so much better: reflective but not somber; commanding but not forbidding; sheltering but not closed.

It’s a magnificent civic achievement.

On Sept. 11, 2001, the forces of death paid a visit to Lower Manhattan and extracted their awful irreparable price. Twenty-five years on, what’s clear, most of all to those of us who saw both sides of that date, is that the forces of life proved much stronger.

OpenAI Says It Has Cracked One of Math’s ‘Millennium Problems’

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

The company’s announcement is the most dramatic sign yet that artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming the field of higher mathematics.

By Cade Metz

OpenAI said on Tuesday that its newest artificial intelligence technology had solved one of the “Millennium Problems,” a collection of important unanswered math questions meant to push the world’s leading mathematicians to new heights.

The announcement is another clear sign that A. I. is fundamentally changing the upper reaches of mathematics, which have long been viewed as a pinnacle of human achievement. The change has excited some mathematicians, while stirring concern among others.

Over the past year, A. I. systems successfully solved a wide range of problems that have bedeviled mathematicians for decades. But these problems were not as complex, nor as closely watched, as the one that OpenAI’s technology has solved over the past several days. The Millennium Problems are among the most heavily researched in the field.

“This is a spectacular culmination of the arc we have seen over the past twelve months,” OpenAI researcher Sébastien Bubeck said of the company’s new solution.

The company announced that one of its latest models, which has not yet been released to the public, needed just 88 hours to solve what mathematicians call “the Navier–Stokes existence and smoothness problem.” This problem involves a series of equations that are often used to predict the weather.

The equations describe the movement of water and other fluids. The Navier-Stokes problem, which has no clear practical value, asks whether these equations completely break down in certain situations. OpenAI’s proof claims to have defined just such a situation.

This would imply, at least theoretically, that the laws of physics themselves would break down under certain conditions: that, for example, water could be made to spontaneously explode. But mathematicians and physicists do not believe that this mathematical breakdown could really lead to such an outcome in the physical world.

The Navier-Stokes problem was one of seven “Millennium Problems” selected by the Clay Mathematics Institute in the year 2000 as a way of tracking the progress of mathematics in the new millennium. The institute, founded by an American businessman named Landon T. Clay, offered a million dollars for the first correct solution to each problem. Before OpenAI’s announcement, only one of the problems had been solved.

“These questions are lighthouses,” said Terence Tao, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, who is regarded by many as the finest mathematician of his generation. “They are great focus points that attract the efforts of human scientists.”

Dr. Tao is among the many mathematicians who have publicly warned that the latest A. I. systems could end up damaging the field of mathematics. If A. I. technologies can solve the most difficult problems with little input from human mathematicians, he says, they could weaken human understanding of the field.

“The effort needed to solve problems is often very instructive. It teaches you something. It’s like going to the gym and having a goal to lift a weight a hundred times,” he explained. “Now, A. I. can solve questions without really getting any value out of them. It’s like having machines that can lift weights for you at the gym.”

But as he and others point out, mathematicians still provide a helping hand as A. I. systems work through these problems. OpenAI said that it deployed vast teams of “A. I. agents” to solve the Navier-Stokes problem and that its researchers passed key ideas between these teams.

“Our role was like a bumble bee cross-pollinating across different groups and delivering different bits of information,” said OpenAI researcher Dan Roberts.

A. I. systems may also draw on key breakthroughs previously made by top mathematicians — or independently duplicate their work. The night before OpenAI made its announcement, Tristan Buckmaster, a professor of mathematics at New York University, said in a post to social media that he had been exploring similar research with another mathematician who works for OpenAI’s chief rival, Anthropic.

In a blog post on Tuesday, OpenAI acknowledged that it focused its resources on the Navier-Stokes problem after hearing that other mathematicians were exploring similar research. But the company said it “did not see any of their work through any means.”

Companies like OpenAI build their A. I. technologies using what scientists call neural networks, systems that learn skills by analyzing vast amounts of digital data. About two years ago, such companies started to hone these systems using another technique called reinforcement learning. Through this process, A. I. systems can learn additional behavior through extensive trial and error.

By working through thousands of math problems, for instance, they can learn which methods lead to the right answer and which do not. Researchers inside labs like OpenAI develop complex feedback mechanisms that show the system when it has done something right and when it has done something wrong.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A. I. systems. The two companies have denied the suit’s claims.)

Reinforcement learning is difficult to perfect in areas like creative writing, philosophy and ethics, where the question of which answers are right or wrong is hard to define objectively. But the technique is ideally suited to mathematics.

Through this process, A. I. systems can learn to prove mathematical theorems using a computer programming language called Lean. The language was originally designed as a tool for human mathematicians. But now that A. I. systems are skillful enough to generate their own computer code, they, too, can use Lean to generate their own math proofs.

In January, OpenAI and another start-up called Harmonic said that together, two of their A. I. technologies had solved one of the “Erdos problems,” a collection of thorny unsolved problems posed by a 20th-century academic named Paul Erdos.

Some mathematicians pointed out that the solution generated by the A. I. systems had not been all that different from earlier work done without help from A. I. “It feels to me like a really clever student who has memorized everything for the test but doesn’t have a deep understanding of the concept,” Dr. Tao told The Times.

But as the months passed, technologies from OpenAI and other companies continued to crack additional problems, sometimes in more impressive ways.

OpenAI said that it solved the Navier-Stokes problem using as many as 10,000 “A. I. agents” working in concert. Running such a large number of A. I. systems is likely to have cost millions of dollars, a result of the enormous amounts of electrical power needed to operate the specialized chips that drive A. I. technologies.

OpenAI research scientist Noam Brown called this a “very expensive process,” before adding that the costs of running A. I. technologies tend to drop as companies like OpenAI improve their efficiency.

On Tuesday, the company released a paper describing its solution, including a Lean proof, allowing outside mathematicians to see how its agents cracked the problem. But to Dr. Tao, it is still a poor substitute for humans solving the problem on their own. He compared OpenAI to a wilderness guide who finds a path to a hidden waterfall.

“This has some value,” he said. “But once someone shows a specific path to the waterfall, people just take that path. They don’t spend as much time looking for other paths.”

As OpenAI’s announcement shows, A. I. is fundamentally changing the upper reaches of mathematics. The question is: what this will mean for leading mathematicians? Academics like Terrance Tao, regarded by many as the finest mathematician of his generation, worry that this will ultimately weaken human understanding of mathematics, because humans will no longer to do the serious work previously needed to solve the hardest problems.

But he and others point out that humans still play vital roles. They dream up the problems in the first place. And as A. I. systems solve these problems, these automated technlogies draw on previous research from human mathematicians. OpenAI acknowledged that human researchers played a role in its new solution.

Cade Metz is a Times reporter who writes about artificial intelligence, driverless cars, robotics, virtual reality and other emerging areas of technology.

Trump’s Latest Makeover Target? Space Force Uniforms.

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

critic’s notebook

The president shared a provocative new look for the next-gen Space Force ’fit.

By Vanessa Friedman

Vanessa Friedman has been chronicling the relationship of clothing to identity, power and politics for The Times since 2014.

After the bulldozer in chief and the redecorator in chief, the designer in chief? So it seems, judging from a Truth Social post from President Trump over the weekend in which he appeared to extend his desire to make over whatever catches his eye to military uniforms. Specifically, the service dress uniforms of the Space Force.

Amid a series of posts showing New Mexico renamed “New America” and George Washington visiting Trump in the Oval Office, the president included what appeared to be an A. I.-generated version of the “next generation” Space Force outfits for his lunar generals. One in “space gray” and “midnight black” featured a Prussian collar, a belted tunic jacket and shiny knee-high black boots.

Sound familiar?

It would be easy to dismiss the post as simply one late-night boondoggle among many. But it is also telling.

According to the post, the style was “inspired by the dignity and functionality of the Starship Trooper uniform.” Given that “Starship Troopers,” the 1997 Paul Verhoeven movie that was inspired by Robert Heinlein’s 1959 book, starts with the phrase “After the failure of democracy” and was meant as a sendup of totalitarianism, this was a provocative model to choose. Think sci-fi Hitler by way of Hollywood, and you will get the idea.

Or think of it as a case of life imitating cartoon art imitating life. Or simply another example of the way the president is merging the pageantry of dictators and the big screen’s schlocky past into a communications chimera that, in its lack of subtlety, may seem like a joke but taps into the totems of mass culture with viral intent. By cloaking the horrors of the past in the costumes of escapism, it normalizes them.

Even if the proposed uniform was more fantasy than realism, many people online did not miss the connection between the look and its historical antecedents in Nazi Germany and fascist Italy and Spain. Especially when such comparisons were already drawn between the former Border Patrol official Gregory Bovino’s preferred overcoat and the wardrobes of classic strongmen.

Besides, the look was entirely in line with the Trump aesthetic.

That’s not just because, as Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan reported in their book, “Regime Change,” Trump believes he is more powerful than Attila the Hun, Genghis Khan, Stalin and Hitler, suggesting that those regimes, with their distinctive aesthetics, are his measuring stick.

Rather, just as gold and marble, the fairy-tale signifiers of palaces and royalty, seem to represent the most desirable physical environment for the president, and superheroes his favored avatars, so, too, the military uniforms that have become communal shorthand for evil armies onscreen seem to be his preferred choice for communicating power and intimidation.

After all, the Space Force outfits resemble not only the uniforms of “Starship Troopers,” but those of the Galactic Empire officers in “Star Wars.”

And they may signal the president’s intent to redesign the look of a lot more than just the White House, even if the proposed uniforms are never made. Emails to the Space Force were not answered, and the Space Force itself introduced new ceremonial dress uniforms during the IndyCar race in Washington last month with a much more traditional look, including sky blue braid, white collars and bright silver buttons. Still, members of the Trump administration prove eager to make the president’s wishes come true — whether that is putting his profile on new gold coins or on special 250th anniversary passports.

Trump has already demonstrated his desire to style the members of his administration, handing out his preferred Florsheim shoes to a number of cabinet members because he didn’t approve of their footwear choices. In that context, the proposed Space Force designs may simply be another … well, lockstep in that direction.

Vanessa Friedman has been the fashion director and chief fashion critic for The Times since 2014.

Trump Administration Asks Supreme Court to Allow Voter-Screening Tool

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Supreme Court Birthright Citizenship Case

Advertisement

Supported by

Voting rights organizations had challenged a Trump administration overhaul of a government database, arguing it could be used to disenfranchise eligible voters.

By Abbie VanSickle

Reporting from Washington

The Trump administration on Tuesday asked the Supreme Court to allow it to use a federal citizenship database to help spot invalid voters ahead of the midterm elections.

The administration is currently blocked from rolling out the tool, which the administration proposed using as part of a larger effort by President Trump to enact additional screening of voters ahead of November.

If the justices allow the administration to proceed, states could use the Department of Homeland Security database to check voter information against federal citizenship and Social Security records.

The emergency application to the justices marks the latest in a dizzying series of legal developments in the fight over the Trump administration’s push to upend voting procedures. The administration has also sought permission from the Supreme Court to change mail-in voting rules even as some states begin sending out ballots.

And it comes as the Trump administration is intensifying efforts to cast doubt on the integrity of voting, with the hotly contested midterm elections less than two months away.

Earlier this month, hundreds of Department of Homeland Security agents began an intensive hunt for noncitizens among the nation’s registered voters, despite little evidence that noncitizens have voted in sizable numbers.

Last week, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, asked the Justice Department to examine whether a commonly used voting machine could be trusted to create a verifiable record, an apparent attempt to cast doubt on the reliability of voting machines.

The Supreme Court gave the challengers until next Tuesday to respond to the Trump administration request regarding the citizenship database.

“The stakes could not be higher: Millions of Americans’ sensitive personal information and the integrity of our elections are on the line, just weeks before the midterm elections,” said Skye Perryman, the president and chief executive of Democracy Forward, which represents the challengers.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that voter fraud is rampant, including by noncitizens, who cannot legally vote in federal elections.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

D. John Sauer, the solicitor general, asked the justices to lift a lower court freeze blocking the citizenship database. He called the court’s freeze “an indefensible order that threatens the integrity of upcoming elections” by limiting the federal government from using Social Security data “when fulfilling its duty to respond to requests by states to verify the citizenship of individuals for voting and other purposes.”

The request was the latest emergency application to the court related to the legality of the president’s efforts to use the federal government to impose voting restrictions.

On Sunday morning, Trump administration lawyers asked the justices to allow the U. S. Postal Service to move ahead with a plan to impose new screening on ballots sent through the mail. A group of Democratic state attorneys general and voting rights organizations challenging the Postal Service plan will respond to that filing by Wednesday.

They argue that the administration’s plan violates the Constitution, allowing the executive to intrude on the authority of states and Congress. The administration has said that the Postal Service is acting lawfully.

The new emergency application filed Monday focuses on the legality of an expansion of a Department of Homeland Security database known as the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, which the government described in court filings as “an online service that enables users to verify a person’s citizenship status, often within seconds.”

The federal database was created in 1986 as a way to enable the federal government and state and local officials to search for immigration status to help determine eligibility for a range of public benefits.

The Trump administration has expanded the database, including by folding in data from the Social Security Administration, which challengers assert can be unreliable and incomplete. They also argue that it would violate privacy protections.

Voting rights groups sued last year to challenge Mr. Trump’s overhaul of the database, arguing that the administration was illegally transforming the system into a nationwide citizenship bank that could be used for states to purge voter rolls. The groups argued that errors in the data could disenfranchise valid voters if it is used in an election context.

On Friday, a divided panel of federal appeals court judges from the U. S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia agreed to keep in place a temporary freeze on access to the database. The majority found that the federal government had not shown that the system could be used without violating laws aimed at shielding Social Security information.

Abbie VanSickle covers the United States Supreme Court for The Times. She is a lawyer and has an extensive background in investigative reporting.
