At 9/11 Tribute, Trump Claims Firefighters Carried Him to Safety

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Sept. 11

Advertisement

Supported by

President Trump has long sought to position himself close to the Sept. 11 recovery effort and has made a series of questionable and provocative statements to burnish his political brand.

By Katie Rogers

At an event honoring those who died on Sept. 11, 2001, President Trump on Tuesday claimed that two firefighters lifted him up and carried him away from a seemingly unstable building when he visited the area shortly after the terrorist attacks.

This was the latest in Mr. Trump’s evolving — and often disputed — account of his actions on Sept. 11 and in its aftermath, when he was working as a real estate developer in New York City.

Mr. Trump was watching television the morning of the attacks, which is verifiable from news coverage of that day, but what he did next has long been a matter of debate. He has repeatedly said that he took a construction crew with him to Lower Manhattan and was deeply involved in cleaning up the site, a claim that has been called into question by at least one former fire official who was involved in the recovery effort.

On Tuesday, Mr. Trump renewed his claim that he had taken a crew to a building near the site where the World Trade Center had stood shortly after the attacks. He said that two large firefighters picked him up and took him to safety when he observed an unstable building.

“I was building a big building in New York, and I took the whole crew down there right after this happened,” Mr. Trump said on Tuesday during an address from the Ellipse.

He went on: “The United States Steel building was creaking, really creaking, and we thought it was going to fall down. The truth is, it creaked a lot. It creaked. It still creaks, but it never came down. And I’ll never forget two firemen. We thought it was coming down on top of us, and two firemen, big strong guys. And I’m not the smallest guy in the world. They grabbed me under the arm, said, ‘Got to get out of here.’ And they literally lifted me up. This is not easy to do. I’m big. They lifted me up and they started running with me. I said, ‘Fellas, I can run myself,’ but they were amazing.”

Almost from the moment the planes hit the towers, Mr. Trump has sought to position himself close to the recovery effort. He has also made a series of questionable and provocative statements to burnish his political brand, notably by sharing a widely debunked claim that Muslims in New Jersey were celebrating after the planes hit.

At least one former official who spent time at the site has disputed Mr. Trump’s claims about his whereabouts over the years. In 2019, Richard Alles, a retired deputy chief with the New York Fire Department, attended a ceremony at the White House where Mr. Trump signed into law a bill that would permanently fund the care of emergency workers who became ill after the attacks.

“I spent many months there myself, and I never witnessed him,” Mr. Alles said in an interview with The New York Times about Mr. Trump, shortly after that ceremony. “He was a private citizen at the time. I don’t know what kind of role he could have possibly played.”

On Tuesday, though, Mr. Trump left the impression that he had been at the site in the immediate aftermath. “I’ve never seen such an unbelievable mass of steel and, unfortunately, bodies and everything you can imagine,” Mr. Trump told the crowd, which had gathered to pay tribute to the police officers and firefighters who had been killed in the attack, including a stock trader and volunteer firefighter named Welles Crowther, whom Mr. Trump posthumously awarded with the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

In response to questions asking for more information about Mr. Trump’s story about being carried by firefighters, the White House press office sent a clip of Mr. Trump delivering a speech on the campaign trail in 2016. In that speech, Mr. Trump said he had traveled to the former U. S. Steel building, now known as 1 Liberty Plaza, in downtown Manhattan with a crew “a couple of days after” the World Trade Center towers came down.

“I must tell you honestly,” Mr. Trump said, “I never knew I could run that fast.”

In an interview on Fox News that was broadcast before Tuesday’s ceremony, Mr. Trump said he traveled to the site of the attacks “very quickly afterwards.” He and a crew “worked long and hard,” he said, “but it was just so terrible and so hopeless. It was so hopeless, such a terrible thing.”

On the day of the attack, Mr. Trump called into WWOR-TV to say that he had a window in Trump Tower that looked directly over the World Trade Center, and talked about a building he had in the area. Trump Tower is about four miles away from the site of the attacks.

“Forty Wall Street actually was the second-tallest building in downtown Manhattan and it was actually, before the World Trade Center, was the tallest. And then, when they built the World Trade Center, it became known as the second tallest,” Mr. Trump said of the building he owned. “And now it’s the tallest.” (It wasn’t.)

In the days after the attack, Mr. Trump became something of a commentator. In an interview with a German television station on Sept. 13, 2001, Mr. Trump was asked if he would be personally involved in the recovery effort.

A photo taken of him on Sept. 18, 2001, has been used in a widely circulated meme that claims Mr. Trump personally traveled to ground zero with hundreds of workers to help uncover victims. Timothy O’Brien, a Trump biographer, said that Mr. Trump would not have had many workers on hand to send to the site, because the Trump Organization “had a dozen people working there” at the time.

Barbara Res, an executive vice president in charge of construction at the Trump Organization, who left the company in the late 1990s, said Mr. Trump was adept at getting news coverage for himself.

“Listen, if he was there and he was escorted by firefighters and first responders, it would be the headline of The Times the next day,” Ms. Res said. “He’d make that happen.”

Susan C. Beachy contributed research.

Katie Rogers is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

Which Republican Senate Candidates Are Skipping Trump’s Convention?

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

For G. O. P. candidates in the most competitive races, deciding whether to appear with President Trump can be tricky. Some are going, while others are staying away.

By Kellen Browning

For Republican candidates running in battleground Senate races, this week’s G. O. P. midterm convention in Dallas represents a thorny conundrum.

Do they attend and risk alienating swing voters in their states by embracing President Trump at a time when many are frustrated with his second term? Or do they skip it, potentially drawing Mr. Trump’s ire and losing out on a chance to fire up the Republican base?

The nine Republicans running in the most competitive Senate races — those considered tossups or leaning toward one party or the other by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report — have made different decisions ahead of the convention, which will unfold on Wednesday and Thursday and feature some of the biggest names in the party.

Here’s a rundown of their choices.

One of the least surprising names on the list of convention speakers is Ken Paxton, the hard-right Texas attorney general who has aligned himself closely with the president and who will need Mr. Trump’s voters to turn out for him. Mr. Paxton, running against James Talarico, a state lawmaker who has Democrats optimistic about flipping Texas, was unlikely to skip a major Republican event in his home state.

Another staunch ally of Mr. Trump set to speak at the convention is Michael Whatley, the former chairman of the Republican National Committee, which is hosting the Dallas event. Mr. Whatley is running for the open Senate seat in North Carolina against Roy Cooper, a popular former Democratic governor who leads Mr. Whatley in polls. Still, North Carolina has gone Republicans’ way in recent presidential elections.

Senator Jon Husted, running for re-election in Ohio after being appointed to serve out the remaining term of Vice President JD Vance, also plans to speak in Dallas. Like Mr. Paxton, Mr. Husted will need to fire up Republican voters in a state that Mr. Trump carried three times. But he faces a tough opponent in former Senator Sherrod Brown, a well-known Ohio Democrat who was ousted in 2024 and is attempting a comeback.

In Georgia, Representative Mike Collins is another Senate candidate who has tied himself closely to Mr. Trump — the president endorsed Mr. Collins in the final stretch of a primary runoff in June — and will speak at the convention. Mr. Collins may face an uphill battle in a swing state, and he faces a formidable opponent in Senator Jon Ossoff, the incumbent Democrat.

Former Representative Mike Rogers of Michigan will also speak in Dallas. With Republicans playing defense across the Senate map, the party sees Mr. Rogers’s bid as a rare chance to go on offense and flip an open Democratic seat. Mr. Rogers is running against Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive former public health official whose bitter primary battle against Representative Haley Stevens, a moderate, divided Democrats in Michigan. Still, Mr. Rogers will have to appeal beyond the MAGA base in a purple state to emerge victorious.

In Iowa, Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican, faces Josh Turek, a Democratic state lawmaker and former Paralympian, as Democrats try to revert the state to battleground status after years of Republican dominance. Ms. Hinson said in a Fox News interview over the weekend that she was “heading down to Texas on Wednesday” and would return to Iowa on Thursday. A spokesman for Ms. Hinson did not respond to an inquiry about her plans, and she was not on the list of convention speakers published last week.

Running for re-election in Maine — a blue state that former Vice President Kamala Harris easily won in 2024 — Senator Susan Collins is skipping the G. O. P. convention, according to her campaign, which said she would be with constituents. Ms. Collins faces Troy Jackson, a progressive former state legislator, in a high-profile contest this fall.

Republicans spy another opportunity in New Hampshire, where John E. Sununu is running for an open seat and trying to make a comeback after serving in the Senate from 2003 to 2009. A spokesman for Mr. Sununu, Mike Schrimpf, said the former senator would not be attending the convention because New Hampshire’s primary is on Tuesday. (The convention is on Wednesday and Thursday.)

And in Alaska, Senator Dan Sullivan, the incumbent Republican, faces a tough challenge from former Representative Mary Peltola, a Democrat, in a state that is conservative but maintains an independent streak. Both candidates have tried to avoid close ties with their parties in the Lower 48. “Senator Sullivan is spending this week campaigning across Alaska,” said Nate Adams, a spokesman for Mr. Sullivan. “The senator looks forward to welcoming President Trump to the state ahead of the November election.”

Kellen Browning is a Times political reporter based in San Francisco.

Smithsonian’s Secretary to Resign as Trump Tries to Rule the Institution

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Attacks on Smithsonian

Advertisement

Supported by

In the face of escalating White House attacks about how museums present American history, Lonnie G. Bunch III has announced his decision to depart.

By Robin Pogrebin and Graham Bowley

After a seven-year run marked most recently by attacks from the Trump administration, Lonnie G. Bunch III announced on Tuesday that he was stepping down as secretary of the Smithsonian Institution.

The White House has escalated its criticism of how the Smithsonian presents American history and values, prompting concern from some about what they see as an assault on the institution’s autonomy and commendation from others for reining in an organization they view as overtaken by liberal bias.

In an interview, Mr. Bunch, 73, said it was not the pressure that had led to his departure.

“It was really just saying, now’s the time,” he said.

“I’m a fighter,” he added.

At the same time, he acknowledged the strain of the role.

“I have to be honest, it has been stressful,” he said. “And at a certain point, I’d like to wake up in the morning and not look at my cellphone.”

In a statement, Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr., who serves as the Smithsonian’s chancellor, said that Mr. Bunch had “pursued excellence in the telling of our nation’s story” and that the Smithsonian had “benefited greatly from his wisdom, vision and leadership.” The Smithsonian said Mr. Bunch was expected to depart at the end of the year.

The White House did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Mr. Bunch sent a poignant farewell letter to his staff on Tuesday, signing it “Your forever colleague.”

“The Smithsonian represents far more than a career to me,” he wrote. “It has become an integral part of who I am. At this moment, I feel like I am in a Frank Capra movie. Thanks to all of you, I have a wonderful life.”

For more than a year, Mr. Bunch has tried to balance diplomacy and openness to criticism with a determination to resist a White House push to present what President Trump calls “patriotic” history. Some admire how Mr. Bunch has managed to quietly hold the line against the White House. Others believe that the Smithsonian has shown too much deference to Mr. Trump and even engaged in self-censorship.

Last year, the painter Amy Sherald withdrew her blockbuster show at the National Portrait Gallery over a disagreement about how the museum would display her portrait of a transgender Statue of Liberty.

But Mr. Bunch said he had no regrets. “My goal has been to win, not to make me feel good,” he said. “To win — to protect the Smithsonian — there were times I would fight, make clear what the red lines were. And there were other times I let things go.”

Mr. Bunch, a widely respected historian who previously oversaw the creation of the National Museum of African American History and Culture, said his next chapter would most likely include teaching or a fellowship.

Created by Congress as a trust in 1846, the Smithsonian has long been viewed as independent of the executive branch. Its governing Board of Regents must now appoint a new leader in the face of withering attacks from the administration.

The 17-person panel, led by Chief Justice Roberts, includes six members of Congress, split along party lines; nine private citizens; and Vice President JD Vance. The terms of three citizen members have recently expired, and the names of replacement nominees have not made it to Congress, an unusual holding pattern that appears to be evidence of the shadow war over control of the Smithsonian.

In the short term, Mr. Bunch seemed to have sufficient board support to stay on. But he has indicated that he is weary of the fray and ready for some form of retirement.

“When you’re Black in America, you’ve got to figure out how to get through, right?” he told The New York Times in May. “You’ve got to figure out how to build allies, when to stand firm, when to bang the table. So in some ways, all of that prepared me for this moment.”

“But do I wish I was in it?” he continued, referring to scrutiny by the Trump administration. “Of course not. Good Lord, I wish that I was doing my goodbye tour.”

Over nearly 40 years in various roles at the Smithsonian, Mr. Bunch developed a reputation as a soft-spoken diplomat adept at raising money and dealing with public officials. As the institution’s first Black secretary, he has at times been a forceful voice on issues of race, particularly after the 2017 white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Va., and in the wake of George Floyd’s murder in Minneapolis in 2020.

Mr. Trump did not pay much attention to Washington’s cultural organizations in his first term but has made them a focus of his second, including through his efforts to govern, close and renovate the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. The Smithsonian has been forced to respond to White House demands or risk potential cuts to its $1 billion budget, which is largely funded by the federal government.

Last month, in a letter to the board, Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, and Vince Haley, a senior White House adviser, made the stakes clear: “Executive departments and agencies cannot in good conscience continue to support the Smithsonian under current leadership.”

The president’s attempt to overhaul the Smithsonian began last year with an executive order that accused the institution of promoting “narratives that portray American and Western values as inherently harmful and oppressive” and called for an end to spending on exhibitions or programs that “degrade shared American values, divide Americans based on race or promote programs or ideologies inconsistent with federal law.”

After the White House demanded that the Smithsonian turn over information about its exhibitions, Mr. Bunch reasserted the institution’s independence while saying that materials had been submitted in an effort to be “transparent.”

The board adopted a resolution that called for its 21 museums to review their content for partisanship or bias. But the administration began its own review of exhibitions, wall text and social media to assess “tone, historical framing and alignment with American ideals.”

Mr. Trump has been unrelenting in his criticism, posting on social media that “the Smithsonian is OUT OF CONTROL, where everything discussed is how horrible our Country is, how bad Slavery was, and how unaccomplished the downtrodden have been — Nothing about Success, nothing about Brightness, nothing about the Future. We are not going to allow this to happen.”

The president also announced online that he was dismissing the director of the National Portrait Gallery, Kim Sajet, calling her “a highly partisan person, and a strong supporter of DEI.” (The Smithsonian insisted it controlled personnel matters, but Ms. Sajet resigned, citing the institution’s best interests.)

The White House pressure reached a new pitch this year with a July 4 report about the National Museum of American History that accused its director of “radical activist ideology” and the museum of undermining “faith in American institutions.”

Many historians expressed serious concern about the report, but some conservatives applauded it, joining Mr. Trump in arguing that exhibits had become overly focused on race, identity and injustice.

“Hardworking Americans don’t want their taxpayer dollars dedicated to Marxist indoctrination,” Senator Mike Lee, Republican of Utah, wrote on social media.

After the report, Anthea M. Hartig, the museum’s director, came under fire at congressional hearings. Mr. Trump ordered warning signs installed to convey his view that the museum did not accurately reflect American history. The signs have yet to materialize.

Mr. Bunch said it had been difficult to have his colleagues attacked by the administration. “I have always tried to protect people,” he said. “So I’ve always said, ‘Let most of the weight fall on me. They don’t deserve it.’ We’re in a time when people are being hurt.”

His priority has been “How do I always make sure that we put the Smithsonian in the strongest position?” Mr. Bunch said. “That we articulate what we believe in, the importance of nonpartisanship and scholarship?”

When Mr. Bunch became the leader of the African American museum in 2005, that institution remained a distant dream.

He worked with Congress to fund it and attracted big-name donors like Oprah Winfrey. He appointed Republicans like Laura Bush and Colin L. Powell to the board and won support by arguing that the museum should recognize the horrors of slavery and the struggle for civil rights while celebrating historical Black achievements.

The museum opened to great fanfare in 2016 and was the Smithsonian’s fourth-most-popular destination last year, with 1.6 million visitors.

In the spring, Mr. Bunch said he was proud of what the Smithsonian had achieved under his leadership despite the barrage of Trump attacks. “Nothing can take that away,” he said. “So I’m trying to make sure I don’t let this moment steal my joy.”

This week, he spoke of how important it was for the Smithsonian to continue to explore the country’s past in all its complexity. “Americans are an amazingly brave people, who have accomplished so much,” he said. “They’ve got to be brave enough to face their own history.”

“To me, that is essential,” he continued. “And I will stand against wind and tide to prevent history from being erased, softened and made palatable. That’s wrong.”

Robin Pogrebin, who has been a reporter for The Times for more than 30 years, covers arts and culture.

Graham Bowley is an investigative reporter covering the world of culture for The Times.

A Doctor Sued 700 Patients for Debts; 81 Were Arrested. Now He’s a Senator.

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

TIMES EXCLUSIVE

Patients sued by Senator Roger Marshall of Kansas were routinely charged 18 percent interest, The Times found. Some had bank accounts garnished.

By Sarah Kliff

Sarah Kliff reviewed thousands of pages of court records and interviewed eight people whom Roger Marshall sued over medical debt.

It was Easter weekend in 2007 when a police car pulled up to Joe Vasquez’s home in rural Kansas.

A doctor had filed a lawsuit against him and his wife over an unpaid $4,561 bill from her emergency hysterectomy three years earlier. They had missed a court date, and the doctor’s lawyers asked the court to issue an arrest warrant.

The police took the couple into custody as their grandchildren prepared for an egg hunt, Mr. Vasquez said. They spent two days in jail before their son could borrow the money to post bond.

“We had no money to pay,” said Mr. Vasquez, now 68. At the time, his wife was working at a manufacturing plant and he was on disability, he said.

The doctor who sued the couple was Roger Marshall, now a senator from Kansas. Mr. Marshall, a Republican who is seeking re-election this fall, filed lawsuits against more than 700 patients with outstanding bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, according to a New York Times analysis of Kansas court records.

Patients were arrested in 81 of those cases for missing court dates, the records show. In an additional 13 lawsuits, Mr. Marshall’s lawyers sought warrants but it is unclear whether an arrest occurred.

They also garnished patients’ paychecks and bank accounts. They routinely charged patients an 18 percent annual interest rate.

The unpaid bills ranged from several thousand dollars to as little as $101. About half the lawsuits were filed under Mr. Marshall’s name and the rest by Heartland Regional OBGYN, the medical practice he solely owned from 1998 to 2012 and then co-owned with another doctor from 2013 to 2019.

Some facing lawsuits were new mothers with outstanding bills from their deliveries. Most lived in Barton County, a rural area with above-average uninsured and poverty rates. Some patients the Times spoke with lacked insurance; others had health coverage but were responsible for part of their bill.

“I had every intention to pay, I was just struggling,” said Kellie Clutts, whom Mr. Marshall sued in 2015 over a $129 bill. Ms. Clutts said the charge was from a postpartum visit shortly after her daughter’s birth.

Mr. Marshall sued Ms. Clutts when her baby was 9 months old and eventually garnished her bank account.

“I was recently divorced, trying to do everything on my own,” said Ms. Clutts, 45. “I told them I could make partial payments, but it seemed like no matter what I said, they wanted the full amount at once.”

In response to detailed questions from the Times, a spokeswoman for Mr. Marshall said that he spent decades caring for patients regardless of their ability to pay.

“Judges issue warrants when people repeatedly miss court dates, not doctors,” the spokeswoman, Payton Fuller, wrote in a statement.

Court records show that Mr. Marshall’s lawyers repeatedly requested arrest warrants, including in Mr. Vasquez’s case. They filed dozens of briefs arguing that warrants were needed because of the defendant’s “refusal to obey Court orders.”

Steven Johnson, a lawyer who often represented Mr. Marshall in debt cases, defended the warrants and ensuing arrests as necessary to ensure that debtors attended court dates.

“If defendants were allowed to appear only when they wanted to without any consequences the court would get no business done,” he wrote in a text message.

He said that Mr. Marshall was “no different” than his other clients in allowing his law firm to take the steps they felt were necessary to pursue an outstanding bill. As a client, Mr. Marshall was not involved in decisions about when to seek warrants, arrests, or garnishments, Mr. Johnson said, but did set the 18 percent interest rate in a contract he had patients sign. Mr. Marshall’s office did not respond to a question from The Times about who set the interest rate.

Doctors have wide discretion in how to handle unpaid bills. They can decide when to involve a debt collector, file lawsuits or drop the debt entirely if a patient seems unable to pay.

“There is a lot of variation,” said Barak Richman, the co-director of the health law program at George Washington University who has studied medical debt litigation in three states. “There are a lot that do bring lawsuits but also a whole lot that don’t. It’s not because they’re in a different position, they’ve just decided they’re not going to do it.”

Some hospitals and doctors have increasingly relied on litigation as insurance deductibles have risen, leaving patients responsible for a great share of their bills.

Even so, wage garnishments and arrests of patients are “definitely on the extreme side,” Mr. Richman said.

Neale Mahoney, an economist at Stanford University, has conducted research in one state finding that lawsuits against patients are relatively rare, with about 1.7 percent of hospital stays resulting in litigation.

“It’s not surprising there are outliers but this does seem to be an extreme case,” in terms of how far a doctor went to pursue debt, Mr. Mahoney said.

Federal law made debtors prisons illegal centuries ago but many states’ laws allow for arrests when the defendant in a debt lawsuit misses a court date.

The Times interviewed eight people Mr. Marshall sued between 2003 and 2015. Most described themselves as living paycheck to paycheck, often deciding between paying medical bills or buying groceries. Two said that the bills Mr. Marshall pursued in court stemmed from late miscarriages that required surgery.

Mr. Marshall stopped practicing medicine after winning election to Congress in 2016. But some of his collection work continued during his time serving in the House of Representatives, from 2017 to 2021, The Times found.

Mr. Marshall spent more than 25 years practicing obstetrics before running for Congress in 2016. In campaign materials, he frequently trumpeted his work delivering babies and the financial success of his medical practice. Both his Senate and his campaign websites refer to him as “Doc Marshall.”

“For 5,000 Kansans, life began here, in the trusted hands of Dr. Marshall,” an ad during his 2020 campaign for Senate said, showing the senator holding two newborns.

His current campaign website says that he was often “the only OB-GYN in the area” in his largely rural region of the state. He has also highlighted his care of low-income patients. Sometimes, he said in 2017, women drove “over a hundred miles” to see him because he accepted Medicaid, the public health benefits program for the poor.

In 1998, he and eight other doctors opened a four-bed surgical center in Great Bend. It steadily grew into a full-service hospital generating tens of millions of dollars in revenue. He served as the hospital’s board chairman, and his family remained co-owners of the hospital until March 2017, two months after he was sworn into office.

Mr. Marshall earned salaries both from his obstetrics practice and the hospital. In 2015, his combined earnings from the two was about $780,000, his 2016 financial disclosure report shows. His current worth is between $3 million and $9.8 million, according to his most recent financial disclosure report.

Great Bend Regional Medical Center also filed hundreds of lawsuits against patients during the years Mr. Marshall was either an investor or board chair.

More than a dozen of those lawsuits occurred while Mr. Marshall served in Congress and before he sold his ownership stake in the hospital, according to Kansas court records and Mr. Marshall’s financial disclosures.

Ms. Fuller, Mr. Marshall’s spokeswoman, said that the hospital “provided millions in uncompensated care” and “used the exact same billing and outside collection procedures as every other business or hospital in Kansas.”

She added, “Sixty days before an election, The New York Times has decided that a rural doctor keeping the hospital’s lights on is some kind of scandal. Kansans know better.”

When Mr. Marshall was elected to Congress, he quickly parlayed his experience as a doctor and health care investor into a central role in Republicans’ 2017 attempt to repeal the Affordable Care Act, the sweeping health care law enacted under President Barack Obama. “I may be the only physician in Congress to help run a hospital,” he said.

In July 2025, he introduced legislation that would prohibit hospitals from suing patients if they did not publicly post their medical prices.

The first time Meischa Zimmerman was arrested for missing a court date related to a C-section bill from Mr. Marshall was in 2011. She was home with her 2-year-old, and eight months pregnant.

“I asked them quietly: Can you not handcuff me in front of my daughter?” said Ms. Zimmerman, 44. “I explained to my daughter I was going for a ride.”

Ms. Zimmerman was arrested twice more, in 2013 and 2016, each time posting $200 bonds that would go toward paying down her debt, according to receipts The Times reviewed. Court records indicate that she was hand-delivered notices of the hearings she needed to attend, but Ms. Zimmerman said she did not receive such documents.

Her last arrest occurred the week after Mr. Marshall won his first congressional election.

Ms. Zimmerman was uninsured during the earlier pregnancy, in 2009, but had explored enrolling in Medicaid. All states offer Medicaid coverage to low-income women during pregnancy and for a short period after. But states set their own income caps, and Kansas has long had one of the lowest in the country, limiting the benefit to women who earn less than 150 percent of the poverty line.

Ms. Zimmerman was not working at the time and thought she might qualify. She made an interview appointment at her local Medicaid office but went into labor the night before, so didn’t show up and never completed the paperwork. Five months later, with her $3,596 bill for the delivery still unpaid, Mr. Marshall sued her.

“I had to choose whether I’d pay my electricity or pay $50 to a doctor who didn’t need it,” she said.

Ms. Zimmerman said she set up a $50 monthly payment plan in 2010 but sometimes could not keep up. Mr. Marshall’s law firm was charging 18 percent interest on her bill, and she recalls being told that it had ballooned to over $7,000 with interest.

Ms. Zimmerman is among 81 patients whose court records indicate that an arrest occurred. Their debts ranged from $114 to $4,683. In some cases, efforts to collect a debt would continue for over a decade and lasted into Mr. Marshall’s congressional career.

Most patients did not attend their original court date, which led to a default judgment. Four of the eight patients The Times interviewed said they never received their summons, which court records indicate were typically delivered by mail. Some sent in handwritten letters asking for leniency.

One, whom Mr. Marshall sued in 2004 for $1,200, asked that she not be held liable for care she received “for me and my twins (who I lost).” She was still found responsible for the bill.

Another hired a lawyer, who wrote a brief protesting a $520 bill for a surgery to remove placenta that remained in a patient’s uterus after childbirth.

“The service that the plaintiff seeks payment for should have been part of the original birthing services for which the plaintiff has already been paid,” the lawyer argued. That case was dismissed.

Mr. Vasquez said he did not recall receiving a summons for his lawsuit or a notice of his court date in 2007. Court records indicate both documents were delivered.

The couple had health insurance, he said, but believe something went wrong with the billing. Mr. Vasquez recalls Mr. Marshall’s office offering a $250 monthly payment plan that he could not afford.

“Every little bit of money we were getting went for rent and bills,” he said.

Mr. Vasquez was recovering from surgery, with fresh stitches in his arm, when the police arrived at his house. Because of that, he was not handcuffed and was kept in a solitary cell.

“It was just me in that itty-bitty room,” he said.

After the arrest, the Vasquezes worked with a law firm to roll this and other debts into a payment plan. Eight years later — 11 years after the emergency surgery — in November 2015, Mr. Marshall’s lawyers filed a letter with the court releasing the judgment against them.

Susan C. Beachy and Stella Raine Chu contributed research.

Sarah Kliff is an investigative health care reporter for The Times.

Iceland Summons U. S. Ambassador Over Provocative Trump Map

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

After voting against talks to join the European Union, Iceland is reacting forcefully to a slight against its sovereignty.

By Amelia Nierenberg

A day after summoning the American ambassador for a formal rebuke, Iceland’s leaders on Tuesday publicly condemned a social media post from President Trump showing the American flag covering their nation along with Greenland, Canada, Mexico and Caribbean states.

“It is an insult to Icelanders, Canadians, Greenlanders,” Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir of Iceland told reporters on Tuesday, referring to Mr. Trump’s Monday post, which did not include any written commentary.

“There is nothing funny or normal about making fun of the sovereignty of states,” she added.

Icelanders have been wary of Mr. Trump since he threatened Greenland, their closest neighbor. Now, this social media post feels like a marked escalation in rhetoric, said Eirikur Bergmann, a politics professor at Bifrost University in Iceland.

“Icelanders are used to looking toward the U. S. as Iceland’s defender,” he said. “Now, our protector has become our intimidator.”

The American Embassy in Reykjavik declined to comment on Mr. Trump’s post or Iceland’s response, and the White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Trump’s post tests Iceland’s resolve just over a week after the Nordic country voted against exploring European Union membership.

That vote sharply divided public opinion, as many of the 400,000 people living in Iceland felt like they were at a turning point. Many said that the vote came down to questions of how to protect their stability and sovereignty.

Some Icelanders, who wanted to explore membership, saw the bloc as a potential protector in a world where superpowers are circling the Arctic and Mr. Trump is shaking international alliances. Iceland, the only NATO member without its own military, relies on the alliance for protection. And Mr. Trump’s aggressive remarks about Greenland have alarmed many Icelanders.

Icelandic voters who wanted to explore E. U. talks said in interviews that they were shocked when Mr. Trump repeatedly confused Iceland with Greenland in a major speech in January. Many, too, were offended by reports that Billy Long, Mr. Trump’s pick to be the new American ambassador, joked in private that Iceland could become the 52nd state. (Mr. Long apologized.)

But late last month, those voters lost out to Icelanders who thought it would be better for Iceland to stay out of the bloc.

Now, Professor Bergmann said, Iceland’s choice to go it alone is heightening the national anxiety.

“Iceland doesn’t have the same options as before of fleeing into the arms of Brussels as a response to an intimidation like this,” he said.

In a show of sovereignty and outrage, Iceland’s government is reacting forcefully to Mr. Trump.

Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir, the foreign minister, summoned Mr. Long to express what her ministry called a “clear message that the image was wholly inappropriate.”

The ministry did not make Ms. Gunnarsdottir available for an interview.

Ms. Gunnarsdottir told reporters that Trump administration officials had repeatedly offered her advice about their boss: “We should perhaps not take the current U. S. president literally, but we should take him seriously,” she said she was told.

This post, she said, crossed a line.

“This is not a joke in my opinion,” she said.

“And if this is supposed to be a joke,” she continued, “it’s a bad joke.”

Egill Bjarnason contributed reporting from Husavik, in northern Iceland.

Amelia Nierenberg is a Times reporter covering international news from London.

Trump Posthumously Awards Top Civilian Honor to ‘Man in the Red Bandanna’

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Sept. 11

Advertisement

Supported by

Welles Remy Crowther, an equity trader and volunteer firefighter, is credited with saving 18 people at the World Trade Center on Sept. 11 before being killed.

By Karoun Demirjian

Reporting from Washington

President Trump on Tuesday posthumously awarded the nation’s highest civilian honor to Welles Remy Crowther, an equities trader who rescued 18 people from the south tower of the World Trade Center on Sept. 11, 2001, before being killed when the building collapsed.

“He just did things that people said were not even imaginable,” Mr. Trump said as he presented the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Mr. Crowther’s mother, Alison Crowther, and his sister Paige Crowther Charbonneau.

“Up and down, up and down, up and down, over and over again, saving life after life,” Mr. Trump added during a ceremony on the Ellipse, a park south of the White House, to honor emergency workers who responded on Sept. 11.

Mr. Crowther, then 24, had been working on the 104th floor of the south tower when United Airlines Flight 175 struck the building. The rescues he is known for happened on the 78th floor, where he heard cries for help while descending the building’s only working stairwell, and came to light in a 2002 New York Times article featuring multiple survivors who recalled having been rescued by “the man in the red bandanna.”

Two months later, Alison Crowther read that article and realized the man was her son, who had trained as a volunteer firefighter. His father, also a volunteer firefighter, had given him the bandanna that he used as a mask against fire and smoke while helping people escape the crumbling south tower that day.

On Tuesday, Ms. Crowther stressed that her son’s training as a firefighter had made it possible for him to rescue others that day.

“Welles would not have been able to do what he did as effectively on 9/11 if it had not been for the training and experience he gained as a member of Empire Hook and Ladder Company, No. 1,” Ms. Crowther said, referring to the volunteer company in Nyack, N. Y., that Mr. Crowther joined when he was 16. Other members of the company were in attendance for the ceremony on Tuesday.

“He was no longer an equities trader on 9/11; he was a firefighter,” she added.

In some cases, Mr. Crowther guided survivors who could walk to the remaining functional stairwell; in others, Mr. Trump stressed, he pulled people from the damaged building and carried them down the stairs. Mr. Crowther was in the lobby of the south tower, the president noted, when it collapsed.

Mr. Trump announced in May that he would be giving the Presidential Medal of Freedom to Mr. Crowther’s family. Representative Mike Lawler, Republican of New York, had been campaigning for that recognition. Mr. Lawler has also filed legislation to give Mr. Crowther a Congressional Gold Medal.

But Mr. Trump said he had decided to award Mr. Crowther the presidential medal long before.

“A while ago, years, I promised Mom and sister that Welles was going to get the Presidential Medal of Freedom,” he said, adding: “We didn’t forget. We never forget.”

Karoun Demirjian is a breaking news reporter for The Times.

What Is Navier-Stokes?

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Artificial Intelligence

Advertisement

Supported by

OpenAI announced today that it had solved the problem, one of seven “Millennium Problems” seen as among the most important in higher mathematics.

By Cade Metz

On Tuesday, OpenAI announced that its latest A. I. technology, which has not yet been released to the public, solved an enormously complex math problem called “the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem.” Mathematicians sometimes call it “Navier-Stokes” for short.

Here is a brief guide to the problem.

It is one of seven “Millennium Problems” selected in the year 2000 by a nonprofit called the Clay Mathematics Institute as a way of advancing mathematics in the new millennium.

The institute, founded by a businessman named Landon T. Clay, offered a $1 million prize to the first mathematician who could solve each of the problems. Before OpenAI’s announcement, only one of the seven had been solved.

It looks at a series of mathematical equations that describe the movement of liquids, like water, and gases, like air.

These equations are often used to predict the weather. They can also be used to model the behavior of ocean currents or the climate as a whole. But mathematicians have struggled to understand parts of these equations.

The Navier-Stokes problem essentially asks if these equations become unreliable in certain situations; if there are cases where they can no longer be solved. This would imply, theoretically, that the laws of physics would break down under certain extreme conditions, that, for example, water could be made to spontaneously explode.

“Is there some initial fluid configuration where water splashes around and, at some point, all the energy implodes and sends all the water particles off into infinite velocity?” said Terence Tao, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles, describing the implications of the result. “Could you set some fluid in motion, watch it flow, and then it blows up?”

Not that we know of. And Dr. Tao adds that simulations of water flow have not shown that it could happen, either. But in its solution to the Navier-Stokes problem, OpenAI seems to have shown that it could happen in theory.

Cade Metz is a Times reporter who writes about artificial intelligence, driverless cars, robotics, virtual reality and other emerging areas of technology.

David Maxwell was among the staffers in the Texas attorney general’s office who accused Ken Paxton of abusing the power of his office, allegations that led to his impeachment. Mr. Paxton was acquitted.

By Beth Reinhard

A former top aide to Ken Paxton, the Republican attorney general of Texas, is appearing in a new online ad endorsing Mr. Paxton’s Democratic rival, James Talarico, in one of the most hotly contested and costly U. S. Senate races in the country.

The aide, David Maxwell, served as Mr. Paxton’s director of law enforcement for several years until 2020, when he and other high-level staffers accused Mr. Paxton of abusing the power of his office to help a campaign donor under federal investigation. The allegations were central to Mr. Paxton’s impeachment trial in 2023, in which he denied any wrongdoing and was acquitted by the Republican-led Texas Senate.

Last year, a judge awarded a total of $6.6 million to Mr. Maxwell and three other former aides to Mr. Paxton who had filed a whistle-blower lawsuit after their dismissals.

“Ken Paxton ended my five-decade career in public service because I blew the whistle on his corruption,” Mr. Maxwell says in the ad, wearing a dark suit and white cowboy hat.

Mr. Talarico, a state lawmaker, has focused his campaign on Mr. Paxton’s impeachment and other controversies in his career, calling him “the most corrupt politician in Texas.” One of Mr. Talarico’s earlier ads featured a story that has become political lore in Texas, in which Mr. Paxton filched a $1,000 Montblanc pen from a courthouse security tray.

But Mr. Paxton has shown striking resilience against accusations of corruption. Though Senator John Cornyn, ran a well-financed re-election campaign arguing that Mr. Paxton was unfit for public office, the attorney general trounced him in a Republican primary runoff earlier this year. In 2022, when Mr. Paxton was running for re-election as attorney general, he beat back a challenge from Republican George P. Bush, who put up billboards calling him a “crook” next to his mug shot from when he was charged with securities fraud. (In a deal with prosecutors, Mr. Paxton never admitted guilt in that case but agreed to pay nearly $300,000 in restitution.)

Tony Buzbee, a Texas attorney who represented Mr. Paxton at what he called a “sham” impeachment trial, said in a recent social media post, “All you naysayers who have written off Ken Paxton and are writing his epitaph clearly don’t know Ken Paxton.”

The new Talarico spot featuring Mr. Maxwell comes as the ad war in Texas is ramping up. The super PAC allied with President Trump recently reported investing $10 million in ads to support Mr. Paxton and attack Mr. Talarico — its first general election spending of the 2026 campaign.

Before he served under Mr. Paxton, Mr. Maxwell spent decades at the Texas Department of Public Safety, first as a highway patrolman and narcotics investigator and then as a member of the agency’s elite Texas Rangers investigative unit.

In an interview with The New York Times, Mr. Maxwell said he was a lifelong Republican who had occasionally voted for Democrats. He said he had never publicly endorsed a candidate before.

“I’m a lawman — I’m not a politician,” he said. “I’ve never asked a crook whom I was investigating if he was a Democrat or a Republican.”

Lauren McGaughy contributed reporting.

Beth Reinhard is an investigative reporter for The Times covering politics.

Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis Edge Back to the Brink of War

The New York Times September 08, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The Saudi authorities said dozens were injured in attacks by the Iran-backed militia and vowed to retaliate.

By Qasim Nauman and Vivian Nereim

Saudi Arabia vowed on Tuesday to retaliate against Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi militia after attacks by the group injured 73 civilians in the south of the kingdom, according to the Saudi authorities.

With the latest attacks, which also hit energy facilities in the kingdom, the two sides appeared to be edging toward full-blown war after weeks of escalating tensions.

The Houthis and the Saudi-backed government of Yemen have been at war since 2014, when the Houthis seized the capital, Sanaa.

Soon after, Saudi Arabia led a bombing campaign to try to restore the internationally recognized government, plunging Yemen into a devastating civil war until a fragile truce was reached in 2022.

The fighting has flared again amid the broader six-month war between the United States and Iran, which has roiled energy markets by choking off shipping routes for the export of oil and gas from the Persian Gulf.

A return to war in Yemen would further threaten the stability of the Middle East and most likely put even more pressure on global energy prices. The Houthis have vowed to attack Saudi energy infrastructure and disrupt the kingdom’s oil export routes in the Red Sea.

The price of Brent crude oil, the international benchmark, touched $99 a barrel following the latest attacks, its highest level since late July.

There has been intense fighting between the Houthis and the Yemeni government in recent days. The Saudi foreign ministry said the Houthi attacks had injured people in four regions of the kingdom, but did not specify when they happened.

The Saudi foreign ministry said Houthi attacks had caused injuries in four places.

Source: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia.

Adina Renner/The New York Times

“I do not believe the door to diplomacy is closed,” said Prince Faisal bin Farhan, the Saudi foreign minister, during a visit to Moscow on Tuesday. “The kingdom will always support peace and diplomatic solutions, but it will not hesitate to defend itself.”

On Tuesday, a Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, said on social media that the militia’s recent attacks in Saudi Arabia had been retaliatory. He accused the kingdom of launching 121 airstrikes in Yemen over the past three days, including one that he said had struck a prison, burying inmates under the rubble.

Saudi Arabia has not commented on those claims. The Yemeni government appeared to assume responsibility for at least some of the airstrikes, saying on Monday that its warplanes had struck Houthi military reinforcements in the west of the country.

The spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition in Yemen, Major General Turki Al-Maliki, said in a statement that the Houthi attacks were “a dangerous escalation.” He added that the coalition would take “all necessary measures and actions to respond to the sources of the threat.”

The Saudi energy ministry said in a statement on social media that the latest attacks on energy facilities had caused fires at some locations and temporarily disrupted operations.

Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst for Yemen at the International Crisis Group, said the country was “sliding back toward large-scale war.” De-escalation is “not impossible,” he said, “but realistically, it is becoming very difficult.”

Video footage released Monday by the Houthis on social media appeared to show the aftermath of a strike on a site that the group said was a prison in al-Hazm city, the capital of Yemen’s northern province of al-Jawf, in Houthi-controlled territory. The New York Times tracked the footage to a compound near municipal buildings in the north of the city.

Al-Masirah TV, a Houthi-controlled broadcaster, reported Tuesday that Saudi jets had struck targets in the cities of Taiz and Marib. The Saudi government has not commented on that claim.

Fighting in Yemen intensified last week as the Houthis tried to capture territory that could give them more control over shipping routes through the Red Sea, according to local security officials. In July, the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi shipping through the Red Sea, and have since launched several attacks on Saudi vessels in the region.

Saudi officials have tried to avoid a direct war with the Houthis, but “it is becoming impossible for them not to do so,” said Farea Al-Muslimi, a research fellow on the Middle East and North Africa at Chatham House, a research group. “Today’s development speeds up the Saudi engagement in this war.”

It is unclear what Saudi Arabia’s goals would be if it were to go back to war with the Houthis. Few observers believe there is a realistic path to routing the militia entirely.

Instead, Saudi Arabia could aim to weaken the group and pressure it to negotiate a resolution to Yemen’s civil war that is more favorable to the kingdom and its Yemeni allies, analysts say.

When the kingdom last embarked on a bombing campaign against the Houthis, in 2015, it turned into a quagmire that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Yemenis from violence, hunger and disease, and failed to displace the Houthis.

Last month, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan signed a pact committing to collective defense against any attacks on the three nations. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif of Pakistan on Tuesday condemned the “cowardly attack” by the Houthis, but it was unclear whether the latest strikes would prompt a military response.

Ismaeel Naar and Sanjana Varghese contributed reporting.

Qasim Nauman is a Times editor in Seoul, covering breaking news from around the world.

Vivian Nereim is the lead reporter for The Times covering the countries of the Arabian Peninsula. She is based in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

A year after the Trump administration laid out its plan to improve the health of American children, we examine where those efforts stand.

Credit... Ricardo Santos

Supported by

By Dani Blum and Alice Callahan

The reporters cover the “Make America Healthy Again” movement and how Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s policies could affect Americans’ health.

Last September, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. released the government’s ambitious plan to improve the health of American children, promising reforms that he said would have been “unthinkable two years ago” and pledging to carry them out “very, very quickly.”

The highly publicized “Make Our Children Healthy Again” report laid out more than 100 goals, some that medical experts praised as worthwhile and many others that they dismissed as unscientific, potentially harmful or unlikely to improve children’s health.

The New York Times assessed the progress on the central promises in the four areas the report outlined — “poor diet,” “chemical exposure,” “lack of physical activity and chronic stress” and “overmedicalization” — and documented actions from the administration that have contradicted some of those goals.

In a statement, Grace Davis Jamison, a health department spokeswoman, wrote that Mr. Kennedy and President Trump have “delivered historic reforms that are fundamentally changing how the federal government approaches food, nutrition and chronic disease,” adding that the administration’s “record speaks for itself.”

REPORT PRIORITY NO. 1

The report proposed initiatives to improve children’s diets, including tightening oversight of chemicals in foods, developing a federal definition for ultraprocessed foods and restricting the marketing of unhealthy foods.

This move was supported by many health experts. But many also criticized the emphasis on meat and whole milk and the lack of transparency in the guidelines’ development, which included research reviews produced in secret by scientists with financial ties to the meat and dairy industries. (The report had promised to improve transparency and to reduce conflicts of interest in policymaking.)

A court has blocked those policies in five states. Many experts support the restrictions, and early research suggests they have reduced sugary drink purchases by 13 percent among SNAP participants.

The policy is intended to close the so-called “GRAS loophole,” which has allowed companies to add chemicals to their products without telling the F. D. A. If finalized, the rule could give the agency a clearer picture of substances in the food supply, but it wouldn’t require federal officials to vet a chemical’s safety before it was used. And experts worry that the F. D. A. lacks the resources to scrutinize new ingredients, much less the thousands of others already in our food, especially after cuts to the agency.

Many (though not all) have promised to do so. Many experts support phasing out the dyes but say that doing so is unlikely to affect rates of childhood diseases.

Mr. Kennedy had said this would be completed by the end of 2025, but the definition — which has been opposed by food industry groups — is still under review at the White House, with an uncertain fate.

There is not clear evidence that consuming more milk fat will improve children’s health. The White House is also reviewing draft rules for school meals, following Mr. Kennedy’s promise to put more “real food” on cafeteria trays. Until those rules are released and finalized, it is too soon to tell if they will lead to healthier school meals.

The money helped schools and food banks purchase produce for students and low-income families.

An estimated 5 million fewer people now receive them, including at least 1.2 million children, leaving more people unable to afford healthy foods.

The administration also eliminated the $536 million SNAP-Ed program, a nutrition education and obesity prevention program that funded cooking classes, community gardens and farmers markets.

Harry Fones, a spokesman from the Agriculture Department, wrote that the number of SNAP enrollees is “constantly changing and is not representative of any one policy,” adding that the department offers support to low-income families.

The report said the administration would develop front-of-package nutrition labels to help shoppers make better grocery choices, but federal officials have yet to take steps toward this. Nor have they moved to limit marketing of unhealthy foods to children.

REPORT PRIORITY NO. 2

The report highlighted chemical exposures as potential drivers of chronic disease and called for more research into air and water quality, microplastics and pesticides.

This includes $130 million in grand prize challenge funding for research into the health effects of chemical exposures and alternatives to pesticides, $100 million for research that could lessen pesticide use and $144 million for microplastics research. The administration also pledged to invest in regenerative agriculture, a type of farming that uses fewer pesticides.

That could theoretically lead to more research funding, but the proposal has not been finalized.

The agency discouraged their use, citing concerns about the chemical’s health effects. But experts said those supplements, already used sparingly, are important for children’s oral health.

Some studies have suggested the herbicide is carcinogenic, though the research is not yet settled. Facing a backlash, President Trump signed another order calling for the Environmental Protection Agency to prioritize approving pesticide alternatives and for studies on the health risks of pesticides. But the order did not provide new federal funding for that research or propose new regulations.

That includes changes that would allow trucks to emit more smog-producing chemicals. This pollution can be especially dangerous for children, whose lungs are still developing.

These “forever chemicals” have been linked to delayed development in children, as well as to an increased risk of some cancers and other health issues.

REPORT PRIORITY NO. 3

The report called for encouraging physical activity and increasing awareness about the effects of screen time.

However, the test is not mandatory, and a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention study found that few states are prepared to implement the test.

The report encouraged parents to delay screen time for “as long as possible.” Surgeon general’s warnings aim to educate the public, but do not change policy.

At the same time, experts have noted, the administration cut scores of other mental health grants.

While the report links chronic stress to factors like excess screen time, experts have noted that actions such as the Medicaid cuts, which could lead to millions of children losing coverage, could undermine youth mental health more broadly.

That funding, approved by Congress after the 2022 school shooting in Uvalde, Texas, supported school counselors and other services. A judge ordered the administration to restore some of it; a legal battle over the cuts is continuing.

Experts say the change could lead more teens to start vaping and become addicted.

REPORT PRIORITY NO. 4

The report made proposals to reduce what it called “overmedicalization,” or the idea that children are being given too many medications and vaccines. These included examining psychiatric drug use and vaccine recommendations, as well as reining in prescription drug advertising.

The administration’s actions included significantly reducing the number of routine vaccines recommended by the C. D. C. (Those changes have been blocked in court.) Mr. Trump also issued several executive orders calling to scale back childhood vaccinations.

This included new trainings to help doctors taper patients off psychiatric drugs. While some psychiatrists welcomed a push for clearer tapering guidelines, others were concerned the moves would stigmatize the drugs and lead to fewer people getting the help they needed from medication.

Mr. Kennedy has said such advertisements have “hooked” Americans on prescription medications. The agency sent thousands of warning letters to drug companies about their ads, including to a company advertising attention deficit disorder medications to children.

While these actions have not yet led to substantial changes in the shots available to American children, experts say the moves have undermined trust in safe and effective shots. They worry that could lead to a further decline in vaccination against diseases like pertussis, measles and hepatitis B. These diseases can lead to chronic health issues that can require medications to manage, two things the report aimed to address.

Dani Blum is a health reporter for The Times.

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.

Trump’s Mail Voting Plan Is Coming to a Head. Here’s What to Know.

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The administration’s plan to screen mail-in ballots remains blocked as the Supreme Court considers challenges to new U. S. Postal Service ballot rules.

By Abbie VanSickle

Reporting from Washington

With only weeks to go before the midterms, the Trump administration continues to try to press forward with plans to restrict voting by mail, even as its new rules remain frozen by the courts.

Prompted by an executive order by President Trump, the U. S. Postal Service adopted new rules for states that allow voting by mail — rules that some states have warned would be nearly impossible to comply with in time for the midterms.

The proposed limits on mail-in voting are the latest effort by Mr. Trump to sow doubt about voter fraud in American elections. Since his loss in the 2020 presidential election, he has repeatedly claimed, without evidence, that fraud is rampant among mail votes.

The new rules remain blocked as of Tuesday, while the Supreme Court considers the legality of the plan. But the scramble over the proposal has left local officials and voters confused less than two months before the midterms.

If the Postal Service plan is allowed to go into effect before the midterms, the agency would not deliver mail ballots in states that do not give voter data to the Postal Service, and it would deliver only ballots that meet certain criteria.

The new rules would force states to send lists of voters who receive mail-in ballots to the Postal Service. Although the Postal Service has said that the lists must be uploaded through a government portal, the portal is not yet live and online.

The rules also require that states use an approved envelope with a special bar code for ballots submitted by voters through the mail. This requirement would force counties and municipalities to get special printers to newly prepare the ballots.

Under the plan, the Postal Service would scan a few ballots out of batches prepared by election officials to be sent to voters, seeking to ensure sure the bar code on each ballot matches one included on a list of voters provided by the state.

If one of those ballots fails to match, the entire batch would be returned to election officials to fix the discrepancy, potentially causing delays.

The Trump administration has unrolled a plan to potentially restrict voting by mail by placing new requirements on states, just before the election. That plan remains frozen by the courts, at least for now.

Since the administration announced the proposal, a legal fight over the plan has made its way through the federal courts. The legal developments have been dizzying, confusing both voters and local officials. But the legal fight may now be coming to a head.

Got a news tip about the courts? If you have information to share about the Supreme Court or other federal courts, please contact us.

On Sunday morning, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to weigh in yet again on the plan, the third time that administration lawyers have asked the justices to clear the way for the new rules.

The case is an emergency application, which means it will be heard on what the court’s critics call “the shadow docket,” a truncated process in which the justices hear cases on a fast-tracked schedule, typically without full briefing or oral argument. A ruling could come later this week.

The Supreme Court is considering whether the Postal Service plan violates the Constitution.

In an executive order in March, President Trump directed the Postal Service to impose new requirements on voting by mail. Several Democratic state attorneys general and voting rights groups challenged the president’s order in court. Eventually, after a series of legal twists and turns, the Postal Service finalized its new rules in late August.

The groups challenging the new rules argue that the plan violates the Constitution’s division of power, which gives states and Congress, not the executive branch, responsibility for elections.

Lawyers for the Trump administration contend that the Postal Service rules are only modest changes and fall within the agency’s discretion to manage the mail under federal law.

The Postal Service plan has raised alarms among critics concerned that a rushed rollout in the weeks before the midterms could lead to chaos and confusion, potentially disenfranchising voters.

For now, it is unclear how states would even be able to transfer voter data to the Postal Service. The agency has said that states would upload data through an online portal, but, so far, none is available.

A whistle-blower report filed last week raised questions about whether the push to roll out the plan before the midterms would lead to errors with large batches of ballots being rejected.

Challengers have also raised fears about a part of the plan that mandates the Department of Homeland Security to draft lists of citizens and send those names to the states, arguing that those lists could be filled with errors, potentially disenfranchising valid voters.

That part of the executive order has also faced court challenges, and the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Tuesday to clear the way for it to make an online tool available for states to compare their voter rolls against federal citizenship and Social Security data.

Critics have also argued that the plan is an illegal move by the executive branch, which is overstepping its bounds and interfering in the role of states and Congress to run elections.

Some states have already begun sending mail-in ballots to voters. Two — North Carolina and Delaware — started mailing ballots on Friday.

Sixteen more are set to distribute ballots in the next two weeks.

It is not clear whether the Postal Service will process ballots without delay if jurisdictions do not abide by the new rules.

Reid J. Epstein, Eileen Sullivan and Nick Corasaniti contributed reporting.

Abbie VanSickle covers the United States Supreme Court for The Times. She is a lawyer and has an extensive background in investigative reporting.
