‘Don’t Let Me Disappear’: The 100-Day Scramble to Free Lue Yang

The New York Times September 08, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Lue Yang, who was convicted in a home invasion as a teenager, was facing deportation to Laos. With a plane on the tarmac, he wondered whether an appeal would be heard.

By Amy Qin

Amy Qin, who writes about Asian American communities, spent time with the Yang family at their home in St. Johns, Mich.

Lue Yang had just finished his overnight shift at a Michigan automotive plant when two unmarked cars with tinted windows pulled into the parking lot and blocked him in.

A man in body armor approached him. Mr. Yang knew that it was Immigration and Customs Enforcement. And, in those early morning hours of July 15, 2025, he knew why the agent was there.

Nearly three decades earlier, as a teenager, Mr. Yang had spent 10 months in jail after he and three friends were caught with stolen cash, electronics and cameras in the trunk of their car.

The consequences had not ended there. Mr. Yang was living in the United States as a war refugee. After his conviction, he lost his permanent residency status and was ordered deported to Laos, the country his family had fled.

For 23 years, the government did not enforce the final removal order. Mr. Yang went back to school, got married, had six children, built a career and became a leader in the Hmong community in Lansing. He checked in with ICE as required. He was never arrested again, said his lawyer, Nancy Xiong.

Now ICE had come for him as part of President Trump’s deportation campaign.

The agent agreed to escort Mr. Yang to his home in St. Johns, Mich., north of Lansing, so he could drop off his motorcycle before being locked up. Mr. Yang gripped the handlebars and tried to stay under the speed limit during the 35-minute ride through verdant fields of corn and soybeans.

As he approached home, he called his wife, Ann Vue, and asked her to come outside. Their children, the younger ones still dressed in their pajamas, trudged down the long gravel driveway alongside her. Mr. Yang hugged each child, and then, before agents placed him in handcuffs, he turned to his wife.

“Look for me,” Mr. Yang said as they embraced. “Don’t let me disappear.”

Those words reflected the start of a race that would stretch over 100 days. Somehow they had to get the deportation order lifted before a government plane flew Mr. Yang to Laos, a country he barely knew. And it would all come down to the last minute.

In a recent interview at her home, Ms. Vue, a U. S. citizen whose parents were also Hmong refugees, exuded the multitasking energy of a full-time working mother of a large brood. She zipped around the house, locating a lost phone charger for her youngest son, checking on Mr. Yang’s 100-year-old grandmother, finalizing details for the family’s upcoming weekend trip to Wisconsin, tending to the chickens milling around the front yard — all while answering a reporter’s questions.

Those juggling skills were put to the test during the months she fought to keep her husband in the country. She persisted even as some Hmong elders advised her not to resurface the shameful memory of Mr. Yang’s conviction and to let him go.

“Just thinking about a life without him was unbearable,” Ms. Vue said.

Mr. Yang spent his first night in detention in Baldwin, Mich., about two hours from home. Soon after, Ms. Vue and her children set up a gamer-style workstation in the basement — a laptop and five computer screens — so she could simultaneously read legal documents and monitor immigration-related news developments.

Her cellphone became a fifth limb. Her notes became a compendium. She took calls from Mr. Yang. She consulted immigration lawyers and advocacy groups for strategies and advice. She lobbied the staff of elected representatives.

But there were obstacles all around.

A lawyer explained that Mr. Yang did not qualify for release on bond since he already had a final removal order. But perhaps they could persuade local officials to vacate his criminal conviction, which would mean effectively erasing the original offense.

So Ms. Vue and her lawyers reached out to the local prosecutor in Clinton County, where Mr. Yang was arrested decades ago. They argued that his Sixth Amendment rights were violated because he was not told that pleading guilty could lead to deportation. But the prosecutor, Tony Spagnuolo, who ran as a Republican, was unwilling to budge. (Mr. Spagnuolo did not respond to a request for comment.)

In early August 2025, Ms. Vue sent a message to the office of Gretchen Whitmer, the Democratic governor, asking for a pardon. On its own, a pardon would not free Mr. Yang, but it could help reopen his federal immigration case and get his removal order lifted.

“Governor Whitmer, my husband is not a danger to anyone,” Ms. Vue pleaded in the letter. “We are asking for mercy. For compassion. For humanity.”

By then, Mr. Yang had been detained for three weeks.

Mr. Yang’s life story has its roots in the Vietnam War and the surrounding regional conflicts.

In Laos, the C. I. A. recruited Hmong to join the fight against communism in a campaign that became known as the “secret war.” Among the recruits was Lo Yang, Mr. Yang’s father, whose job included rescuing downed American pilots. To this day, the elder Mr. Yang still has shrapnel lodged in his skull from that time, Ms. Vue said.

After the United States withdrew, the Laotian government persecuted Hmong people for taking the other side in the war. In 1978, Lo Yang and his family fled to Thailand, where Lue Yang was born in Nong Khai, a refugee camp.

The next year, the family came to the United States as part of the resettlement of more than one million Southeast Asian refugees, an effort that many Americans saw as a moral obligation for the country’s role in the Vietnam War. They joined the tens of thousands of Hmong refugees resettling in cities like Lansing; St. Paul, Minn.; and Fresno, Calif. A black-and-white photo from a local Michigan newspaper in 1980 shows Mr. Yang’s parents posing alongside a patterned wall hanging they had woven as a thank-you gift to the church that had sponsored them.

Six more children came along, all American citizens by virtue of their birth in the United States. Mr. Yang’s parents worked constantly. His mother made doughnuts at a local convenience store chain. His father worked as a church janitor and, later, opened a small bait shop.

Through middle school, Mr. Yang excelled academically, particularly in math. But in 1997, his sophomore year of high school, he started to ditch class with a group of Hmong kids, some of whom were involved in gangs.

“It was like, ‘We’ll do some break-ins, but not when anyone’s home,” Mr. Yang recalled. “It was stupid.”

That spring, he sat in a car while three friends broke into an empty house. They tried to drive away with the goods, but the driver, Mr. Yang recalled, didn’t know how to work a stick shift.

A police officer stopped to help, and then realized the car matched a burglary alert, Mr. Yang said. Mr. Yang went to jail, and in 2002, the U. S. government ordered his deportation to Laos. At the time, though, the Laotian government was refusing to accept large numbers of U. S. deportees.

That diplomatic tussle allowed Mr. Yang to remain in the United States on supervised release for 23 years.

In 2025, with President Trump back in office and applying pressure, Laos and other countries began accepting much larger numbers of deportees. That is how Mr. Yang became locked up and faced the prospect of a one-way trip to Laos.

Ms. Whitmer’s office seemed receptive to a pardon. Her staff emailed Ms. Vue a blank application.

Ms. Vue scrambled to complete the forms. Yes, Mr. Yang was married. Yes, he had children — five sons and a daughter. Yes, the state had expunged his conviction in 2018 because his crime was old and he had demonstrated rehabilitation. Yes, he had paid all fines and restitution.

Was he a changed man? On that point, there was much to say. After getting out of jail, Mr. Yang had earned his G. E. D. and enrolled in community college. He had gone on to hold a series of jobs in car manufacturing facilities. To make ends meet, he had also worked at a McDonald’s flipping burgers.

By the time ICE arrested him, he had worked at the same automotive parts manufacturer for nearly a decade. He had worked his way up to becoming a torque technician, which requires meticulous precision to ensure that every nut and bolt is fitted to the exact specifications. He served as the president of the Hmong Family Association of Lansing, which provided translation, social services and food assistance for community members in need. And he was a Hmong spiritual healer, performing traditional blessings at births and other important life events.

The governor's office needed more than just Mr. Yang’s word. So Ms. Vue sent a mass text that reached the Hmong community and beyond. More than 200 people from California to Michigan wrote letters testifying to the man they knew.

A relative said that Mr. Yang had given him and their younger cousins “endless talks” about making good choices and staying in school, rewarding them $25 for each “A” that they received. A colleague wrote that Mr. Yang had risen at their company with his “bright attitude” and “natural leadership abilities,” even receiving an award for perfect attendance, a “stark contrast to his current absence.”

The president of a Hmong veterans association emphasized the risk of persecution that Mr. Yang could face as the son of a C. I. A.-allied fighter if he were deported to Laos.

In public and behind the scenes, Mai Xiong and Stephanie Chang, both Democratic state lawmakers in Michigan, lobbied for Mr. Yang’s release. And in a rare show of bipartisan support, United States Representative Tom Barrett, a Republican and an Army veteran, also joined the campaign to free Mr. Yang.

Still, the pardon application felt like a Hail Mary. Michigan rarely granted pardons. And requests typically took months to process.

But for Mr. Yang, having a team fighting for his release helped push him through some dark moments.

“That was pretty much what gave me a lot of strength in there,” Mr. Yang said. “Because otherwise it felt like the system was made to break people down.”

During their almost daily phone calls, Ms. Vue updated her husband on the status of his pardon application, even as they made plans for his deportation to Laos. Their children, who had never traveled abroad, had to get passports so they could visit. And they needed to find someone, perhaps a distant family friend, who could sponsor Mr. Yang’s release from the government-run detention facility once he arrived in Laos.

Mr. Yang told of his experiences in detention. An elderly Vietnamese man fainted because he had not received his medication for days. A young Indian guy, Sahil, paced in his cell and struggled to find enough food that complied with his vegetarian diet. On another day, Mr. Yang and a few others put together a birthday cake for another detainee with items from the commissary — white cake with jelly and a sprinkling of crushed Lemonhead candy.

Ms. Vue wrote down all the details. Mr. Yang was keeping his own journal, but he also wanted her to keep a record, partly so he could track his friends as they were separated, transferred around and ultimately deported.

The Department of Homeland Security has long insisted that detainees receive adequate care. In a recent emailed statement, Chandler Rebel, a department spokesman, said that detainees were given “three nutritious meals a day” with special religious accommodations and “comprehensive medical care from the moment an alien enters ICE custody.”

At the end of August, Mr. Yang was moved to a staging facility in Arizona, where some detainees are taken before being deported. He was shackled at the wrists, waist and ankles and led onto the tarmac with the other detainees, where a plane they were told was bound for Asia waited in the desert sun.

By the time Mr. Yang shuffled to the front of the line to board the plane, he was sweating from the heat. He had worn all the clothes he had with him, including four layers of socks to pad the ankle shackles. He was unsure if he would ever return to the United States and didn’t know when he might see his family again.

An officer patted Mr. Yang down to look for sharp objects and to check that the shackles were secure. Then the officer looked for Mr. Yang’s name on the list. It was missing.

Mr. Yang was pulled aside and then walked back to a holding cell, where he waited until he was loaded into a van with several other detainees who had also been removed from the plane at the last minute.

“I felt like I had dodged a bullet,” Mr. Yang recalled.

It wasn’t until nearly two months later that he was put on a plane that actually took off.

It was Oct. 22, 2025: 99 days into Mr. Yang’s detention. A deportation flight bound for Asia was scheduled to leave the next day.

Mr. Yang called Ms. Vue, this time from a staging facility in Louisiana. When Ms. Vue saw the “Prison” caller ID flash across the phone, she picked up immediately.

She couldn’t wait to share the news. Mr. Yang had been pardoned by Governor Whitmer.

From his holding cell, Mr. Yang flagged down an officer and explained the situation. His lawyers were at that very moment appealing to D. H. S. to stop his removal, he said.

The officer left and came back with a sheaf of papers. She had to follow orders, and Mr. Yang’s name was still on the deportation list.

His heart sank.

He was flown from Louisiana to Baltimore, where the plane was scheduled to stop for refueling before heading the next morning to Asia.

There was no way for Mr. Yang’s wife and lawyers to get in touch with him now. All they could do was watch the little plane icon on the online flight tracker as they worked into the night to draft motions to stay Mr. Yang’s removal.

The motions had to be filed in person at the Board of Immigration Appeals in Virginia. But the courier could not make it until the afternoon of Oct. 23, after the flight to Asia was scheduled to leave. If Mr. Yang were deported, it would be much more difficult for him to return to the United States.

On the morning of Oct. 23, Ms. Chang stood in the Michigan Senate chamber and pleaded with ICE to release Mr. Yang. Mr. Yang’s flight had been scheduled to take off from Baltimore two hours earlier, but his exact whereabouts at that moment were unknown.

“This morning, we believe Lue Yang is still in the United States,” Ms. Chang said, sniffling as she held back tears. “We still have a chance.”

On a large airliner, Mr. Yang shivered in the frigid cabin air and prayed. He had recited the Hmong soul-calling prayer countless times for relatives and friends who had looked to him for spiritual guidance in times of distress. Now, as his airplane hurtled down the runway, he found himself saying those familiar, comforting words for himself.

“Hey spirit, I’m leaving the United States now,” Mr. Yang remembered whispering to himself. “So if you are still behind, follow your body.”

Across the plane, Mr. Yang heard another deportee yell that he could see the ocean. This was it, Mr. Yang thought.

As the plane continued its journey, Mr. Yang’s thoughts turned toward his children. Had he been too hard on his youngest son when he took away his screen time for acting out on the school bus? Why hadn’t he taken his only daughter, Lily, a die-hard Hulk Hogan fan, to a wrestling event, as she had asked?

And what would he do in Laos?

Suddenly, Mr. Yang felt the aircraft tilting sharply. The other passengers on the plane — deportees from India, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Laos and Cambodia — cried out in confusion.

They were turning around.

Soon they were back in Louisiana, at the staging facility near the airport. Rumors spread that the plane had run into trouble getting clearance over international airspace.

That night, officials lined up the detainees once more and called out their names by country to shackle them again so they could re-board the plane. Mr. Yang listened as they made their way through the list of those going to Laos.

“You didn’t call my name,” Mr. Yang told the immigration officer.

The officer looked at his clipboard. “Are you from Detroit?” Mr. Yang recalled him asking.

“Yes,” Mr. Yang replied.

“We can’t send you anymore,” the officer said. He didn’t seem to know why.

As soon as he could, Mr. Yang called his wife. For 24 hours, she had been anxiously tracking the plane. Their three youngest kids were sleeping around her, as they had taken to doing ever since their father had been detained.

“Everyone’s gone,” Mr. Yang told her. “I’m still here.”

She heard a roar in the background. The plane was taking off again for Asia — without Mr. Yang.

It took more than a month for Mr. Yang to reopen his immigration case, get the removal order lifted, return home and reunite with his family. Once home, Mr. Yang went back to his old job, putting in extra hours so he could start paying back his legal fees. Last month, he finally had his permanent residency status restored.

But the joy of returning to familiar routines has been tempered by lingering uncertainty. The Department of Homeland Security maintains that Mr. Yang should have been deported and accused Ms. Whitmer in a recent emailed statement to The Times of endangering Michiganders with her decision to pardon Mr. Yang, whom the department called a “public safety threat.”

There is also the survivor’s guilt. During his time in detention, Mr. Yang became close to many people who, like him, were child war refugees who had committed crimes decades ago. Unlike him, they were still deported.

Since he has left detention, he and Ms. Vue have continued to help others in the Hmong community facing imminent deportation, offering advice about the pardon application process and emotional support for worried relatives. It was a way to pay forward the camaraderie that had sustained Mr. Yang through his months in detention.

“I miss the guys,” Mr. Yang wrote in his journal, not long after he was pulled off the plane some of his friends were still on. “Hope they are doing good.”

I’ve spent the past few months reporting on how recent deportation efforts are impacting Southeast Asian war refugees. Lue Yang’s case immediately stood out for its drama, but during my reporting, I found his story is far from unique. Many who came to the U. S. as young children were convicted of offenses as teenagers—sometimes relatively minor ones. Decades later, they face deportation to countries they barely remember or, as in Mr. Yang’s case, have never set foot in.

With state-level pardons often serving as their only line of defense, these cases raise a deeper question: How should our legal system—and society—define who is deserving of forgiveness? Does that change when the consequences are deportation?

Amy Qin is a national correspondent for The Times, writing primarily about Asian American communities.

OpinionGuest Essay

Credit...

Supported by

By Maxi Heitmayer

Dr. Heitmayer is an assistant professor at Rowan University who studies technology distraction, attention economics and digital culture.

Every decade or so, adults discover that young people are consuming media that corrupts their minds — and a moral panic ensues. Comic books were going to produce a generation of delinquents. Television would make children into couch potatoes. Video games and rap music would inspire them to do violent stuff. The internet would keep them shut away in the basement, typing in chat rooms to dangerous strangers.

Now the panic surrounds “brain rot” — the state of being entranced by an infinite stream of nonsensical TikToks and Instagram reels. Perhaps you overheard some of these videos this summer. The dancing cappuccinos and singing toilets and muscular fruit. The random bursts of noise and strobe flickers and wild visual effects. This can’t be good.

I research how digital environments shape human behavior. My co-author, Anna Götzfried, and I recently published a study interviewing Gen Z-ers aged 13 to 26 about how they experience brain rot — what these videos mean to them and why they watch them. What we discovered is a generation that is achingly self-aware of what brain rot is doing to their minds. They are struggling with the social media environment they have been given, and they are searching for a way out.

The panic over brain rot assumes that the brain-rot content itself is the problem. That Gen Z-ers’ engagement with absurd, low-quality videos, because they are young and impressionable, necessarily leads to cognitive decay. Our participants described the inverse: The mental state comes first. After scrolling algorithmically curated feeds long enough, they experience a “brain-rot feeling” — a fogged-out, low-selectivity state in which they simply consume whatever appears.

Brain rot emerged from social media platforms like TikTok and YouTube where the amount of attention you attract determines your success. Every piece of content on these platforms competes for the finite attention of users. This competition then pushes everything toward faster, louder, more stimulating but also simpler material. Simple content wins our attention.

The business model of social media treats user focus as a commodity to be extracted and sold. The more time we spend, the more advertising revenue we generate for the owners of the platforms. This attention economy increases engagement — it does not promote high-quality content.

What struck us in our interviews, however, was how clearly Gen Z understood this dynamic. (The interviews are anonymous, following social science conventions.) One participant told us: “You’ll watch something anyway, so why not brain rot? It’s actually better than an ad because it doesn’t demand anything from you.” Another argued: “If everything is content now, then brain rot is anti-content. It’s the only way to be free online, which is to do something so stupid it can’t be monetized.”

When we spoke to Gen Z-ers about brain rot, we heard sophisticated — if uncomfortable — statements outlining a generation’s response to the cultural conditions and the overbearing information environment it inherited. Like every generation before them, they are making something out of the conditions they were given. In this case, they are participating in deliberate nonsense.

To describe this process, my co-researcher and I introduced the concept of anti-gratification. Traditional media theory, going back to the 1970s, assumes people choose media to satisfy needs: They want information, emotional engagement, social connection, relaxation. But in an environment inundated with content that seeks to monetize your attention under the guise of educating you, entertaining you, motivating you or improving you in some other way, content that proudly offers nothing becomes a relief.

Brain rot breaks the mold of social media through its absurdity, its deliberate refusal of narrative, purpose or message. A century ago, artists responded to the horrors of World War I by creating deliberately irrational, anti-aesthetic work. Dada rejected the cultural logic that had led to industrialized killing.

In its own meme-driven way, brain rot refuses to participate in the attention economy on that economy’s terms. The joke is that there is no joke. The meaning is that there is no meaning. And for a generation that grew up with its every digital interaction tracked, measured and monetized, that refusal is experienced as a form of honesty in a dishonest system.

Our participants explicitly told us that because brain-rot content is visibly fake and/or A. I.-generated, it feels less exploitative than polished influencer posts pretending to be candid. “Everyone knows it’s generated,” one participant said, “so it feels less manipulative than posts that act like they’re just normal life.” When the simulation admits it is a simulation, it becomes more trustworthy than content that pretends to be real.

By no means do I seek to romanticize brain rot. Our findings were marked by profound ambivalence. The same participants who described brain rot as liberating also described feeling drained and guilty, and referred to the practice of watching until they fell asleep as “death scroll.”

One told us, “I’m scared I won’t find something I’m actually good at mainly because I don’t really have any hobbies. I guess brain rot is my hobby. Also, there is no more time during the day once you start watching.” Another broadly commented on her peers’ viewing behaviors: “They know it’s not good for them, but it gives that little hit and escape. And you just kind of ride it out, like the same way you do with any other vice.”

This ambivalence communicates the emotional register of people living inside a system they cannot escape. They see the manipulation, understand what the algorithms are doing. But they keep scrolling anyway, because they cannot imagine a life outside this system; most of them never lived one.

Consequently, nearly every one of the Gen Z-ers we spoke to explicitly asked for systemic, top-down change to social media platforms. Not through self-control apps or screen-time reminders but through the only mechanism they believe could work: regulation. One participant drew a direct parallel to tobacco: “Before the government regulated the tobacco industry, everyone was smoking, even though they knew it was bad. Because the environment encouraged and allowed for that to happen. Yeah, the doctors would smoke. Now we need to get into a state where the environment shifts so young people’s habits shift.”

The real story here is obscured by the moral panic. Brain rot is not evidence that young people are getting stupider. It is evidence that the attention economy is working exactly as designed, and that the people most immersed in it can see this more clearly than the people watching from the outside.

Brain rot is the collective recognition of a shared cognitive state; we have all been through the same algorithmic meat grinder. “The humor is deeply tied to feeling like you are part of an inside joke,” as one participant put it. “Brain rot gives you the sense that you’re in on something.” Repetitive catchphrases from brain-rot videos migrate out of digital spaces and into offline conversation, becoming part of everyday speech, without anyone’s “even understanding what those terms really mean.”

In this way, brain rot functions like slang: meaningless to outsiders, rich with social significance to those inside. Outsiders look at videos of singing toilets or a chimpanzee-banana hybrid set to a looping audio track and see cognitive decline. Those who have experienced brain rot see in-group membership and a brief reprieve from a media environment that otherwise demands something of them at every turn.

During the Great Depression, Donald Duck, a character who constantly failed at everything, offered millions of people emotional relief by turning their social conditions into comedy. Brain rot similarly channels the collective mood of Gen Z. The key difference is that Donald Duck was a corporate product pushed from above and brain rot is user-generated, spread through memes. This gives it a grass-roots authenticity that traditional media cannot replicate, even as the platforms hosting it remain corporate.

This leads us to the central problem we have encountered in our research: The paradox of anti-gratification is that it remains embedded within the boundaries of the system it opposes. Brain-rot content still generates engagement metrics, feeds data to algorithms and may make money for its creators, ultimately keeping users on a platform. Sure, the livelihood of human influencers may be affected as the sponsored content they put out loses market share, but the platforms continue to harvest user attention without any threat to their business model. I should also note here that stuffed toys and other merchandise based on brain-rot characters are widely available and in demand. Gen Z’s sense of rebellion through watching nonsense is sincere. Whether it is effective is a different question.

Henry David Thoreau is credited with first using the phrase “brain-rot” in “Walden” to critique traditional society’s suppression of curiosity, which he thought gave rise to simplistic, shallow thinking. Today’s suppression comes from an infrastructure so pervasive and so well designed that the people living inside it can describe its mechanisms in detail and still not escape them.

We should be worried. But not about our kids or the content they produce and consume. We should be worried about the infrastructure of social media that has made sustained, focused attention — the very capacity required for individual growth, deep personal connection and societal participation — feel unattainable for an entire generation. Instead of debating whether teenagers are ruining their brains with Ballerina Cappuccina, we should be asking why the world’s most sophisticated technology companies are systematically optimizing for cognitive depletion to harvest our attention.

To treat brain rot, we need to treat the infrastructure problem it lays bare. Platforms could measure success not by time spent, but by users feeling their time was spent well. They could endeavor to make algorithmic decision-making more transparent rather than more opaque. When they recognize that users have entered states of cognitive depletion, they could design for relief rather than exploiting them for additional engagement. They could allow groups of users to support each other with sticking to their social media times, rather than isolating the individual against an algorithm designed to blow past any limits. None of this is technically difficult, but it is commercially inconvenient. And that is why it will not happen voluntarily.

In my more than a decade of research on technology distraction, not one participant has ever reported spending too much time on a device using maps, checking the weather or Shazaming songs. We all know where the problem lies. Gen Z is behaving as expected by the system we have put them in. Brain rot is a cry for help.

This piece really resonated with me. As a high school teacher, how do I compete for a student's attention when I'm going up against a technology that has been perfected by tens of thousands of engineers, marketers, and designers with hundreds of billions of dollars on the line? It's an asymmetric information contest which is incredibly draining.

@Gregory Ancmon Thank you for sharing this! I am afraid it is worse than asymmetric information. In an earlier study we filmed people using their smartphones in everyday life and found that 89% of interactions were initiated by the user, not by a notification. People reach for the phone roughly every five minutes and afterwards often don't fully remember why they did it. So you aren't competing with a device that buzzes and pushes information. You are competing with a habit developed over years, and no teacher should be expected to win that alone.

Maxi Heitmayer is an assistant professor at Rowan University who studies technology distraction, attention economics and digital culture.

A Place Where Memories of the 9/11 Victims Have Faded Away

The New York Times September 08, 2026

Sept. 11

Advertisement

Supported by

Relatives who traveled to the U. S. Navy base in Guantánamo Bay left memory stones and messages for those killed in the attacks 25 years ago.

By Carol Rosenberg

Reporting from Guantánamo Bay, Cuba

A few years ago, relatives of people killed in the Sept. 11 attacks began leaving messages at a monument in Guantánamo Bay near the courtroom built to put accused terrorists on trial. It was a way to remember a loved one in the enormity of the tragedy.

Inside a heart drawn on a stone, Deborah Garcia wrote a love note to her husband, David, and left it beneath the American flag at the site.

“Here to get you justice,” someone else wrote on a conch shell.

“Never forget 9/11,” another message said.

The words are now all gone.

With the approaching 25th anniversary of the attacks that changed the United States, a grim reality has overtaken the place of remembrance. The messages, written on shells, stones and chunks of coral, have been washed away by tropical rains and bleached white by the Caribbean sun.

Time and justice have not been kind to the families of the nearly 3,000 men, women and children who were killed on Sept. 11, 2001. The 19 hijackers died in the attack, and U. S. commandos hunted down and killed Osama bin Laden in 2011. But none of the five prisoners charged in the plot have gone on trial.

A military judge recently set June 5, 2028, for the start of jury selection. But the death-penalty case at the U. S. Navy base in Guantánamo is in its 14th year, and with appellate questions mounting, there is no end of the effort to find justice in sight.

Ms. Garcia has been coming to Guantánamo since 2023 to watch the hearings and seek justice for her husband, a computer programmer from Long Island.

She said she went that first time “for my presence, my story and my husband’s life to be acknowledged. To not let them take my power.”

Hers has been a tragic road to Guantánamo, as recounted in her blog. Her husband died at 40, leaving her with two young sons. Their eldest son, Davin, died of suicide in 2020.

Still reeling from that loss, she became interested in a long-running lawsuit against the government of Saudi Arabia, the homeland of most of the hijackers, and the case at Guantánamo Bay. She has met with prosecutors and told her story to lawmakers in Washington.

Only one memorial remains at the Camp Justice signpost, as the place of pilgrimage is known: a sturdy, metal plaque for Ronald P. Bucca, a New York fire marshal who was killed when the South Tower of the World Trade Center collapsed.

Mr. Bucca, 46, also was an Army reservist, and a U. S. detention site in Iraq — Camp Bucca — was named for him.

His memorial appeared as the others were fading away. Someone recently left a card there from the funeral of his mother, Astrid Marie Bucca. She died in April at the age of 98.

Since the first arraignment in the case in 2008, the office of the chief prosecutor has brought relatives of 173 of the victims to the base to watch the proceedings from behind soundproof glass at the rear of the courtroom. At least 19 of those visitors have since died, including fathers, mothers and grandparents.

Air Force Lt. Col. Michael Schrama is the fifth judge to preside in this version of the case. He was an undergraduate English major at Georgetown University and a defensive end on the football team when hijackers slammed American Airlines Flight 77 into the Pentagon, across the Potomac River from his campus.

Children with no meaningful memories of that day have come to observe the proceedings, which take place in a courtroom that was built specifically for the Sept. 11 case. It has been going so long that the Coast Guard emblems around the compound, a sign of that service’s contributions to security, have been replaced with the symbols of the U. S. Space Force, an entity that was created nearly two decades after the attacks.

Cindy McGinty came to Guantánamo just once, to watch a hearing in 2023, wondering what could constitute justice for the loss of her husband, Michael G. McGinty. The father of two and U. S. Naval Academy graduate was 42 when he was killed in the World Trade Center.

On her stone, she wrote: “Michael McGinty — Never forgotten.” She added “9/11” and drew a small dragonfly. Now, as the words at the memorial disappear, she fears that the horror of the attacks is also fading.

“My feelings are however very complicated,” she said. “I feel like the men in Guantánamo will never actually see a trial, and one of two things will happen — I will die, or they will and hence be declared innocent.”

The youngest of those charged is 47, and the oldest is in his early 60s. Their health has been declining from their time in C. I. A. detention and a lack of specialized medical care at Guantánamo to address their trauma and other disorders, their lawyers say.

During discussions of a plea deal in the case, prosecutors told family members that a trial followed by appeals could take years. In military justice, if a convicted prisoner dies while appealing, the conviction is vacated. He would die innocent in the eyes of the law. A conviction through a guilty plea could prevent that possibility.

Camp Justice can feel like a cruel, claustrophobic place for the families who travel to Guantánamo. A grief counselor accompanies them on their weeklong trips, starting with when they assemble at the distinguished visitors lounge at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.

Soldiers on temporary deployment to the prison operation and other chaperones escort the family members around the base. The courtroom has a special blue privacy curtain that can be pulled closed to shield them from the eyes of other observers.

Carol Rosenberg reports on the wartime prison and court at Guantánamo Bay. She has been covering the topic since the first detainees were brought to the U. S. base in 2002.

Cockroach Milk, How to Blow Your Nose, and Mosquito Printers: The Ig Nobels of 2026

Wired September 08, 2026

Achievements that first make people laugh and then make them think. That’s the motto of the Ig Nobel Prizes, an annual competition that—parodying the Nobel Prizes—recognizes some of the world’s most unusual scientific studies. The organization Improbable Research has been hosting the event since 1991 with the aim of showing that science also has a humorous side in its quest to meaningfully answer questions about the world.

This year the ceremony was held in Zurich, Switzerland, and recognized 10 research projects ranging from an attempt to scientifically define what a kiss is to an experiment that used buried underwear to assess soil health.

What exactly is a kiss? A group of researchers decided to establish a scientific definition that would apply to all animals, not just humans. They came up with the categorization that a kiss is “a non-agonistic interaction involving directed intraspecific oral-oral contact, with some movement of the lips or oral structures and without the transfer of food.” By this definition, other great ape species are also kissers, so are domestic dogs and cats as well as pigeons, penguins, squirrels, black bears, and tortoises—though not all of these kisses have the same meaning.

In the study “Higher Social Class Predicts Increased Unethical Behavior,” published in PNAS, researchers conducted seven experiments to investigate whether socioeconomic status was linked to unethical behaviors, such as breaking traffic rules, failing to yield the right of way, cheating, and even taking candy from children. Spoiler: Yes, it seems that more money does mean more problems—creating more problems at least. The results suggest that people from higher social classes have, on average, a greater tendency to prioritize self-interest. Who knew.

Yet another study suggesting that the future of nutrition may lie in insects. The “milk” in question is a high-protein substance produced by mother cockroaches of the species Diploptera punctata, which concentrate proteins, fats, and sugars into an extremely energy-dense form. A team of scientists analyzed the crystals that form inside the embryos to understand how these crystals store so many nutrients in such a tiny space.

The researchers behind the study on nutritious cockroach milk.

This is probably the most popular study in the competition because of the story behind it. It’s a posthumous award to scientist Unno Tokuji, who spent his final years studying the correct way to blow one’s nose. He analyzed everything from the aerodynamics and volume of nasal breathing to the pressure exerted on the ears. The recommendation was to blow one nostril at a time when one is more congested than the other and to do so with a long, relatively forceful exhalation, rather than a short, weak blow.

To determine what triggers a defensive bite, researchers applied pressure to different parts of the bodies of Bothrops jararaca snakes—a highly venemous species of South American pit viper—and observed how they reacted. Wearing a boot and in a controlled manner, they stepped on different parts of the snake. Stepping on the head resulted in a 44 percent probability of a bite. Applying pressure to the body yielded a 20 percent probability of an attack. If for some reason you need to step on a snake, aim for the tail, where the risk is only 11 percent.

One of the researchers who measured how snakes react to being stepped on.

According to mathematical models, there’s an optimal angle for a stream of liquid to hit a urinal if you don’t want droplets to bounce back. The researchers found that lower angles of impact significantly decreases splashing, and they designed prototypes based on that principle. Such scientifically backed urinals can help with keeping public restrooms sanitary.

The price of 3-D printers has gone down significantly in the past decade, and now you can make one with something as low-cost as a dead mosquito. The proboscises that mosquitos use to suck our blood function as extremely fine needles. One of the most delicate parts of a 3-D printer is the nozzle, which is essentially an ultrathin tube. In looking to develop new components for precision instruments, the researchers realized there was no need to invent everything from scratch. Evolution had already come up with a great solution by optimizing the mosquito’s mouthparts.

One of the researchers who discovered that the mosquito proboscis that turned out to be very well-suited for 3D printing.

Once again, science confirms something you probably could have guessed. Researchers analyzed how parents perceive their children’s body odor at different ages. Participants rated the smell of young children more favorably and that of teenagers much less so. Surprise, surprise. The team believes that smell plays an underappreciated role in communication within a family and may be related to the recognition and strengthening of the bond between parents and children.

What kind of person do people typically want as a best friend? To answer this question, researchers administered questionnaires asking participants about how their friend should behave toward them, toward a stranger, and toward an enemy. In general, people prefered a friend who is kind to them but cruel to their enemies, suggesting that the ideal friend is not necessarily a “universally good” person.

About 1,000 participants buried cotton underwear and returned some time later to check how much had decomposed. The result: the “underwear index.” The more holes in the undergarments, the more biological activity, namely that of microorganisms capable of breaking down cellulose, a natural molecule in the cell walls of plants. A population of these kinds of microbes is key for the health of farmland, and now all you need to test for their presence is an old pair of underwear.

The entire ceremony is now available to watch online.

Muse, Meta’s New Personal AI Agent, Needs You to Trust It

Wired September 08, 2026

Meta announced Tuesday the release of Muse, a personal AI agent that people can message to automate digital tasks in a secure cloud environment, all while relying on security and privacy that the company says is “built into it” from the start.

Meta says Muse is rolling out today for iOS and Android users in a dedicated Muse app, as well as the website Muse. ai. The company also says users can directly message Muse in WhatsApp to interact with the agent. Meta says users of its AI glasses will soon be able to interact with its Muse agent as well. Meta says people can try out Muse for free, but users who want to automate lots of digital tasks will need one of the company’s AI subscription plans.

Muse is Meta’s latest attempt to compete with viral AI agents such as OpenClaw and Instinct, which users can message with to automate digital tasks. Muse is a product of Meta Superintelligence Labs, the AI unit CEO Mark Zuckerberg formed roughly a year ago to catch up with OpenAI and Anthropic, offering some researchers eye-popping compensation packages to join. The unit was built on the belief that AI agents will transform how everyday users navigate the internet, as well as Meta’s products.

WIRED previously reported that Meta has been testing Muse internally under the codename “Hatch,” and that employees have been using it to autonomously operate third-party applications and browse the web on their behalf.

Meta claims in a blog post that anyone can use Muse out of the box, and that the product was designed “so there’s no learning curve.” The company says users can prompt Muse in natural language, and the agent will work on its own to send emails, book travel, or even help sell a car on a user’s behalf.

Muse is also capable of making purchases on behalf of users, checking out using special payment infrastructure designed by Stripe. The payment tool, which Stripe calls Link, issues a single-use card number so that agents aren’t going around entering a person’s real financial information across the internet. Meta says Muse is the first AI agent covered by Link’s purchase protections for agents, which guarantees no-fee returns.

Meta is late to release a personal agent, but it seems to be seeking to differentiate itself by focusing on security and privacy features for Muse. The agent is debuting with an architecture for all users dubbed Secure VM, which is meant to isolate each user’s activity in a so-called virtual machine to keep untrusted data from the web and any integrations separate from the part of the agent that can actually take action on a user’s behalf.

A personal AI agent requires a lot of user trust, something Meta in particular has struggled with significantly over the years. To get users to try out Muse—and allow the agent to be integrated with users’ third-party apps and services—Meta is attempting to convince people that they can trust the company to handle their data appropriately.

“We know it’s really important, if we’re going to build a product like this that can access a lot of sources of personal data, that we’re really responsible with that, so we’ve designed this system very deliberately,” says David Singleton, Meta Superintelligence Lab’s vice president of engineering for consumer products. “And we’ve built what we call the Sentinel that actually looks out for everything that’s moving out of the VM and either matches it to an existing policy where the user or the system has given permission for that to happen or presents a human-in-the-loop dialog to ask you to approve the action it’s going to take.”

Singleton notes that these check-in prompts for humans come directly to the user and aren’t filtered through the model, to protect against attacks like prompt injections.

While Secure VM is built to maintain user security and privacy, it is not a truly locked box. Singleton notes that while Meta is barred by policy from accessing user Muse data, it would still be technically possible. Users can opt out of allowing their data to be used for training.

The architecture of Secure VM is noteworthy from a privacy standpoint, if only as a way to set a new industry standard for AI agents. Eventually, Meta will also offer Muse “Confidential VM,” designed so each VM runs in a “trusted execution environment” and users manage their own access keys locally on their devices. This way no one else, including Meta, can access that user’s agent VM.

Confidential VM comes as part of Meta’s work with Moxie Marlinspike, creator of the end-to-end encrypted messaging app Signal who also developed the privacy-focused AI platform Confer in recent years.

WIRED viewed an advance draft of a technical white paper describing Confidential VM. In addition to structuring the system so the user controls their access keys, Meta is also giving select security firms access to the Confidential VM source to regularly audit and verify its privacy guarantees. Meta will also publish the Confidential VM binaries (machine-readable instruction files) and a transparency log, so users can verify the validity and integrity of their connection to Muse.

Singleton emphasizes that Muse Secure VM has already been extensively vetted, including by Meta’s human and agentic red teams as well as through the company’s private bug bounty. And now Meta is adding Muse to the scope of its public bounty as well, with payouts up to $300,000 for valid vulnerability findings, including up to $130,000 for successful prompt injection attacks that affect a single user.

Apple and Google Miss Deadline to Block Child Nudity on Their Phones in the UK

Wired September 08, 2026

In June, the UK government told Big Tech it had three months to make taking, viewing, or sharing images of child nudity on their devices impossible. “I expect tech firms to make that happen,” said then prime minister Keir Starmer. “But if they choose not to, then we will act and change the law.”

That deadline arrived on Tuesday, and the government says that the likes of Apple and Google have failed. As a result, they will be changing the law to introduce what the UK government claims will be world-first legislation of its kind.

While engineers from Apple and Google had been working with the government since June to make changes, “they do not meet the scale of this crisis,” Lisa Nandy, the secretary of state for digital, culture, media, and sport, told lawmakers on Tuesday as she introduced the legislation.

Under the new plan, companies failing to build the child protection solutions into all existing and newly sold smartphones and tablets in the UK would face fines and potential criminal liability for their bosses. “We know that this is a sector that can—when required—innovate at an extraordinary pace when the chips are down,” Nandy added.

Nandy also plans to explore placing similar legal requirements on apps used by children, like Instagram and Snapchat. Neither Meta nor Snap immediately responded to a request for comment.

“For too long, technology companies have failed to protect children from the worst harms,” Nandy said, “and to be frank, I am not prepared to give them the benefit of the doubt that progress will continue at the pace we need it to while harm is being done now.” Still, she said she would reassess whether legislation is necessary if platforms implement solutions while it is being drawn up.

“Apple and Google needed to urgently introduce these protections to ensure online sexual abuse is disrupted and prevented on children’s devices,” says Chris Sherwood, chief executive of the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children. “Now the deadline is up, government must crack down and legislate.”

Not everyone is so keen on the measures, which would not impact adults who had verified their age. In June, messaging app Signal accused the UK government of using the measures to rush “invisible surveillance infrastructure” into law. It warned that forcing UK residents to prove their age and have their content scanned in the name of child safety could be a slippery slope into wider surveillance.

Apple, meanwhile, says it is working with the UK government in the name of protecting kids. “We share the UK’s commitment to combating exploitation and abuse online and have shared with UK officials future plans to strengthen Communication Safety and other tools even further to help keep kids safe,” an Apple spokesperson tells WIRED in a statement, pointing to its Communication Safety feature launched in 2021, which blurs photos or videos detected to contain nudity on a child's device.

A Google spokesperson says in a statement that their team is “pleased to have made progress and are fully committed to continuing to work with experts, legislators, app developers and device manufacturers to keep children safe, while also protecting privacy and access to information.”

Globally, governments taking more extreme measures to protect children from online harms have been met with backlash over privacy and other digital rights. In the European Union, civil rights activists opposed extended legislation allowing tech firms to voluntarily scan users’ private messages for child sexual abuse material. Elon Musk’s X complained that the information-gathering powers imposed by Australia’s social media ban risk interfering with international law.

In the UK, Nandy also said the government was considering going further with its sweeping social media ban for children under 16, which was announced earlier this year and remains on track to go into effect in spring 2027. She is also looking at strengthening the law around AI chatbots to protect children on those platforms as well.

OpenAI Just Claimed a Huge Math Discovery. Some Academics Are Crying Foul

Wired September 08, 2026

OpenAI said today that it has found an AI-generated solution to one of the biggest problems in mathematics—a 200-year-old equation that describes the natural behavior of fluids like water and air.

The announcement appears to demonstrate the stunning power for AI to advance mathematics. But it has been marred by claims from another mathematician, Tristan Buckmaster, who says that OpenAI rushed ahead to solve the problem after learning of the work of Buckmaster and a colleague—Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge. Buckmaster claims OpenAI also tried to influence who got credit for the work.

The proof concerns the Navier-Stokes equation, one of the unsolved problems in the Clay Millennium prizes, which are each worth $1 million.

Sebastien Bubeck, a mathematician and AI researcher at OpenAI, said in a press briefing that the company began training a new AI model with advanced mathematical capabilities on August 28.

After reading rumors that Anthropic was making progress toward solving Navier-Stokes, Bubeck said the company decided to dedicate more resources to tackling the problem. The company had more than 1,000 agents tackle the problem over more than 50 hours; eventually, as many as 10,000 agents were hard at work before the company discovered that it had come up with a solution.

“I thought there must be a mistake somewhere,” Bubeck said. “And on Sunday morning we had the final solution, Lean-formalized and everything.” (Lean is a programming language that can be used to formalize mathematical proofs.)

OpenAI noted that solving this problem required using considerably more computing power than it had previously spent on solving mathematical problems. The amount required cost “in the millions of dollars,” said Mark Chen, head of research at OpenAI.

On Monday, Alpöge and Buckmaster, a mathematician at NYU, posted documents claiming key advances in an area relevant to the Navier-Stokes problem. The pair says they used several AI models, including Claude and Codex, to complete their work.

Buckmaster also posted a statement claiming that, last week, he learned that OpenAI had become aware of his and Alpöge’s work and had started putting significant resources toward the problem. Buckmaster claims that he asked OpenAI leaders about whether the company had accessed the pair’s Codex logs. He says he was told the model “didn’t look up user data” but claims the company didn’t respond to questions about training. He then says that OpenAI offered several “proposals,” including one in which Buckmaster could publish a paper announcing the Navier-Stokes problem had been solved by an internal OpenAI model but without Alpöge’s name included.

In a post on social media, Bubeck pushed back on the idea that the company had suggested removing Alpöge’s name. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman also stepped into the fight, and defended the team's work.

Buckmaster, Alpöge, and Anthropic did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

In the briefing, Bubeck and other OpenAI executives denied that the company had ever inspected the pair’s Codex prompts in order to inform their work. “We, whether it’s the researchers or the agents, did not see any of their work until it was released publicly last night,” he said.

In a blog post detailing the work, the company wrote, “while unlikely, we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models⁠.”

“I want to be extremely clear that we recognize the priority of Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster’s work on unforced Euler, and we have nothing but congratulations to them on this monumental achievement that they have made. To be clear, we did not use their prompt or proof to prompt our models or direct our agents,” said Bubeck.

Ven Chandrasekaran, a mathematician at the company, also emphasized that their solution was significantly different in nature from the one produced by OpenAI’s model.

The spat over who gets credit for solving one of the biggest problems in math may rumble on for a while. As AI takes on more of the work involved with finding proofs, such fights could perhaps become more common.

Here’s Samsung’s Advice for Apple and Its Upcoming Folding iPhone

Wired September 08, 2026

On the eve of Apple’s highly anticipated folding iPhone, Samsung isn’t feeling threatened. Instead, the folding smartphone pioneer says the competition is “absolutely welcome.”

That’s according to Hee-Cheul Moon, head of Samsung’s Advanced Mechanical R&D Group, who sat with WIRED on a virtual Zoom call with Seungki Choi, head of Samsung’s Smartphone R&D Group. Before the talk veered toward Apple, the pair spoke about how the company managed to shave 75 grams off the weight of its latest Galaxy Z Fold8 in the seven years since it debuted the original.

Weight is integral to a folding phone’s success. If the device is too chunky and heavy, you’re less likely to want to use it. Over the past two years, folding devices from Honor, Google, and Samsung have rapidly gotten lighter, with each iteration featuring thinner designs. It may be why Samsung saw preorders for its latest folding handsets increase 30 percent globally versus last year’s models, with the Fold8—the device with a new smaller shape that’s easier to hold—accounting for nearly half.

“Seeing these other brands entering the market, we feel very proud of ourselves that the value that we pioneered with this new category of foldables is being acknowledged and recognized,” Moon says through a translator.

When I asked what advice the company had for Apple ahead of its folding debut, Moon said, “The key to providing the highest customer value in this market is all about the weight of the device. As you know, it’s not easy." Apple’s folding iPhone, rumored to be called the iPhone Ultra, is expected to weigh between 230 and 241 grams (the iPhone 17 Pro Max weighs 233 grams), heftier than Samsung’s latest.

Samsung has made notable strides this year in making its main Galaxy Z Fold8 smartphone lighter than top-end candybar-shaped smartphones. The single-screen Galaxy S26 Ultra weighs 214 grams, but the Fold8 is merely 201 grams, thanks to its smaller, passport-style shape. The company says its own customer data and YouGov survey data from 2024 show that bulky designs were a chief concern for people uninterested in folding phones.

The company says it analyzed every single component in the latest Fold8 and Fold8 Ultra—approximately 270 components and more than 180 auxiliary parts—from circuit boards and antennas to tapes and fastening components.

The team looked everywhere to cut weight. For example, it redesigned the printed circuit board to remove unnecessary circuits and improve component layout, reducing the space requirement. Samsung says it even eliminated 15 auxiliary parts and machined the internal display support plate down to roughly 0.2 millimeters. To keep that thinner panel durable, Samsung developed its “Flex Titanium” screen—a titanium alloy film roughly one-third the width of a human hair designed to maintain surface flatness and keep the crease from worsening over years of folding.

You’ll also notice Samsung’s primary folding phone no longer has three cameras on the back. Instead, it’s powered by a dual-camera system, a main camera and an ultrawide—there’s no more telephoto. For those who still demand high-end zoom and a 200-megapixel primary shooter, Samsung points to the larger Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra, framing the Fold8’s camera cutback as an intentional concession to deliver that lightweight, passport-style design.

Apple’s folding iPhone is also expected to have a wider and shorter passport-style shape, and it’s likely to have a similar camera setup. Both Apple and Samsung made similar concessions last year chasing ultrathin and light smartphones.

Choi says this came down to user feedback as Samsung’s customers wanted a folding device that was “effortlessly portable” yet could be unfolded for an immersive multimedia experience. “We continue to always monitor the voice from the market, and we are open to any possibilities,” he says. We spend most of our time consuming multimedia with our smartphones, and the Fold8’s new shape is specifically tailored for media, with less obvious letterboxing than previous Folds.

Yet chasing that slim, lightweight profile leaves foldables exposed where traditional flagships excel: durability and ingress protection. Most candybar smartphones sport an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance, meaning they’ll be fine even after spending some time at the bottom of a pool, but the Galaxy Z Fold8 series is still stuck at IP48—it can get wet, but dust will cause problems. Dust notoriously forced Samsung to delay the launch of the first Galaxy Fold in 2019, as little specks could get through the hinge and damage the screen.

Google’s folding Pixels are the only models with an IP68 rating. Still, even with the higher rating, dust can pose a problem, according to Elizabeth Chamberlain, iFixit’s director of Sustainability. The repair company’s teardowns show that dust can get inside the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, making the hinge sound “crunchy” and causing what could be a serious liability over time.

“We still haven’t seen a solution for that,” Chamberlain tells WIRED. “Repair is still a problem for foldables.” iFixit’s recent teardown of the Galaxy Z Fold8 gave it a 4/10 for repairability. “The hinge is buried under all the other components, and the hinge is the thing most likely to get damaged,” Chamberlain says. She did give Samsung props for its new adhesive system that makes battery removal easier.

Moon reiterated that Samsung’s Folds have the “best-in-class” dustproof and waterproof performance in the industry and that the company isn’t just “chasing the numbers for the sake of it.” He also emphasized that, despite the Fold8’s slim profile, internal components are far easier to detach and service than in earlier iterations.

That tension between engineering finesse and long-term durability is what Apple is stepping into. While Samsung enjoys a boost in Fold8 preorders, the broader foldable category was staring down a double-digit decline after five consecutive quarters of losing steam.

Nabila Popal, senior research director at the International Data Corporation, says this niche market is stabilizing, and the upcoming iPhone is expected to help the category grow nearly 13 percent year over year—the only bit of growth in the smartphone market right now. Drew Blackard, Samsung’s senior vice president of Mobile Product Management, previously told WIRED that more competition will help bring visibility to the category.

Popal says foldables are more durable and dependable now, arguing Apple is entering just as hardware anxieties have eased.

Chamberlain isn’t convinced the category is truly mature. “I want a phone that is durable and repairable, and I think it’s highly unlikely that Apple will have solved the hinge problem,” she says.

Even with the durability question unanswered, Samsung’s engineers believe they’ve finally landed on the right formula. When I asked what device everyone in the room was using, a sea of Galaxy Z Fold8 models appeared in the air. Moon held up both the Z Fold8 and the Fold8 Ultra, smiling and saying, “We use the Fold8 Ultra also.”

Richard Kelly on Donnie Darko at 25: ‘It’s a Miracle That Any Movie Gets Made’

Wired September 08, 2026

All products featured on WIRED are independently selected by our editors. However, we may receive compensation from retailers and/or from purchases of products through these links. Learn more.

For a diehard fan of Donnie Darko, meeting director and screenwriter Richard Kelly is a thrill in itself. But to first encounter him as a silhouette in a darkened movie theater is to feel almost like a character in one of his films—unmoored by indefinite space and physics, questioning your altered perception.

It’s a hot Friday in mid-August when I sit down with Kelly, 51, at Santa Monica’s Aero Theatre, a beloved repertory venue that makes a key appearance in Donnie Darko, his remarkable debut feature. Released in October 2001 with virtually no marketing due to the tragic events of 9/11 weeks prior (the plot hinges on a plane accident), it couldn’t get a toehold at the box office. But in the months and years that followed, the film became a hit on the home video market and gained a fervent cult fandom thanks to its unique supernatural mystery.

To mark its 25th anniversary, Fathom Entertainment will mount a limited theatrical rerelease of the film in a new 4K presentation, complete with a special introduction by Kelly—he’s just wrapped recording when I walk into the Aero. Screenings begin on October 2, the date that launches mentally disturbed suburban teenager Donnie Darko (Jake Gyllenhaal) on a surreal journey that may or may not lead to the end of the world. Snippets of the movie play without sound as Kelly and I settle into a back row to talk.

“My memories of this film run the entire spectrum from fear to love,” Kelly jokes, alluding to the corny pop psychology peddled by Patrick Swayze’s self-help guru in the film. This occasion, Kelly says, is all about the “love,” as he couldn’t be more grateful to “all the people who have continued to support” his work.

That camp should be pleased to hear that on December 15, Kelly will publish his mammoth first novel, The Philosophy of Time Travel, available for preorder now. The 800-page volume picks up right where the movie left off and is intended to set the stage for a film sequel as well. “It’s been very inspiring for me to remain focused on continuing the journey that began 25 years ago, on my own creative terms,” Kelly says. “This film has defined my entire career, but at the same time, it’s set a benchmark in the sense of the movies that I want to continue to make.”

Here, the auteur revisits the unforgettable dreamscape that put him on the map, and considers the artistic possibilities still ahead.

On when he realized Donnie Darko was becoming a cult hit:

There was one specific moment, I think in March of 2002, when I was in New York City. I was walking through the East Village, and I walked past a pizza restaurant called Two Boots, and my poster for Donnie Darko was hanging in their window. I saw the poster and I was like, “What’s going on? This is bizarre. Why does a pizza restaurant have a movie poster?” I went inside and I asked the manager, and he said, “Well, we have a little theater in the back, the Pioneer, and we’re playing your movie every Saturday night at midnight—and it’s selling out.”

I showed up the next Saturday night at about two in the morning, when the movie was finishing. I expected there’d be maybe 10 people there, and he wasn't joking, it was sold out, and there were people with camcorders and lights in my face, and Michael Musto from the Village Voice was there. I was just completely bowled over by the fact that there were people who cared, who were really, really connecting with the movie. That was the moment I knew that it wasn’t over, that the movie was going to have a second wind.

On how Drew Barrymore and Jason Schwartzman saved the screenplay from Hollywood purgatory:

It all started with Jason Schwartzman. He attached to play Donnie, and by virtue of his attachment, the script got sent around to a whole new round of people. It had been circulating for about a year, and the story was, “Oh, the writer won’t sell it. He wants to direct. It's his first movie, it’s too ambitious. It’s just a writing sample, he’s never gonna get that movie made. He won’t let anyone else take it away from him.”

Then the script got sent to Nancy Juvonen, who’s partners with Drew Barrymore [at Flower Films]. She read it and flipped out and wanted to meet me, so we went down to the set of Charlie’s Angels. We went into Drew Barrymore’s trailer, and she was finishing the script, and we just immediately hit it off. I’m like, “Drew, would you like to play the English teacher, Mrs. Pomeroy?” And she’s like, “Will you let my company, Flower Films, produce the movie with you? And I’m like, “Of course.” She had a one week window in August of 2000 before she was going to do a Penny Marshall film called Riding in Cars with Boys. We had to meet that deadline and get Drew to shoot her out in one week.

Jason Schwartzman had a scheduling conflict, and then in walks Jake Gyllenhaal. So it all happened really quickly. Nancy and Drew really deserve an enormous share of the credit in getting this whole thing off the ground—and Jason Schwartzman, too. Had he not attached, I would not have a career.

On having real-life siblings Jake and Maggie Gyllenhaal anchor a fictional on-screen family.

I heard from Joseph Middleton and Michelle Morris Gertz, our wonderful casting directors—they told me that Jake has an older sister, her name is Maggie Gyllenhaal, and she’s a brilliant actress. She had only appeared in one movie thus far, Cecil B. Demented, a John Waters film. I think she had a tiny cameo, but she had done a lot of theater and was obviously an enormous talent, like her brother, and once I realized there was a possibility of getting her, I was just like, “We have to get Maggie. It will anchor the family with real siblings, and Maggie will be this great foundation for Jake, and for the whole cast, and she was just so essential.” Sometimes the cards are dealt in your favor in terms of who’s available, who is interested, and so much of filmmaking is just the timing. It’s a miracle that any movie gets made.

On giving Seth Rogen his first film role (as a high school bully):

He had done Freaks and Geeks, and he was a standup comedian, performing in comedy clubs. Seth was one of these prodigy kids, really wise beyond his years and ahead of the game. He was maybe 19 years old when we shot the movie, the same age as Jake—incredibly observant, very articulate and funny young actor and writer and comedian, he was already pursuing all these different avenues. I felt like we had access to all the cool LA kid actors, because we shot in Los Angeles, it was the summer of 2000, and there was a commercial [actors] strike where all of the commercials were dark.

On creating the 1980s setting of Donnie Darko.

When we were doing the ‘80s, it was the year 2000, and we were capturing 1988, which is completely insane. That’s 12 years. So you subtract 12 years from 2026 and we are in 2014, which seems completely insane to do a period piece about 2014, because things don’t look that different than they did in 2014—but the disparity between 2000 and 1988 aesthetically was pretty significant. The cars looked completely different, the TVs looked different, the clothing looked different.

In terms of the ’80s aesthetic, we wanted it to feel subtle, we didn’t want a lot of big ’80s hair, and we didn’t want someone wearing a “Beat It” Michael Jackson jacket. We didn’t want it to be kitschy. April Ferry, our incredible, Oscar-nominated costume designer, who we lost a few years ago, was so wonderful in bringing the ’80s fashion for Mary McDonnell and Beth Grant—you see them with the shoulder pads and the different ’80s suburban costuming.

On the movie reference from his original script that didn’t make it to the screen:

In the original script, Donnie and Gretchen went to go see C. H. U. D., just because I thought it was a funny ’80s horror movie. Linda McDonough, who was an executive at Flower Films, was trying to track down the licensing permission for the movie C. H. U. D. as we were approaching the shoot date here at the Aero Theatre, and she was getting nowhere. It was one of the big studios, and there was some woman in charge of licensing at that studio who was just like, “You’re never getting this.”

You would think we were trying to license Lawrence of Arabia or Citizen Kane. They wanted so much money, and we were three days from shooting the scene, and we didn’t have a movie to show. Linda, to her enormous credit, said, “Richard, I am friends with the producers at the studio that owns The Evil Dead, they own the negative. Sam Raimi is a great guy, and they will let us have the poster to show at the front in the lobby of the theater. They’ll let you show any clip from The Evil Dead you want, the music, you can have it basically for free.” It was like a deus ex machina in the form of Sam Raimi. That led to the whole Evil Dead sequence in the movie, that was so perfect. Then we were able to do the marquee with The Last Temptation of Christ—we weren’t showing a clip from the Scorsese film or the poster, just showing the title. That’s an easier ask.

On the influential soundtrack of post-punk and new wave music:

I wasn’t thinking that deep. I was just like, “I love this song.” Like, “Head Over Heels” [by Tears for Fears] was written into the script because I knew that when Donnie and his friends jump out of the school bus, when Donnie’s feet hit the pavement, that first big piano note of “Head Over Heels” starts. When the camera flies through the window and you see all the kids sitting down and Drew Barrymore gathering the class together … “Time flies.” I had to get from the feet hitting the pavement to when they said, “Time flies,” and I had to edit the song down. It was just me doing a music video and loving that song and the vibe and the energy of it.

I have to give an enormous amount of credit to Manish Raval and Tom Wolfe, my music supervisors, who really expanded the canvas of the music in the movie to include Joy Division and Echo and the Bunnymen. It really did form a cohesive musical narrative. We were very fortunate, because no one was really trying to license a lot of that music in the year 2000.

The one song that we could not get—if you go back and watch the dailies, the Sparkle Motion dance scene was choreographed to Pet Shop Boys, but that was a no-go, we could not afford it, so we replaced it with Duran Duran.

On the dialogue that has had a surprising impact—such as the line “Sometimes I doubt your commitment to Sparkle Motion,” as delivered by actor Beth Grant:

It’s so ridiculous. You never know it’s gonna connect. Literally that’s gonna be in my obituary, that line of dialogue, the only thing people remember that I wrote. Beth Grant is the best.

On what the social media reaction would be like if Donnie Darko came out today:

I can’t even wrap my head around it. Online discourse is terrifying, and you kind of try to stay away from it. Any filmmaker that gets too caught up in online discourse, that can only have a negative impact on one’s art. You have to be cognizant of what’s going on in the world, but I think you need to curate your own art as the artist. We need more of that, art that is purely what the artist wants to say.

But I’m emboldened and excited about the younger generation going back to the theaters and reading books. Launching a book, the enormous amount of work that’s gone into writing a novel—it’s very gratifying to get to the finish line on something like that because you realize how a novel can help be the engine for something that is very difficult to get made because of the budget.

On the newer films and filmmakers to catch his eye:

Like everyone else, I saw Obsession. I thought it was terrific. Incredibly well done for such a small budget. The performances were great. I love Ari Aster’s work. I love Jane Schoenbrun’s work. I’ve not seen [Sex and Death at] Camp Miasma, that’s next on my list.

On the movie he most wants to make (besides a sequel to Donnie Darko):

There are so many scripts I’ve written and projects that have hit roadblocks for various reasons. I would love to get my Rod Serling biopic made. That is a very ambitious project that tells the life story of Rod Serling using a fantasy and science-fiction language, in conjunction with his daughter Anne Serling and her memoir about her father. It’s an expensive movie to make, given the fantasy elements and the period elements and the scope. If there are big influences, they would be Defending Your Life, the Albert Brooks film, A Matter of Life and Death by Powell and Pressberger, and All That Jazz by Bob Fosse.

Update on Tuesday, September 8 at 1:30 pm: This story was updated with more information about the 25th anniversary release and to add a link to buy tickets.
